## The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Avengers and Philosophy Earth's Mightiest Thinkers, The" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction Earth’s Mightiest Philosophers" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Mark D. White introduces the volume: the Avengers fascinate because they are equal parts superhero epic and soap opera, and the contributors' questions mirror that mix. He previews the book's guiding questions—whether Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor embody three different moral philosophies, whether the Kree-Skrull War bears on the ethics of war, why the team keeps admitting reformed criminals like Hawkeye, Quicksilver, and the Scarlet Witch, whether Kang can kill his past self, whether we secretly admire Norman Osborn's Dark Avengers, and whether the android Vision can truly love the Scarlet Witch. It frames the collection but applies no philosophical framework itself.
- ch. 7 "Part One What Would an Avenger Do" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Ethicists Assemble!" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; Deontology; Virtue Ethics — White casts the 'Avengers Prime' as three living ethical systems: Tony Stark is the utilitarian who, during Civil War and the registration crisis, bets on outcomes he alone claims to foresee (stopping the Crimson Dynamo's heart, enlisting the Thunderbolts, exiling the Hulk); Captain America is the deontologist who refuses registration on principle ('we maintained the principles we swore to defend... you sold your principles') and rejects the Punisher and the Negative Zone prison regardless of consequences; Thor is the virtue ethicist who condemns Iron Man not by utility or duty but for violating loyalty, trust, and friendship in cloning him, and who refuses the Twilight Sword because using it would make him 'the same demon'. The chapter argues all three frameworks still demand judgment and conviction, which the heroes share.
- ch. 9 "Just How Dark are the Dark Avengers" **·** Plato, Socrates — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Justice in the Republic; Allegory of the Cave; Theory of Forms — Donovan and Richardson read Osborn's Dark Avengers through the Republic: Osborn is a modern Thrasymachus for whom justice is merely the advantage of the stronger, managing Bullseye's murder of Lindy and the team's image exactly as Glaucon's ring of Gyges predicts—villains like Moonstone, Daken, and Venom appearing good while doing injustice. Captain America, who tells Stark 'who made you the moral compass of us?', embodies the Socratic belief in a justice beyond human advantage, backed by the Forms and the allegory of the cave. Ms. Marvel, Noh-Varr, and Ares choose being just over appearing just, defecting or dying (Ares torn in half during the Siege) rather than serve Osborn's fraud.
- ch. 10 "Let there be an Ending!" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Southworth and Tallman ask why fans blame Hank Pym for Ultron's killings while never crediting Magneto for fathering two heroes, and answer with Aristotle's account of character formed by habitual imitation, renewed as 'moral exemplarism': praise and blame track exemplarship, not biology. Scott Lang earned credit because he actively taught Cassie right and wrong, making her the hero Stature; T'Chaka and stepmother Ramonda shaped T'Challa, while Heinrich Zemo's Nazi upbringing warped Helmut into the new Baron Zemo. The Avengers themselves—Cap's patient mentoring of Hawkeye, Stark hiring ex-con Scott Lang—function as moral exemplars for reformed villains, so the mentoring 'parents', not the siring ones, deserve the credit or blame.
- ch. 11 "Part Two Who is an Avenger" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Are you the Next Goliath" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory) — Nelson tests body theory and psychology theory of personal identity on Avengers cases—a Rogers/Pym body swap in the spirit of Locke's prince-and-cobbler experiment, and a Pym brain-hemisphere duplication puzzle—before proposing a distinct 'mantle theory' of superhero identity requiring an appropriate heroic role plus legitimate pedigree, like intellectual property. Legitimacy explains how John Walker (appointed by a government commission) and Bucky Barnes (endorsed by Stark and then Rogers) each really were Captain America. The same theory rules Pym can wear only one of Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath, Yellowjacket, and the Wasp at a time—confirmed by Clint Barton snapping his bow in half when he shed Hawkeye to become the new Goliath.
- ch. 13 "Maybe Jen’s Reading this Chapter Right Now" *(no index entry yet)* — Cook analyzes John Byrne's and Dan Slott's She-Hulk runs as metacomics: Jen breaks the fourth wall to threaten readers into buying her book, deduces how long she was unconscious from comic-book time, steps across the gutter between panels to travel, and even attacks her own creator. Weezie's line 'We're inked and colored! Printed!' raises the problem that once published, the characters' actions are fixed, while her backstory (staying in print to stop aging) exploits comic conventions. The chapter ends by asking whether the Official Handbook's conflicting retcons make Jen's meta-awareness a delusion or a superpower, and what that uncertainty means for truth in metafiction and our understanding of comics storytelling itself.
- ch. 14 "Hoist by his Own Petard" **·** Plato, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus) — Powell reads Norman Osborn's Dark Reign as a living lesson from Plato's Gorgias and Alcibiades: Osborn's media-staged killing of the Skrull Queen and his hollow rebranding of S.H.I.E.L.D. into H.A.M.M.E.R. are the sophistic 'knack' of persuasion substituting for the genuine craft of statecraft, just as Polus's ideal Sophist imagines power without self-control. Like Alcibiades, Osborn lacks the Socratic self-knowledge that comes only through critical self-reflection with honest friends, and instead surrounds himself with flatterers and villains while his own Goblin persona—mirrored in the Sentry's Void—grows stronger. Loki's goading of the unsanctioned Siege of Asgard completes the cautionary tale: the sophist who created fake institutions is destroyed by them, hoist by his own petard.
- ch. 15 "Part Three Should the Avengers Do More Than Avenge" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Avengers, Forgive!" **·** Hannah Arendt, Jacques Derrida — Forgiveness; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Malloy builds an account of forgiveness around the Avengers' habit of recruiting ex-villains: Arendt's 'predicament of irreversibility' explains why we cannot undo Wonder Man's revenge scheme against Stark, so resentment must be overcome; Derrida's claim that only the unforgivable is truly forgivable frames the House of M question, whether Quicksilver's manipulation of Wanda's reality-warping is a crime beyond forgiveness. Forgiveness means relinquishing resentment without excusing responsibility or condoning the wrong, so Iron Man has the 'moral power' to forgive Hawkeye, while the team's charter-based standing lets the Avengers forgive Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch on the community's behalf. The chapter closes by separating avenging (justice) from revenge, and punishment (retribution that repays debts) from forgiveness, which is why expelled members like Iron Man and Hank Pym could be readmitted.
- ch. 17 "Neither Gods nor Beasts But Political Animals" **·** Aristotle — Man as Political Animal; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Spanakos denies the official line that the Avengers assemble from necessity—Thor beats Loki alone—arguing instead through Aristotle that the team is a polis: heroes join for safety but stay for the good life, since outside the polis one is either a god or a beast. Ms. Marvel's miserable solo run (unrecognized by Stilt-Man, a 'Where Are They Now?' has-been) ends only when she returns to lead the Mighty Avengers among friends who share her arete; the self-loathing Jessica Jones finds eudaimonia through philia with Carol, Luke Cage, and the team that delivers her baby; even the arrogant Hank Pym regains excellence by defending Tony and leading a new team. Even gods like Thor and near-beasts like the Hulk, the chapter concludes, need the Avengers to flourish.
- ch. 18 "Avengers Rehabilitate!" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Terjesen asks whether Cap's Kooky Quartet-style rehabilitation really works, pitting Aristotle's fixed-character virtue ethics against John Doris's situationist 'local traits' (backed by Milgram's experiments): Hawkeye succeeded because his regional traits—hotheadedness and a need for approval—were redirected to heroism, not erased, as when he cheats the Grandmaster to save the universe. Aristotle's continence-versus-virtue and vice-versus-incontinence distinctions explain why Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch keep backsliding, why Moonstone's true viciousness defeats rehabilitation while Songbird and MACH-1 reform. Against deterrence and retributivist theories of punishment, rehabilitation is defensible when applied early and to the unhardened—the Avengers Academy children and Young Avenger Patriot—so the Avengers can rehabilitate as well as avenge.
- ch. 19 "Part Four Do the Avengers Ever Go Too Far" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "And the war Rages on" **·** Michael Walzer, Immanuel Kant — Just War Theory; Humanity as an End in Itself; Consequentialism; Deontology — Robichaud runs the Kree-Skrull War (Avengers #89–97) through Michael Walzer's just war theory: the Avengers' defense of Earth against Ronan's Plan Atavus is justified self-defense meeting proportionality and last resort, while Ronan's preventive 'devolve humanity' war fails for lack of evidence and exhausted diplomacy. The Skrulls' shape-shifting trick that gets Mar-Vell to build the Omni-Wave Projector might squeak through on consequentialist grounds, but the emperor's threat to make Captain Marvel watch the Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver die counts as torture—and is impermissible on the Kantian ground that it treats a person merely as a means, whatever the consequences. The point is that even a cosmic comic war displays the real moral complexity of military ethics.
- ch. 21 "“This is the Kind of Thing that is Going to Bite US in the Butt”" **·** Michael Walzer — Deontology; Just War Theory; Consequentialism — Melançon pictures Avengers ethics as Hawkeye's arrow sliding along a line from deontological duty toward consequentialist results, focusing on secrets and lies: Doctor Strange's deception—disguising his Sanctum Sanctorum as a coffee shop to shelter the underground New Avengers after Civil War—is tested against Michael Walzer's 'supreme emergency', the wartime exception (Allied bombing of Germany, the ticking time bomb) that permits violating your own values so they can survive. Strange keeps sliding—possessed by a demon against the Hulk—until the Eye of Agamotto strips him of his title, showing emergencies must stay rare and the agent 'worthy of surviving'. Steve Rogers's secret black-ops Secret Avengers repeat the danger: unlike democratic intelligence agencies, they have zero oversight or accountability, so the WikiLeaks-style leak of their informant dealings threatens the reputation of the whole Avengers enterprise.
- ch. 22 "Captain America’s mighty S.H.I.E.L.D. . . . Well, Sort Of" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Philippa Foot — Doctrine of Double Effect — Bogaerts asks why every proactive superhero comes to grief: Nick Fury's unauthorized Secret War in Latveria, Tony Stark's exile of the Hulk and registration crusade, and the Illuminati's blunder all backfire (World War Hulk, the Skrull invasion), and Aquinas's doctrine of double effect—elaborated by Foot and Anscombe—cannot absolve them, since the foreseen harms were massive and disproportionate to the intended goods. Comics theory supplies the deeper cause: Reynolds's status quo defense and Jewett and Lawrence's American monomyth (via Campbell's hero's journey) make the superhero genre intrinsically reactive, guarding a paradise rather than remaking it, so heroes who 'move up into governance'—Thor as Lord of Earth, the Squadron Supreme's utopia—slide into supervillainy. Foot's act/omission distinction and the priority of negative over positive duties explain the trap, and why even Steve Rogers, as the new top cop, retreats to being Captain America again.
- ch. 23 "Part Five What Kind of World do the Avengers Live In" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Time to End" **·** The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Jones uses Kang to walk through the physics and metaphysics of time travel: Einstein's twin paradox (Quicksilver aging one year while Wanda's clock runs twenty), Gödel's spinning universe and van Stockum's cylinder yielding closed timelike curves, Thorne's wormhole time machine, and Hawking's Chronology Protection Conjecture against energy-stealing paradox loops. Applied to the comics, Prime Kang's purge of his flawed selves, Immortus's Forever Crystal, and Iron Lad's murder of his future self all confirm the fixed-timeline view: attempts to change the past only prune variants or create transient branches that snap back, so Kang can never un-become Kang. The Avengers end up as the Marvel Universe's Chronology Protection Agency, enforcing the rule that even where time travel exists, the past cannot be rewritten.
- ch. 25 "Equal Opportunity—for Deities" **·** Immortality and the Soul; The Problem of Evil — Barkman argues the Marvel Universe's 'One-Above-All'—depicted as Stan Lee and Jack Kirby—is the eternal Judeo-Christian Creator, and arranges its beings in a graded hierarchy: the Living Tribunal as God's judge, cosmic beings like Eternity and Galactus, elders, sky fathers Odin and Zeus, down to mortals, with only God eternal and everything else, gods included, able to die yet enduring by His decree. Ontological rank guarantees nothing morally—Mephisto, the Goddess, and Hera are powerful and wicked, and even Hercules can be beaten by the Wrecking Crew. A free-will theodicy answers where evil came from: 'no other gods before me' never denied other gods' existence but commands loving the Good above all, which mortal Avengers like Thor, loving justice perfected by sacrificial love, manage as well as any deity.
- ch. 26 "Love American Style" **·** Peter Singer, Charles Sanders Peirce — Philosophy of Love; Speciesism; The Pragmatic Method — Klayman asks whether the android Vision can love the human Scarlet Witch, working through C.S. Lewis's four loves to show affection, friendship, Eros, and charity are all open to human-android pairs, with their marriage best read as Eros—preoccupation with one irreplaceable self rather than sexual desire. Peter Singer's attack on speciesism is extended into 'organicism', the prejudice that dismisses synthetic beings: the Vision suffers, has interests, and laments that 'we artificial life-forms are still the least accepted', so denying androids love is arbitrary bias. Peirce's pragmatic maxim settles the question by practical effects—the Vision's care, kindness, attentiveness, and intimacy with Wanda just are loving—whether the lover is flesh or machine.
- ch. 27 "The Way of the Archer" **·** Laozi, Zhuangzi — Wu Wei (effortless action); Taoism (Daoism); The Tao (the Way); Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream) — White reads Clint Barton through the Tao Te Ching and Chuang Tzu: Hawkeye's instinctive archery—'use your bow gently, naturally, instinctively'—is wei wu wei, while his bragging, his glory-chasing failure against Iron Man, and his attempt to become Goliath all violate it by striving against his own nature, until the Kree-Skrull War teaches him the bow is his way. Chuang Tzu's butcher carves the lesson that the effortless path (the straightforward shot) is the skilled one, and Lao Tzu's sage-leadership—lowering oneself, deflecting praise—is exactly how Captain America handles Clint's insurrections. Lao Tzu on sages putting themselves last illuminates Hawkeye's sacrificial death and his legacy passed to Kate Bishop, while the butterfly dream frames his resurrection and the House of M's rewritten reality: with no way to compare the states, life and death are both to be welcomed as parts of the Way.
- ch. 28 "Appendix Why are there Four Volumes of Avengers" *(no index entry yet)* — A fan-guide appendix, not a philosophical essay: it untangles the Avengers' publication history to show which comics the book's chapters draw on—the original 1963–1996 volume, the thirteen-issue Heroes Reborn relaunch ('never cited in this book—for a reason'), the 1998 volume ending in Avengers Disassembled, then New Avengers, Young Avengers, the Civil War split, Mighty Avengers, Osborn's Dark Avengers, and the Heroic Age's fourth volume alongside Secret Avengers and Avengers Academy. It makes no philosophical argument; its point is navigational, mapping the canon that the essays' examples come from.
- ch. 29 "Contributors Avengers Academy" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "Index From Jarvis’s Secret Files" *(notes)*

## The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*

- ch. 6 "PROLOGUE “WHAT’S THAT SUPPOSED TO MEAN ”" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Will to Power — The prologue closely re-watches Bob Dylan's 1965 Newport 'going electric' set and argues that the famous booing began for mundane musical reasons — the bassist missing the change to the five chord in 'Maggie's Farm' and an under-rehearsed band — not ideological betrayal by folk purists. It contends that the audience collectively transmuted a flawed performance into an epochal myth of folk-vs-rock rupture, and that this shared fiction, not how the music actually sounded, is what mattered culturally. Framed by the Nietzsche epigraph on self-overcoming, it reads Dylan as a catalytic, quasi-messianic figure who performed the 'necessary murder of the old order' (culminating in the 1966 'Judas!' shout), enjoyed even the booing as part of the cultural drama, and refused every label by calling his new style 'vision music.'
- ch. 7 "I. “STANDING IN THE GATEWAY”" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "CHAPTER 1 “LET’S GET REAL, REAL GONE FOR A CHANGE”" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, William James — The Dialectic; Authenticity; Geist (World Spirit); Zen Buddhism — The chapter argues that Elvis's Sun recordings — the staged rupture in 'Milkcow Blues Boogie' ('That don't move me. Let's get real, real gone for a change') and the accidental 'acting the fool' emergence of 'That's All Right' — enacted an epistemological revolution: a leap out of modernity's rationalized, disembodied mode into repressed bodily affect, defining American cool as affective authenticity against Bill Haley's affected performativity. Elvis's immersion in a Black Memphis neighborhood and his emulation of Black performers made him a catalyst for racial-musical integration and the 'visceral empathy' that prepared desegregation, while the panic of critics (Sinatra, the Times, Congressman Celler) is reread via Hegel's 'tarrying with the negative' as the resistance Geist needs for its self-overcoming. Creative novelty is described with Whitehead's and William James's metaphors — the 'lure of feeling,' sudden phase transition, radical empiricism in what Elvis kept or dropped onstage — with his 'did it make me feel good' studio criterion and a Zen-like mushin statesmanship of loosing egoic control in the band.
- ch. 9 "CHAPTER 2 “A CREATIVE TENSION”" **·** William James, René Descartes — Authenticity; The Dialectic; The Cogito — The chapter traces the Beatles' rise as a case study in how novelty enters culture: Lennon and McCartney polarize into transgressive truth and melodic beauty, their 'creative tension' producing an emergent whole greater than either (the 'holding a mirror' songwriting method, their fused harmonies, the Decca audition versus Hamburg swings between commerce and authenticity). Hamburg is the underworld initiation where 'Mach Schau!' humiliation, absurdist humor read as Freudian catharsis, and Preludin-fueled marathon sets broke them out of English propriety into ecstatic physicality, before Epstein's suits and George Martin's harsh Abbey Road critique dragged the pendulum back toward rational professionalism. Against the Cartesian thesis that humanity is defined by the thinking mind ('I think, therefore I am'), the chapter reads 'Please Please Me,' Beatlemania's screaming crowds (citing Ehrenreich on female assertiveness and solidarity), and Rubber Soul as successive dialectical phase transitions integrating affect with intellect — a rock-and-roll answer to rationalized modernity, in James's wave-crest image of novelty flung ahead of history.
- ch. 10 "CHAPTER 3 “LOOKING FOR THE INNER HEAT”" **·** Thomas Kuhn, G.W.F. Hegel, Jean-Paul Sartre, William James — Paradigm Shifts; Authenticity; Existentialism — The chapter reads Dylan's self-becoming as a chain of identity-emulations and overcomings — Hank Williams, Woody Guthrie, Ramblin' Jack Elliott — with Jon Pankake's folk-police critique and the Mike Seeger epiphany acting as Kuhnian anomalies that force a paradigm shift from folksinger to songwriter, each gatekeeper playing the 'Hegelian negative' Dylan needed. It argues Dylan fused folk, beat poetry, and rock and roll into an 'archaic revival' of mythic, enchanted consciousness against modern rationalization, rejecting the Sartrean/beat existentialism of a meaningless world in favor of co-creating meaning, and treating authenticity as the refusal of fixed identity (the Zimmerman-to-Dylan renaming, 'I'm gonna get me a new Bob Dylan'). The Newsweek exposé, Irwin Silber's open letter, and Johnny Cash's guitar-gift blessing stage his passage from 'King of Folk' to electric rock, with the little-known 1962 cut of Presley's 'That's All Right' showing that going electric was a return home — folk having been, in Dylan's words, 'just an interruption.'
- ch. 11 "II. “YOU REALLY DON’T KNOW UNTIL YOU STEP INSIDE”" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 12 "CHAPTER 4 “A REVELATION TO BEHOLD”" **·** William James, Aristotle, G.W.F. Hegel — The Will to Believe; The Four Causes; Truth as What Works; The Leap of Faith — Argues that the Beatles' devotion to rock and roll was a literal religious phenomenon rather than loose metaphor: Lennon's first hearing of Elvis is analyzed as a William James-style conversion, the Radio Luxembourg broadcasts were treated 'like scripture,' Hamburg was a 'baptism by fire,' and Epstein's new suits at the Cavern were announced as 'a revelation.' Drawing on James's Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism, the chapter reads Beatlemania's screaming crowds as collective ecstatic ritual and the 'toppermost of the poppermost' chant as the will-to-believe making its own truth, in the way James says truth 'happens' to an idea. Aristotle's four causes supply the metaphysical frame — the 'magic' of Liverpool and the sacred quality fans reported are formal-final causation against the material-efficient causation of disenchanted modernity — while the band's double irony ('tarrying with the negative,' after Hegel) let them hold skepticism inside belief, as in Lennon's 'flaming pie' origin parody and the 'more popular than Jesus' episode.
- ch. 13 "CHAPTER 5 “AN EXTREME SENSE OF DESTINY”" **·** Aristotle, William James, Heraclitus, Thomas Kuhn — The Four Causes; The Will to Believe; Fate and Foreknowledge — Reads Bob Dylan's 'extreme sense of destiny' as lived Aristotelian final causation: Dylan's passivity about fame ('It happened like anything else happens'), his 'Jack Fate' persona, and the odyssey of 'goin' home' all treat his future self as the telos drawing him forward rather than his past pushing him. William James's Will to Believe ('faith creates its own verification') explains the self-fulfilling portents Dylan found in Gorgeous George's wink, his felt succession to Woody Guthrie, and his premonition of Joan Baez, while the chapter insists this destiny is not fatalism since Dylan could have ignored the signs and 'gone off another way.' It closes by taking Dylan at his word that 'Bobby Zimmerman' died when his namesake was killed in a 1961 motorcycle crash — a Jungian synchronicity that seals the shamanic death-and-rebirth 'transfiguration' Dylan claims for himself, where Heraclitus's river captures that the old self cannot be recovered.
- ch. 14 "EPILOGUE “THROUGH THE MIRROR”" **·** William James — The epilogue reads the three pairwise meetings — Elvis and the Beatles at his Bel Air home in 1965 ('Long live the King!'), Dylan turning the Beatles on to cannabis on August 28, 1964, and Dylan's refusal to ever meet Elvis, memorialized in 'Went to See the Gypsy' — as mirrors through which each figure's transformation passed to the next. Its central argument is that the 'marijuana summit' was an epistemological watershed: following Terence McKenna's claim that a culture's sanctioned drugs select its ways of knowing, cannabis (against caffeinated, speed-fueled rationalism) opened the affective, intuitive mode that became the counterculture, audible in Lennon's turn from 'Help!' to 'Come Together.' The song's gypsy and 'pretty dancing girl' are finally read as the Jungian anima, the archetypal feminine drawing the West back to embodied, enchanted experience — a book-length thesis the epilogue attributes to the 'radical empiricist' lineage of James, Jung, Bergson, and Whitehead.

## The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke

- ch. 1 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*

- ch. 4 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Dean Kowalski's introduction pitches the volume: philosophy's big questions about what is really real, how we ought to behave, and what we can know brought to Sheldon's spot on the couch. It previews the essays to come — Aristotle weighing Sheldon's way of life, Hobbes applauding the roommate agreement, Kant deriding 'un-unravelable webs' of lies — and frames the book's running thought that comic-book and sci-fi geekery can be put to serious philosophical use, while even Sheldon cannot escape the 'inexplicable need for human contact.'
- ch. 8 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics (arete); Aristotle on the Soul — Greg Littmann tests Sheldon's geek existence against Aristotle's ideal of living well: since humanity's distinctive function is reason (the DVD-player-and-screwdriver argument), a life devoted to thought like Sheldon's — down to his fantasy of being a thinking satellite in orbit — has genuine Aristotelian worth. The chapter argues Aristotle could even bless geek obsessions, because poetry explores universal hypotheticals (Terminator causal loops, Superman's laundry) and adventure fiction purges emotion much as tragedy's catharsis does. But Sheldon's arrogance ('Captain Arrogant'), rigid clinging to his spot on the couch, and selfishness toward Leonard and Howard would earn failing marks in virtue, so the modern geek gets a mixed yet partly vindicating report card.
- ch. 10 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Kowalski maps Aristotle's three kinds of friendship onto the gang: pleasure-friendships (Halo and paintball nights, and Raj's fury when Howard abandons their kite fight for a jogger), utility-friendships (Sheldon's failed Friendship Algorithm bid on Kripke for lab access, and the roommate agreement's Friendship Rider invoked over the CERN trip). Complete friendship — mutual care for the other's own sake between moral equals — looks closest in Leonard and Sheldon, yet Sheldon's pancake-breakfast apology collapses the moment Leonard refuses to take him to Switzerland ('Drat. No Frodo for you'), exposing contractual utility where genuine care should be. The chapter concludes no pairing in the show achieves Aristotle's rare complete friendship, and asks whether similarity is really required for true 'besties.'
- ch. 11 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); Man as Political Animal — Sayles sorts the show's technology use by Aristotle's doctrine of the mean: healthy supplements (Raj webcamming his parents in India, Sheldon and Amy's video dates) versus unhealthy substitutes (Penny's Age of Conan spiral into unwashed hair and sick days, Sheldon living as a 'mobile virtual presence device,' one-sided 'virtual vengeance' videos against Penny's Wi-Fi theft and Kripke's helium prank). Since the mean is relative to the person and situation rather than a mathematical midpoint, moderation must be found case by case, and man as a social being must keep his social skills exercised. The chapter finds Penny and Amy — not the four scientists — best model balanced technology use.
- ch. 12 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Philosophy of Disability; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Clifton asks whether fans are moral monsters for laughing at behavior that looks autistic, running Sheldon through the DSM criteria for Asperger's syndrome: missing Penny's sarcasm about doctors who 'remove shoes from asses,' hedging the bath-item Christmas gift, and inflexibly clinging to nonfunctional routines like Saturday-night laundry. Setting the writers' stated intentions aside as one fallible piece of evidence (the intentional-fallacy debate), he weighs the medical model of disability (leveling and normalizing) against the social-constructivist model in which disability is a misfit between trait and environment. Because Sheldon has built a world — theoretical physics, accommodating friends, the comic book store — where his traits are advantages, even an 'alpha nerd' leader, they constitute an 'enability' rather than a disability, and the laughter is morally innocent.
- ch. 14 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Gottfried Leibniz, Hannah Arendt, Martin Buber — The Problem of Evil; Will to Power; The Banality of Evil; The Best of All Possible Worlds — Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.
- ch. 15 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, John Stuart Mill, Jeremy Bentham, Plato — The Social Contract; The State of Nature; Higher and Lower Pleasures; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — The Bocks test three answers to the good life against the show: Howard as hedonist (laser-obstacle-strip-chess, the 'whore of Omaha') read through Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, and Aristippus; ethical egoism via Glaucon's ring of Gyges and Howard's offer to Skype rather than visit the deported Raj; and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract read into Sheldon's roommate agreement, whose lack of a Hobbesian sovereign leaves 'I settle all ties' arbitrary and rule-following too thin for ethics. Aristotle's virtue and practical wisdom crown Leonard — the nucleus of the social group, as Amy says — as the closest thing to the phronimos. The gang's sabotage of Dennis Kim with a manufactured girlfriend closes the chapter by asking who really ruined whose life.
- ch. 16 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Lawhead reconstructs Sheldon's 'fundamentalist scientism' — an inverted pyramid of knowledge with fundamental physics as the load-bearing point — and tests it through 'Sheldonology,' a mock special science that predicts Sheldon's behavior from the Parking Principle and his seven-restaurant dinner rotation. He grants Sheldon that a grand unified theory would be maximally general (against Amy's claim that neurobiology could 'subsume' physics as rank psychologism), but argues that a successful brain simulation would just be a system that does physics, and that the special sciences trade generality for usefulness — so choosing Sheldonology over fundamental physics to find a Sheldon-approved restaurant is perfectly rational. Science thus contains an ineliminably pragmatic element, deflating Sheldon's haughty derision of Howard, Raj, and the humanities.
- ch. 18 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Karl Popper, Thomas Kuhn — Falsificationism; Paradigm Shifts — Jones explains the Leonard–Leslie breakup ('Tell me, Leonard, how would we raise the children?') as a genuine clash of research commitments: string theory with its demanded extra dimensions versus Leslie's loop quantum gravity. Along the way he uses Popper's falsifiability and Kuhn's paradigms — the 1998 dark-energy discovery as falsification at work, Sheldon's alien-parasite hypothesis as paradigm-protecting refusal to accept that Amy is aroused by Zack — and the Dirac-to-Anderson antimatter story alongside Sheldon's North Pole monopole expedition to weigh theoretical against experimental science. Leonard emerges as the Feynman-style skeptic ('At best you can say, hey, my idea has internal logical consistency'), which is exactly what Leslie cannot forgive.
- ch. 19 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, René Descartes — Is–Ought Problem — Pigliucci argues the gang is funny because their scientistic worldview misfires in ordinary life: Howard's Drake-equation-derived 'Wolowitz coefficient,' Sheldon's friendship algorithm that Howard must rescue from an infinite loop, and Leonard's 'bio-social exploration' kiss experiment with Leslie all fail because courtship and friendship resist quantification. Tracing scientism's appeal to the Cartesian method of reductionism, he criticizes E.O. Wilson's Consilience, Sam Harris's science of morality (defending Hume's distinction between empirical facts and values), and the Churchlands' eliminative materialism — the tequila sunrise and the rock wall's qualitative feel escaping the neuro-reductive gaze. Sheldon's chocolate-based operant conditioning of Penny and the Tuskegee syphilis study show why science needs ethical evaluation from outside itself.
- ch. 20 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Alvin Plantinga, John Locke, Peter van Inwagen — Faith and Reason; The Watchmaker Argument (design) — Barkman and Kowalski mine the Cooper household for science-and-religion lessons: Mary's 'Third-World demon' diagnosis of Raj raises religious diversity (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), her 'But intelligently designed by a creator, right?' prompts an assessment of Behe's irreducible complexity against Darwinian counterexamples like the flagellum-turned-syringe and a warning against god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Her claim that 'all that science stuff comes from Jesus' occasions Plantinga's argument that Darwinian naturalism undermines trust in our cognitive faculties, plus origin-of-life and fine-tuning probability arguments, tempered by Kitcher's caution that such estimates rest on unknown background conditions. Van Inwagen on why Genesis need not teach literal science, and Locke's advice to proportion belief to evidence, frame the mutual education Mary and Sheldon owe each other.
- ch. 21 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, John Locke — Language Games; Tabula Rasa — Pötzsch reads Sheldon as the early Wittgenstein trapped in the Tractatus's picture theory — taking Penny's 'How've you been?' as a question about existence and replying 'I can't be impossible, I exist' — living among speakers of the later Wittgenstein's language games, where meaning is use within forms of life and social conventions (the tea that must be an invitation, the pizza-for-helping-moving protocol). Family resemblance, the childlike learner whose slate of social convention is blank (the Lockean tabula rasa applied to Sheldon's social mind), and lying as a language game Sheldon plays badly — the fake cousin Leopold Houston's fabricated Facebook trail, the orangutan hair — all dramatize the passage from logic-bound to use-based meaning that Sheldon, like Wittgenstein, may eventually make.
- ch. 23 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Democritus — Possible Worlds; Problem of Induction — Mackonis shows Sheldon is wrong about being wrong: Stuart's tomato counterexample ('it's very wrong to say it's a suspension bridge') refutes his claim that wrongness admits no gradation, and closeness to truth is cashed out with possible-worlds similarity — vegetable theory sits one small alteration from actuality, echoing Sheldon's own many-worlds refusal to dance in any of them. The Raj exchange ('So you were wrong' / 'I didn't say that') motivates many-valued logics in which degrees of truth let both be partly right, while the 'Cooper-Wrongness Paradox' argues that if Sheldon always knew when he was wrong, he could never know that he was wrong. Hume's problem of induction then shows his post-Toby confidence in his other beliefs can never be inductively verified, only sometimes falsified, and his French-sprinkled 'victory' over an exhausted Stuart is sheer logical fallacy.
- ch. 24 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Isaiah Berlin, Richard Rorty — Two Concepts of Liberty — Lowe stages a 'Tolerance Bowl' between Sheldon's scientism and Mary's fundamentalism, opened with Berlin's liberal answer to pluralism — everyone entitled to their opinion, yet Sheldon insists 'evolution isn't an opinion, it's fact' and Mary's tolerance becomes its own tyranny. Davidson's argument that there is no very idea of a radically different conceptual scheme shows mother and son argue from shared concepts (DNA, intelligent design), but both remain metaphysical realists who cannot brook disagreement, while Rorty's 'the world does not speak' antirealism encourages fallibilist tolerance only to congeal into a 'what-we-have' dogma of its own that cannot account for genuine plurality. Nobody wins the bowl: each worldview makes tolerance hard in its own way.
- ch. 25 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Augustine of Hippo, Gilbert Ryle — The Categorical Imperative; The Noble Lie; Deontology — Fallis uses Sheldon — a lousy liar with an elaborate theory of lying — to probe the philosophy of lying: Kant's absolute prohibition (even 'out of frivolity'), Bok's presumption against deceit, Plato's noble lies reserved for philosopher kings, and Nietzsche's self-deceiving overmen, whose counsel explains the 'un-unravelable webs' of fake Facebook and blog evidence for the imaginary cousin Leopold Houston. Ryle's knowing-how versus knowing-that split explains how Sheldon can state the rules ('casually, no rapid breathing') yet botch the performance, while the Bazinga! pranks and the insincere courtroom apology break the Augustinian definition that lying requires intent to deceive. Grice's norms of conversation then ground the author's own definition — lying as intending to violate the norm against saying what you believe false — until a hypothetical, convention-oblivious liar like Kripke forces him to concede a counterexample and admit he was wrong.
- ch. 26 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Nel Noddings, Plato — Virtue Ethics (arete); Caring as the Ground of Ethics; Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Barkman diagnoses four mama's boys: Raj's selective mutism under his parents' webcam meddling, Sheldon's comfort-seeking from a fundamentalist mother ('Soft Kitty,' mandatory grace), Howard's learned helplessness with his foghorn mother, and Leonard raised as Beverly's lab subject, his hugging machine echoing the wire-mother monkey experiment. Plato and Aristotle ground the charge of injustice — receiving less than one's station deserves, and wrongs against intimates are 'more terrible' — so parents bear special obligations their neglect breaches, a contemporary point pressed in the care-ethics tradition of Noddings. Cognitive-dissonance theory and Putman's Aristotelian 'psychological courage' prescribe honest self-reckoning for mothers and sons alike, with Leonard furthest along after confronting Beverly in 'The Maternal Congruence.'
- ch. 28 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Evans defends the Penny–Sheldon friendship as genuine by three universal marks — mutual care (two Saturnalia-miracle hugs), intimacy (keeping Penny's community-college secret; friends who direct and interpret each other's conduct), and shared activity (singing 'Soft Kitty' in the round) — and then argues its deep differences are not an obstacle but the engine of moral growth. Against Aristotle's similarity-based complete friendship, oriented to a shared eudaimonia, he offers a modern pluralist account: Sheldon's self-aware jokes, dancing, and social awareness and Penny's physics lessons show each growing toward the other's way of flourishing without becoming alike, which a friend as similar as Amy could never force.
- ch. 29 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" **·** Judith Butler, Simone de Beauvoir, John Stuart Mill, Plato — Gender Performativity; One Is Not Born a Woman; Woman as the Other; The Subjection of Women — White and Fisher run the show's women (and men) through feminist philosophy: the sex/gender distinction from Plato's Republic Book V and Mill's Subjection of Women through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' and Butler's antiessentialist performativity. Penny's hyper-femininity reads as Butlerian parody that satirizes the script, the Penny–Bernadette–Amy lineup exposes the custom that smarts and beauty must trade off, and Elizabeth Plimpton and Leslie Winkle ('come for the breasts, stay for the brains') break it — while the four guys fail every 'real man' stereotype beside Penny's muscle-bound exes like Zack. Gender emerges as an artificial label that limits everyone, and seeing that would be the show's ultimate change through parody.
- ch. 30 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" *(notes)*
