- ch. 8 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Foreword" *(no index entry yet)* — James S. A. Corey (Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck) frame both philosophy and science fiction as 'acts of critical imagination': philosophy advances into questions before data and measurement exist, and science fiction imagines what we do not yet know until it stops being speculative. They describe The Expanse as a collaborative project built from the science fiction they read growing up (Bester, Niven, Clarke, Cherryh) and from real history, its boundaries clear only at a distance. The foreword presents this volume as the conversation they inherited carrying forward, with The Expanse as touchstone, hoping it leaves readers 'a little more awed, a little wiser.'
- ch. 10 "Introduction" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Jeffery L. Nicholas declares Leviathan Wakes 'that book' and the TV series 'that show' of philosophical science fiction, and explains that his own aphantasia makes the series especially precious to him (watching the Rocinante on screen, Naomi's torture to save lives). He frames the volume's guiding questions over the first five seasons with hints from Babylon's Ashes: whether Amos or Avasarala is more evil and Naomi or Holden good, the costs of interstellar migration through the Ring Gates, and whether humanity even has a choice about expansion. Like Joe Miller holding Julie's necklace, the contributors offer their love of the show through interrogation of Miller, Holden, Amos, Bobbie, Naomi, and Avasarala herself.
- ch. 11 "First Orbit FROM EARTH TO THE STARS" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Howl at the Moon If You Want To" **·** Immanuel Kant, Blaise Pascal — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Free Will vs Determinism — Michael J. O'Neill argues that infinite space is The Expanse's most constant on-screen character, conveyed through chiaroscuro cinematography that deliberately echoes the seventeenth century (the Don Quixote references, 'Dulcinea', the Rocinante's name), when humanity first confronted infinite space. He reads Pascal's terror at man as 'a middle point between all and nothing' into Avasarala's losing debate with Nancy Gao over the Ring gold rush and into Miller's agoraphobic quest for Julie, then contrasts this with Kant's mathematically and dynamically sublime: spacewalks, the Behemoth dwarfed at the Gate, the Arboghast disassembled over Venus, and Inaros' asteroid attack as the weaponization of the infinite. Against Pascal's insignificance, Kant's sublime reveals our freedom — Holden's 'crazy notion about free will' while descending to the Ring station, Drummer's 'nothing in the void is foreign to us', and Amos' 'we're still here' — so the awe the show's visuals provoke is an intuition that we are greater than all nature's power.
- ch. 13 "What Really Matters" **·** Derek Parfit — Existential Risk; Second-Order Desires (personhood) — Margarida Hermida deploys Parfit's comparison of peace, a war killing 99 percent of humanity, and one killing everyone to argue extinction is categorically worse than mass death, and makes the stakes concrete through The Expanse's threats: the protomolecule, all-out Earth-Mars-Belt war, and the Free Navy's asteroid attack that kills billions. She rejects Miller's 'stars are better off without us' pessimism by arguing human existence is a good when suffering is fought (Belter disease and Ceres trafficking are contingent injustices, not necessities), values humanity as the only species with civilization and as the universe 'starting to understand itself', and distinguishes the desirable biological colonization of lifeless worlds from the protomolecule makers' morally objectionable disregard for native life like Ilus'. Against Phil Torres' worry that human speciation means endless war, she points to the mixed Rocinante crew and Naomi's line that the real divide is 'people who want more violence and the ones who want less', concluding with Parfit's On What Matters that what matters most is avoiding the end of human history and of rational beings.
- ch. 14 "Actual Threats to Our Existence" **·** Derek Parfit, Nick Bostrom — Existential Risk — Leonard Kahn takes the season-four debate between Avasarala and Nancy Gao over Ring colonization and asks who should have won. Using Parfit's extinction asymmetry, Bostrom's 'astronomical waste', and Toby Ord's definition of existential risk, he calculates that the 1,300 Ring gates could make accessible between 10^34 and 10^71 future lives (versus the Epstein-drive Nauvoo's century-long crawl to Tau Ceti), yet because using the rings risks the annihilation that befell the protomolecule's creators, the loss of humanity's long-term potential outweighs Gao's 'unimaginable opportunities' — so Avasarala's caution should have won. He ends skeptically: like Socrates arguing against the execution of the Arginusae generals, philosophical Cassandras rarely prevail, Gao was probably right that ring colonization was politically inevitable, and we face the same dilemma with nuclear war, engineered pandemics, and runaway AI.
- ch. 15 "Conclusion Whatever I Goddamn Like" **·** Aristotle, David Hume, Mary Wollstonecraft, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Feminism; A Vindication of the Rights of Woman — S. W. Sondheimer argues that Avasarala's election loss to Nancy Gao is explained not by competence but by millennia of gender expectations. She excavates the lineage: Aristotle's form/matter hierarchy ('matter yearns for form as the female for the male', women as incomplete 'deformed males' with 'fewer teeth') used to bar women from politics, Hume's portrait of women as near-livestock incapable of the sublime, and Romantic-era bodily confinement — mapping each onto Avasarala's staff recasting her as a 'nurturing, caring family matriarch', her forced public apology for the failed Inaros boarding raid that a male commander like Errinwright would never have had to make, and Arjun seizing control of the narrative of their son Charanpal's death. Closing the loop with the 2016 US election (Clinton versus Trump), the chapter argues that even in 2350 voters punish the 'nasty woman' and reward the comfortable mold Gao fits, and demands we 'dig this garbage philosophy out of our shared consciousness and set it on fire.'
- ch. 16 "Second Orbit IS IT THE PROTOMOLECULE, OR JUST HUMAN NATURE" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "Should Mao Be Pardoned" **·** Hannah Arendt — The Banality of Evil — R. S. Leiby stages the trial of Jules-Pierre Mao alongside Hannah Arendt's report on Adolf Eichmann to ask whether someone can commit great evil without being evil. Mao, like Eichmann, would plead 'not guilty in the sense of the indictment': he mourns Julie at her tree, momentarily defends the children on Io ('We're torturing children'), yet lacks the imagination to think from the standpoint of his victims on Eros, the Canterbury, and Ganymede — unlike the genuine fanatics Dresden and Cortázar, whom appeals to morality cannot touch. The 'anyone would do it' defense is tested through Milgram's obedience experiments and Miller's killing of Dresden ('I killed him because he was making sense'), showing how seductive moral tradeoffs are; following the Eichmann court's rule that responsibility increases with distance from the fatal instrument, the chapter concludes that Mao — a free, autonomous agent with even less excuse than Eichmann — should not be pardoned.
- ch. 18 "Amos Is No Superman" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality; Ressentiment; Will to Power; The Übermensch — Pankaj Singh reads Amos through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: Amos' division of people into 'bad ones, ones you follow, and ones you need to protect', his outsourcing of moral judgment to Naomi and Holden ('Naomi wouldn't like it'), his fearlessness, and his violent spontaneity make him 'evil' by slave morality yet good by master morality. Unlike Prax, who has to be stopped from shooting Strickland out of ressentiment, Amos kills without revenge ('I am that guy'), and his fistfights with Miller and Alex discharge hostility immediately so it never poisons — the strong natures Nietzsche praises that 'form, mold, recuperate and forget.' His 'crew comes first' and 'better to go down swinging' express the will to power as discharge of strength rather than mere self-preservation, but because he never sublimates or overcomes his drives, the chapter concludes Amos is no Übermensch — 'but then again, who is?'
- ch. 19 "The Upsides of Amos" **·** Hannah Arendt — The Banality of Evil; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Diana Sofronieva asks whether Amos is evil and answers no — in some ways he is better than most. Drawing on psychopathy research (Blair's moral/conventional distinction), Glover's 'moral resources', and Damasio's somatic markers to explain both his emotional absence (cauterized by a Baltimore childhood where children were sold for sex) and his difficulty making choices ('I've been trying to make choices of my own lately, and I can't seem to make the right ones'), she distinguishes him from bloodthirsty killers like Murtry and from Cortázar, who surgically chose the emotionless life Amos wants to escape. Against Arendt's banality of evil, Amos is no thoughtless 'joiner': he holds an uncompromising inner code (family first, bullying punished), deliberately selects good people — Naomi, Anna, Holden — as his moral compass after verifying their reasons, and his honesty, loyalty, trust in competence, and selflessness make him paradoxically less capable of evil than nearly anyone else on the Roci.
- ch. 20 "What Promotes Moral Behavior" **·** Michael Walzer — Just War Theory; Consequentialism; The State of Nature — Matthew D. Atkinson and Darin DeWitt use the Canterbury's ignored mayday in 'Dulcinea' — Captain McDowell's 'let the good God Darwin sort it out' versus Ade Nygaard's appeal to law, karma, and obligation — to ask what binds people when no central authority enforces rules. Through Michael Walzer's just war theory they read the Earth-Mars war: moral language is not 'cheap talk' (even Errinwright must dress aggression as peace and manipulates Reverend Volovodov's words), aggression and imminence govern when to fight, and five 'how to fight' principles — noncombatant immunity on Eros and Ganymede, POW rights for the Martian marines on the Kittur Chennamma, leaders' rather than soldiers' responsibility (Fred Johnson's defection after Anderson Station), proportionality in Errinwright's 'a base for a base' Deimos strike, and the rejection of ends-justify-means utilitarianism — discipline even Holden and Amos as they reflect on free will and culpability. The chapter concludes The Expanse is optimistic: human decency survives even in the anarchic Belt because characters keep reflecting on what their obligations to one another are.
- ch. 21 "A Crossroads in Human History" **·** Michael Walzer, Hannah Arendt — The Ethics of Political Violence; The Banality of Evil — Trip McCrossin reads season five's asteroid strikes on Earth as a 9/11 allegory (Delgado's 'at least now they know it's an attack') and applies Michael Walzer's five conditions to define Marco Inaros' terrorism: deliberate harm to randomly selected innocents, meant to terrify a cohort into political change, as in Marco's 'crossroads in human history' broadcast. This yields the terrorist's dilemma — justice toward victims versus compassion toward beneficiaries — while Avasarala's opening gravity-torture scene and her 'dirty hands' assign the opponent blame for failing to relieve the oppression that makes terrorism seem a last resort. Lydia's 'churn' ('float to the top or sink to the bottom') and her lesson that one can 'lead a good life without being a good person' explain how Amos and Clarissa redeem each other on the road to Baltimore, whereas Marco, like Arendt's Eichmann, cannot think from anyone else's standpoint ('everything we ever dreamed of'); the chapter ends with Avasarala's proposed Inners-Belters union as her own redemption — 'this is how we win.'
- ch. 22 "Third Orbit REMEMBER THE CANT!" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "A More Human Future" **·** Frantz Fanon — Black Skin, White Masks; The Ethics of Political Violence — Sid Simpson argues, through Frantz Fanon, that Marco Inaros' asteroid attacks must be judged as anti-colonial violence rather than simple monstrosity. Using Black Skin, White Masks' ontological division (Belters as 'skinnies', 'possessions, animals', the dehumanization that made Eros an acceptable testing ground and Anderson Station a 'message'), reinforced by Columbus and las Casas on Spanish colonization, he shows why the Inners' 'peace' is merely the status quo of ongoing extraction — Fanon's 'hypnotherapy' — that no treaty or Ring can fix. Fanon's Wretched of the Earth then recasts anti-colonial violence as a 'cleansing force' that shatters the colonial ontology and lets the colonized create a 'new, better, more human form' of humanity, so that Marco's personal narcissism and possible insincerity do not settle the political question: for the Belt, violence may be not only the last option but the most just one, against Avasarala's champagne-toast universalism that never takes Belter grievances seriously.
- ch. 24 "Against Love of Nation" **·** Cosmopolitanism — Applies George Orwell's distinction between patriotism (defensive devotion open to critique) and nationalism (obsessive, unstable, indifferent to reality) to Belt politics, reading Drummer as the patriot — she works for the Earther Fred Johnson, turns her guns on Belter radicals in 'Pyre', and refuses to whitewash Marco's massacres ('We're scavengers') — and Marco Inaros as the nationalist, whose asteroid genocide, treatment of Naomi as a welwala, and brainwashing of Filip ('All I did, I did for all Belters') display obsession, loyalty-transfer, and indifference to reality. The chapter's twist is that by Season 5 the patriots lose, because nationalists can always outbid defenders who play only defense, so neither Drummer nor Marco has the right attitude; Avasarala's finale call to 'turn every Belter, Martian, and Earther into this [the Rocinante crew]' makes cosmopolitanism — shared humanity over national loyalty — the show's real answer.
- ch. 25 "“I Want to Conquer the World”" **·** Michel Foucault, Hannah Arendt, Karl Marx — Totalitarianism; Class Struggle; Power/Knowledge — Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.
- ch. 26 "Tilting at Windmills" **·** Theodor Adorno, Francis Bacon — Ecofeminism; Anthropocentrism — Reads Protogen through Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment: like Odysseus tied to the mast while his sailors take the wax, Dresden's team had empathy surgically removed ('we modified our science team to remove ethical restraints'), Mao weeps at Julie's protomolecule corpse yet calls her death 'lucky', and Strickland experiments on Katoa and Mei Meng — self-made monsters serving the Baconian dream of conquering nature (New Atlantis, witch-trial language of 'penetrating her holes and corners'). Via Maria Mies and Carolyn Merchant's ecofeminism, it traces this domination of nature to pastoralist castration and the control of women's reproduction, culminating in Marco's theft of Filip and 'She left us. She left us both' — Naomi cast as nature to be mastered. Against them, Holden's childhood on the family farm, a cooperative 'let grow and make grow' world, is why Avasarala cannot play him and why he withholds broadcasts at Ilus: he is a knight who wants everyone to grow and speak for themselves, not to conquer.
- ch. 27 "Fourth Orbit THEY STILL DREAM" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "“Doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing”" **·** Anthropocentrism; Climate Ethics — Reads The Expanse as a portrait of a survived-but-unlearned Anthropocene: Bobbie's mourning encounter with Earth's dead, walled ocean in 'Cascade', Prax Meng's cascade of cascading failures killing Ganymede's artificial ecosystem and manufacturing Belter climate refugees overnight, and the slum outside the UN gates where children drink sewer water. Drawing on Brian Henning's 'Technozoic' critique, Katie McShane, Keekok Lee's intrinsic value of inanimate nature, and Henry Shue and Kyle Whyte on climate justice and colonialism, it argues humanity simply exported its anthropocentric, colonial worldview to Mars terraforming, Ilus, and the Ring worlds instead of changing it — Belters standing in for the Global South — so the Roci's creed that 'doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing' becomes a demand for environmental justice and a non-anthropocentric ethics.
- ch. 29 "“What happens to us now ”" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill, Francis Bacon, René Descartes, John Dewey, Charles Sanders Peirce — Utilitarianism; Pragmatism; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Tests the moral limits of science against Dresden's defense of Eros ('hardly a rounding error', 'we become our own gods'): Descartes' evil demon explains why Holden can never verify the protomolecule-ghost Miller — or even the Roci's bulkhead — is real; Baconian induction and mastery of nature explain why Protogen feeds biomass to the protomolecule ('we can only learn by letting it learn'), though Bacon himself demanded knowledge be shared for universal good; Peirce's pragmatism explains how the Donnager infers stealth ships from their effects and why protomolecule victims count as no longer human; and Dewey's inseparability of means and ends indicts Fred Johnson's readiness to negotiate with Dresden. It culminates in Miller shooting Dresden — 'I killed him because he was making sense' — as the straightest critique of utilitarian calculation, concluding that when empathy is excised (Cortázar's stimulation) or ignored, even science aimed at saving humanity produces Eros, Project Caliban, and the Earth-Mars war.
- ch. 30 "It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, Thomas Kuhn — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Paradigm Shifts — Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.
- ch. 31 "Fifth Orbit TILTING AT WINDMILLS" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "The Burden of the End of the World" **·** Hannah Arendt, Plato — The Philosopher King — Reads Naomi's escape from collapsing Ganymede — sedating Amos to leave the freighter, then stepping out before a crowd of more than a hundred stranded Belters to propose saving only the youngest — as Arendt's 'doing' politics, action justified by the seeing-and-being-seen of shared speech rather than by the strategic 'making' calculus Melissa and Amos use to justify abandoning the crowd. Naomi must alternate between the two — Champa's measured violence organizes the crowd — without letting making become the ethical metric, because, as she says, 'every shitty thing we do makes the next one that much easier.' Marco embodies politics reduced to pure making (abandoning six million on Ceres), Holden stays trapped in righteous strategizing that never defeats the protomolecule's uncertainty, and the chapter closes on Arendt's story of Plato's philosopher-king: trying to eliminate uncertainty by preemptive rule only multiplies risk, so resilience comes from doing politics together.
- ch. 33 "Knuckles and the Augustín Gamarra" **·** Kimberlé Crenshaw — Intersectionality — Deploys Crenshaw's intersectionality to explain why Naomi — the only Belter and only woman aboard the Rocinante — reads as a serial traitor: giving the protomolecule to Fred Johnson out of loyalty to the Belt, leaving Filip to escape Inaros's control of her through motherhood, and siding with Miller after the Dresden shooting ('as a Belter, Miller wasn't wrong'). It scales the analysis up to Belters as a collectively intersectional group — race, class, refugee status, and colonial occupation at once, as with the Weeping Somnambulist fired on carrying 55 refugees and the Ilus colonists framed through the European conquest of the Americas — then walks through Naomi's past with Marco (the Augustín Gamarra bombing that killed 516 people, her suicide attempt, 'the right to walk away') to show that resisting intersecting oppressions forces impossible, betrayal-laden choices, with her chosen family on the Roci as a model of solidarity that crosses identity lines.
- ch. 34 "Risky Tradeoffs" *(no index entry yet)* — Maps conflicts between incommensurable kinds of value across the series: moral versus epistemic value in Dresden's 'we become our own gods' defense of Eros and Strickland's knowingly continued torture of children on Io; moral versus aesthetic value in Cortázar calling protomolecule-infected Julie 'beautiful' and Anna Volovodov ignoring Nemeroff's suicidal pleas on the Thomas Prince because she craves the sublime Ring; and epistemic versus prudential value in Iturbi and Janus losing the Arboghast and Okoye calling Holden's nightmares 'an acceptable tradeoff'. The chapter argues that because we can rarely be certain which value should govern, every such tradeoff is itself a moral risk — even a correct choice leaves a residue of sacrificed value, and Dresden's and Cortázar's certainty is reckless because unjustified — before weighing dilemma, permissibility, and ranking models and settling on pluralism, with Holden 'pushing buttons as we find them'.
- ch. 35 "Sixth Orbit RIDING THE ROCI" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Immortality and the Soul; Aristotle on the Soul; Personal Identity — Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.
- ch. 37 "One and Multitudes" **·** W.E.B. Du Bois — Double Consciousness — Reads Naomi through Latina feminist phenomenology — Ortega's 'multiplicitous subjectivity', Lugones's 'world-traveling', Anzaldúa's borderlands — as one subject inhabiting several incompatible social worlds at once: Belter and Roci crewmate, Marco's former partner and Holden's lover, who experiences Miller's killing of Dresden simultaneously as her captain does and 'as a Belter, Miller wasn't wrong.' Du Bois's double consciousness names her two-ness when the Inaros faction pulls her back into a world she can still slip into 'as if she'd never stopped', and Ashford's list of her identities ('radical, betrayed, hid with the Inners, big hero') shows the borderlands Belters occupy between Inner and Outer worlds. The chapter argues this unsettlement is not a defect but a critical vantage: one stream of experience can carry multiple, conflicting meanings simultaneously, and all of it — no part more than another — is who Naomi is.
- ch. 38 "On the Other Side of the Ring A Difficult Consequence" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Uses Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk, we would not understand him' and his shift from the Tractatus picture-book model to the Investigations' language-game model to explain why Inners and Belters, though they share a language, still cannot understand each other: 'Rocinante' and 'MCRN Tachi' name the same ship but mean differently, Earth plays the post-scarcity-superpower game around Basic assistance while Mars plays the driven-upstart game and the Belt the liberation game, and Holden's family's casual 'skinnies' slur shows even love cannot supply missing context. The chapter runs through Okoye's lab 'scalpel' joke and the use–mention distinction to make the model precise, then draws the dark consequence: understanding fails at every scale, from Avasarala versus Dawes to Bobbie versus the Laconians to humanity versus the Ring Builders and Unknown Aggressors ('Some of them are even playing the language game of genocide'), leaving Star Trek-style optimism naive and only the small, personal understandings — Naomi, Amos, Bobby — attainable.
- ch. 39 "Season 5" *(front)*

- ch. 9 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Socrates — The book's introduction argues that the trilogy is at root the truth 'about violence against women, and the men who enable it' in a distinctly Swedish, Stockholm-centered story. It casts Lisbeth Salander as a latter-day Socratic gadfly: like Socrates in Athens, she is an annoying pest who forces the city's sophists to face their hypocrisies, and like him she is tried and pre-condemned in the court of public opinion. Against the old ideal of eternal capital-T Truth (Keats's 'truth is beauty'), it sets Salander the anti-beautiful Pippi Longstocking heir for whom truth 'can be a moody bitch,' and previews the volume's questions about whether journalists and hackers are the new philosophers who will suffer the hemlock backlash.
- ch. 10 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Using Erving Goffman's Stigma and Asylums, the chapter reads Salander's psychiatric record as a textbook spoiled identity: her silence, refusal of medication, and tattoos are recorded at St. Stefan's as symptoms, and the same behaviors that pass unnoticed in 'normals' (Giannini's earrings, Teleborian's own youth) are recoded as pathology in the Hornet's Nest courtroom. It shows labels slipping from 'mentally ill' to violent, promiscuous 'lesbian Satanist,' allies divided into Goffman's 'wise' (Palmgren, Armansky) and those before whom she must pass (Blomkvist, Mimmi Wu), and real Ontario Mental Health Act hearings that generalize single incidents into dangerousness. The chapter's conclusion is that the trilogy's point is not that Lisbeth was wrongly labeled but that no one—including the 'rightly labeled'—should be reduced to a label, since sane/insane is a shifting continuum we all occupy.
- ch. 12 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — The Panopticon (surveillance); Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies — The chapter uses Foucault to explain how Salander could leave school without a certificate yet master Fermat-class mathematics: schools 'cut' students into fabricated 'human kinds'—the problem-solving child and the at-risk child (Popkewitz's alchemy)—and under No Child Left Behind that sorting licenses surveillance and discipline of everything an at-risk student does. Lisbeth's case shows the machinery: her correct answer marked wrong from the textbook key, her Rubik's-cube brilliance ignored, her 381 days strapped to a bed under Teleborian's silhouette-like gaze recasting Bentham's Panopticon, and her subsequent guardianship extending the watch over her money and behavior. Because power 'produces reality,' the at-risk label becomes self-fulfilling, and Lisbeth's refusal to be disciplined—her silence, tattoos, and asocial style—only supplies fresh evidence for the label.
- ch. 13 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Judith Butler, Michel Foucault — Gender Performativity; Heteronormativity; Feminism — Reading Salander as genderqueer rather than simply a woman, the chapter argues her feminism lies in swift retaliation against those who abuse women and in economic and sexual independence from men, while her refusal of every identity label ('I don't know what I am') aligns her with queer theory's anti-identity politics. Judith Butler's performativity grounds the reading: Salander's body modifications and wardrobe 'undo' conventional gendering, and her drag-like aliases—the big-busted heiress Monica Sholes and the quiet Irene Nesser—succeed at fraud and flight only through absolute adherence to heteronormative femininity, proving gender is continuously constructed. Foucault's History of Sexuality frames her pathologization, institutionalization, and regulated sexuality as the medicalization of the sexually peculiar, a disciplinary script she reverses by hacking, surveilling, and exposing the authorities who pathologized her, tattooing i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist onto Bjurman.
- ch. 14 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Humanity as an End in Itself; Objectification; Philosophy of Love — Why do Berger, Cecilia, Harriet, Salander, and Figuerola all bed the unprepossessing Blomkvist? Testing Kant's claim that sexual desire makes 'the loved person an Object of appetite... a lemon which has been sucked dry,' the chapter argues his appeal is that he treats women as ends in themselves—he works beside them as equals, is 'not going to compete with you' with Figuerola, and never manipulates or controls—so his sex is the least objectifying in a Sweden full of men who hate women. Against Kant and Baumrim, Irving Singer's reply that desire can respond to the whole person explains why his no-strings honesty attracts powerful women, though his refusal to define, own, or 'cherish' any lover—walking in on Erika just as Salander arrives with the Elvis cabin ad—still leaves Salander heartbroken and Figuerola in sadness.
- ch. 16 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Simone de Beauvoir — Zen Buddhism — A cultural history of the coffeehouse frames Larsson's caffeine-soaked cast: the 'penny universities' where Addison brought philosophy out of closets to coffee-house tables, Diderot and Marx plotting at the Café de la Régence, Trotsky at the Café Central, and the Viennese 'meridians of loneliness' that fit Salander's i am an alien T-shirt, Blomkvist hearing his sentence at Kafé Anna, and Niederman's need to sit among people he despises. Ritzer's McDonaldization and 'Starbuckization' explain the characters' Billy's Pan Pizza and chain-café habits as rationalization's homogenizing disenchantment, against which Henrik Vanger's slowly sipped Norrland coffee stands for an older ethics of conversation and community. The chapter closes with the counter-image Larsson's addicts never reach: the Zen tea ceremony of Suzuki and Kakuzo, tranquility emanating from inner consciousness and 'the cup of humanity.'
- ch. 17 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** The Public Sphere; Democracy — The chapter reconstructs the real Swedish journalist behind Kalle Blomkvist: the 1950s reporter as the welfare state's mouthpiece alongside heroic police, the 1970s radical investigative journalist epitomized by Jan Guillou—whose exposure of the secret IB organization earned him a prison sentence and a revenge vindication, the direct template for Blomkvist—and the 1990s–2000s slide into 'sensation, scandal, and spectacle' around crime. It shows journalism decoupling from crime statistics—about a hundred killings a year in a country of 9.4 million, falling, yet alarmist coverage fueling tougher sentencing and the Nazi-rooted Sweden Democrats' entry into parliament—so the watchdog ideal of the muckraker who draws aside the veil on 'men who hate women and democracy' becomes a question: where have you gone, Kalle Blomkvist?
- ch. 18 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Philosophical Skepticism; Free Will vs Determinism — Philosopher Sven Ove Hansson's memoir shows the trilogy's realism came from Larsson's decades of unpaid extremism-watching: patiently archiving Nazi and racist networks, exposing the Sweden Democrats as Per Engdahl's 1979 repackaging of fascism in anti-immigrant dress (the same strategy as Britain's National Front), and forcing Skeptics' scrutiny onto the publisher of David Irving's Holocaust-denying Göring biography. It presents Larsson's anti-pseudoscience skepticism—astrology, faith healing, pyramidology, racist biology—his rejection of the postmodern idea that knowledge is mere social construction ('The Holocaust was not a social construction'), and his philosophically interesting argument that astrology's deterministic worldview is a stifling, self-fulfilling spiritual posture. The honor-killing analysis pairing Fadime Sahindal with Melissa Nordell demonstrates his method of using philosophical case-comparison to expose moral prejudice in taken-for-granted categories—habits of mind that resurface in the novels' hidden power structures and rationalist heroine.
- ch. 20 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Martha Nussbaum, Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche — Asking whether the Millennium Trilogy is popular fiction or literature, the chapter proposes Wittgenstein's family resemblances instead of an essence: Larsson's books are devoured like genre series, yet they tackle the 'moral seriousness'—violence against women, corruption, journalistic ethics—that Sartre called committed literature, so the whodunit becomes the exposé. Nussbaum's account of reading as moral perception, not mere grasp of facts, is applied to Lisbeth's 'Bitch' verdict on Harriet Vanger—should we see a culpable sister or a victim?—and the paradox of fiction explains why we feel real pity and fear for characters we know are invented, down to the detective plot's 'consolatory fiction' that truth can be found. The verdict: socially conscious popular fiction whose high/low distinction (Arnold versus Meisel's level field) matters less than the words-as-force-for-justice theme summed up in 'an insufferable do-gooder who thought he could change everything with a book.'
- ch. 21 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Plato, Martha Nussbaum — Why do we prefer the narrative where Bjurman handcuffs and rapes Salander to a boring one where Zalachenko is a good father? Rejecting Plato's Republic censorship of disturbing art—which would leave us nothing but nice stories—the chapter applies Aristotle's Poetics: Salander is an imperfect, exaggerated tragic hero whose flaws (defiant independence that keeps her from reporting Bjurman) arouse pity and terror, and reading the trilogy produces catharsis understood, with Nussbaum, as clarification rather than purgation. Thus the rape scenes illuminate how guardianship and power enable men who hate women (Bjurman's 'She had to understand who was in charge,' Martin Vanger's 'godlike feeling'), the heavy-metal concert models safe purgation of anger, and Salander's axing of Zalachenko joins Clytaemnestra's 'man-killing ax' tradition while her tattooed revenge on Bjurman, per Aristotle, yields moral satisfaction rather than tragedy.
- ch. 22 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** The Male Gaze; Objectification; Feminism — Applying Laura Mulvey's visual pleasure to the printed page, the chapter argues that Larsson's protest against woman-hating is compromised by styling Salander—four-eleven, ninety pounds, 'childlike breasts'—as a sexual spectacle whose rapes (Bjurman's coerced oral sex, the anal rape, the trial's play-by-play of implements) are the trilogy's most explicit scenes while consensual sex stays off-screen, making the books 'torture porn' for the voyeuristic reader. The films shift the gaze further: the revenge on Bjurman runs longer than the rapes, Salander actively watches Martin Vanger burn, and her bisexuality with Mimmi Wu is reduced to one silent morning, changes that make the violence against men more acceptable than against women. The chapter ends ambivalent: Laurie Penny and Gail Dines charge that 'Misogynist violence is appalling; now here's some more,' yet the distributor's RAINN partnership and a rape survivor's testimony that Salander was the first active, aggressive survivor she had ever seen show the books also work as Larsson intended.
- ch. 23 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Democracy — The chapter reads Salander's hacking beside Julian Assange's WikiLeaks: both are hard to classify as criminal or activist, and both live by the hacker ethic Stephen Levy codified—unlimited access, all information free, mistrust authority, judgment by skill—which later versions soften with privacy and social responsibility, matching 'Salander's Principles' (a bastard is always a bastard) and Assange's 'capable, generous men do not create victims; they nurture victims.' Through David Brin's Transparent Society it asks who watches the watchers—the police-camera city of the state or the citizen-accessible city—and argues for WikiLeaks-style reciprocal transparency that keeps the 'mighty' (governments, the Vanger Corporation, Wennerström) exposed while protecting whistleblower anonymity. Blomkvist's choices—suppressing the Vanger murders, encouraging Salander to steal Wennerström's files, planting disinformation—mark him as the journalist half of Larsson's new information-age hero pair.
- ch. 25 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Hannah Arendt, bell hooks, Aristotle, Karl Marx — The General Will; Feminism — Against Blomkvist's 'I don't believe in collective guilt,' the chapter argues the Section is not a few bad apples: with Rousseau, institutions outgrow the people's will and preserve themselves (the guardianship agency cannot welcome its own obsolescence; the Fälldin directive lets Säpo stand inside and outside the law at once), and with Arendt, institutions protect only those they already recognize, so the excluded Salander cannot be heard by Teleborian, Prosecutor Ekström, or the court that doubts Giannini. Through bell hooks's definition of patriarchy it shows the police, psychiatry, and Säpo prize rationality, stability, and power in a masculine code under which Salander's responsiveness to her mother's abuse and her retaliation read as insanity—her very self-sufficiency (pepper spray, Taser, forward planning) proving she needs no 'guardianship.' Rancière's policing-versus-politics distinction supplies the conclusion: perpetual political contestation of who institutions exclude, not Prime Minister-initiated cleanup, is the only answer to a hidden Section in every institution.
- ch. 26 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — Defending gossip against Sissela Bok's verdict ('trivializing' and 'reprehensible'), the chapter reads the trilogy as showing that loose talk is knowledge: Blomkvist's libel conviction, Bjurman's appointment through Björck, Gullberg's suspiciously empty reputation, and the Section's detection via the missing panic-talk at Millennium all run on trust and 'trust capital,' while Salander's hacking is electronic gossip—Solove's diary made public—in the old tradition of rumor as resistance from colonial India to pre-revolutionary Parisian libelles. Kant supplies the warning that Salander's principle turns people into 'mere means': her schadenfreude is 'moral' (Portmann) when it denatures powerful abusers like Wennerström but mere revenge against the condescending realtor, and the Malleus Maleficarum lineage shows the powerful gossiping best, their 'lesbian Satanist' smear a modern witch hunt. The trilogy closes on reciprocity—he knew her secrets just as she knew all of his—making mutual confession, not one-way scrutiny, the ground of trust.
- ch. 27 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Using the Nicomachean Ethics and the Rhetoric, the chapter vindicates the pleasure readers take in Salander's Taser-and-tattoo revenge on Bjurman: Aristotle distinguishes revenge, done for the satisfaction of the one wronged, from punishment, and requires that the wrongdoer know who avenges and why—which is why Lisbeth waits until Bjurman wakes before inking i am a sadistic pig, a pervert and a rapist across his torso. Proper anger on the right grounds is a virtue (hatred alone is corrosive), Larsson is cast as the rhetorician who must keep our trust to 'put the judge into a certain frame of mind,' and the revenge emerges as the deliberated, rational means toward the end Aristotle calls eudaimonia: independence from a bogus guardianship and a life worth living, since under 'proportionate reciprocity' those who cannot requite evil with evil are slaves.
- ch. 29 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Autonomy of the Will — Salander shares Kant's detestation of the criminal's hypocrisy: Martin Vanger's meticulous, unimpulsive murders and Wennerström's hubristic paper trail fail the universal-law formulation because each supremely rational villain casts himself as the exception to rules that bind everyone else. But Salander fails Kant too—she hacks 'for the kick' rather than from duty, encroaches on innocent privacy, and takes justice into her own hands (tattooing Bjurman, stealing from and arranging the death of Wennerström) where Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' would forbid even lying to a murderer; the chapter finds her closest to Benjamin Constant's rejoinder that truth is owed only to those worthy of it, matching her maxim that 'a bastard is always a bastard.' Her strict promise-keeping, her cultivation of mind and body per the Doctrine of Virtue, and her refusal of guardianship and of Blomkvist's money make her, in Kantian terms, a champion of autonomy who is nonetheless a work in progress.
- ch. 30 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Taking J. L. Austin's distinction between justifying conduct (showing it was the right thing to do) and excusing it (accepting wrongdoing but denying full blame), the chapter audits the trilogy's deceptions: Blomkvist's lottery trick on the pedophile Björck, his intention to double-cross him, the fake-collapse 'double game' at Millennium, and the disinformation fed to the Section's bugs are justified, since they deceive only dangerous criminals engaged in murderous conspiracies. Salander is shakier—her hacking of the innocent Blomkvist and the tax-tip revenge on the realtor expose the flaw in 'a bastard is always a bastard' (she cannot know guilt in advance), though her lies to Bjurman, Forbes, and Zalachenko earn excuse or justification. The verdict falls hardest on the cover-up of Martin Vanger's murders—trading truth for Harriet's protection and crisis-center funding, it might have warned other women, so Blomkvist's 'unforgivable' stands—and on her final lies under oath to honest police, excusable only if she still cannot trust the state.
- ch. 31 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust

- ch. 1 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** Personal Identity; Immortality and the Soul — The editors' introduction argues that His Dark Materials is philosophy-rich rather than a mere children's fantasy: its metaphysics of parallel worlds, dæmons, angels, armored bears, and mulefa poses genuine epistemic questions and ethical dilemmas. It frames the volume around the controversy over whether exposing children to Pullman's anti-religious vision is spiritual violence or an education in thinking for oneself like Lyra. It also sets up the trilogy's alternative afterlife, where Lyra frees the dead from the drab land of the dead to dissolve into Dust, and flags dæmons as puzzles of personal identity and soul-body interaction.
- ch. 10 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Death of God; The Übermensch; Will to Power; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.
- ch. 12 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** The Problem of Evil; Fate and Foreknowledge — Robison measures Pullman's Authority against the three attributes that make the Christian God worthy of worship and finds it fails all three: the suffering of intercision victims like Tony Makarios and the Authority's delegation to the malevolent Metatron defeat omnibenevolence, because unlike with the real God we know no free-will theodicy applies, since the Authority simply does not care; his ignorance of Lyra's destiny (which witches and the Consistorial Court learn long before he does) defeats omniscience; and his demented weeping in the crystal litter before dissolving in open air defeats omnipotence. Since the Authority never created the universe and lied about being its creator, he is not God at all, so Pullman's plot never refutes the God of the philosophers. What the books do establish, she argues, is a powerful attack on organized religion: the Magisterium's suppression of Dust research and harming of children mirror real religious institutions' punishment of Galileo, resistance to evolution, and persecution of dissenters.
- ch. 13 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, John Stuart Mill, Socrates, Jean-Paul Sartre — On Liberty; The Death of God; Bad Faith — Fairweather casts the campaign against Pullman's books as Socrates's trial rerun (impiety plus corrupting the young) and asks whether legally protected speech can still be morally wrong, weighing Mill's On Liberty point that children lack the 'maturity of their faculties' against the charge that Pullman's 'killing God' rhetoric inflicts spiritual violence on young believers, by his own image of intercision. The answer comes through Nietzsche's Three Metamorphoses: Asriel, Will, and Lyra play the lion that slays the great 'thou shalt' of the Authority, but the lion's destruction is only the possibility of freedom, since full freedom is Nietzsche's child creating its own values rather than lapsing into nihilism or Sartrean bad faith. Pullman's Republic of Heaven, with its virtues of courage, compassion, love, kindness, and curiosity held in community, is a social ideal rather than a radically Nietzschean one, so the charge of corrupting young readers is deflated.
- ch. 14 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** David Hume — Faith and Reason; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Yuen reads the silver guillotine of intercision against infant circumcision: both cut unconsenting children as acts of faith, Mrs. Coulter's belief that severing dæmons prevents original sin mirroring the Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 17. Deploying W.K. Clifford's shipowner ('It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence') and Hume's claim that belief is an involuntary feeling no will can command, he argues that the real moral fault lies in acting on uninvestigated beliefs in ways that harm others, while Mrs. Coulter's non-consensual experiments on kidnapped children are wrong independently of what she believes. He concludes that if cutting Pantalaimon from Lyra is wrong, circumcision is wrong for the same reasons though less severely, at worst as irresponsible as exposing a child to chicken pox.
- ch. 15 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** The Noble Lie — Vaclavik follows Lyra's career as liar and trickster, from the Silvertongue performance that goads Iofur Raknison into fighting Iorek Byrnison, up to the reversal in the Land of the Dead where the harpy screams 'Liar!' and only true stories can feed the ghosts. She frames Lyra's boast that she is the best liar there ever was yet is not lying as a version of the Liar Paradox, then dissolves the puzzle by showing that lies continue after the katabasis (Will's comforting fib, Mrs. Coulter's noble treachery with Metatron) just as truth-telling appeared before it. Truth triumphs in the underworld not for its own sake but because it suits the audience: the dead need the world they have lost, so storytelling, truthful or invented, is judged by what it does for its listeners.
- ch. 17 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Mackey tracks the ontological migrations of Lyra, Pantalaimon, and the alethiometer from black marks on a page into the Listening Library audiobook with fixed voices, the National Theatre's puppet dæmons whose black-clad puppeteer stunningly turns out to speak as Lyra's death, the film's computer-graphic Pan with its explanatory opening voice-over, the dæmon-assignment website, a videogame that reduces Pan's shape-shifting to four player-chosen forms, and a Tonner collectible doll with a resin Pantalaimon. She asks whether 'reinforced fiction' supported by extratextual evidence (publisher websites, playbill portraits supposedly showing historical dæmons) makes stories feel more real, and what essential qualities make each embodied version still count as Lyra or Pan. Her conclusion is a research program: understanding how readers conjure fictional beings 'out of all air and thought' across media would be a giant step toward understanding the intricacies of the human mind.
- ch. 18 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** Everything Flows / Logos — Russell argues that in Pullman's universe stories generate Dust and truth is a product of the telling: Lord Asriel defends the Adam and Eve story as an 'imaginary number' that lets you calculate what you could not otherwise imagine, and Mary Malone must first tell a lie to a guard and later narrate her own story of leaving her convent to bring Lyra and Will to the moment of free will. Reading the companion pieces Lyra's Oxford and Once Upon a Time in the North, she shows Lyra and Lee Scoresby (guided by Hester and Iorek) learning to read clues, birds, maps, and attached ephemera without closing too fast on meaning, Lyra's detective-story certainty proving mistaken about the alchemist Sebastian Makepeace. The self that emerges, citing Santiago Colas, is relational and becoming rather than being: we become the stories we tell and read, and Dust is renewed by each narrative interaction rather than settled into final answers.
- ch. 19 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato — Possible Worlds; Free Will vs Determinism — Auxier tests Pullman's many-worlds premise, setting Asriel's coin-toss explanation and the Barnard-Stokes hypothesis against Book III's claim that unchosen possibilities are 'snuffed out like candles,' then measures the trilogy against David Lewis's causally independent possible worlds, which forbid the subtle knife's transworld travel and leave the chill Lyra feels at the thought of 'another Lyra' in Will's Oxford as an unresolved transworld-identity puzzle. Compiling fourteen kinds of conscious beings from humans and dæmons to specters and the Abyss itself, he argues Pullman's cosmology is panpsychist and aesthetic rather than moral or epistemic, ordered by what the alethiometer, the knife, and the spyglass can and cannot do, with the alethiometer submitting to the knife and love alone able to break it, as Will's love for his mother and for Lyra does twice. Peirce's agapicism, evolution by creative love alongside chance and mechanical necessity, supplies the closest philosophical analogue to Pullman's 'Matter loved Dust.'
- ch. 21 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** Harry Frankfurt — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Moral Luck — Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.
- ch. 22 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** René Descartes, David Lewis, G.E. Moore — Methodological Doubt (evil demon); Philosophical Skepticism — Michaud wonders whether the Magisterium's censorship of Dust research could be epistemically justified, building the answer from Descartes's dreaming and deceiving-demon doubts (imagine waking to find your dæmon was only a dream), Moore's common-sense 'I know I have two hands' reply, and Dretske's relevant alternatives, arriving at Lewis's 'Elusive Knowledge': inquiry itself ratchets up the standards for knowledge until certainty dissolves, which is exactly what happens to Lyra, and to readers, once they start asking questions about Dust and other worlds. On this view the Magisterium had a Lewisian motive to suppress inquiry, since unquestioning belief preserves the certainty on which its power and promise of salvation rest. But because philosophical questions like 'Is God good?' can never meet the raised standards anyway, the chapter concludes that a little doubt is preferable to the dogmatism and bigotry certainty breeds.
- ch. 23 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Finley puts Pullman's parallel worlds beside philosophers' possible worlds: the twin Oxfords sharing Simon Parslow's scratched initials invite the inference that Lyra's world has its own Madagascar, while modal realists like Lewis ('out there going on') take possible worlds to really exist and more skeptical theorists treat them as convenient fictions like 'in the story.' She contrasts their origins, quantum splitting at the level of elementary particles versus eternal logical possibility, explains why the indexical 'actual world' is one we can never leave, and argues that Lewis's underdetermination of fiction means the books describe not one possible world but vast numbers differing in unmentioned details like the population of alternate Madagascar. Lewis's counterpart theory then resolves Lyra's chill at 'perhaps there was a Lyra': the counterpart in Will's Oxford could never be her, only someone remarkably like her.
- ch. 25 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit, René Descartes, David Chalmers — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Mind–Body Dualism; Immortality and the Soul — Harris and Baer use the Boatman scene ('Pan is me... we'd die') to test criteria of personal identity against the trilogy: Lyra and Will's inference to a thinking third part, the ghost, reenacts Descartes's dualist reasoning about mind-body distinctness, Iorek's lack of a ghost exemplifies the same-body criterion, and Pantalaimon's instant shape-shifting favors the psychological criterion, spelled out through Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory thought experiment and Parfit's psychological connectedness and continuity. They ask whether Lee Scoresby's dissolution into conscious atoms that reunite with Hester's counts as genuine survival, best accommodated by Locke's consciousness criterion or a panpsychist matter criterion, with Chalmers cited as the contemporary defender of conscious matter. The chapter closes with individuation, whether Lyra and Pan are one person or two, applied to a Primal Fear-style multiple-personality murder trial, the hypothetical of Pan killing someone while Lyra is innocent, and living wills in persistent vegetative states.
- ch. 26 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" **·** Epicurus — Death Is Nothing to Us; Immortality and the Soul — Greene applies the philosophy of death to Pullman's worlds, starting from the Epicurean puzzle that death is bad only if experienced, so it cannot be bad, plus the asymmetry puzzle about prenatal non-existence, then testing the Deprivation View (Father Gomez's bullet would rob Lyra of Oxford, the alethiometer, and love) and the Desire-Frustration View (Iorek's frustrated desires) against a universe whose dead do persist as ghosts. The world of the dead, with its harpies, eternal boredom, and the pain of leaving Pan with the Boatman, seems to refute Epicurus by making death a miserable experience after all. But the twist reframes everything: the dead who stream through Will's knife-hole to dissolve into Dust are choosing death over the afterlife, and since for them the good things of life are already off the table, death is not bad at all, which is exactly why they choose it.
- ch. 27 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 28 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" *(notes)*
