- ch. 8 "Welcome Everything Is Great!" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction argues that The Good Place is unique among TV comedies in taking real moral philosophy seriously instead of playing the professor for a fool: Chidi Anagonye is a deontology-focused ethics professor whose 'mini ethics lessons' ground the plot, and philosophy becomes the vocabulary Eleanor and the others use to make sense of themselves. It recounts the show's premise (Eleanor waking in Michael's Neighborhood 12358W with Janet the 'vessel of all knowledge'), explains why a philosophy-professor character is rare on television, and sets out the volume's title conventions and spoiler warning.
- ch. 9 "Thanks" *(notes)*
- ch. 10 "I The Demons in the Details" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic" **·** Hannah Arendt — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Reads the show's automatic, unquestionable point system as Hannah Arendt's bureaucracy — 'rule by Nobody' in which no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority over the system ('He's not God, he's a bureaucrat'). It argues via Arendt's power/violence distinction that bureaucracies deprive everyone subject to them of the power to act, leaving only resistance or violence, which is why Michael's Season Two plea before Gen ('the very method we use to deem them good or bad is fundamentally flawed') and his Season Three interference amount to revolt. Chidi's 'Most Improved Player' defense of Eleanor and Michael's case that souls can grow after death show the system cannot accommodate rehabilitation, only retribution.
- ch. 12 "2. How Can Torture Be This Funny" **·** Henri Bergson, Philippa Foot, Bernard Williams — The Trolley Problem; Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living) — Asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny and answers with incongruity theory (circus music under Michael's dejection; a comedy set in Hell) plus Bergson's view of comedy as social correction that deflates those who deserve it — Tahani's name-dropping, Michael failing 802 reboots. It centers on 'The Trolley Problem': Michael teleporting Chidi's ethics lesson into real runaway trolleys ('not real, but the pain is') is both incongruous humor and genuine torture, and invoking Bernard Williams shows the real wrongdoer is Michael, who rigged the situation, not Chidi who must choose. Eternal torture, it concludes, only works as endless low-grade everyday crappiness, which is comic in twenty-two-minute doses — and Eleanor's twice-given forgiveness of Michael, after seeing the centuries of torture in Janet's VR device, is the show's real moral marvel.
- ch. 13 "3. Sympathy for the Devils" **·** William James — Pragmatism; Free Will vs Determinism — Argues, against Michael, that the Soul Squad still belongs in the Bad Place: drawing on William James's conditions for actions having moral worth (foreseeable consequences, no do-overs) and his meliorism about an unfinished, responsive universe, it shows the points system is contextualist (the tricycle fix worth +4.79 or +0.04; the two Dougs' rose gifts), but the afterlife simulation is a context where nothing the humans do is consequential or permanent, so their moral growth earns no points. Worse, their growth adds net unhappiness — Michael's suffering, the demon cast's misery, Judge Gen's distress — so becoming better ironically confirms they belong in the Bad Place. Only Michael, whose retirement is a real, irreversible consequence and whose sacrifices add genuine good, deserves the Good Place.
- ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" **·** David Hume, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Friedrich Nietzsche, Thomas Hobbes — Bundle Theory of Self; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; Non-Self (anatman) — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Bad Faith — Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.
- ch. 16 "II Somewhere Else" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "6. A Better Bad Place" **·** Anselm of Canterbury — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Utilitarianism — Asks whether Judge Gen could ever justly consign Team Cockroach to eternal torment. It reconstructs the Anselmian infinite-desert defense (God as 'than which none greater can be conceived', every sin against an infinite being meriting infinite punishment) and shows it fails on the show since no such God appears and neither Gen nor Michael is infinitely great; the continuing-sin model fails because the Bad Place's physical tortures (eyeball corkscrews, bees with teeth) preclude sinning, and Gen's own tests (Jason's Madden game, Tahani's hallway, Chidi's two hats) show vice persisting without added desert. Punishment as retribution also fails on utilitarian grounds (Jason's hypothetical spray-paint-can sentence adds only pain), so the chapter proposes a non-retributive 'Bad Place 3.0' where people face the natural consequences of their vices, comparing it to C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce.
- ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" **·** Albert Camus, Susan Wolf — Meaning in Life; The Meaning of Life; Immortality and the Soul; The Myth of Sisyphus — Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.
- ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — The Death of God; Authenticity; Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd — Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.
- ch. 20 "III Everything Is Fine" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; The Ends Justify the Means — Asks whether a show about ethics may lie to its audience for a whole season: the Season One twist breaks the viewer's implicit contract even though the show keeps its internal 'truth in fiction'. Through 'The Eternal Shriek' it stages the debate — Chidi's Kantian ban on lying (the red cowboy boots saga with Henry, ending in a confession that defeats Henry) against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means plot to 'kill' Janet — and reads the show's cascade of confessions as its answer that truth-telling absolves. Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' lets Chidi lie his way through Hell, leaving viewers to decide whether the twist's ethical education justifies the deception.
- ch. 22 "10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism — Casts Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis in an allegorical love story: Chidi's Kantian universalizability about lying and his utilitarian lesson (confess, because the neighborhood's welfare outweighs you) only move Eleanor when she sees Theory enacted — Michael's willingness to absorb eternal torture in her place convinces her the theory 'has legs'. Praxis repays the debt when Eleanor's moral particularism pushes Chidi to lie to demons and play his part in the Bad Place party, and Michael's conversion from torturer to someone who sacrifices his portal pin for Eleanor ('Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent') completes the union. The moral: theory is born in the world, but only practice lets it thrive there.
- ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" **·** Immanuel Kant, Philippa Foot — The Trolley Problem; The Categorical Imperative — Treats Chidi's indecision (rock-paper-scissors panic, the soul-mate dilemma, the boots lie) as the show's authentic portrait of how hard moral life is, not just a professor joke. Michael's live-action Trolley Problem — Foot's thought experiment made literal, with Henry's bloody boots flying at Chidi — is read as torture precisely because it weaponizes Chidi's defining trait, and the show pointedly never hands the audience a right answer. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired movies-vs-er argument ('Your boy Kant would say never break a promise') finally lets Chidi act, and Scanlon's What We Owe to Each Other frames his arc's resolution: we choose to be good because of our bonds with others, as when he kisses Eleanor in 'Somewhere Else' and Michael 'solves' the trolley by sacrificing himself.
- ch. 24 "IV The Brainy Bunch" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "12. How the Fork Did I Get Here" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Personal Identity; Aristotle on the Soul — Asks what makes the person sitting in Michael's office numerically identical to the person who died on Earth. The same-body theory fails because bodies stay behind (buried or cremated) with no spatiotemporal continuity; the same-mind theory of psychological continuity fails on the 802 memory-wiping reboots and the duplication case of two psychologically-continuous Eleanors; the same-soul theory cannot say what makes two souls the same soul. The chapter concludes that 'Janet(s)' — essences reconstituting themselves in Janet's void — quietly commits the show to Aristotelian and Aquinan hylomorphism, while leaving open how anyone (even Janet) could tell that two persons share an essence.
- ch. 26 "13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts" **·** Frank Jackson, Boethius, Thomas Aquinas, Averroes (Ibn Rushd) — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Knowledge Argument (Mary's Room) — Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.
- ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; The Trolley Problem — Defends Kant against the charge that he is why everyone hates moral philosophy professors: it explains the two-question Categorical Imperative test via frozen-yogurt maxims and Eleanor's selfish 'won't help unless it benefits me' principle, shows Kant never actually forbade lying to the murderer at the door (his crotchety 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' was an obscure legal point), and reads Chidi's trolley-track switch but refusal to harvest Eleanor's organs as the humanity formula — never treat a person merely as a means. Tahani's $60 billion in charity and Eleanor's failed point-chasing in 'What's My Motivation?' illustrate the good will: deeds lack moral worth unless done for the right reasons. Aristotle explains the residual puzzle — theory mastery does not make you skilled at ethical practice, any more than a nutritionist is a great cook.
- ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" **·** John Dewey, Immanuel Kant, Carol Gilligan, Aristotle, Jeremy Bentham — The Ethics of Care; Deontology; Utilitarianism; The Golden Mean — Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.
- ch. 29 "V No Exit" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "16. Is Hell Other People" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Bad Faith; Authenticity — Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.
- ch. 31 "17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Bad Faith; Existentialism — Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.
- ch. 32 "VI The Leap to Faith" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "18. Heaven Is Other People" **·** Emmanuel Levinas — The Face of the Other; Forgiveness; The Meaning of Life — Treats the show as a theological sitcom whose afterlife (Gen's algorithmic judgment, cubicles, the Jeremy Bearimy timeline) critiques a pop-Christian eschatology of disembodied Heaven and eternal conscious torment while missing the bodily resurrection of Nicene and N.T. Wright's account. Levinas supplies the positive frame: ethics precedes ontology, the face of the Other demands responsibility before any impersonal verdict — which is why Gen's points system 'wouldn't cut it' and why the show's two-shots, Eleanor's spontaneous good acts, and Chidi's 802 yeses to teaching her matter. Bonhoeffer's religionless Christianity completes the reading of Eleanor's repentance, Donna's and Tahani's confessions, and Michael's self-sacrificing Christ figure: salvation comes through intersubjective, grace-infused transformation, so 'Heaven is other people'.
- ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" **·** Dharma; Atman and Brahman — Argues Hinduism 'gets more than five percent right' via the Bhagavad Gita: the show's point system mirrors karma, Eleanor's failed point-chasing and quiet departure for the Bad Place enact nishkama karma (desire-less action), and the 802 reboots are rebirths without memory. The characters form a ladder of unfoldment — Jason's unknowing wrong action below Eleanor's knowing one, Tahani's corruptly motivated good deeds, Chidi's knowledge without decision, Michael swerving from his demonic dharma, and Janet highest: desireless, rebooting like cyclical rebirth, her void echoing boundless Brahman. Chidi's logic-bound indecision versus Eleanor's knowledge-producing logic completes the Gita reading.
- ch. 35 "VII What’s My Motivation" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "20. Moral Health Warning" **·** Immanuel Kant — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Categorical Imperative — A health warning from Jonathan Dancy himself: the show's premise that Chidi's lessons in Kant, Scanlon, and the Trolley Problem can make Eleanor better is false, because becoming good requires a change in motivation and intellectual study shapes motivation at most indirectly — and might attach to the wrong as easily as the right, since moral philosophy studies both. Worse, studying ethics looks like self-indulgence, time spent on Kant that could have gone to doing actual good. Against the Kantian thought that only acting from a sense of duty earns moral credit, Dancy argues that sympathetic love — Doug Wynegar bringing his grandmother roses simply for her sake — is enough, which undermines both Kant and Chidi's entire teaching project.
- ch. 37 "21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good" **·** Socrates, Aristotle — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Argues that no one can improve without first admitting they are bad: the rigid Good Place/Bad Place binary is ethical dualism whose cracks show in Mindy St. Claire's Medium Place and Jason, a naive moral neutral who fits neither side. Socrates' Apology supplies the method — wisdom is knowing what you do not know, so self-aware fault-finding precedes growth — while Aristotle's account of virtue as learned by practice, like an instrument, grounds the claim that goodness can be acquired even in the afterlife, though unlearning old habits is harder. Eleanor's trash storm, Tahani's failed party, and Chidi's theory-practice gap mark each character's admissions of error, and the worst offenders, Eleanor and Michael, improve most because they confess unprompted.
- ch. 38 "22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience" **·** John Dewey — Embodiment (the lived body); Experience and Education — Brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings are evolved, body-based shortcuts built from a lifetime of social interaction that prune options in real-time moral choice, so Chidi's classroom mastery paired with real-world collapse mirrors Damasio's ventromedial patients — except Chidi has the alarms and refuses to trust them, insisting ethics is pure calculation. Mark Johnson's moral imagination (his own draft-number dilemma) and Scanlon's contractualism (morality is other people) reinforce that we are not disembodied reasoners. Combining Dewey's 'morals is education' with Damasio's claim that somatic learning never stops, the chapter explains how Eleanor and friends keep growing morally even after death — bodies, social bonds and all.
- ch. 39 "23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness" **·** Immanuel Kant — Authenticity; Humanity as an End in Itself — Begins with Schur's traffic-light story — the fourth car sneaking through the left-turn arrow as 'negative twenty points' — to argue the show is, before it is about ethics, an attack on selfish inauthenticity: Tahani's name-dropping charity, Eleanor's lunch-table declaration of friendlessness, Chidi's moral filibustering, and Jason's Acidcat gig each pursue a self at others' expense. Using Charles Guignon's On Being Authentic and Kant's language of means and ends, it traces the movement from authenticity that uses others to an authenticity that lives for others — Chidi's 802 unconditional yeses, Michael's shift from torturer to self-sacrificer to paralyzed would-be hero, and Eleanor giving up Chidi in 'Pandemonium' as the endpoint. Being true to yourself, the show teaches, is only ethical when it helps others be their truest selves.

- ch. 8 "Welcome Everything Is Great!" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors' introduction recounts how Eleanor Shellstrop wakes in Michael's fake Good Place with the indecisive ethics professor Chidi as her reluctant guide, and argues the show is unique because philosophy is not a gag but the vocabulary the characters use to understand themselves and their predicaments. It frames the volume as extending Chidi's ethics lessons to the audience and sets out the book's terminological conventions for the show, the fake neighborhood, and the real Good Place.
- ch. 9 "Thanks" *(notes)*
- ch. 10 "I The Demons in the Details" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic" **·** Hannah Arendt — Westfall uses Hannah Arendt's account of bureaucracy as 'rule by Nobody' to read the show's afterlife: the point system runs itself, and no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority to alter the automatic calculation of a life's score. Because bureaucracies deprive everyone subject to them of the power to act and thereby invite violence, Chidi's 'Most Improved Player' plea for Eleanor and Michael's Season Two argument before Gen that the system is 'fundamentally flawed' amount to the only recourse Arendt leaves: resistance against the system itself.
- ch. 12 "2. How Can Torture Be This Funny" **·** Henri Bergson, Philippa Foot, Bernard Williams — The Trolley Problem; Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living); Integrity Against Utilitarianism — Pavelich asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny, answering with incongruity theory and Bergson's view of comedy as social punishment, seen in Tahani paired with a silent monk and Michael failing 802 reboots. The centerpiece is 'The Trolley Problem': Michael drops Chidi into Foot's thought experiment so Chidi becomes the instrument of his own agony, and by Bernard Williams's principle the real wrongdoer is Michael, who set up the situation. Eternal torture works as comedy only because everyday crappiness is watched on a twenty-two-minute scale, and Eleanor's forgiveness of Michael after seeing the tortures in Janet's VR makes her the show's real moral hero.
- ch. 13 "3. Sympathy for the Devils" **·** William James — Consequentialism; Free Will vs Determinism — Bromhall contends the Soul Squad's moral growth cannot earn them Good Place points, because the contextualist point system rewards only the happiness an action actually adds to the universe, as the two Dougs' rose gifts show. Using William James's conditions for morally valuable action, foreseeable consequences and no do-overs, he argues the afterlife is the wrong context for human action since Michael can rewrite reality and wipe memories at will. Ironically the humans' growth only makes Michael and the demons miserable, while Michael's own high-stakes, irreversible self-sacrifice meets all of James's conditions and so alone deserves The Good Place.
- ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, David Hume, Thomas Hobbes — Bundle Theory of Self; Non-Self (anatman); Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; Moral Relativism — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Bad Faith; Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation — Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.
- ch. 16 "II Somewhere Else" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "6. A Better Bad Place" **·** Anselm of Canterbury — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; Utilitarianism; The Ontological Argument — Grosz asks whether Judge Gen could justly condemn Team Cockroach to eternal torment, testing the classic 'sins against an infinite being deserve infinite punishment' defense built on Anselm's God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived, and finding that no such being exists on the show. He rejects the continuing-sin model of Hell because the Bad Place's physical torture precludes both further sinning and moral reform, and argues purely retributive eternal punishment fails the utilitarian test. His proposal, a non-torturous 'Bad Place 3.0' modeled on C.S. Lewis's The Great Divorce where people face the natural consequences of their vice until they reform, could be justified as what is best for the person.
- ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" **·** Susan Wolf, Albert Camus — The Meaning of Life; Meaning in Life; The Myth of Sisyphus; Immortality and the Soul — Yang frames Eleanor's predicament as a dilemma: a finite life seems drained of value by its ending, while an immortal one collapses into boredom or into the disconnection of the 802 memory-wiped reboots. Camus's Sisyphus and Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view prove inadequate, so he adopts Susan Wolf's account of meaning as loving what deserves to be loved, which Eleanor's study of moral philosophy, her friendships, and her romance with Chidi satisfy even without God or eternity. John Martin Fischer's narrative approach then redeems the reboots as self-contained episodes, and Eleanor's note to herself in Scanlon's book shows memory wipes need not sever the story of a life.
- ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — The Death of God; Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; Authenticity — Montoya reads Chidi's breakdown upon learning he has been tortured for three hundred years as Nietzsche's death of God, quoting the Parable of the Madman from 'Jeremy Bearimy' to show how the guaranteed meaning of Chidi's worldview collapses into nihilism. Michael's midlife-crisis makeover and partying embody Camus's embrace of the absurd, while Sartre's existence precedes essence, abandonment, and anguish explain why Eleanor's confession to Michael and her sacrifice in the Judge's test count as authentic choices. With the Judge's verdict stripping away any hope of reward, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake, which the chapter presents as the show's answer to nihilism.
- ch. 20 "III Everything Is Fine" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place" **·** Immanuel Kant, Niccolò Machiavelli — The Categorical Imperative; The Ends Justify the Means — Sheldon argues the Season One twist makes the show itself a moral paradox: a series about ethics that lies to its audience for thirteen episodes, breaking the informal contract it built through 'truth in fiction'. Through Chidi's red-cowboy-boots lie and Eleanor's plot to murder Janet, 'The Eternal Shriek' stages Kant's absolute prohibition on lying against Eleanor's Machiavellian ends-justify-means reasoning, with confession portrayed as the only release from escalating deception. The chapter ends with Eleanor citing Jonathan Dancy's moral particularism to get Chidi to lie his way through the Bad Place, leaving viewers to decide whether the show's own deception is justified by the ethical conversation it forces.
- ch. 22 "10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Utilitarianism — Altmann allegorizes Chidi as Theory and Eleanor as Praxis, whose 'love story' shows each completing the other: Chidi's lessons in utilitarianism and Kant's Categorical Imperative give Eleanor reasons, and eventually a lived example in Michael's feigned self-sacrifice, to confess her lie, while Eleanor's pragmatism in the Bad Place teaches Chidi that principles useless in the world must be revised. Michael's arc from designing psychological torture to giving Eleanor his portal pin demonstrates a theory of human nature, that people cannot change, being falsified by praxis. The chapter closes with Eleanor re-entering the cycle by finding Chidi's lectures online, recommending the union of theory and praxis as how anyone becomes a better person.
- ch. 23 "11. Those Agonizing Choices" **·** Immanuel Kant, Philippa Foot — The Trolley Problem; The Categorical Imperative; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Romanowski traces Chidi's indecision from the cowboy-boots lie through the rock-paper-scissors panic attack, arguing the show treats the agony of deciding as the universal human moral condition rather than a professor joke. 'The Trolley Problem' makes Foot's dilemma literal torture, and the show pointedly never gives the right answer, confirming Chidi's claim that there are no clean solutions to hard moral questions. Eleanor's Dancy-inspired particularism pitch in 'Rhonda, Diana, Jake, and Trent' and Michael's 'I solved the Trolley Problem: you sacrifice yourself' moment, together with Chidi finally kissing Eleanor, show that acknowledging uncertainty is no excuse for inaction.
- ch. 24 "IV The Brainy Bunch" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "12. How the Fork Did I Get Here" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Aristotle on the Soul — Tepley uses Eleanor waking in Michael's office to pose the problem of numerical personal identity: what makes the person in the chair the very same person who died seconds earlier on Earth? He eliminates the same-body theory, since bodies stay behind and lack spatiotemporal continuity, the same-mind theory of psychological continuity, which fails on the 802 reboots and implies the absurdity that two duplicates would both be Eleanor, and the same-soul theory, which offers no criteria for sameness. The 'Janet(s)' revelation that the humans are recomposed from 'essences' turns out to be Aristotelian-Thomistic hylomorphism, committing the show to a same-soul theory of identity it never defends.
- ch. 26 "13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts" **·** Boethius, Frank Jackson, Thomas Aquinas, Averroes (Ibn Rushd) — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Knowledge Argument (Mary's Room) — Schiltz tests Janet's claim to know 'literally everything' against the philosophical definition of omniscience as believing all true propositions, finding she lacks knowledge of Michael's demonhood, of the future, and of current events on Earth. Divine-omniscience puzzles drawn from Averroes and Aquinas, and Boethius's solution that God sees all things in an eternal present, frame why Janet's ignorance of the future is what protects the characters' free will and moral responsibility. Frank Jackson's Mary thought experiment illuminates Judge Gen's failure to know what human life is like, and Janet's gradual acquisition of empathy across her reboots shows why her imperfect knowledge is a feature rather than a glitch.
- ch. 27 "14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; The Trolley Problem; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Duindam defends Kant against the charge that he makes moral philosophy professors insufferable, walking through maxims and the two-question Categorical Imperative test with frozen-yogurt and stealing examples, and arguing that Kant's notorious 'you cannot lie to the murderer' essay is an obscure legal point whose actual test permits lying to demons. On the trolley, the bridge, and Michael's forced organ-harvesting scenario, Kant's humanity formula, never treat persons merely as means, explains both Chidi's refusal to kill Eleanor and the difference between switching tracks and pushing a man. Tahani's sixty billion dollars in charity earning no points, and Eleanor's fruitless 'What's My Motivation' blitz versus her costly confession, vindicate Kant's claim that only a good will gives actions moral worth, while Aristotle supplies the closing lesson that being good takes practice, not just study.
- ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" **·** John Dewey, Immanuel Kant, Carol Gilligan, Jeremy Bentham, Aristotle, John Stuart Mill — The Ethics of Care; Deontology; Utilitarianism; The Golden Mean — Vannatta argues Chidi's indecision exposes the shared flaw of the Big Three theories, Kantian deontology, Bentham and Mill's consequentialism, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of the golden mean: their rationalism pretends moral conflict can be eliminated by applying the correct rule, when Chidi's trolley terror shows moral situations are experienced as genuinely uncertain. Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals', the Good of desire, the Right of duty, and the Virtuous of communal praise, legitimizes that felt uncertainty and explains Eleanor's talent for finding option C between binary dilemmas. The chapter concludes that the show's real, unspoken moral theory is care ethics: partiality, relationship maintenance, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as Eleanor learns from Chidi's friendship rather than his lectures.
- ch. 29 "V No Exit" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "16. Is Hell Other People" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — The Look (hell is other people); Bad Faith; Authenticity — Berk compares the show to Sartre's No Exit, where Garcin, Inez, and Estelle are locked in a drawing room as each other's torturers, and notes that Michael's experiment 'in the spirit of Sartre' fails because the four humans befriend and improve each other instead. She then corrects the standard reading: Sartre himself insisted 'Hell is other people' is conditional on twisted, bad-faith relationships of over-dependence on others' judgment, as with Tahani's craving for her parents' approval, and the footnote in Being and Nothingness about a 'radical conversion' to authenticity leaves room for healthy relations. Read this way, the show's message that flawed people can find salvation through each other is compatible with, not a refutation of, Sartre.
- ch. 31 "17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Radical Freedom and Responsibility; Bad Faith; Existentialism — Hubbard-Mattix frames the show's central paradox, each person is responsible for her choices yet those choices are formed by her relationships, as a collision between the existentialism of Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and the feminist idea of relational autonomy. Each character embodies a failure mode: Eleanor's futile rejection of social dependence, Chidi's evasion of accountability in bad faith, Tahani's destruction by living for others' approval, and Jason's unexamined loyalty to Pillboi, Donkey Doug, and the Jaguars. Their failures before Judge Gen teach the audience to choose relationships that enable growth while still owning one's choices.
- ch. 32 "VI The Leap to Faith" *(front)*
- ch. 33 "18. Heaven Is Other People" **·** Emmanuel Levinas — The Face of the Other; Immortality and the Soul; The Meaning of Life — Mayward examines the show's eschatology, arguing its points algorithm critiques the popular picture of Hell as eternal conscious torment, in the lineage of Jonathan Edwards, while missing historic Christian teaching about embodied resurrection. He then reads the series through Levinas, for whom ethics arises in the face-to-face encounter with the Other prior to any impersonal judgment, a structure mirrored in the show's two-shots and in Eleanor's spontaneous good deeds done before she understands them, and through Dietrich Bonhoeffer's 'religionless Christianity', in which Michael's self-sacrifice and the humans' repentance enact responsibility for neighbors without hope of reward. Salvation in the show is intersubjective transformation: where Sartre said Hell is other people, The Good Place suggests Heaven is other people.
- ch. 34 "19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right" **·** Karma and Rebirth; Dharma; Atman and Brahman — Kaur and Gupta argue Hinduism got far more than five percent right, mapping the show's points onto karmic theory and the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of action: right action, inaction, and wrong action. Eleanor's fruitless point-grubbing and selfless departure exemplify nishkama karma, desire-less action, while the 802 reboots and Janet's memory-wiped revivals mirror the birth-death-rebirth cycle on the way to self-realization. Ranking the cast on the Gita's ladder of unfoldment, desire-driven Eleanor and Jason below Tahani and knowledgeable Chidi, with Michael straying from his dharma and detached, duty-bound Janet nearest to Brahman, they show the series dramatizes the Gita's teaching that motivation, not the deed itself, determines an act's worth.
- ch. 35 "VII What’s My Motivation" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "20. Moral Health Warning" **·** Immanuel Kant — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); The Categorical Imperative — The moral philosopher Jonathan Dancy issues a warning against the show's premise that studying moral philosophy can make you a better person, the assumption behind Chidi's entire tutelage of Eleanor. What makes someone good is their motivation, and reading Kant and Scanlon is at best self-indulgent study that never redirects the will toward the right; indeed anyone genuinely motivated by the good would stop reading moral philosophy and go do good instead. He also contests the Kantian thought that only action done from a sense of duty earns moral credit: Douglas Wynegar's roses for his grandmother, given out of love, should count without any thought of obligation.
- ch. 37 "21. You Gotta Be Bad if You Wanna Be Good" **·** Socrates, Aristotle — Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Virtue Ethics (arete) — Shearer argues the show dismantles ethical dualism, the good/evil binary that sorts people wholly into the Good Place or the Bad Place and that underwrites real-world 'us versus them' thinking. Following Aristotle, being good is a learnable skill like reading or an instrument, acquired by practice and unlearning, not a fixed nature. Following Socrates in the Apology, progress begins with admitting you do not know, and the chapter shows that the characters who self-generate that admission, Eleanor confessing and Michael realizing he loves the humans, grow the most, while Jason's moral neutrality exposes a case the Good Place/Bad Place binary cannot classify at all.
- ch. 38 "22. Professor Stomachache Needs Neuroscience" **·** John Dewey — Embodiment (the lived body); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Zebrowski brings Antonio Damasio's Somatic Marker Hypothesis to bear on Chidi's stomachaches: gut feelings built from a lifetime of social experience are essential decision-making shortcuts, not noise corrupting pure reason, as the tirelessly deliberating frontal-lobe patient shows. Chidi's failure is not brain damage but a refusal to trust his own somatic alarms while insisting ethics can be computed, exactly the mind-body split that Scanlon's contractualism, where morality is negotiated with other people, and Dewey's 'morals is education' both reject. Combined with Mark Johnson's moral imagination, this explains how the dead humans keep growing morally after death: bodies, relationships, and culture continue tuning their ethical instincts.
- ch. 39 "23. Like Boxing Gloves of Sadness" **·** Immanuel Kant — Authenticity; Humanity as an End in Itself; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Benko argues the show's deepest target is selfishness understood as inauthenticity: an over-investment in a self whose real motivations, Tahani's name-dropping, Chidi's moral filibustering, Jason's Acidcat fiasco, Eleanor's aggressive solitude, are hidden from the person herself. Drawing on Charles Guignon's account of authenticity, he shows that being true to yourself is not enough unless your self-expression enables others to become their authentic selves too, which is why Chidi's keeping of his promises across all 802 reboots is the show's moral core and why treating people as mere means fails on Kantian grounds. Eleanor's final willingness to lose Chidi rather than her better self demonstrates authenticity reoriented toward others, the show's answer to Schur's fourth-car-at-the-left-turn driver.

- ch. 41 "Residents of Neighborhood 12358W" *(notes)*
- ch. 42 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia

- ch. 1 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Authenticity; Feminism — The editors introduce the book by contrasting The Good Wife with earlier law shows like Law and Order: for the first time we see lawyers at home, and the central figure is Alicia Florrick, juggling teenagers, a firm in bankruptcy, and a marriage wrecked by Peter's prostitution scandal while keeping up appearances as the 'good wife' and taking lover Will Gardner. They argue the show refuses a single right answer - her choices are selfish, cowardly, vengeful, or simply her being true to herself - and that her growth as a woman, mother, and lawyer challenges preconceived social norms about women and about lawyers. Philosophy enters as the natural sequel: ethics, justice, feminism, privacy rights, epistemology, and social-political philosophy are all sewn into the episodes.
- ch. 9 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); On Liberty — Judith Andre uses the show's cases - Alicia's overnight prison visit to Peter for case information in 'Conjugal', snatching evidence before the police in 'Hi', Kalinda's inadmissible but coercive evidence in 'Heart', and Will's advice to use perjured testimony in 'Long Way Home' - to ask whether the profession's zealous advocacy actually serves justice. She explains the adversary system's two-level defense (each side's pursuit of victory supposedly forces truth out, mirroring sport) and its weaknesses: money decides outcomes, and no one in the courtroom is responsible for the truth, as the buried Childs tapes in 'Hybristophilia' show. Individual liberty against state power justifies criminal defense at most, and she endorses David Luban's sober conclusion that the system is justified yet 'cannot mandate lawyers to cut throats', with Alicia remaining the show's uneasy, unreconciled conscience.
- ch. 11 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Aquinas, Augustine of Hippo, Cicero — Just War Theory; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Jai Galliott takes the Season Three episode 'Whiskey Tango Foxtrot', in which Nevada-based drone operator Sergeant Elkins kills twelve Afghan civilians and is convicted of murder despite Alicia's scapegoating defense, as a case study in the ethics of drone warfare. Tracing just war theory from the Mahabharata through Augustine to Aquinas's jus ad bellum and jus in bello framework, he applies proportionality and discrimination to the strike and argues that sensor limits and the physical and emotional distance of push-button killing (Grossman's spectrum from knife combat to drones) erode operators' capacity for discriminate targeting. He concludes that drones are a moral hazard but a legitimate asset, and that blame must be apportioned among operator, manufacturer, and commanders rather than dumped on Elkins alone.
- ch. 12 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; Consequentialism — Rod Carveth maps Bentham's act-utilitarianism onto Lockhart Gardner's defense-side reasoning and Mill's rule-utilitarianism onto the prosecution's, then tests the pairing on the firm's recurring client Colin Sweeney. Sweeney's cases - the wrongful-death suit in 'Bad' where Alicia says 'Of course' he killed his wife, the manslaughter plea and merger opportunism in 'Hybristophilia', and the perjured testimony Alicia may still use in 'Long Way Home' - show the firm letting the end of client and firm gain justify the means. Sweeney walking free, restored to his company, and a father despite admitting the murder is the counter-intuitive consequence that makes Carveth question whether act-utilitarianism should ground our decisions at all.
- ch. 13 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Socrates — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Philosophy of Love; Feminism — Celine Morin reads Alicia's love life through the Greek triad agape, eros, and philia as laid out in Plato's Symposium: her unconditional agape for Peter is eroded by his demands for forgiveness ('Stripped', 'Boom'), while the Socratic myth of Eros born from Penia's lack explains why she tells Will their affair is 'romantic because it didn't happen'. She argues Alicia abandons the romantic soul-mate model of her pearl-necklace marriage for Giddens's egalitarian 'pure relationship' with Will, but stays moored to the old family structure, hesitating on the doorstep in the Season Three cliffhanger 'The Dream Time'. Her discovery of feminism through Diane Lockhart is what lets Alicia weigh leaving that structure without destroying her family.
- ch. 15 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Carol Gilligan, Immanuel Kant, Nel Noddings — The Ethics of Care; The Categorical Imperative; Caring as the Ground of Ethics — Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.
- ch. 16 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Mark D. White uses the show's bench - umpire-like Judge Park, the 'cleanse'-addled judge of 'Double Jeopardy', Judge Lessner's 'in my opinion' ritual, liberal Judge Abernathy, and Judge Baxter's sentencing kickbacks in 'Lifeguard' - to ask how far judicial bias infects rulings. He walks through legal formalism's chess-like model, legal realism (Holmes's law as 'prophecies of what the courts will do in fact', Will's lesson to Ms. Cabrini in 'Mock'), Hart's open texture of law, and Dworkin's principles-and-integrity theory, on which Abernathy and Lessner facing the same case would each reach their own 'right answer'. The upshot: judges cannot be neutral umpires, so winning lawyers like Will predict the judge, not just the law.
- ch. 18 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Blaise Pascal — The Categorical Imperative; Pascal's Wager — Lisa McNulty asks what could oblige us to believe someone: Peter's lying fails Kant's Categorical Imperative (a world of universal liars makes lying impossible), while friendship explains Alicia's readiness to believe client Kenny Chatham even before the evidence does. The 'Death Zone' libel trial over an Everest death shows that one's position of power fixes whom one owes presumptive belief - a reader should side with Cardiff, a judge must presume Lambrose innocent - and Pascal's Wager supplies the method of 'behaving like a believer': withholding rumors, withholding conviction, and Alicia publicly playing the wife and sleeping with Peter in a bid to believe in her marriage again. She concludes Peter forfeited any right to be believed, so Alicia has no moral obligation to behave like a good wife.
- ch. 19 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Deontology — James Edwin Mahon sorts the show's plots by the gap between deed and motive: Patti Nyholm helps save Marjorie Garnett's liver in 'In Sickness' purely to leverage her firm, Lockhart Gardner sues Chumhum in 'Great Firewall' for the mercenary reason Alicia laments, and the Demorys bribe a juror in 'Fixed' out of altruism. Working through Mill's exchange with Llewellyn Davies and Kant's shopkeeper, he argues motives can be good or bad but never right or wrong, and that no good motive makes a wrong action right - Kant denied even a philanthropic right to lie. Hence Alicia's persuading Shen Yuan to lie about his torture, however compassionate, was wrong.
- ch. 20 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Plato — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Skyler King and Robert Arp catalogue the excuses cheating men offer - 'my wife let herself go', 'so much eye candy', 'a moment of weakness' - and add evolutionary psychology's parental investment theory to explain why Peter Florrick-types stray while women like Alicia cheat less. The centerpiece is Glaucon's Ring of Gyges story from Book II of Plato's Republic: politicians such as Peter, Bill Clinton, and Eliot Spitzer wear the invisibility ring of power and come to think moral rules no longer bind them. The chapter closes with prudential and moral reasons against infidelity - scorned spouses, broken promises, wounded children - capped by Eli Gold fielding questions about a Brazil-shaped birthmark in 'Anatomy of a Joke'.
- ch. 22 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Roger Hunt treats Louis Canning, Peter Florrick, and Colin Sweeney as psychiatric cases read through Freud's later drive theory, in which a life drive (Eros) and a death drive (Thanatos) fuse in varying proportions. Sweeney is the purest death-driven type, deriving low-grade sadistic pleasure while feigning personhood to escape punishment; Peter's paranoia assembles a protective barrier of handlers (Eli, Jackie, Alicia, the DNC); Canning may convert self-attack into the very tardive dyskinesia symptoms he weaponizes before juries. The chapter's claim is that the show's evil is not absolute lawlessness but pathology seen from the other characters' perspective, and that the death drive accounts for much of the wickedness on screen.
- ch. 23 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Jennifer Swanson asks whether Alicia can 'have it all', starting from Aristotle: Peter fails the moral virtues (faithfulness, honesty, courage), Jackie's intrusive moments undermine her kindness since Aristotle's unity of the virtues ties them together, and Eli Gold's perfect frankness leaves no room for perfect tact. Following Michael Slote's partial values and impossibility of perfection, she argues career and family are paired values in which gaining one loses the other, as Alicia discovers being pulled between Molly the nanny, Cary's 'she'll have something to fall back on', Diane's partner-track warning, and dumping Will after Grace's twelve butt-dials in 'Parenting Made Easy'. Since perfection is impossible in principle, the answer is balance across all the values of a good life, not Caitlin's retreat into 'I just want to be a mom'.
- ch. 25 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Betty Friedan — The Feminine Mystique (the problem with no name); Feminism — Karen Adkins argues the show exposes the 'choice' to stay home as neither free nor innocent: Betty Friedan's Feminine Mystique and Linda Hirshman's Get to Work frame how Alicia's more-promising-than-Will-or-Peter career was sacrificed to Peter's ambitions and now constrains her, while Peter's 'thanks for playing the breadwinner', Cary's condescension in 'Fleas', and Jackie's 'we stay in the shadows' speech treat her work as a hobby. The show's feminism goes bland, she contends, when Alicia declines to fight Caitlin's resignation in 'Long Way Home' and endorses choice feminism against her own history. The chapter's evidence runs both ways, though: the 'We're not the cops, honey' double standard, and Alicia's mom skills and lawyer skills flowing productively between nursery and deposition room.
- ch. 26 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — John Fitzpatrick asks whether voters should care that Alicia stands beside Peter, from the Season One resignation press conference to the finale's withheld hand. After a rapid tour of right-action theories grounded in the show - Eli Gold's egoism, Peter's 'pitted' evidence tip as consequentialism, Alicia keeping Jonas Stern's dementia secret as deontology, the Florrick-Childs no-children pact as social contract - he turns to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia as a life weaving pleasure, friendship, and practical activity, in which mentors like Will and Diane let us contemplate virtue in others and improve our own character. His conclusion: Alicia's endorsement matters not because she is a good wife but because she is a good person whose judgment reveals Peter's character.
- ch. 28 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Justice in the Republic; Virtue Ethics (arete); Ethical Egoism — The Azevedos read Plato's Republic Book I as a manual for professionalism: Socrates argues the practitioner - doctor, ruler, lawyer - serves the patient, citizen, and client rather than himself, while Thrasymachus's cynicism that injustice pays and people only seem just is embodied by Eli Gold ('I lie for a living') and by stunt lawyers Nancy Crozier, Patti Nyholm, Louis Canning, and the secretive Jonas Stern. Alicia answers with Aristotle's virtue ethics: professionalism as a cluster virtue cultivated through habituated action, hitting the mean and doing the right thing at the right time for the right reasons. Saint Alicia shows how costly being good all the time is, yet the chapter sides with her striving for virtue over Thrasymachus's goldbrick glory.
- ch. 29 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Feminism — Offered as a salute to The Good Wife's female lawyers (Alicia, Diane, Caitlin, Geneva Pine, Dana Lodge, Elsbeth Tascioni), this piece collects good, bad, and memorable real women attorneys: pioneers Bettisia Gozzadini, Arabella Mansfield, Myra Bradwell - barred by Justice Bradley's 'wife and mother' dictum in Bradwell v. Illinois - and Charlotte E. Ray; notorious figures like accused murderer Mary Leonard; and trailblazers Gloria Allred, Sandra Day O'Connor, Constance Baker Motley, and Ruth Bader Ginsburg. The parade of firsts grounds the show's fictional women in the real feminist struggle to enter and practice the legal profession.
- ch. 30 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" **·** Protagoras, Jeremy Bentham, Cicero, Plutarch, Averroes (Ibn Rushd), Francis Bacon, René Descartes, Gottfried Leibniz — This companion piece profiles philosophers who actually practiced law or rhetoric: the sophists Thrasymachus and Protagoras (whose 'man is the measure' relativism was rhetoric for hire and whom Plato and Aristotle despised), Demosthenes, Cicero - called 'the closest thing to a Philosopher King any society has ever seen' - Plutarch with his virtue-and-vice maxims, Cordoba's jurist Averroes, legal-team veteran Francis Bacon, natural-law theorist of war Hugo Grotius, law-degree holders Descartes and Leibniz, Montesquieu of the separation of powers, Bentham (panopticon architect whose utilitarianism lets ends justify means like waterboarding), and legal positivists Hart and Dworkin. Its running joke is that the lawyer-sophist connection is as old as philosophy itself, which is precisely the stereotype The Good Wife plays against.
- ch. 31 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — The book's comic interlude: eleven numbered lawyer jokes, from the vacuum-cleaner dirt bag and the drowning lawyer thrown his partners to 'God doesn't think he's a lawyer' and the closer that 'only three lawyer jokes exist; the rest are true stories'. The list spikes the same lawyers-are-scoundrels stereotype that Judith Andre's opening chapter analyzed seriously and that the editors' introduction answered with Dick the Butcher's 'first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers'.
- ch. 32 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Grateful Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Foreword" **·** Zen Buddhism — Steve Silberman's foreword frames Dead shows as 'half baseball game and half church' — a space of collective permission where fans could dance, weep, or trip while taking stock of their lives. He argues the band's philosophical import lies less in doctrine than in the total experience: Robert Hunter's allusive lyrics (shaped by Joyce and Eliot), Garcia's improvising that made each show a story within stories, and the band's very name, which lands you in the middle of what Zen teachers call the Great Matter, life and death, with a grinning skeleton as your guide. He closes by likening thirty years of Dead tours to Kerouac's 'floating zendo' from The Dharma Bums — a movable refuge where any Bodhisattva could find a spot among friends.
- ch. 6 "Saying Thank You for a Real Good Time" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Some Folks Trust to Reason" *(no index entry yet)* — Editor Steven Gimbel's introduction argues that whenever norms are challenged there is philosophy to be done, and the Dead challenged norms everywhere: as house band for the Acid Tests they probed the nature of mind, musically they broke the three-and-a-half-minute song template and genre walls, and as an organization they let fans tape shows and sold their own tickets. He maps how the book's essays apply different traditions to the band — Buddhist and Taoist lyrics, analytic logic applied to the storyteller's choice in 'Lady with a Fan', the justice of the narrator's murder in 'Me and My Uncle', continental thought on Deadhead community and gratitude for death, and American philosophy reading 'Eyes of the World' and the band's Beat roots. Philosophy, he insists, does not end discussion but advances insight — 'some of the time you do see the light in the strangest of places if you look at it right.'
- ch. 8 "In the Parking Lot—Fireworks, Calliopes, and Clowns - The Culture of the Dead" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Need that Cash to Feed that Jones" **·** Adam Smith, Karl Marx — The Invisible Hand; Alienation; Social Darwinism — Steven Gimbel and Brendan Cushing-Daniels argue that the Dead's parking-lot economy — tie-dye shirts priced at ten, twelve, or fifteen dollars, veggie burritos, dueling bootlegs — realized Adam Smith's classical picture of capitalism, not the corporate capitalism Marx attacked. They trace Smith's Newtonian invisible hand and market equilibrium, his ethics of sympathy tempering self-interest, then the Social Darwinist twist given Smith under industrialization and Marx's four types of alienation under postwar white-collar work that pushed hippies to drop out. The punchline: deadhead sellers were not alienated — making shirts was creative self-expression — and buyer-seller sympathy ('it was simply uncool to screw over a fellow deadhead') made the lot a sustainable, kinder 'caring capitalism' that kept the scene alive.
- ch. 10 "The Gathering of the Tribe Ironic Sacramentalism" **·** John Stuart Mill, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, John Rawls — Anarchism; On Liberty; The Harm Principle; The Social Contract — Horace Fairlamb argues the Grateful Dead were the Sixties' real revolutionary success: where the New Left failed by keeping confrontational politics, the Dead changed consciousness first, extending Mill's liberal 'experiments in living' into a whole alternative culture. He reads the total improvisation learned at the Acid Tests ('the form that follows chaos'), the band's leaderless 'functional anarchy' — Lesh: if anyone tried to take charge 'it would just dissolve in their hands' — and its flat business hierarchy with roadies as corporate presidents as a spontaneous order lived at the edge of chaos. The Deadhead community's ritual communitas, analyzed through Victor Turner's separation-liminality-reincorporation model, amounts to an 'ironic sacramentalism' that achieves what social contract from Hobbes (force), Locke (property), and Rawls (self-interest) cannot: unity that transcends difference while leaving it in place.
- ch. 11 "Forgetting the Love We Bring" **·** Herbert Marcuse, Martin Heidegger, Ludwig Wittgenstein — One-Dimensional Man; Language Games — John Drabinski argues that the Deadhead parking lot is an 'occasional community' offering real hope against modernity's managed, one-dimensional life. Starting from his own Amherst-to-Worcester commuter routine read through Wittgenstein's forms of life — a community of nodding strangers at the same mini-marts — he stages Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Bauman's managed death as the deadening background against which such moments crack open. Where the commuter's community stays merely occasional, the parking lot's saturated friendship and shared undergoing (com-passion, good trip and bad, frat guy comforting and comforted) converts occasion into a genuine alternative ethos, drawing on Heidegger's sense of ethos as dwelling place — an everyday miracle of conversion he says we need now more than ever.
- ch. 12 "A Solution Dissolving Special Status" **·** Labor Theory of Property — Peter Bradley uses the Dead's taping ethos and the 2005 Archive.org shutdown to argue copyright wrongly grants authors special status. Distinguishing natural from conventional morality (the four-year-old who knows hitting Jenny stays wrong even if the teacher allows it), he contends that respect for irreducibly unique creative expression — not authorial intent, and not Bob Weir's appeal to the covered songwriters' rights — grounds the tapers' moral code, since Olivier could not copyright his double-cast Hamlet ghost and Woody Guthrie welcomed copyists. Ownership means control, from one's own labor outward; but a performance, like another person, is metaphysically impossible to control, and in the digital world (per Barlow) recordings escape physical control entirely — so authorship should be dissolved into improvisational performance, with published works treated like live recordings rather than rigid canonical objects.
- ch. 13 "Soundcheck - Describing a Band Beyond Description" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "The Music Never Stopped" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Apollonian and the Dionysian — David MacGregor Johnston reads the Grateful Dead through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy: the Acid Tests and Dead shows revived the Dionysia, with LSD-fueled crowd ecstasy playing the Dionysian chorus and the concert's structure, set lists, and amphitheater-like outdoor venues supplying the Apollonian form Nietzsche required for the highest art. Leary's Psychedelic Experience — built on the Tibetan Book of the Dead as an Apollonian guide to the trip — parallels the band's dictionary-derived name, 'a song meant to show a lost soul to the other side'. Following Nietzsche's story of Euripides and Socratic rationalism destroying tragic music, he argues the Dead restored music's power to carry listeners (even sober Wharf Rats) beyond language into dispossession and the primordial unity of existence.
- ch. 15 "Tough and Tender, The Dead Keep Truckin’" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, William James, Aristotle, Cornel West — Self-Reliance; The Will to Believe; Eudaimonia (flourishing); Pragmatism — Gary Ciocco traces a line from Emerson and James through Kerouac, Ginsberg, and Neal Cassady to the Grateful Dead: Emerson's nonconformist 'infinitude of man' and James's 'live options' and religious appetite for being 'more fully alive' become, in the Beats, the project of living life itself as art ('the only people for me are the mad ones'). He argues the Beats splintered because each chased an atomistic, individual epiphany — Kerouac swinging wholesale from tender- to tough-minded temperament — while the Dead turned the same Jamesian hunger into a shared communal religious experience, a 'kindler, gentler' scene that better achieves Aristotle's eudaimonia. Cassady, muse of On the Road and driver of the Pranksters' bus, literally connects the two movements, but the Dead's unity-in-diversity made them the evolution, not the echo, of the Beats.
- ch. 16 "High Art and Definition" *(no index entry yet)* — Michael Gettings argues that on Tolstoy's definition of art in 'What Is Art?' — the communication of sincerely lived feeling that 'infects' audiences and unites them in joy and spiritual union — the Grateful Dead rank among the greatest art of the last century. Collective, improvisatory Dead performances (the band found songs by experimenting until 'the music played the band') meet the sincerity condition that mass-produced TV, film, and pop fail, and the grief of American Beauty, traceable to Garcia's mother's death, shows real feeling handed on to listeners. Tolstoy's prescriptive (not merely descriptive) definition even condemns Beethoven's Ninth as bad artificial art while 'Dark Star' succeeds — so a theory ranking the Dead above the high-art canon is a feature, not a reductio.
- ch. 17 "Was Jerry Garcia the Soul of the Grateful Dead" **·** Aristotle, John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — John Uglietta asks what made the Grateful Dead the Grateful Dead when they swapped five keyboardists yet stopped being themselves the moment Jerry Garcia died, prompting the rename to The Dead. Testing Aristotle's essential versus accidental properties, Peter French's structural account of group identity (the Yankees, the Glenn Miller Orchestra), same-stuff theories via a VW bus rebuilt piece by piece from its old parts — a Ship of Theseus puzzle — and Locke's memory theory applied to Phil Lesh's liver (but feared brain) transplant, he proposes that the band's essence was a group spirit born of members 'surrendering their own little trip'. The soul of the Dead was bigger than Jerry but smaller than the whole band, and its loss at his death was something the survivors could recognize but not replace.
- ch. 18 "Set One—Who’s to Guide You - Ethical Questions in the Lyrics of the Grateful Dead" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Encore" **·** The Buddha, Immanuel Kant, Socrates, David Hume — Immortality and the Soul; The Four Noble Truths; The Problem of Evil; The Categorical Imperative — Randall Auxier adopts 'I trust Phil' — Phil Lesh the bass player who hears the whole sound — as his epistemic principle for asking whether death is to be dreaded, staging the essay around interview riffs with Deadheads Dale, Robbie, and Cory. Socrates in the Phaedo and the Buddha's Four Noble Truths converge on welcoming death — samsara is the 'Samsonite Scenario', bad luggage your own wishing keeps repacking — while Hume's Dialogues make God's power, goodness, and evil an inconsistent triad, so immortality is 'not that cool'. Kant's postulates (God, freedom, immortality) and categorical imperative prove too rule-bound for creative life; Whitehead's self-creativity and 'objective immortality of the past' supply the real bass line: even God cannot unmake what you have played, and the properly Grateful response is gratitude for the chance to add your riff to the Acid Test.
- ch. 20 "Once I Was the Student, Now I Am the Master" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Socrates — The State of Nature; Justice in the Republic; Ethical Egoism — Johannes Bulhof reads 'Me and My Uncle' — the Dead's most-performed song, though hardly a fan favorite — as a parable against rational self-interest. The nephew learned everything from his uncle: how to cheat at cards, steal, and shoot first, so he rationally guns down the cowboys, takes the gold, and leaves his uncle's 'dead ass there by the side of the road' — the student out-mastering the teacher. Framing the song with Thrasymachus's Republic I claim that the unjust always profit (and his own students' admission they would cheat if they could get away with it), then with Hobbes's state of nature where equality, contested goods, and anticipatory striking make everyone enemies — even family — Bulhof argues the song's drunken lesson is that rational self-interest is communally irrational.
- ch. 21 "Analyzing Emptiness" **·** The Buddha, Nagarjuna — Emptiness (sunyata); Non-Self (anatman); The Four Noble Truths; Impermanence (anicca) — Paul Gass reads the Dead's hippie milieu (the Beats, the Acid Tests, Buddhist-monk lyricist Peter Monk) as a conduit for Buddhist doctrine, taking the 'Eyes of the World' chorus as an invitation to awaken to Buddha-nature. He explains the Four Noble Truths, karma, and the five aggregates to argue the self is an illusion, using the image of a flame passed between lighters at a Dead show to picture rebirth without a persisting soul. The chapter then presents Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka middle way — emptiness itself must not be clutched as an absolute truth — and reads the 'redeemer... wagon loaded with clay' verse of 'Eyes of the World' as the Mahayana bodhisattva liberating all beings, with emptiness finally discarded like the boat after crossing the river.
- ch. 22 "I’ve Got Time to Hear His Story" **·** Emmanuel Levinas — The Face of the Other — Stephen Stern reads the 'Wharf Rat' narrator's decision to give August West not a dime but time to hear his story as an enactment of Levinas's ethics: hearing the other's call ipso facto obligates us, and listening restores the face that the label 'wharf rat' stripped away, just as Levinas was stripped of his 'human skin' as vermin in a Nazi POW camp. He parallels West's hope that the absent Pearly Baker 'been true to me' with Levinas's hope in his absent wife and daughter, locating traces of God not in a friendly maker but in human commitment and responsibility for the other. The chapter closes on the narrator walking downtown to his own Bonny Lee, suggesting that responding to August West liberates both parties from isolation.
- ch. 23 "Santayana, the Grateful Dead, and Self-Knowledge" *(no index entry yet)* — Jessica Wahman argues that 'Eyes of the World' restates George Santayana's ontology: the chorus's 'you are the eyes of the world, but the heart has its beaches' captures Santayana's distinction between consciousness (spirit) and the organism's blind, material psyche. She reads the second verse's redeemer fading away with his clay and the seeds bursting into bloom and decay as Santayana's acceptance of natural cycles and mortality — life as a carnival to be danced rather than escaped. The chapter treats the Dead show itself, from Drums and Space to the parking lot, as Santayana's 'spiritual life': a holiday of the mind in which spirit contemplates the play of essences, ending with the self-knowledge the author gained by comparing the two.
- ch. 24 "Set Two—What Shall We Say Shall We Call It by a Name - The Nature of Nature" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Dizzy with the Possibilities" **·** Henry David Thoreau — Deep Ecology; Climate Ethics; Wilderness and Nature Aesthetics — Allen Thompson treats 'Throwing Stones' — 'the future's here, we are it, we are on our own' — as voicing the existential dread of anthropogenic global warming and the felt 'end of nature' Bill McKibben named, defending the song as the band's a-political polemic against heartless powers. He argues via Steven Vogel that humans cannot literally end nature unless we are supernatural, and recasts the crisis with Thoreau and Gary Snyder as civilization's assault on the wild, the self-willed order we too belong to. Deep ecology then supplies the response: re-identify the self as wild — as Deadheads do by dancing wildly to the music — and build a civilization wildness can endure, with the band's 1988 rainforest-benefit press conference as evidence of the Dead's own ecological consciousness.
- ch. 26 "“Just Like Mary Shelley, Just Like Frankenstein”" **·** Aristotle, Plato — Free Will vs Determinism; Compatibilism; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Chuck Ward uses 'Mama Tried' (the meek family's rebel son doing life without parole) and the mysterious birthmark in 'Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodleloo' to ask whether character is fixed from birth, setting the songs' fatalism against Aristotle's account of character as habituated choice and Plato's claim that traits tend to be inherited. He surveys behavioral genetics, twin studies, The Bell Curve, and the supposed 'criminality gene' before arguing that genetic determinism is a mistaken reductionism: like the groovy atmosphere of a Dead show, which shapes the very individuals who produce it, complex systems admit top-down causation, so genes never act alone. The chapter's payoff is that the songs' studied ambiguity — mama tried, yet 'that leaves no one but me to blame' — shows art expressing, rather than resolving, the tension between free will and determinism.
- ch. 27 "So There’s No Accounting for Taste" **·** J.L. Mackie, David Hume — Moral Relativism — Mary MacLeod stages her quarrel with her husband over the musical value of the Dead's Space jams as a problem in metaethics: she claims Space objectively lacks merit, Eric claims it has value, and the chapter asks whether either 'should' claim can be true. She lays out Value Realism (value as intrinsic, detectable properties), Subjectivism ('no accounting for taste'), Mackie's Humean error theory (we project feelings onto the world as we do with color), and the 'oughts by agreement' view that expert or social consensus makes things right the way traffic conventions make right-side driving correct. The Dahmer and torture cases show why subjectivism fails for ethics, and the chapter concludes that 'beauty by agreement' quietly collapses back into Realism — so Deadheads' fierce debates about Space are legitimate disagreements after all.
- ch. 28 "The Storyteller Makes No Choice" **·** Blaise Pascal — Stephen Dillingham takes at face value the storyteller's challenge in the Terrapin Station parable 'Lady with a Fan,' where a lady throws her fan into the lion's den and demands a sailor and a soldier risk 'uncertain pains of hell' to win her. Using decision theory rooted in Pascal and Fermat's probability and the subjectivist (Bayesian) reading of probability as degree of belief, he runs five expected-value cases in 'roses,' varying the soldier's and sailor's estimates of success and the values of winning the lady, being eaten, or refusing. The upshot is that 'you decide if he was wise' is a genuine question: the soldier's refusal and the sailor's dare can each be rational or foolhardy depending on probabilities and utilities no listener can observe.
- ch. 29 "Encore—Mysteries Dark and Vast - Metaphysical Quandaries" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "Sometimes We Live No Particular Way but Our Own" **·** Epictetus, Baruch Spinoza, Zhuangzi — The Dichotomy of Control; Wu Wei (effortless action); Substance Monism (Deus sive Natura); Compatibilism — Matthew Turner argues that a 'Playin' in the Band' jam — the band drifting from the tune into long collective improvisation and back — models a Stoic solution to free will shared by Epictetus, Spinoza, and Chuang Tzu: freedom is not uncaused choosing but responding well within constraints, so by the dichotomy of control there is no point resenting the band when it flubs a climax. Spinoza's definition of the free thing as one determined by its own nature, and Chuang Tzu's butcher who cuts oxen by spirit beyond skill, show the band letting the music 'play them' — Jerry's 'Tennessee Jed' riff never played the same way twice — as learned skill becomes second nature.
