Because the Dead jam within banks (keys, mutual listening, ability) yet generate something genuinely new and transcended every genre of 1960s music where the Monkees merely copied the Beatles, the Stoic attitude proves creative rather than quietist, an analogue for living freely within our own constraints.
- ch. 31 "I’ll Get Up and Fly Away" **·** Martin Heidegger, Epicurus, Socrates — Death Is Nothing to Us; Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Immortality and the Soul — Ian Duckles and Eric Rubenstein use the community's losses of Pigpen and Jerry Garcia to ask whether death is bad, running Epicurus's argument that being dead is no experience and hence no harm, the tedium-of-immortality argument that eternal life would eventually exhaust every fundamental desire, and Socrates's Phaedo claim that death frees the soul to philosophize — which disturbingly implies Pigpen's early 'burn out' was the better fate. Their resolution is Heidegger: authentically confronting death as the end of all possibilities strips socially imposed values (consumerist 'keeping up with the Joneses') and frees us to create our own projects, so mortality itself is something to be grateful for. On this reading the Deadhead counterculture — rejecting 1950s suburban scripts for free love, psychedelics, and life on tour — lived Heideggerian authenticity, and it is better to fade away (like Garcia) than to burn out (like Pigpen).
- ch. 32 "Goin’ Down the Road The Grateful Dead Discography" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "Playin’ in the Band" *(notes)*
- ch. 34 "The ABCs We All Must Face" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "The Grateful Dead and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "ALSO FROM OPEN COURT" *(notes)*
- ch. 37 "The Grateful Dead and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 38 "Copyright Page" *(front)*

## The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Handmaid’s Tale and Philosophy A Womb of One’s Own" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Handmaid’s Tale and Philosophy A Womb of One’s Own" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Dedication" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Thanks" *(notes)*
- ch. 9 "Resisting Dystopia" **·** Utopia and Dystopia; Objectification; Feminism — The editor's introduction argues that The Handmaid's Tale disturbs us because it shows how tenuous our civil liberties are, so we must actively watch political events for warning signs. It insists that a woman's value is not fixed by her body, fertility, or attractiveness—Handmaids are treated as incubators and commodities—and that the caring work women do is a power, not a weakness. It closes on the lesson that facts, not politicians, control the narrative, ending with 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum.'
- ch. 10 "Part I But They Were Godless" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "1. A Great Darkness Filled with Echoes" **·** Utopia and Dystopia; Totalitarianism; Feminism — De Vaul argues Gilead terrifies because social cycle theory structures it: every detail, from the Puritan wedding-night sheet to Stalin-style purges and the Nazi and residential-school seizure of children, already happened, so Gilead reads as speculative rather than science fiction. Atwood's three stated influences—Puritan New England, the 1980s religious right, and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four—show history cycling back, with June as the apolitical 'backlash' daughter her second-wave mother Holly and the activist Moira both predicted. The pattern repeats at small scale (June relives the former Offred's Scrabble-and-affair story, Omar's family suffers June's own fate) and in the Historical Notes, where Pieixoto strips Offred of authorship, proving 'the past is a great darkness, filled with echoes.'
- ch. 12 "2. Dystopia from a Woman’s Point of View" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Søren Kierkegaard, Simone de Beauvoir, Aristotle, Karl Marx — Utopia and Dystopia; The Leap of Faith — Robison-Greene reads The Handmaid's Tale as Atwood's answer to Nineteen Eighty-Four—a dystopia 'from the female point of view'—comparing how both regimes suppress critical thought by banning women's reading, rewriting texts (the Marx slogan 'from each according to her ability' passed off as St. Paul), and manufacturing perpetual war. She deploys Nietzsche's 'monumental' abuse of history, Kierkegaard's leap of faith (Offred's three contradictory versions of Luke's fate), and doublethink to show that believing contradictions becomes both the regime's tool and the victim's survival strategy. The woman's lens adds that reducing women to reproductive function (Marthas, Aunts, Jezebels) thrives where thinking is suppressed, that Beauvoir's point about women's complicity in their oppression is embodied by the Aunts, and that Offred and Nick's affair, like Winston and Julia's, is the act of freedom the Party can never quite own.
- ch. 13 "3. Gestational Totalitarianism" **·** Hannah Arendt, Aristotle, Plato, Karl Marx — Totalitarianism; Feminism; Allegory of the Cave — Kolb reads Gilead through Arendt's The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism: when reproduction becomes the means of production, women's labor is targeted, forcing fertile women into Animal laborans status as 'national resources' while denying them the creative freedom of Homo faber. She traces the polis/oikos split from Aristotle through Puritan capitalism to show Gilead overcorrecting into Aunt Lydia's 'freedom from'—totalitarian control of birth legitimized by the Rachel and Bilhah story and a Pauline creation story. The chapter ends with the transitional generation's forgetting (Offred's cave-delusion with Nick evoking Plato's Allegory of the Cave, the Holocaust documentarian 'thinking about how not to think') and Ofglen's bomb, arguing that thoughtfulness and literacy, not violence, are the only hopes against totalitarianism.
- ch. 14 "4. The United States of Gilead" **·** Totalitarianism; Feminism; Utopia and Dystopia — Greene argues that the contemporary United States under Trump exhibits early Gilead-like symptoms, detailing five shared techniques: othering (the Aunts' stereotypes of pre-Gilead women vs. Trump on Mexicans and Muslims), separating children from parents (Handmaid births and seizure of Hannah vs. immigrant detention camps), gaslighting (Janine's 'her fault' Testifying vs. inauguration-crowd and Mueller claims), discrediting dissent (Gilead's ban on reading vs. 'fake news'), and lying (Gilead's founding promise of elections vs. thousands of false claims and 'alternative facts'). He grounds the danger in the correspondence theory of truth: once leaders detach belief from how the world actually is, society is a small step from Atwood's dystopia.
- ch. 15 "Part II Faith Is Only a Word, Embroidered" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "5. Inside Gilead’s Misogynist Parlors" **·** Richard Rorty, Friedrich Nietzsche, Sigmund Freud, Albert Camus — Just War Theory; Moral Relativism; Utopia and Dystopia — Hirschbein unravels the Genesis story of Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar as the script Gilead rereads to rationalize its 'misogynist parlors,' arguing that Gilead's exegesis is propaganda rather than scholarship—cherry-picking scripture that Nietzsche joked would appall the actual Jesus. He then spins the reader's moral compass: with Rorty's ironist he asks whether anyone initiated into Abraham's tribe or raised in Gilead can be blamed—are even Hitler and Commander Waterford products of their time?—and weighs Ofglen's suicide bombing of the Rachel and Leah Center against just war criteria of proportion, innocence, and chance of success. Finally, with Freud and Niebuhr, he suggests the Sons of Jacob built their surveillance state on a depraved view of human nature, so utopian schemes—Gilead included—are doomed from the founding.
- ch. 17 "6. Serena Joy, Miserable, Despicable" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Aristotle, Boethius — Bad Faith; The Ethics of Ambiguity; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Elsby refuses to see Serena Joy as a self-determined villain, arguing she annihilates her own freedom—negating her humanity in Beauvoir's sense—to become an empty vessel for Gilead's will. Working through Aristotle on coerced and 'mixed' actions and the bad-upbringing excuse, Sartre on freedom and responsibility in Being and Nothingness, and Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity, she asks how much blame an oppressed woman deserves who nonetheless helped build her own subjugation and holds June down during the Ceremony. The answer runs through bad faith: Serena deceives herself until raping June is no longer a necessary wrong but a good in itself, and the 'unwomen' logic echoes Boethius's claim that evildoers cease to be human—comprehensible, but still abhorrent.
- ch. 18 "7. Remix in Gilead" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Gilles Deleuze, Karl Marx — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Walker frames Gilead as a remix: the Sons of Jacob sample scripture under restrictive rules (the Bilhah Ceremony, the doctored Beatitudes, Marx's slogan misattributed to St. Paul), like Danger Mouse's Grey Album, while Offred herself remixes the Lord's Prayer and 'Amazing Grace.' Using Pieixoto's line that Gilead's 'genius was synthesis,' he argues via Baudrillard that no original Christianity exists against which to judge Gilead—we live among simulacra, so Gilead is 'presented as unique in order to hide that it is Christianity'—and via Deleuze that Pieixoto and Wade's assembly of Offred's cassettes is a new original rather than a degraded copy. The payoff is that the question of authenticity is misguided, and gradual, unnoticed change is what lets regimes like Gilead assemble themselves.
- ch. 19 "8. From the Handmaid’s Tale to the Handmaids’ Tale" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The Problem of Evil; The General Will; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society — McCrossin reads Offred's silent prayers ('I want to know what I did to deserve this') as channeling the Book of Job, using Susan Neiman's distinction between the theological and secular problem of evil: even if we stop demanding explanations from God, we must still make evil intelligible, as Janine's Testifying cruelly refuses to do. He sets Rousseau against Voltaire on whether morality requires making evil intelligible, finding June Rousseauian for piecing together Gilead's hidden prehistory at the Boston Globe and for acting from compassion, as with the bread-truck driver's secret Quran. The Salvaging refusal—Ofglen first, then Offred, then sixty-five stones dropped with 'I'm sorry, Aunt Lydia'—shows compassion becoming solidarity and solidarity becoming a general will, transforming The Handmaid's Tale into The Handmaids' Tale.
- ch. 20 "Part III Dying of Too Much Choice" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "9. A Rose by Any Other Brand" **·** Heraclitus, Aristotle, Socrates, Plato — Everything Flows / Logos; The Four Causes; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Callis treats Gilead's rise as a marketing campaign, reading it through Thom Braun's philosophy of branding built on Heraclitus (brands as false stability amid flux, the 'hidden connection' of the 'Balm in Gilead' hymn), Socratic questioning that Gilead forbids its citizens, Plato's brand-as-becoming, and Aristotle's four causes (the Sons of Jacob as efficient cause, the subjugation of women as the brand's function). She argues the brand was doomed because its core premise—that women exist to breed—is false, so Waterford's quip that love is 'lust with a good marketing campaign' foreshadows its Shakespearean collapse. The resistance works the other way: handmaids reclaiming their real names ('My name is June—and I will survive') is what breaks the brand.
- ch. 22 "10. Babies and Pleasures" **·** Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — The Panopticon (surveillance); Discipline and Docile Bodies; Power/Knowledge — Wesch uses Foucault's Discipline and Punish to explain how ordinary women so quickly served Gilead: power is exercised rather than possessed, so Offred enjoying the Guardians' frustration, the 'Her fault!' Testifying, and the Particicution show everyone wielding whatever power is within reach. Gilead is a panopticon in Bentham's sense—the Eyes, paired shopping, 'Under His Eye'—where unverifiable surveillance makes citizens their own overseers, while biopower sorts desirable from undesirable populations, 'making live' fertile Handmaids (shatterproof glass against suicide) and letting Unwomen and unbabies die in the Colonies. Resistance is Foucauldian too: Offred's remembered food, Moira's bathroom gossip, and sex with Nick are the 'bodies and pleasures' that counterattack the deployment of sexuality.
- ch. 23 "11. What about the Men" **·** Feminism; Epistemic Injustice — Jones argues that Nick is coerced as surely as June—ordered by Serena, married off to Eden, unable to refuse without Gilead's punishments—so calling his unwilling sex rape should be uncontroversial. Yet he then argues the 'what about the men?' question itself is inappropriate: because politics and film are male-dominated (19 percent women in Congress, 4.1 percent of top films directed by women), women's lived experience rarely gets center stage, and male readers instinctively bend such rare texts back toward themselves. Pieixoto's flirty, fact-obsessed keynote is the model of this failure, and the challenge for male viewers is to listen to what the show says about women's experience—including #MeToo-era sexual violence—without making it about men.
- ch. 24 "12. Gilead as Palimpsest" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Jacques Derrida, W.E.B. Du Bois — Deconstruction; The Face of the Other; Double Consciousness — Ketcham likens Offred's existence to holocaust by degree: her name is overwritten as the Nazis tattooed forearms, and her past survives like ink bleeding through a palimpsest. Using Derrida's sous rature (via Spivak's introduction and Heidegger's crossed-out words)—the word crossed out yet necessary—he reads her memories as 'under erasure,' and through Levinas's 'useless suffering' shows how her cocooned passivity severs her from the responsibility-for-the-other in which Levinas locates freedom, which is exactly what the he-theonomy needs to rule. With Du Bois's double consciousness and the Hitler parallel, the chapter warns that ideologues promising to cure suffering—Hitler, the Sons of Jacob—only write a new, more oppressive text over the erased old one.
- ch. 25 "Part IV How Easy It Is to Invent a Humanity, for Anyone at All" *(front)*
- ch. 26 "13. Gilead vs. the Self" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle — Humanity as an End in Itself; Respect for Persons; Feminism — Holberg argues that on Kantian grounds Gilead is morally incoherent—Handmaids are treated as mere means, vessels without agency—and that it sustains itself by attacking self-respect through two temporal modes: the quick onset of fear (Aristotle's account in the Rhetoric applied to the machine-gun arrests of women at their jobs) and the slow grind of shame (empty time that turns women into 'objects not in use' and manufactures a veneer of consent: 'nothing is going on here that I haven't signed up for'). Agency needs recognition from others—love as the most basic acknowledgment, or invoking Moira ('Moira would never stand for this shit')—so June's 'I tell, therefore you are' and the reader's duty to affirm her judgment carry the feminist-Kantian point: dependency on others does not negate the self, it is what constitutes it.
- ch. 27 "14. The Value of a Handmaid" **·** Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx — Humanity as an End in Itself; Commodity Fetishism; Moral Relativism — Pérez assesses a Handmaid's value through Kant—Gilead gives women a price, not a dignity, so the Gilead–Mexico trade deal is human trafficking dressed as diplomacy—and through Marx's use value and exchange value, with fertility the commodity and Jezebels carrying both market and affective price. He adds Bourdieu's forms of capital to show Offred's social and resistant cultural capital against Janine's collapse, then weighs cultural relativism (via Renteln and Herodotus) before rejecting it for Gilead: its values were improvised and forced rather than naturally evolved, so the culture itself earns no pass. The Handmaids' refusal to stone Janine shows their collective worth: 'They should've never given us uniforms if they didn't want us to be an army.'
- ch. 28 "15. June the Stoic" **·** Epictetus, Albert Camus, Jeremy Bentham — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; The Ethics of Care — Lequien asks how June might endure Gilead and answers with Epictetus: like the slave-philosopher, she can locate freedom in what is 'up to her'—detaching from her body during the Ceremony ('What he is fucking is the lower part of my body'), relinquishing property, and learning not to call husband or daughter her own. He tests alternatives—Camus's question of suicide (the shatterproof glass), utilitarianism (the coerced 'We are very happy'), Tronto's care ethics (Gilead smothers the sorority that could make care meaningful), and the Particicution as a licensed Two Minutes Hate—before concluding that 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum' functions as June's Stoic mantra: mastery of her own responses is the one victory the Sons of Jacob cannot take.
- ch. 29 "16. Who Is the Meanest of Them All" **·** Hannah Arendt, Immanuel Kant — The Banality of Evil; Totalitarianism; Humanity as an End in Itself — Frunză and Grad apply Arendt's banality of evil to Gilead: the Commander is 'not Iago, not Macbeth' but an Eichmann—sheepish, Scrabble-playing, 'thinking about how not to think'—and no character holds a monopoly on evil because everyone is 'too banal' for demonic profundity. They test his 'just doing my duty' against Kant (duty requires universalizing what reason can will and never treating persons as means, so the Aunts' reeducation camps fail the test) and use The Origins of Totalitarianism to read Handmaids as rightless people whose 'two-legged wombs' status mirrors statelessness. Arendt's web of guilty complicities explains why resistance is scarce, and the chapter ends with banality eroding all criteria for judging—leaving Offred's 'the darkness within; or else the light' as the final choice.
- ch. 30 "Part V I Tell, Therefore You Are" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "17. The Red and the Black" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Aristotle, Walter Benjamin, Theodor Adorno — Language Games — The chapter reads Gilead's color system philosophically: Aristotle's On Colors already treated color as a signifier of something beyond itself, and Goethe's red-as-dignity-and-awakening sits ironically against the Handmaids' sexual servitude, a meaning the show deliberately 'mutilates' and reassigns. Wittgenstein supplies the core apparatus—colors mean by use within a language game—so red signifies sexual servitude only inside Gilead's rigid classificatory system, and when June burns her dress in 'June' red flips to blood and freedom. Walter Benjamin's child's view of color (the subversive blending crushed when a mix gets fixed as a name, like the Wives' teal) and Adorno's claim that radical contemporary art is black close the argument: Gilead's violence is to impose one univocal, authorized meaning on what should stay open to play.
- ch. 32 "18. Smoke and Mirrors in Gilead" **·** Plato, Socrates — Justice in the Republic; Allegory of the Cave; Ring of Gyges (why be moral?) — St. Martin structures Gilead with Plato's Republic: Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger' is the Sons of Jacob's operating principle (the Wall, the cattle prods, 'removing the damaged ones' from the ambassador's reception), and Glaucon's claim that it is best to do injustice without paying the penalty describes Commanders, while Handmaids suffer injustice with no revenge. She maps Socrates's division of labor onto Gilead's color-coded castes (Handmaids, Marthas, Aunts, Wives), then uses Glaucon's mocking 'city of sows' to show Gilead betraying even that model, since the regime exists to keep men powerful rather than babies alive—baby Charlotte recovers only when reunited with Janine. Serena's awakening after Eden's execution is an emergence from the cave, and the chapter closes that justice must be chosen for its own sake, with biases checked.
- ch. 33 "19. How Language Shapes Reality in Gilead" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Guerra and Barkman use Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations—words have no precise boundaries, family resemblance replaces strict definitions, meaning is use—to explain how Gilead engineers reality. Its two maneuvers are coining negations ('unwoman,' 'unbaby') that turn feminists, lesbians, and disabled infants into disposable non-persons, and assigning role-titles ('Commander,' 'Handmaid,' 'Angels') whose inherited connotations slot people into social positions before they can speak. Offred's riff on the word 'chair' (the leader of a meeting, a mode of execution, the French word for flesh) shows she intuits the lesson: because meaning lives in use, whoever controls use controls what counts as real.
- ch. 34 "20. Under a Watchful Eye" **·** Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham — Power/Knowledge; Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Panopticon (surveillance) — Timm gives a full Foucauldian reading: the Sons of Jacob's biblical 'knowledge' is a regime of truth produced by power (via the genealogical method Foucault took from Nietzsche), and Gilead rules less by sovereign violence (particicutions, the Wall) than by disciplinary power that defines, sorts, confines, and retrains—precisely the asylum-prison-school trajectory of Foucault's History of Madness and Discipline and Punish. The Red Center is that institution in miniature (Janine's 'Her fault, her fault'), the black vans with painted Eyes enact Bentham's Panopticon—power 'visible and unverifiable'—and biopower's medicalized control of women's reproductive bodies ties Gilead to Iowa's 2018 fetal heartbeat law. Offred's small refusals—her hidden name, the night that is 'mine,' the act of telling her tale—are the resistance Foucault always found inside disciplinary power.
- ch. 35 "Part VI Gilead in the Rearview Mirror" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "21. A Response to Professor Pieixoto" **·** Aristotle, Simone de Beauvoir — Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Eudaimonia (flourishing); One Is Not Born a Woman; The Golden Mean — Doll writes a fictional keynote by 'Professor Anadicrad' answering Pieixoto's 'our job is not to censure but to understand': the fact that we view the past through an anachronistic lens does not forbid normative judgment, since Aristotle's practical wisdom—honed by hindsight, aiming at the golden mean and eudaimonia—gives historians a standard for judging whether a society cultivated virtue or vice. Gilead fails that standard spectacularly: it banned the reading that shapes values, reduced women to reproductive function, and required heteronormative forced procreation, blocking the relationships and habits flourishing needs. Beauvoir corrects even Aristotle's own biology-based view of women, and the chapter closes that a purely descriptive history would doom us to repeat Gilead's atrocities.
- ch. 37 "References" *(notes)*
- ch. 38 "Mayday Members" *(notes)*
- ch. 39 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 40 "The Handmaid’s Tale and Philosophy A Womb of One’s Own" *(front)*

## The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way

- ch. 1 "capa.xhtml" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "COPYRIGHT" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "rosto.xhtml" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "creditos.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "sumario.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "introd.xhtml" **·** Plato — Allegory of the Cave — The editors' introduction frames The Hobbit as Plato's Allegory of the Cave retold 'there and back again': like the freed prisoner, Bilbo leaves his comfortable hole, has his eyes opened by a frightening journey, and returns 'queer' to neighbors who cannot accept that life offers more than order and routine. It lists the book's guiding questions - whether adventures are worth missing dinner, whether food and song outrank gold, whether powerful technology can be trusted or must be destroyed, and the duties of friends - as the essays' shared agenda.
- ch. 7 "a1-parte-1.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "a2.xhtml" **·** Aristotle, Socrates, William James, Seneca — Virtue Ethics (arete); Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know) — Bassham reads The Hobbit as a story of moral growth: the comfort-loving Bilbo who trembles like jelly at the dwarves' plans grows into the hobbit who volunteers to carry the Ring to Mordor. Growth in wisdom comes from Socratic self-examination (learning how little one knows) and from broadened experience of the wide world; growth in virtue comes either from sudden conversion (Thorin's Scrooge-like deathbed repentance) or, as Aristotle taught, from slow habituation - Bilbo's repeated courageous and generous acts (sparing Gollum, returning the elf-keys, giving up the Arkenstone) build lasting character. Seneca's view that hardship strengthens supplies the framework for why Bilbo's trials on the road ennobled rather than broke him.
- ch. 9 "a2.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 10 "a3.xhtml" **·** Zhuangzi, Laozi — The Tao (the Way); Wu Wei (effortless action); Yin and Yang — Brannigan reads Bilbo's tug-of-war between Baggins security and Took adventure through Taoism: the two desires are not contradictory but the interplay of yin and yang, and true dwelling is found in the journey itself, as the 'Roads go ever on' song says. Greed is the great weight - Thorin enslaved by the treasure he 'never forgot', Smaug hoarding for hoarding's sake, even the orc-loving of machines - and the cure is the mirror-mind of Empty Mind that reflects without grasping, illustrated by the Taoist masters tale of 'Gold-Is-Heavy' and 'Empty-Mind'. Beorn, who lives on honey indifferent to gold, and Bilbo, who in the spirit of wu-wei sheds his desire for the Arkenstone and finally lets go of the Ring, embody life in harmony with the Tao.
- ch. 11 "a3.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 12 "a4.xhtml" **·** Henry David Thoreau, Michel de Montaigne, Zhuangzi, The Buddha — Taoism (Daoism); Buddhism; Walden (deliberate living) — Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.
- ch. 13 "a4.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 14 "a5.xhtml" **·** Kwame Anthony Appiah — Cosmopolitanism — Knepp maps Appiah's cosmopolitanism onto Bilbo's journey from provincial hobbit - the Shire-folk who find even across-Brandywine hobbits odd - to citizen of the world who wants the good of dwarves, elves and men. Shared adventure, not argument, teaches tolerance: Bilbo and the dwarves never convert each other but learn to live together through meals, bickering and shared survival, exactly Appiah's 'conversation' that helps people get used to one another. The elf-made swords and the mithril coat show 'cultural contamination' as a good; Gimli and Legolas illustrate fallibilism and pluralism; Smaug and the orcs are anti-cosmopolites who impose their single way by force.
- ch. 15 "a5.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 16 "a6_parte-2.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "a7.xhtml" **·** Plato, Augustine of Hippo, Cicero, Socrates — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); The Unexamined Life — The chapter sets the bloody classical ideal of glory (Homer's kleos, Beowulf, Alexander modeling himself on Achilles) - which Augustine already condemned as libido dominandi - against Plato's alternative of a life aimed at the good, the true and the beautiful. Thorin's last charge at the Battle of Five Armies fits the heroic tradition, but Tolkien's real point is that Bilbo, the 'grocer' who feels the dwarves' treasure-lust yet walks away from it, and who ends by inviting the dwarves to four-o'clock tea instead of a victory feast, shows glory subordinated to domestic beauty and humility. Socrates' question in the Apology - why care so little for wisdom and the soul's improvement while chasing wealth, honor and reputation - is exactly the temptation Bilbo resists, and the Symposium's move from battle to a drinking-party of love-of-beauty mirrors Tolkien's placement of heroism in hobbits rather than warriors.
- ch. 18 "a7.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 19 "a8.xhtml" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Cardinal and Theological Virtues — Garcia argues Tolkien writes with a virtue-ethical moral theory: Middle-earth peoples are characterized by moral traits (noble eagles, cruel orcs), intentions matter (Bilbo is not to blame for the discomforting barrel escape because he meant rescue, and he turns back through the mountain tunnels because loyalty and courage demand it), and the book's drama is the tension between Aristotle's 'great-souled' proper pride and Aquinas' Christian humility. Thorin's pride (self-styled 'King under the Mountain', refusing Bard's just claim), Smaug's vanity that Bilbo flatters to find the bare patch, and the dragon-sickness illustrate pride as vice, while Bilbo's growth - believing after the spiders that 'there was more in him' yet accepting Gandalf's 'you are only quite a little fellow in a wide world' with a laugh - exemplifies correct self-assessment between vanity and undue humility.
- ch. 20 "a8.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 21 "a9.xhtml" **·** Thomas Aquinas, The Buddha, Laozi, Henry David Thoreau — The Four Noble Truths; Non-Self (anatman); Taoism (Daoism) — The chapter argues Tolkien's clearest moral in The Hobbit is against possessiveness, starting from Aquinas' definition of greed as 'immoderate love of riches': dragon-sickness ruins Thorin and drowns the Master of Lake-town starving in the wilderness with his gold, and Gollum shows the isolating end of a life organized around a 'precious'. Buddhism reframes the diagnosis - Gollum's craving (tanha) is rooted in ignorance (avidya) of the self's illusoriness, since grasping enriches a self that does not exist, per the Four Noble Truths - while Laozi's 'he who knows he has enough is rich' and Thoreau's 'a man is rich in proportion to the things he can afford to let alone' are embodied by Beorn and the gift-giving, nearly government-less hobbits. Bilbo's generosity - giving away the Arkenstone worth 'more than a river of gold', taking only two small chests, later giving Sting and the mithril coat to Frodo - is the book's counter-example to greed.
- ch. 22 "a9.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 23 "a10.xhtml" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Thomas Aquinas — Just War Theory — Johnson tests the Battle of Five Armies against just war theory as developed from Augustine through Aquinas: the men under Bard satisfy legitimate authority, just cause and last resort (they bargained, even using the Arkenstone as leverage and trying economic pressure), the Elvenking explicitly waits rather than start 'this war for gold', while the dwarves fail the criteria because greed and pride are not just causes and a thirteenth-share was a cheap price for peace. The war that actually happens - the three armies uniting against Bolg's orc-host - is justified self- and other-defense, whereas the orcs' motives (revenge, plunder, conquest) are unjust. Against apparent pacifist evidence (Tom Bombadil, Frodo at the Shire 'scouring', Gandalf's 'pity' for Gollum), Johnson reads Tolkien's letters as endorsing war as sometimes necessary and sometimes 'in the right', though Tolkien rejects the theory's reasonable-chance-of-success condition given the hopeless stands at Helm's Deep and the Morannon.
- ch. 24 "a10.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 25 "a11.xhtml" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Immanuel Kant — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Tallon reads The Hobbit as an exercise in aesthetics: Tolkien half-accepts the Kant-era 'art for art's sake' settlement - dwarves once made 'things of beauty for pure delight', elves sing 'lovely nonsense' without shame, Gandalf blows smoke-rings and fireworks - while rejecting both Victorian moralism and Wilde's amoralism. Instead aesthetic sensitivity is a moral thermometer grounded in Augustine's ordo amoris: orcs 'make no beautiful things, but many clever ones', dragons cannot tell good work from bad nor mend a loose scale (which is how Bard's arrow finds Smaug's bare patch), and Aule creates dwarves out of love so others might enjoy the beauty of Ea while Saruman's 'mind of metal and wheels' breeds Uruk-hai for domination. Beauty also acts morally: the dwarves' song awakens Bilbo's 'love of beautiful things made by hands' and, as Scarry and Murdoch hold, that awakening of desire beyond oneself is what prepares us for justice.
- ch. 26 "a11.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 27 "a12.xhtml" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Charles Sanders Peirce, Plato — Respect for Persons — O'Hara argues that play is what makes hobbits - and us - fully human: Bilbo's childhood games of throwing stones, riddles and smoke-rings turn out to be training for the quest (his stone-throwing fells the spiders, his riddle-practice buys time with Gollum), and even Gollum's riddle-game makes him momentarily 'less a monster and more a person'. Following Schiller's and Huizinga's Homo ludens thesis that play completes humanity, he distinguishes play from idleness (Aquinas held recreation continues in heaven; Peirce called play 'vigorous exercise'), places leisure among the goods of Aristotle's 'we play in order to be serious', and contrasts Gandalf's beauty-directed fireworks with the orcs' merely useful explosions and work-chants. But play has limits: Kant warns against treating persons as toys, and Bilbo's lesson is 'Never laugh at live dragons!'
- ch. 28 "a12.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 29 "a13_parte-3.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "a14.xhtml" **·** David Hume, Henry David Thoreau — On Miracles; Wilderness and Nature Aesthetics — Stewart argues Middle-earth magic is rule-bound engineering rather than Hume's miracle as 'a violation of the laws of nature': spells fail, the Ring hides neither shadow nor wet footprints, and magic comes in strengths like gravity, so fear of Gandalf is fear of superior knowledge of nature's laws, not of lawlessness. The deeper point is Tolkien's linkage of magic with technology as the impatient will to make one's will effective quickly - Sauron is 'Lord of magic and machines', the Ring is the supreme technological artifact, Saruman's forged men and blast-fires embody domination - while elvish 'Art' is sub-creation and Beorn's communion with animals models harmony with nature. Like Thoreau pricing possessions in 'how much life' they cost, the chapter ends with Tolkien's warning that 'if a thing can be done, it should be done' is the great false assumption of our age.
- ch. 31 "a14.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "a15.xhtml" **·** Martha Nussbaum, David Hume, William James — Kind uses our genuine reactions to Bilbo - pity when he sits forlorn at the Lonely Mountain, anxiety at the riddle-game, outrage at Thorin's rebuke - to stage the paradox of fiction: how can emotions be rational toward someone we know never existed? She walks through the failed solutions: Radford's verdict that fiction-emotions are irrational like fearing a mountain lion after the sighting is debunked; Walton's 'quasi-emotions' of make-believe, which cannot explain why we cannot switch our fear of the wargs off at will; and thought theory's mental images, since what we fear is Smaug, not our mental image of Smaug. Her preferred route, following Richard Moran, relaxes the belief requirement itself - as Hume noted passions resist rational assessment and as Nussbaum argues fiction cultivates moral character, many emotions (grief for the dead Tolkien, fear of future floods) need no existence beliefs.
- ch. 33 "a15.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 34 "a16.xhtml" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Grimwood turns the riddle contest in the dark into a lesson in hermeneutics: Bilbo interprets like Hirsch's intentionalist, asking what Gollum means (and suspecting he means to eat him), while Gollum answers each of Bilbo's riddles by fusing the words with his own forgotten past - sun on daisies, eggs at his grandmother's hole - exactly Gadamer's claim that understanding is a dialogue of horizons shaped by 'prejudices'. Bilbo's final 'What have I got in my pocket?' breaks the game because it severs the good will that makes interpretation a genuine exchange, leaving Gollum no horizon to fuse with, so he simply constructs his own 'truth' that the hobbit stole his precious. The chapter generalizes: Gandalf's dismantling of 'Good morning' shows interpretation is everywhere, and there is no view from nowhere outside our horizons.
- ch. 35 "a16.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 36 "a17_parte-4.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 37 "a18.xhtml" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Nagel, Immanuel Kant, John Rawls — Moral Luck — Jensen dissects Bilbo's run of luck - the fish that leaps to his feet mid-riddle, the drunken elf-guards, above all his hand falling on the Ring in the dark - using Aristotle's account of luck as the rare, uncontrolled coincidence of ordinary causes (an orc leaving the back door ajar plus a hobbit's six-meals-a-day girth). He then deploys Nagel's kinds of moral luck: Bilbo's constitutive luck (born a Baggins with Took blood, Rawls' 'natural lottery'), circumstantial luck, and resultant luck (finding the Ring, which he could not control but which dooms Sauron). Against Kant's good will that is 'like a jewel' beyond luck and Plato's 'no harm can befall a good man', the chapter argues that Thorin's dragon-sickness, the orcs' unlucky birth, and Bilbo's outcome-dependent standing show that praise and blame do - and should - reach beyond the agent's control.
- ch. 38 "a18.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 39 "a19.xhtml" **·** Boethius — Fate and Foreknowledge; The Consolation of Philosophy; Free Will vs Determinism — Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.
- ch. 40 "a19.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 41 "a20.xhtml" **·** Aristotle — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Watson uses the company's decisions under uncertainty - whether to approach the troll-fire that nearly gets them eaten, the elf-lights in Mirkwood, Bilbo's descent of Smaug's tunnel - to teach decision theory: expected utility (assigning probabilities and values shows they should have stayed put rather than follow the troll-light), conditional probability (the Mirkwood lights are treated as dependent events, dodging the gambler's fallacy), and simplifying the outcome set. He then judges Bilbo by Aristotle's doctrine that courage is the mean between the vice of cowardice and the vice of rashness, felt with respect to the appropriate passion, fear: Bilbo fears as he should (kettle-whistles and jelly-trembles), avoids unforced risks, yet risks death for his companions' lives - so he has acted courageously and is developing, not yet fully possessing, the virtue, which Aristotle says requires long practice.
- ch. 42 "a20.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 43 "a21.xhtml" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson — Self-Reliance; Transcendentalism — Kraus argues The Hobbit is two different books depending on the reader's experience: read cold it is a fairy-tale of adventure, but reread after The Lord of the Rings - knowing what the Ring did to Bilbo and what 'precious' means - it becomes a song of innocence and experience like Blake's Songs and Wordsworth's 'emotion recollected in tranquillity', where Elrond's opening description points to the deep Silmarillion history a first-time reader cannot yet feel. Emerson's 'transparent eye-ball' from Nature - the self stripped bare and made original in the woods - becomes Bilbo's first use of the Ring, where invisibility lets him see Gollum's miserable humanity and choose pity; but the image darkens into Sauron's Lidless Eye, the totalizing knowledge that defines and devours selves. 'There and back again' thus echoes nostos turned nostalgia: Bilbo never truly gets back, having traded the child's innocence Thorin praises on his deathbed for an experience he cannot undo.
- ch. 44 "a21.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 45 "a22.xhtml" *(notes)*
- ch. 46 "colofao.xhtml" *(front)*
- ch. 47 "saiba-mais.xhtml" *(notes)*

## The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason

- ch. 1 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** The Unexamined Life; Utopia and Dystopia; Philosophical Skepticism — The editors' introduction frames the trilogy as Katniss's quest to peel away Panem's layers of lies, likening her self-examination and self-control to the Delphic 'Know Thyself' and 'Nothing in Excess' and calling her skeptical spirit the engine of her wisdom. It poses the book's driving questions: why we enjoy watching others suffer, whether ordinary morality survives the arena, and how easily our own reality-TV-shaped world could slide into Panem's, noting that Collins modeled the Games on the Roman Colosseum. It presents dystopian exaggeration (children slaughtered for entertainment, tyrants, starving workers) as a cautionary mirror of trends already present in our society, and casts the contributors' chapters as a therapeutic game of 'Real or Not Real' played with the reader.
- ch. 8 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Augustine of Hippo — Utopia and Dystopia — Brian McDonald opposes two arts in Panem: Peeta's Aristotelian mimesis, which delights and instructs (his camouflage station skill and the 'right shade for sunlight on white fur' speech that eases the dying morphling's last moments), and the Capitol's 'perverse imitation' of tragedy in the arena and Caesar Flickerman's interviews, where the audience feels catharsis's pity and fear with none of its insight because they are complicit in inflicting the tragedy. Drawing on Phillip Rieff's notion of 'de-creation,' he links the Remake Center's freakish body modifications to the arena's cruelties as one abandonment of aesthetic and ethical limits, and uses Augustine's 'deceptive sense of omnipotence' from the Confessions plus Ernest Becker's causa-sui project to explain the Capitol's flight from any fixed identity ('You almost look like a real person'). The chapter closes with Katniss's recognition scene in Mockingjay: choosing the artist Peeta over the hunter Gale is how she survives having become a monster herself.
- ch. 10 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Socrates — Justice in the Republic; The Philosopher King — Anne Torkelson reads Panem through the Republic and the Laws: because mousike imitates states of soul and slowly molds character, Socrates polices music and poetry in the just city and fears innovation in musical modes, and the Capitol's own outlawing of songs quietly confirms music's power. She shows 'The Meadow Song' replacing Katniss's grief with hope and inspiring the flowers for Rue, the forbidden 'Hanging Tree' planting the Socratic question of whether an unjust life is a fate worse than death (paralleling Socrates's own unjust execution, the hemlock, and the nightlock pact Katniss, Gale, and Peeta make), and Rue's four notes mutating from an orchard work-signal into a salute of defiance when the District 11 man whistles them on the Victory Tour, at the cost of his life. Music, which Katniss dismisses as 'somewhere between hair ribbons and rainbows,' turns out to be the force that shapes her character and carries the revolution.
- ch. 11 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Jill Olthouse applies hermeneutics, crediting Gadamer as its key philosophical developer, to Panem's ideological battle of words and images: paradoxical metaphors like 'the girl on fire,' 'tribute,' and 'mockingjay' carry contestable associations, so interpreting them is a creative act through which Katniss is either defined by her enemies or defines herself. She traces Katniss's reinterpretations, from squirrel-prey to hunter after Peeta saves her, from staged 'star-crossed lovers' to a bond that becomes literal, to the berry suicide ploy that denies the Capitol its victory, and reads the hijacked Peeta's 'she's some kind of mutt' as the Capitol winning an interpretive round by stealing her metaphor. The chapter culminates in Katniss's creative reading of Snow's confession and her assassination of Coin, the moment she finally claims the mockingjay identity on her own terms as a fighter and messenger rather than a weapon used by others.
- ch. 12 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Nagel, Seneca — Moral Luck; The Wheel of Fortune; Stoicism — George Dunn tests Katniss's luck-saturated life against Kant's claim that the good will shines 'like a jewel' regardless of fortune, with Peeta's vow to 'die as myself' as the stronghold the Gamemakers cannot touch, and with Seneca's dictum that what Fortune has not given she cannot take away. He then runs Nagel's four kinds of moral luck through the trilogy: Haymitch's reaping-made alcoholism as constitutive luck, Rue's death sparing Katniss an impossible final choice as circumstantial luck, Peeta's rooftop words echoing unconsciously behind the flowers for Rue as causal luck, and the revolution's success as resultant luck without which Katniss would have been the destroyer of District 12 rather than its torchbearer. Framing the Gamemakers as Fortuna on her wheel, he ends with the berries: since Katniss can never untangle whether she held them out from love, defiance, or self-protection, even moral worth proves hostage to luck and to the opacity of our own motives.
- ch. 14 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Immanuel Kant, Friedrich Nietzsche — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Andrew Shaffer imagines Capitol patrons at Caesar's Bar & Grill cheering the Quarter Quell bloodbath and asks what makes their enjoyment possible, answering with Schopenhauer's 'devilish' verdict on Schadenfreude as the mark of a worthless heart, Kant's calling it a 'diabolical' vice, and Nietzsche's account of another's misfortune as the social equalizer that appeases envy. He argues the spectators need dehumanization, from Effie's 'savages' rhetoric and the prep team's scrubbing to the wolf mutts wearing Glimmer's eyes, to enjoy innocent children dying, and that the star-crossed-lovers story humanizes the tributes enough to force the unprecedented double-victor rule change. The chapter closes by turning the diagnosis on us: readers thrill to the arena too, the whole trilogy arguably runs on Schadenfreude, and even Snow's execution is staged as a spectacle of righteous pleasure in a villain's death.
- ch. 15 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Jennifer Culver explains Katniss's 'I hate owing people' through Marcel Mauss's gift-exchange theory, extended to modern private gifts by Lewis Hyde: Peeta's bread creates an unpayable burden because gifts carry invisible strings of reciprocity, which is why Thresh's 'we're even then. No more owed' makes instant sense to her, and why in Catching Fire she contemplates shooting Finnick before she can owe him more. She contrasts debts handled gracefully, quietly patronizing the Hob sponsors, thanking District 11 in words rather than cash equivalents, and treating loyalty as a gift in District 13's uniform economy, with Katniss's initial resentment of any bond that constrains her self-sufficiency. The chapter ends with the gift of memory, the mourning book and Peeta's small gestures after the war, by which Katniss finally accepts that the point of gifts is the bond they forge, not the debt they impose.
- ch. 16 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Immanuel Kant, David Hume — Social Darwinism; Ethical Egoism; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Abigail Mann argues that the Games only look like 'survival of the fittest': Darwinian natural selection runs on chance ('one slip in thousands') and explicitly rejects the social-Darwinist use of 'unfit' against the poor, while Darwin's Descent of Man explains the tributes' kindness through kin and group selection and an evolved moral sense, so Katniss's unhesitating volunteering for Prim is kin selection and Thresh's conflicted sparing of her shows conscience overriding self-preservation. She tests this against Kant, for whom only duty-motivated action is truly moral, which would make Thresh's inner struggle the more moral act and Katniss's instinctive sacrifice mere animal impulse, and against the egoism of Hobbes (giving to a beggar to relieve one's own distress) and Dawkins's selfish gene, answering with Hume and psychologist Daniel Batson that genuine altruism is real. Her coda: Katniss ultimately rejects Gale not only because his firebomb killed Prim but because it was engineered to trap and kill altruists, and her closing habit of listing 'every act of goodness' is the trilogy's verdict that simple kindness is not an illusion.
- ch. 18 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Boethius, John Locke — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life) — Jason Eberl treats the muttations, jabberjays that mimic speech without understanding, tracker jackers, the wolf-mutts with Glimmer's eyes that torment Cato, and the lizard-mutts hissing Katniss's name, alongside real chimeras (geeps, the SCID-hu mouse, Balaban's quail-chick brain transplants, Weissman's human-neural mouse) to ask whether biotechnology could create a person. Working through Boethius's definition of a person as an 'individual substance of a rational nature' and Locke's 'thinking intelligent Being' that can consider itself the same over time, he argues that human DNA alone confers no personhood, while a chimera genuinely capable of self-conscious rational thought would be a person whose weaponized creation and lab captivity would violate its rights, which is why ethicists allow mouse chimeras but hesitate with primates. He notes that the Gamemakers' refusal to see tributes as persons is exactly the move that made slavery and Nazi dehumanization possible, and that Katniss's suspicion about whether the mutts remember their deaths is the right ethical question to keep open.
- ch. 19 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, Seneca, Zeno of Citium — Stoicism; Preferred Indifferents; The Dichotomy of Control; Living in the Present — Abigail Myers runs Stoic doctrine against Katniss's biography: Zeno's thesis that only moral goodness is good (with Plutarch Heavensbee's renunciation of Capitol privilege as indifference to wealth and status), Seneca's 'On the Shortness of Life' against deferring living, Epictetus's dichotomy of control including the uncomfortable advice to kiss wife and child as mortals, and Marcus Aurelius's practical Meditations as the gentler 'Stoic for beginners' who would be president of Panem. Katniss comes out Stoic in her frugality, her mortality-shadowed appreciation of small joys, and her firm moral code, but decidedly un-Stoic in her fierce attachments to Rue, Peeta, and Prim. Yet her final choice of Peeta over Gale is itself Stoic, Myers argues: she forgives what Peeta's hijacking made him do since it was never in his control, refuses a noble friendship that would endorse Gale and Coin's slaughter of innocents, and chooses in accordance with nature and reason so as to survive as herself with her values intact.
- ch. 21 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler — One Is Not Born a Woman; Gender Performativity; Woman as the Other; Heteronormativity — Jessica Miller shows Katniss coded masculine, since Collins built her from Theseus and Spartacus and her breadwinning, hunting, and defiance fit masculine norms, while Prim embodies everything Beauvoir says civilization 'produces' as feminine, and Panem itself proves oddly gender-neutral: women work the mines, Finnick is the sex symbol sold by Snow, and Coin is as ruthless as any man. She then reads Katniss's romance performance through Judith Butler: the kisses, caresses, and televised wedding gowns do not express a preexisting femininity but constitute one, down to Butler's radical claim that sex itself is a cultural norm, which reframes even the Games' reaping of one boy and one girl as a gendered ritual rather than a presocial biological fact. Cinna's burning bridal gown that transforms Katniss into the mockingjay makes the political payoff explicit: gender performed strategically becomes the rebellion's power, and the hunter-and-baker partnership offers an alternative to the dominant romance script.
- ch. 22 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings, Immanuel Kant — The Ethics of Care; Caring as the Ground of Ethics; Autonomy of the Will — Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge. Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.
- ch. 23 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; The State of Nature; Authenticity — Coatney explains why Katniss fails at everything she fakes — the disastrous first propos ('that is how a revolution dies'), the studio Mockingjay shoots, the cover-story mission to kill Snow — through Rousseau's distinction between amour de soi (natural self-love) and amour-propre (vanity born of society): she is a natural person in a corrupt world of seeming. The chapter contrasts district self-preservation with Capitol vanity (Posy asking green-skinned Octavia 'Are you sick?'), and reads Haymitch's smooth deception as a costlier, self-destroying alternative to Katniss's inability to dissimulate. Since Rousseau doubts any return to the state of nature, Katniss's refusal to flee into the woods — 'I'm going to stay right here and cause all kinds of trouble' — shows her Nietzsche-noted fate of being punished for her virtue, still preferable to becoming like Effie.
- ch. 25 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** John Locke, David Hume, Plutarch, Gottfried Leibniz — Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity; Bundle Theory of Self — Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.
- ch. 26 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Immanuel Kant — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself — Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.
- ch. 28 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Just War Theory; The Ethics of Political Violence — Melançon tests the Mockingjay revolution against the just-war tradition's three parts: jus ad bellum, jus in bello, and jus post bellum. The districts satisfy just cause, right intention, last resort, and proportionality against the Capitol, but stumble on competent authority — no legitimate state authorizes their rebellion — a problem the chapter says forces the tradition to admit popular self-determination. Both sides then violate jus in bello: the rebels' avalanche on the Nut fails military necessity and proportionality, and the bombing of the Capitol's child shields plus the medics treating them breaches distinction twice, making the rebels as bad as the Capitol. The contemplated final Hunger Games with Capitol children would violate jus post bellum, so the revolution was not a just war and only stumbles into peace.
- ch. 29 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Jones models Panem with game theory: the tesserae system is a rigged, house-favoring gamble on the reaping (Katniss's twenty entries versus Madge's three), the Training Days are a subgame for winning sponsors, and arena alliances formalize the prisoner's dilemma, where betray-betray is the stable equilibrium even though mutual cooperation would leave everyone better off. Iterated-play tit-for-tat wins computer simulations but fails in the arena because a betrayed tribute usually dies before retaliating — as Katniss's repeated misreadings of her allies show. Katniss's genius is stepping outside the game: with the nightlock berries she denies the Gamemakers a victor and forces a new game, and at the climax she plays terminal tit-for-tat against President Coin, showing the world need not follow the rules of the models.
- ch. 30 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Michel Foucault — Discipline and Docile Bodies; The Panopticon (surveillance); Power/Knowledge — Van Dyke uses Foucault's account of discipline and 'docile bodies' (with Susan Bordo's feminist elaboration) to explain how the Capitol rules: citizens satiated with abundance channel their hungers into fashion, body modification, and self-surveillance, and this self-focused discipline trains their attention away from the injustices that sustain them — which is how the genuinely affectionate prep team can weep over Katniss yet love the Games. She shows that District 13 disciplines just as totally through rigid schedules, rations, and punishment (the prep team chained for taking bread), so neither Snow's hidden indulgence nor Coin's overt regimentation leaves room for autonomy. Cinna's styling of Katniss demonstrates the alternative: body modification as internally generated self-expression and resistance that helps Katniss become the Mockingjay rather than a docile body.
- ch. 32 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Seneca — Stoicism; Preferred Indifferents; Stoic Cosmopolitanism (citizens of the world) — Barkman reads the trilogy's Roman texture — panem et circenses, gladiatorial Games, tyrants named Coriolanus and Caesar — through the Stoic Seneca, who lived under Nero just as Katniss lives under Snow. Seneca's distinction between the good (virtue alone), the merely preferable (wealth, fame, power), and the bad (vice) explains the Capitol: Snow and Coin traded virtue for preferables and so became vicious, while the citizens' binge-and-purge luxury mirrors the Roman decadence Seneca condemned. The Hunger Games are the gladiatorial 'pure murder' that corrupts emperors, crowds, and tributes alike, and the districts are slaves whose liberation — like Katniss declaring 'I'm done killing their slaves' — is Seneca's freedom from slavery to fear and vice. Katniss and Peeta's self-sacrificial love and refusal to be changed exemplify the Stoic virtue the Capitol cannot take away.
- ch. 33 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" **·** Socrates — Cultural Hegemony; Ideology and False Consciousness — Timm uses Bourdieu's forms of capital (economic, social, cultural) and habitus to explain why Panem needed no brute force for seventy-five years: District 12's school teaches the Hunger Games as normal, doles out history as 'what we owe the Capitol,' keeps districts ignorant of each other, and trains Seam children for the mines, so education reproduces inequality instead of curing it. Katniss and Gale's hunting and trading skills are only 'resistant cultural capital' — worthless to Capitol taste but a habitus of lawbreaking that made rebellion thinkable for them alone. Katniss's public defiance exposes the 'wavy squares' in the force field of taken-for-granted power, and the chapter likens her fate to Socrates, condemned by Athens's holders of capital yet igniting a revolution in values.
- ch. 34 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 35 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Setting Up the Game" **·** Plato, Socrates — Socratic Method (elenchus) — Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction: he argues videogames, and the Zelda franchise in particular, deserve philosophical attention, then frames the book's spirit with Plato's Meno. Just as Socrates' questioning leads the slave boy from thinking he knows to actually knowing that a double-sized square has area sixteen, the gamer's struggle through dungeons is rewarded with the item-room fanfare (the ladder, the silver arrow) as an 'AHA!' feeling of insight. The chapter lists the franchise's games and the book's guiding questions, stressing that the gamer guides Link rather than passively watching.
- ch. 8 "Level 1 - Emotion, Experience, and Thought" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Evaluating Zelda" **·** Plato — Tripartite Soul — Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, or care when Tetra's identity is revealed, though we know none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never suspend disbelief enough to call the police), Carroll's thought theory (fear is too fast and too vivid for mere thoughts), and Walton's pretend theory (involuntary pretending and the uniform way all players see the sail break it). Instead he argues for a multi-level mind, modeled on Plato's divided soul in the Republic and Fodor's mental modules: local unconscious appraisals react to the fire as if real, while a global appraisal of reality-status keeps us in our chairs.
- ch. 10 "Game versus Place" **·** Embodiment (the lived body) — Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warp sacrifices environmental presence for goal-oriented play: the long, uneventful sails where waves, cloud patterns, and quiet soundscapes dominate are precisely when Hyrule feels like a place, and teleporting turns it into a disposable grid of destinations. Drawing on Castells' spaces of flows versus places, Schivelbusch's 'annihilation of space and time' by the railway (the player becomes a 'human parcel'), and de Certeau's opposition between the panoptic map view and the embodied everyday view, he contends the very existence of the warp option colors all distance traveled. Even panoramic pleasures like hang-gliding over Outset Island, he notes, must be balanced against pure map-grid travel.
- ch. 11 "End Game" *(no index entry yet)* — Arp and Milarker use Zelda examples to teach informal logic: Rob's 'all gamers are geeks' is a hasty generalization, the argument that the original Zelda is chronologically first commits equivocation (Earth release order is not Hyrule chronology, since Miyamoto named Ocarina of Time earliest), and debates over banning violent games trade in false dilemmas, ad hominem, and slippery slopes. The chapter sets out premises, conclusions, deductive versus inductive arguments, validity and soundness, strength and cogency, with worked examples from Clawshot reasoning to Best Buy Wii lines. Its point is that fallacious reasoning harms real lives, so readers should audit every argument in the book and in the gaming world.
- ch. 12 "Level 2 - Dodongo and Death" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, Viktor Frankl, Friedrich Nietzsche — Existence Precedes Essence; The Myth of Sisyphus; Man's Search for Meaning (logotherapy); The Death of God — Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.
- ch. 14 "Game Over" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, G.W.F. Hegel, Bernard Williams — Immortality and the Soul; The Death of God; The Meaning of Life — Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.
- ch. 15 "Level 3 - Don’t Get Manhandled by Manhandla—or . . . Mind-handled" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Master and Slave Morality — Drzaic and Rauch argue Link is 'good by default' because ludus play (rule-bound, goal-directed, winning the designed story) locks the player into the designers' morality, while paidia play, player-invented goals like the Ocarina of Time flying glitch or the Fierce Deity rampage in Majora's Mask, escapes the story's moral frame entirely. They then map this onto Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil: protagonist Link embodies slave morality (reactive, fear-avoiding, pity, patience, restoring the old Hyrule Ganon disturbed), while the elite paidia player is value-creating like the master, honoring power and secrecy (Huizinga) rather than the protagonist's virtue. The chapter concludes that in videogames the good/evil opposition is welded to ludus, and Zelda fans' naughtiness shows play can go beyond good and evil.
- ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Ship of Theseus; Personal Identity — Robison asks how Link stays the same person through Ocarina of Time's child/adult switches, Twilight Princess's wolf form, and Wind Waker's consciousness-projection into seagulls and mages. Physical-continuity views fail because Link's body changes or is left behind; Locke's memory-based psychological continuity fails because adult Link's past hasn't happened yet when he travels back. After a Ship of Theseus variant (Ganon reassembling Tetra's sunken planks) she proposes that in Zelda's stipulative metaphysics, destiny, the goddess-given roles of courage, wisdom, and power, is the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, fitting videogame universes whose metaphysics are fixed by designers.
- ch. 18 "Level 4 - The CDi Games Don’t Count! Timelines and Miyamoto" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Putting Together the Triforce" **·** David Lewis — Possible Worlds — Duncan and Gee study the Nintendo NSider forum threads where fans build Zelda timelines, showing that their marshaling of evidence (Ganon's trident, whether the Master Sword is 'legendary' because of an earlier hero or its sage creators, Hyrule's geography as a marker of time) mirrors scientific argumentation. Using Latour and Woolgar's Laboratory Life, they argue that what 'counts' as evidence, even down to excluding the BS Zelda and CD-i games as non-canon, is socially constructed within a community of practice, not value-free data. David Lewis's plurality of worlds supplies the metaphysics for the split-timeline debate after Ocarina of Time, and the chapter concludes that knowledge in general, in labs and in fandoms alike, is constructed through tools, discourse, and interaction.
- ch. 20 "Zelda Is a Communication Game!" **·** Martin Heidegger, William of Ockham, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gottfried Leibniz — Ockham's Razor — Johnson argues that because Zelda has no single authorial vision (teams, outside developers, cryptic Aonuma interviews), the timeline is a 'communication game' fans play together. Interpretation follows the hermeneutic circle of Heidegger and Gadamer (parts inform the whole, as when Wind Waker's references to Ganon's earlier attacks make sense of the series), faces Leibnizian underdetermination since infinitely many theories fit the games, and uses Ockham's razor, whose failures (the y=2x formula) show that simplicity is relative to a community's training, as in Wittgenstein's pupil who suddenly counts '1,004, 1,008'. Hence Miyamoto's own claim that Zelda is a communication game: designers supply puzzle pieces, and the fan community creates the meaning.
- ch. 21 "Level 5 - Time and Space in Hyrule" *(front)*
- ch. 22 "The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — Eternal Recurrence — Sherlock reads Majora's Mask's repeating three days as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence from The Gay Science, the demon's demand that we affirm the same life 'innumerable times more', but then shows the Ocarina disrupts the mapping: the Inverted Song of Time and Song of Double Time make each cycle a non-repetition, dissolving the recurrence test's existential weight into a new anxiety about fragmented time. Items that survive the reset and rupees banked in Clock Town give time a material value, while the Deku Scrub transformation scene ('You'll stay looking that way forever') is analyzed as uncanny temporality via Freud's Das Unheimliche, with Derrida's claim that there is no non-metaphysical concept of time framing the conclusion that even game time cannot be separated from its representation.
- ch. 23 "Hyrule Regained" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games — Through an opening dialogue where a Tax Inspector absurdly appears in Level 9, Siabra-Fraile distinguishes physical from logical space in the NES Zelda: obstacles are chains of conditions (locked door needs key, key needs rupees, rupees need octoroks, octoroks need a sword), and this logical distance, not geometry, is what makes the adventure. Sprites mean what you can do with them (a tree burns, a rock explodes; water is 'the thing that blocks movement and holds zolas'), characters and objects combine like words in semantic fields and like words, phrases, and discourse build screens, levels, and the map. The rules that make Hyrule coherent and playable are, in Wittgenstein's sense, a language game woven into an activity or form of life, so Link can finally prove the inspector out of place.
- ch. 24 "Level 6 - Treasures of the Hyrulopolis" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "A Win for Zelda" *(no index entry yet)* — Cuddy argues that Zelda games can genuinely be art by adapting three aesthetic theories: Walton's make-believe account (art styles are rules for how to 'look', and a novice friend who plays A Link to the Past like a shooter is applying the wrong rules), Rosenstein's transparent/translucent/opaque artwork-worlds (Zelda's avatar, music, terrain, and story make it translucent, while Adventure is mere message and Second Life too close to life), and Panofsky's claim that objective properties demand aesthetic experience. The decisive third property is freeplay, gameplay not tied to beating the game, like exploring with the flippers to find the bottle under the bridge. Some games (Tetris, Super Mario Brothers) fail the test, so some videogames are art and some are not.
- ch. 26 "Paradise Found" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Søren Kierkegaard — Utopia and Dystopia; Justice in the Republic; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Man as Political Animal — Brown reads The Minish Cap's Hyrule as a working utopia: its Royal Family, guards, and market traders loosely realize Plato's Republic classes from Book V onward, but with fluid social boundaries (Zelda wanders the festival unharassed), no slavery, and relaxed state control that Plato's static order lacked. The town matches Aristotle's polis design (walled, defensible, right-sized, river-powered yet self-sufficient), while the surrounding pastoral landscape embodies Kantian disinterested beauty in nature and the Schillerian idea that through beauty we arrive at freedom. Its vague, prophet-free Picori religion of benevolent Christs-in-miniature needs no Kierkegaardian leap of faith, so unlike Hitler's Germany or Stalin's Russia, Hyrule is utopia actually achieved, and explorable, through Link.
- ch. 27 "Level 7 - You are Nearing the End of Your Quest . . . Grumble, Grumble . ." *(front)*
- ch. 28 "A Link to the Present" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Immanuel Kant, Michel Foucault, Daniel Dennett — The World as Will; Transcendental Idealism; Free Will vs Determinism; The Cartesian Theater (critique) — Compagno argues that the word 'I' in Zelda simultaneously names Link, the virtual body, and the player, the invisible will, and builds this into a 'Schopenhauerian Console': as Schopenhauer held, we have freedom of action but not freedom of will, since the decisions of the unknowable will never appear in consciousness (against Descartes' free mind and Dennett's Cartesian theater critique). Kant's transcendental subject, standing at the border of experience, becomes the player's perspective from which Hyrule exists, what Foucault would call an empirical-transcendental doublet. The payoff: Link's quest is fated and scripted, yet the player wills it in a perpetual present, enacting Schopenhauer's lesson that a determined life is still lived as one's own free act.
- ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Eternal Recurrence; Will to Power; Amor Fati (love of fate); Theory of Forms — Bruce finds Nietzsche's eternal return in the NES Zelda's clockless, endlessly restartable structure: the same game recurs every time you press start, yet since the player changes, each playthrough manifests the forces anew, and the demon's question 'do you desire this once more?' becomes 'do you will to play once more?'. Link's growth through eight dungeons to face Ganon is read as will-to-power, personal strength and self-overcoming rather than mere domination, and saying yes to the struggle is amor fati. Against Plato's two-worlds doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly (both Nietzsche's targets), the original Zelda offers no guide, no Bible, and no linear time to a final judgment: this looped world is the only one, so it must be affirmed.
- ch. 30 "Level 8 - The Triforce—Need I Say More" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "The Golden Power" **·** Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Dugan reads the Triforce through Lacan's psychology of the dyad and the social symbolic: Link is the player's dyadic anchor ('Miyamoto's Framework' avatar, named because he links us to the system), while the gameworld we progressively master and explore is the social symbolic. Each Triforce piece maps onto the triangle: Courage completes the two-way player-Link bond, Power is the sword/bomb/arrow system consummated in the A Link to the Past final battle, and Wisdom is the realization that these tidy symbolic trinities (Father/Son/Holy Ghost, Brahma/Vishnu/Shiva, the three branches of US government) are simplifications. The 'golden power' is seeing that all such systems are representations posing as totality, offering pre-designed, illusory choice, and inferring who designed the games we are in.
