- ch. 9 "The Office and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Plato — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Argues that the standard trio of moral failure - malice (Creed ogling Pam, Andy sabotaging Dwight with the toll-receipt trick), weakness of will (Jan returning to Michael, Meredith relapsing with alcohol), and ignorance (Pam trading away Jim's teapot in 'Christmas Party') - misses a fourth category: moral blindness, embodied by Michael Scott, who can recite moral rules but cannot see when they apply (his Martin Luther King name tag on Diversity Day, defending Phyllis from Todd Packer with a harassing kiss, the fake-firing prank on Pam). Against Plato's view that all wrongdoing is ignorance, the chapter claims knowledge of rules neither helps nor harms decency; what matters is moral perception - seeing what a situation requires - shown by Jim getting Dwight to the hospital and rescuing the Dundies, Pam protecting the Dwight-Angela secret, and Toby patiently answering Dwight's anatomy questions.
- ch. 11 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Utilitarianism; Deontology — Weighs the morality of Jim and Pam's workplace flirting (while Pam is engaged to Roy) using three ethical frameworks: act utilitarianism has them tot up their own happiness against effects on co-workers' morale and Dunder-Mifflin's bottom line; rule utilitarianism models HR's blanket anti-dating policies and asks whether Jim and Pam could justify an exception without destroying the rule (the Hawaiian shirt day analogy); deontology searches for duties against office romance (favoritism in evaluation, distraction from duties) and finds none once harassment is set aside, concluding that in the absence of a deontological prohibition, Jim and Pam may keep flirting until 5 p.m.
- ch. 12 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** David Hume, Adam Smith, Bertrand Russell — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; The Impartial Spectator; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Asks whether Michael can (not will) ever learn empathy, distinguishing cognitive empathy - explained via Russell's argument-by-analogy account of other minds, which Michael manages only with people like himself, hence his sales success in 'The Client' - from affective empathy, which he lacks (Kevin's possible skin cancer is 'terrible news for both of us'; he cannot read Phyllis's oven mitt in Yankee Swap). Traces his cluelessness to egocentrism, and following Hume and Smith's sentimentalist account of morals - decentring the ego toward the impartial spectator via emotional contagion - argues his only hope is a real friendship (Jim's) that could drag him outside himself, since sycophantic Dwight and one-sided Todd Packer never will.
- ch. 13 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Autonomy of the Will; Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Reads Tim Canterbury of the UK Wernham-Hogg as an autonomous moral agent who nonetheless cannot act on his own judgments: Kant's categorical imperative is applied to Tim's stapler-through-the-window prank (universalizing the maxim of disposing of disputed objects passes the test, so Tim is in the clear), before the chapter diagnoses the office's pointlessness with Durkheim, Fromm and Merton's notion of anomie - David Brent's management produces moral lawlessness and boredom. Tim's dice speech, his swallowed resignation and accepted promotion, and his last-second failed dash to Dawn in the finale show a weak-willed conscience: he knows what he should do but lacks the conviction, making him the moral conscience of the show without being its moral hero.
- ch. 14 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); The Golden Mean; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics account of wit as a character virtue lying in a mean to map the UK office: David Brent is the buffoon of excess, the 'slave of his sense of humor' who cannot not joke (the 'crack of Dawn' line, the cruel Post-It Notes firing prank on Dawn), Gareth Keenan the boor of deficiency whose literalism leaves him unable to make or take a joke, and Tim Canterbury the ready wit whose responsive irony ('Does anybody have the right time?') hits the mean. Because humor, like morality, is uncodifiable - there is no Having a Sense of Humor for Dummies - the trio illustrates that virtue is qualitative appropriateness guided by practical wisdom, not moderation or rule-following.
- ch. 15 "The Office and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "The Office and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Gives a crash course in epistemology (knowledge vs hypothesis, mistake, and opinion; empirical and rational evidence) to solve the puzzle of how Pam can simultaneously know and not know that she loves Jim: the evidence is public (Jim is 'onto' her, the teapot gift, Angela's 'Pam Pong' tally, her inspection of Jim's bedroom in 'Email Surveillance'), yet she tells the camera she and Jim are 'just friends' and angrily rejects the evidence (being picked up in 'The Fight', the 'first date' remark in 'The Client'). The chapter models self-deception as two kinds of knowledge plus an unjustified belief - she rationalizes the lie with genuine reasons (security with Roy, fear of losing control) until second-order knowledge of her own lying erupts as anger and despair, concluding the show is great because it is honest about the lies viewers tell themselves.
- ch. 17 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Plato, Epicurus, René Descartes — The Noble Lie; The Categorical Imperative; Death Is Nothing to Us; Tripartite Soul — Tests the deceptions swirling around Dwight: Kant's two arguments against lying (universalizing the maxim 'lie whenever it saves face', and treating the deceived as a mere means) are set against Plato's noble lie from the Republic - Michael's empty 'Assistant Regional Manager' title may be a morally tolerable verbal lie because after 'The Fight' it restores their friendship, though it does not medicate the office as Plato's lie does the city. Epicurus' claim that only what is experienced can harm you ('what you don't know can't hurt you') is refuted by the thought of Angela's hypothetical fake love for Dwight: undetected deception is itself a harm. Finally Dwight's self-deception (believing the false promotion, Jim's telekinesis prank, the fax from his future self) is modeled by dividing the self - Plato's tripartite soul versus Descartes' simple, indivisible mind - suggesting cognitive science's modular brain as the better picture, and asking whether one can even wrong oneself.
- ch. 18 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Socrates — Authenticity; The Unexamined Life — Pits authenticity - understood both as self-discovery and as existentialist self-creation after Sartre and Heidegger, requiring self-knowledge and meaningful relationships - against happiness as subjective well-being, in a case study of Michael Scott. Michael's closest 'friendships' are relationships of convenience (Dwight's betrayal in 'The Coup', the fear-induced Packer bond, self-destructive Jan), his 'Packer norms' of locker-room humor are unshakeable, and Shelley Taylor-style positive illusions (his self-image as progressive on Diversity Day, 'The World's Best Boss' mug) keep his moods afloat while truth-tellers like Jan and the Chili's bar patrons knock them down. The conclusion challenges Socrates' dictum: since Michael is psychologically incapable of achieving authenticity, perhaps for some people the examined life is simply not available, and trying for it only produces misery.
- ch. 19 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Henri Bergson, Thomas Hobbes — Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Against Hobbes's view that laughter expresses superiority and Bergson's that comedy humiliates the socially disruptive into conformity, argues that viewers of The Office feel humiliation 'by proxy': Michael Scott is immune to humiliation because his narcissism blocks the minimal condition for feeling it - recognizing he could do wrong (Prison Mike, his MLK name tag while stereotyping Kelly, reneging on the pledge to Oscar's nephew, Carol's rejection at Diwali). We blush, look away, and feel his shame in his place, which transforms neither Michael nor us but reaffirms our own decency, compassion, and grip on values like self-awareness - and the chapter answers the worry that this merely endorses 'Hollywood' values by noting the standards Michael violates (moral sight, honesty with oneself) cross value systems.
- ch. 20 "The Office and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Karl Marx, Walter Benjamin — Alienation; Class Struggle; Historical Materialism — Answers The New Yorker's claim that the American Office 'doesn't care about class' by reading it through Marx: capital's growth logic and surplus value explain the degraded office labor the show depicts (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock type of situation' truck unloading, Pam's tepid watercolors, Roy's 'unloading trucks without meaning', Ryan's rejected assembly line), while the salaried masses' class position survives precisely as unnamable and denied - Michael's botched condo purchase, his fury at Ryan's business-school ambition, and Prison Martin's observation that office and prison are both 'doing the same thing every day'. Drawing on Kracauer, the chapter argues the show's comedy walks between distraction and awakening, and ends with Walter Benjamin's 'authentic humanity' located in the gap between professional and private life: Michael's failures make him an unwitting critique of the system that produced him.
- ch. 22 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Michel Foucault — The Look (hell is other people); Bad Faith; The Panopticon (surveillance) — Applies Sartre's Being and Nothingness to the mockumentary: Pam's bad faith consists in pretending she has no choice between Jim and Roy (her garbled 'I'm not into Jim' conversation with Karen in 'Ben Franklin'), while the camera's Look - Sartre's keyhole peeper caught in the hallway - turns her into an object not of her making when she is caught watching Jim and Karen in 'The Merger', and her shame finally lets her own her feelings. David Brent's pride (posing with his Inside Paper magazine cover) tries to control the Other's look and fails, since the freely respected gaze he craves cannot be extracted; and the ever-possible camera functions as Foucault's panopticon (Bentham's prison design), visible and unverifiable, silencing Jan on speakerphone in 'Cocktails' and forcing Dwight and Angela's 'Don't linger. Break left' choreography, which makes the viewer a complicit co-worker.
- ch. 23 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Aristotle — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Uses Baudrillard's three orders of simulacra to read the UK office: Neil Godwin embodies the first order where the boss's signs reflect real virtue (Aristotle's practical wisdom), Gareth's health-and-safety training of Donna - which degenerates into interrogation about her sex life - is the second order where virtuous signs mask desire, and David Brent is the third-order hyperreal, his management-speak ('team individuality', 'mutual likewise reciprocated', the 'rape' role-play outburst) signs with no referent masking that he is not a boss at all. The chapter's sting is that laughing at Brent we tacitly endorse the 'real' managerial system that produces Neil and redundancies, while Gareth - who models himself on Brent and pushes his codes to suicidal extremes ('will there ever be a boy born who can swim faster than a shark?') - instantiates Baudrillard's fatal strategy, a system carrying the seeds of its own destruction.
- ch. 24 "The Office and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 25 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle — Kraft uses Dunder Mifflin to test whether stockholder profit or stakeholder welfare should drive business decisions, introducing stakeholder theory via Ansoff and the Mitchell salience model. Michael's exclusive patronage of national chains (Chili's, Starbucks, USA Today) versus the staff's loyalty to local spots like Poor Richard's becomes a Millian case: by Mill's point that most good action benefits particular individuals, shopping locally spreads happiness through the Scranton community while Michael's habits export money and decision-making elsewhere. Dwight oscillates between stockholder logic (the cheapest health plan, poaching Jim's client in 'Diversity Day') and stakeholder-minded customer service, while 'Halloween,' 'Health Care,' and 'Branch Closing' show profit trumping people; Michael's successful sale to Christian at Chili's in 'The Client' balances both, and his 'Show me that farm' speech insists workers like Stanley and Phyllis are not replaceable cogs.
- ch. 26 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Thomas Nagel — Consequentialism; Utilitarianism — Johnson works through the standard objections to affirmative action using Scranton material: Ryan's paralysis before the all-Black management team in 'Traveling Salesmen' shows a single-race workforce is not intrinsically bad, while Michael's Chris Rock routine and his do-it-yourself slur exercise in 'Diversity Day' show that Dunder Mifflin meeting every quota does nothing about racism. A hypothetical about Dwight's grandfather refusing to hire Stanley's grandfather at the beet farm frames the compensation objection, answered by the 'cycle of poverty' account of the present effects of past discrimination. Finally, a fictitious hiring of guard Hank Tate over a better-qualified white candidate - justified, following Nagel, by the consequences of calming branch unrest - sets up the conclusion that education, not racially preferential hiring, would break minority poverty without discrimination, so affirmative action is ultimately unjustified.
- ch. 27 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Harry Frankfurt, John Stuart Mill, Karl Marx — Objectification; On Liberty; Ideology and False Consciousness; The Harm Principle — Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.
- ch. 28 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Catharine MacKinnon — Objectification; Dominance Approach (pornography and gender); Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Dromm asks what makes Michael's behavior wrong even where the law cannot touch it: as an 'equal-opportunity harasser' of Pam, Ryan, and Oscar, Michael seems to escape Title VII's discrimination requirement. He tests Edmund Wall's 'wrongful communication' definition against the filthy emails, 'that's what she said,' and Michael's solution to the Kevin-Angela dispute in 'Conflict Resolution,' finds it too broad and too dependent on the victim's objection, then turns to MacKinnon's sex-discrimination account and Crosthwaite and Priest's oppression account to explain the distinctive harm to women (pressuring Pam to be a cheerleader in 'Basketball,' calling the party-planning committee his 'bitches'). He concludes that both views are needed, and that in the end harassment wrongs workers by undermining their legitimate expectation of being judged only on job-relevant merit, leaving Dwight's extra effort done for nothing.
- ch. 29 "The Office and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Johnson asks what Dunder Mifflin morally owes after the obscene watermark scandal in 'Product Recall': stockholder theory says only refund and apologize insofar as that protects the bottom line, while stakeholder theory demands real amends to Barbara Allen and the Dunmore High prom attendees even at a profit cost. He then argues corporate responsibility cannot attach to a mindless company, and builds a criterion of blameworthiness - failing to do what it is one's job to do when that failure causally contributes to the incident - which convicts Creed (skipping his weekly mill quality checks all year), Michael (never verifying the inspections happened, despite his 'escape goat' apology video), and Jan (retaining an incompetent manager), all of whom should have been fired.
- ch. 30 "The Office and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 31 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Zeno of Citium — Philosophy of Love; Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Humanity as an End in Itself — Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.
- ch. 32 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, Saul Kripke, W.V.O. Quine, Aristotle, Plato — Naming and Necessity (rigid designators); Language Games; Theory of Forms; Potentiality and Actuality — Nys uses Brent's quiz grievance about Mr. Spock (half-Vulcan, half-human) and his Crufts pedigree-dog analogy, Gareth's 'look at the ears' classification test, the dwarf/midget/elf/pixie interrogation of Alex, and Tim and Dawn's 'lethal blow' prank to introduce the problem of natural kinds. Realist answers come from Kripke (water is H2O whatever we call it), Aristotle's matter-and-form essences, and the DNA evidence separating Bornean clouded leopards from mainland cousins, while Wittgenstein's language games and Quine's point that our innate similarity senses mislead support the constructivist that we lay classification on an unstructured world. The verdict: nature supplies real differences but never carves itself into kinds, and the line-drawing remains up to us.
- ch. 33 "The Office and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Luck defends Gareth's announcement that he 'knows no one is present' when Tim hides behind his wall of files: since Tim's presence is a fifty-fifty gamble, the Rule of Acceptance (believe only what is more likely than not) plus the Conjunction Principle commit Gareth to believing Tim both present and absent, so announcing is the only act consistent with both beliefs. A Brent-style redundancy lottery - rationally believing of each of thirty employees that they will not be fired while knowing someone must be - shows the same tolerable inconsistency, and the chapter concludes, following Graham Priest, that Gareth is an unwitting practitioner of paraconsistent logic.
- ch. 34 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, René Descartes, David Hume, Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas — Personal Identity; Struggle for Recognition; The Cogito; Bundle Theory of Self — Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.
- ch. 35 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard — Being-Toward-Death; Authenticity; Subjectivity Is Truth — Lonergan and Wisnewski read 'Grief Counseling' and 'Safety Training' as a case study in death-denial: Michael cannot parse the euphemism 'we lost Ed Truck,' Kelly must teach him to be sad, and Creed's report of the decapitation forces the Heideggerian realization that death is his own not-to-be-outstripped possibility, not just a fact of life. The office deflects with movie plots and euphemism (Jim's 'seriously hurt' about the rooftop stunt), Pam's eulogy for Toby's bird shows how mourning ritual copes with mortality, and Michael's longing to be remembered - hospital wings named after him, saving his own life - exemplifies Kierkegaard's 'world-historical' life as an ego defense, with living subjectively the recommended but unexplained alternative. Becker's thesis that all culture is a fabricated protest against death frames the whole chapter.
- ch. 36 "The Office and Philosophy" **·** Jean Baudrillard, Plato, Aristotle, Augustine of Hippo — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Written as a fake email thread among University of Scranton faculty, the appendix has junior professor Joe Kraus propose reading the town through Baudrillard's simulacrum - the 'Scranton Welcomes You' sign from the credits becoming real for him only as a TV image - while senior colleagues tutor him through the history of representation theory. Stephen deploys Plato's Ion (Socrates' magnet-and-iron chain of imitation, with Ion's Brent-like obliviousness) and Aristotle on mimesis, pity, fear, and catharsis to explain the show's tragicomic discomfort, while Maria adds the Antiochene, Alexandrian, and Augustinian fourfold senses of scripture applied to Scranton; Michael Friedman contributes a Chekhovian reading of Pam's bird eulogy as subtext about Michael's fear of dying alone. The thread itself mirrors an Office plotline as the senior faculty quietly decide to cut the untenured Joe out of the project.
- ch. 37 "The Office and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — This appendix compiles Dwight's talking-head 'facts' episode by episode through season four - his beet farm and volunteer sheriff's deputy credentials, the Assistant (to the) Regional Manager obsession, Schrute Bucks, the resorbed twin, shunning, bear lore, and recorder performances - followed by entries from his blog. It advances no philosophical argument and engages no philosopher; its role in the volume is to supply, in Dwight's own deadpan and self-contradictory idiom, the raw character material that the book's chapters on identity, classification, and workplace ethics draw on.
- ch. 38 "The Office and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 39 "The Office and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Olympics and Philosophy

- ch. 1 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics — Michael Austin argues that a truly Olympic greatness requires moral, not merely athletic, excellence, reading Aristotle's magnanimity (megalopsychia, 'greatness of soul') as the crowning virtue that unifies all others. He tests this against three Olympians: bobsledder Eugenio Monti, who lent a rival team a part and lost gold; sprinter Wilma Rudolph, who forced her homecoming parade to be integrated; and runner Emil Zatopek, who gave away his gold medal and defied the Soviet invasion of Prague. Using Robert Adams's idea of 'modules of virtue,' he explains why some champions show self-control in sport but not in life, whereas the magnanimous person holds every virtue across every domain.
- ch. 9 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli — Virtù and Fortuna; The Ends Justify the Means — Raymond Belliotti reads the twenty-year Olympic career of Italian sprinter Pietro Mennea, 'The Southern Arrow,' through Machiavelli's concept of virtu, the excellence relevant to one's function that lets a person master Fortuna. He distinguishes Machiavelli's military, political, civic, moral, and artistic virtu (using the Agathocles passage and the Life of Castruccio Castracani) and argues Mennea's physical prowess, mental toughness, and turning of anti-southern prejudice into motivation exemplify athletic virtu. Machiavelli would scoff at Olympic ideals of peace and brotherhood but relish the fierce international competition and the discipline of sport that Mennea embodied through his 1980 Moscow gold and later political career.
- ch. 10 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ralph Waldo Emerson — Amor Fati (love of fate); Self-Reliance; Will to Power — Scott Parker argues that distance runner Steve Prefontaine, who finished a medal-less fourth at Munich 1972, embodied the true essence of the Olympics better than any champion, an essence he identifies with Nietzsche's 'higher man' and Emerson's self-reliance rather than winning. He aligns Pre's front-running, effort, confidence, and will with Nietzschean self-overcoming and life-affirmation and Emersonian self-valuation, arguing value is what the valuer assigns himself through hard work. Reading Pre's exhausted stumble to the finish as a possible enactment of amor fati, love of fate, Parker holds that if Pre did his best he should love rather than merely accept his defeat.
- ch. 11 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Socrates — Tripartite Soul; The Apollonian and the Dionysian — Paul Cantor and Peter Hufnagel use Nietzsche's essay 'Homer's Contest' to argue that the competitive spirit the Greeks called thumos links philosophy and athletics, presenting Plato's dialogues as 'the Olympics of philosophy' in which Socrates is the last man standing. They trace thumos as the spirited third part of the soul in Plato's Republic, the guardians' quality that reason must tame through gymnastics and music, and as the force Socrates enlists to win the thumotic youths Glaucon and Adeimantus to philosophy. They then read Achilles in the Iliad and its funeral games in Book XXIII as a build-up/discharge/calm cycle of thumos, offering athletics as Homer's alternative channel for the same warlike energy.
- ch. 13 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Albert Camus — Virtue Ethics (arete); Eudaimonia (flourishing); The Myth of Sisyphus; The Golden Mean — Through an imagined Greek play featuring the Spartan 'trembler' Aristodemus and an Avery-Brundage-like IOC president, Jesus Ilundain-Agurruza argues for rethinking the Olympic motto and creed around three Greek virtues, aretE (excellence), andreia (courage), and kalon (noble beauty), grounded in Aristotle's virtue ethics, the mean, and eudaimonia. Using the Spartans exercising on the eve of Thermopylae, he defends a collaborative, non-instrumental conception of competition against record-obsession and cheating, exemplified by Eugenio Monti and Cecil Healy. He closes with Camus's Sisyphus, arguing the athlete pushes the rock in the spirit of aretE, spending energy joyfully 'just because,' turning punishment into sport.
- ch. 14 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Socrates — Virtue Ethics (arete); Tripartite Soul; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Heather Reid interprets the Olympic Charter's first Fundamental Principle through the ancient ideal of aretE, arguing the metaphysical structure of sport, contests that create purposeless obstacles, exists to cultivate and celebrate human excellence rather than to beat opponents or make money. Citing Plato the wrestler, Suits's definition of game-playing, and Homer's funeral games, she maps five virtues onto sport: eusEbeia (reverence for ideals beyond oneself), andreia (courageous endurance in agOn), sOphrosynE (harmonious power and control), dikaiosynE (justice as rule-order and proper function), and sophia (the athlete's pursuit of truth about human capacity, akin to 'flow'). The goal she proposes is the 'Olympian soul.'
- ch. 15 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Edmund Husserl, Emmanuel Levinas, Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Phenomenology; Intentionality; The Face of the Other — Douglas McLaughlin and Cesar Torres argue that Coubertin's vague Olympism is best clarified by the phenomenological concept of intersubjectivity developed by Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, and Levinas. Treating competitive sport (via Suits's lusory attitude and the 'testing family' notion of a mutual quest for excellence) as inherently social, they use intersubjectivity to dissolve the apparent contradiction between the motto's excellence and the creed's participation, since one's victory is meaningful only through worthy opponents one is answerable to. Invoking Levinas's ethics of the face, they ground Olympic values of mutual respect, fairness, and peace in the reciprocity athletes owe one another 'running shoulder to shoulder.'
- ch. 17 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — Cosmopolitanism; The End of Grand Narratives; Struggle for Recognition — Milan Hosta traces a dialectical line from the individual athlete through nationalism and internationalism to the transnational Olympic movement, arguing individualism 'turns into itself again' since the whole order is reproduced by individuals like Paavo Nurmi ('I run for myself, not for Finland'). He reads Coubertin's 'sincere internationalism' as a moral epistemology of knowing others (glossed via Morgan and a Hegelian account of tolerance as recognizing but not truly accepting difference) against the hollow cosmopolitanism of tourism and 'popular ethnography.' Drawing on postmodern pluralism and the end of grand narratives, plus Hardt and Negri's Empire, he frames the IOC as a peace-preaching yet blood-bathed transnational power sustained by record-seeking individuals.
- ch. 18 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Plato — The Categorical Imperative; Virtue Ethics; Euthyphro Dilemma — Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.
- ch. 19 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** John Rawls — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Utilitarianism; The Veil of Ignorance — Stephen Kershnar examines the three strongest arguments for the IOC's ban on performance-enhancing drugs, harm-to-self, harm-to-others, and unfairness, and argues each fails, using cases such as Ben Johnson's stripped 1988 gold and Marion Jones. Against harm-to-self he cites anti-paternalism and the far greater accepted risks of NFL play and boxing; against harm-to-others he shows PED pressure is no different from the pressure of rivals' superior training (a Prisoner's Dilemma leagues need not solve); against unfairness he tests four accounts of fairness, including a Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance model whose choosers might find banning steroids while allowing Lasik and high-tech gear arbitrary. He concludes the ban, if justified at all, rests only on contested utilitarian grounds like audience preference and protecting children.
- ch. 21 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(no index entry yet)* — Lewandowski argues Olympic boxing suffers from suboptimal 'constitutive rules' and applies Jon Elster's constraint theory, using Odysseus lashing himself to the mast to hear the Sirens as the model of 'constrained maximization' where a self-chosen constraint enables an otherwise impossible action. He contrasts the near-ruleless ancient pyx (the fatal Kreugas/Damoxenos bout) with modern boxing's over-tight constraints (short rounds, mandatory headgear, computerized scoring), showing both extremes fail to produce skilled, safe, creative competition. He proposes replacing headgear and button-scoring with safety monitors tracking headshots and holistic round-based judging of punches and ring generalship.
- ch. 22 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill, Aristotle — Utilitarianism; Practical Wisdom (phronesis); The Hedonic Calculus — Reitsma defends keeping the 'second-rate' Olympic men's football tournament against Bob Harig's 'Simply the best' litmus test, which would de-roster any event that is not the pinnacle of its sport. He likens Harig's proposed 'Olympic calculus' (scoring sports on tradition, parity, marketability) to Bentham and Mill's utilitarian maximization of a single value, and rejects both as oversimplifying an irreducibly plural decision. He argues the IOC instead rightly practices casuistry, case-by-case judgment that requires Aristotelian practical wisdom, and that dropping men's football (an under-23, FIFA-hampered tournament) would sacrifice the Olympics' global breadth for a false ideal of excellence.
- ch. 23 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Cornel West, W.E.B. Du Bois — Ressentiment; Double Consciousness — McDaniels reads Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Mexico City raised-fist protest as an expression of an 'oppositional consciousness' rooted in the memory of slavery and Jim Crow. He deploys Nietzsche's notion of ressentiment, the oppressed sufferer's rebellion against a dominant slave-making morality and need to release rage, and Cornel West's 'prophetic pragmatism', which frames struggle as tragic yet guided by integrity and justice, to interpret the sprinters' silent gesture. He also invokes the athletes' Du Boisian 'twoness' as black athletes and citizens, casting Smith and Carlos in a Douglass-to-Edwards lineage of public dissent as a vehicle of black liberation.
- ch. 25 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Judith Butler — Gender Performativity; Feminism; Objectification — Jonsson argues that modern sport enforces masculine norms and that the East German 'wonder girls' (Koch, Ender, Krabbe), along with Stella Walsh, Jarmila Kratochvilova and Caster Semenya, were 'gender radical' Amazons who challenged the link between masculinity and maleness by winning with 'masculine' bodies. Drawing on Judith Butler's claim that gender ideals are not static and women's sport can rearticulate them, he treats the doping-built Eastern Bloc athletes as progressive because they contradicted how female athletes are 'supposed' to look. He critiques Jane English's appeal to 'permanent biological differences' and laments that after 1989 commercialized sport (symbolized by Flo Jo's marketed femininity) hardened conservative gender norms again.
- ch. 26 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Martha Nussbaum — Objectification; Feminism; The Male Gaze — Weaving argues from a liberal-feminist standpoint that the FIVB's mandatory bikini-bottom rule for women's Olympic beach volleyball sexualizes and objectifies the athletes, contradicting Coubertin's ideals of universal humanity. Using Paul Davis's distinction between acceptable sexuality and objectionable sexualization (deliberate focus on body parts, freezing postures, punning captions like 'Buns of Gold'), and citing Nussbaum, Baker and Bartky on when treating someone as a sexual object becomes wrong, she shows the rule detaches athletes' bodies from their athletic agency. She traces harms including physical risk, the APA-documented effects of sexualization, a 'trickle-down' to school volleyball short-shorts, and exclusion of Islamic women.
- ch. 27 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Mahatma Gandhi — Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Just War Theory — Taliaferro and Le Gall examine when a nation or athlete may justifiably boycott the Olympics, distinguishing 'material' from 'formal' contribution and weighing available alternatives and the stringency of values (e.g., Gandhi's boycott of British goods, apartheid boycotts, the Lysistrata sex strike). They argue attending is not itself endorsement of the host regime, so the heavy, often irrecoverable cost to individual athletes places a strong burden of proof on any boycott. Surveying the 1956, 1980 and 1984 boycotts (which changed little) and the 1936 Berlin Games (where Jesse Owens's participation did real good), they conclude only a credible threat of serious bodily harm clearly justifies boycotting.
- ch. 29 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** John Rawls — Cosmopolitanism; Justice as Fairness — Hardman and Iorwerth argue that Olympic 'nation-swapping' should be judged by Coubertin's 'sincere internationalism' and Stephen Nathanson's 'moderate patriotism' (grounded, they note, in Rawls's justice as fairness), which permits a special but non-aggressive concern for one's country. They contrast the 'reflective national', whose national attachment evolves genuinely over time (the runner Wilson Kipketer settling in Denmark), with 'enlightened' and 'nomadic' cosmopolitans (Kenyan-born Qatari Saif Saaeed Shaheen bought for money, Jamaican-born Slovenian Merlene Ottey), whose transfers are economic and thin. They propose using Olympic Solidarity funding to offset the poverty that drives talent transfers rather than merely tightening Rule 42.
- ch. 30 "The Olympics and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Walter Benjamin, G.W.F. Hegel, Jean Baudrillard, Karl Marx — Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Aura of the Artwork; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); Commodity Fetishism — Sharpe analyzes the Olympics as an aestheticized 'spectacle' (Debord, after Marx's commodity analysis) whose real product is the shareable 'Olympic moment.' Reading Kant's Critique of Judgment through Terry Eagleton, he argues the games trade on the sensus communis Kant finds in the judgment 'this is beautiful', an intimated universal harmony among humans that mirrors the ancient Olympic ekecheiria (truce). He links Beijing 2008's simulated fireworks and lip-synced girl to Baudrillard's simulacra, and uses Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay, Riefenstahl's Olympia and Hegel's account of Greek sculpture to show how the Nazis' 1936 Games weaponized this aesthetic power, warning the spectacle serves both good and evil.
- ch. 31 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 32 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "The Olympics and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Onion and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "For Crying Out Loud" *(no index entry yet)* — Sharon M. Kaye's introduction recounts the legend that The Onion got its name from an uncle's suggestion while the founders ate onion sandwiches, then argues the dictionary definition of 'onion' fits perfectly: 'bulbous' things are inherently funny and 'pungent' things penetrate and burn. The Onion's satire is therefore philosophical, she concludes, because philosophers have always been critics of the society in which they live—an uncomfortable wake-up call, like heartburn—and the chapters ahead will 'unpeel' the connections.
- ch. 6 "Science and Technology" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Ridicule Is a Survival Strategy" **·** Thomas Aquinas — The Five Ways; Virtue Ethics — Kaye argues that the highest form of ridicule, which The Onion has mastered, targets not stupidity but cheating—specifically 'asscheating,' believing what you want to be true. She reads 'I Believe In Evolution, Except For The Whole Triassic Period' as skewering people who understand Darwin perfectly but exempt humans from evolution because admitting we are just another animal means admitting we die like everything else, the move behind Aquinas-style teleological add-ons that only invite a regress of gods supplying 'extras.' Articles on breast implants, the 'New Nietzschean Diet,' and Tour de France doping all show asscheats artificially inflating their evolutionary fitness; since natural selection stamps every organism with the purpose of survival and reproduction, asscheating is a vice, and ridiculing the asscheats who pollute the gene pool is itself a survival strategy.
- ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" **·** David Hume, William Paley, William of Ockham — Ockham's Razor; Falsificationism; The Watchmaker Argument (design); The Problem of Evil — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- ch. 9 "Area Philosopher (Me!) Is Sick Of The Stupid Debate About Stupid" **·** Philosophical Skepticism; Problem of Induction — Cuddy stages the generational-decline debate between Mark Bauerlein's The Dumbest Generation and Stephen Johnson's Everything Bad Is Good for You, showing that Onion stories can be marshaled for both sides: Aristophanes complaining that today's audiences 'just don't get me' vindicates the perennial declinist, while 'US Students Lead World in Detention' wryly supports Johnson's sleeper curve. Comparing Bauerlein to Aristophanes and the 'Our Dumb World' entry on Aristotle and Plato's schools closing, he concludes every era teems with idiots, so The Onion could have existed in any century. Because induction from earlier generations' failed predictions cannot settle whether Millennials really are dumber, he suspends judgment and toasts The Onion as the smartest perspective around.
- ch. 10 "Opinion" *(front)*
- ch. 11 "In All Fucking Seriousness" **·** Aristotle, Confucius — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics (arete); The Junzi (exemplary person) — Arp asks why well-placed 'fucks' in Onion headlines like 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' are funny, and answers with the golden mean traced to Aristotle and Confucius, who both prized self-control and being a good role model to children: swearing is virtuous when it hits the mean between the vice of too much (gangsta rap's every-other-word profanity, the cemetery gardener's rant, Glengarry Glen Ross) and the vice of too little. He sorts Onion stories into vice tables—'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer' illustrates the vice of cowardice, with courage as the hitting-the-mark mean—and concludes that a well-placed fuck is both funny and virtuous precisely because so many people treat the word as taboo.
- ch. 12 "More Asshole Morality" **·** Peter Singer — Hallquist observes that Dan Savage's 'Savage Love' column, syndicated in The Onion, treats 'asshole' not as a mere expletive but as a property that can be discovered, disagreed about, and used to explain behavior—raising exactly the puzzles philosophers raise about morality. He defends an expressivist account modeled on Ayer's: 'Dan Savage is an asshole' expresses an attitude while picking out a range of behavior defined by shared attitudes, and he answers the classic objections (logic requires truth-aptness, moral disagreement seems factual, we ask third parties who the asshole is) by adapting Singer's point that logic applies to commands and attitudes too, and by showing disagreement over assholery is a conflict of attitudes we still have urgent practical reason to resolve. Since the standard arguments against moral expressivism would equally refute this intuitively plausible asshole-expressivism, the objections must fail, giving moral expressivism a modest positive argument.
- ch. 13 "Jesus Delays Second Coming Because Of Offensive Article" **·** David Hume, John Stuart Mill — The Problem of Evil — Littmann runs Hume's Dialogues argument from evil through Onion headlines: 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy' (Timmy Yu's resounding no), 'God Outdoes Terrorists Yet Again,' 'God Wastes Miracle On Running Catch In Outfield,' and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways As Motive In Killing Of 3,000 Papua New Guineans.' He dispatches the theodicies one by one: limiting God's power or goodness (as Mill's lesser deity would) abandons the God of the tradition; the free will defense fails because police rightly restrain gunmen and no human freedom explains hurricanes; soul-building is pointless for a being who could implant compassion innately or stage fake evils; the 'no best possible world' dodge would excuse the reporter who watches a man burn; and the mystery defense makes reason useless. He concludes no all-knowing, all-good, all-powerful God exists, while insisting readers think it through for themselves.
- ch. 14 "Politics" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Area Man And Woman Wonder What They Are Good For" **·** Feminism — Benatar uses The Onion's 'Area Man' to stage the Hart–Devlin debate: Lord Devlin made the man on the Clapham omnibus's 'real feeling of reprobation' the test for when law may enforce society's morality against private homosexual acts, and H.L.A. Hart replied that shared values can be wicked (Nazi Germany) and that societies transform rather than disintegrate when values change—confirmed by Onion Area Men who hate their gay coworker, have gay sex to dodge the office blood drive, or have spent eight years 'experimenting,' none of which dissolved Britain or America. The chapter adds the feminist complaint that treating the Area Man as the norm erases Area Woman, and closes with Joel Feinberg's crowded-bus thought experiment from Offense to Others: average disgust is relevant to regulating public offense but never decisive, so the ordinary person interests legal philosophy without being its arbiter.
- ch. 16 "A Newspaper Gone to the Dogs . . . Enlightened Dogs" **·** Diogenes the Cynic, Socrates — Cynicism (living according to nature) — Bayan traces 'cynic' to the Greek kynikos ('doglike') and the philosophy to Socrates' virtue, poverty, and integrity, through the proto-Cynic Antisthenes to Diogenes of Sinope—the man in the tub, the plucked chicken at Plato's Academy, 'you can step out of my sunlight'—arguing that Cynicism is fierce moral opposition to sham and hypocrisy, which is exactly why the powerful smear cynics. Distinguishing The Onion's cool, Swiftian irony from postmodern 'pseudocynicism,' he concludes the paper is genuinely Cynical: headlines like 'Black Guy Asks Nation for Change' (the Obama reveal), 'God Angrily Clarifies Don't Kill Rule,' and 'Dictator Slays Millions in Last-Minute Push to Be Time's Man of the Year' nuzzle the kind, bark at the greedy, and bite scoundrels, so Diogenes would have read The Onion with paternal fondness.
- ch. 17 "Banal Sex" **·** Heteronormativity; Objectification; Feminism — Marinucci reads The Onion's sex coverage as 'terminally ambiguous': 'Nation's Gays Demand Right To Library Cards,' 'Massachusetts Supreme Court Orders All Citizens To Gay Marry,' and 'New Bill Would Defend Marriage From Sharks' ridicule the idea that gay marriage threatens straight marriage, while 'Area Homosexual Saves Four From Fire: Heroic Neighbor Praised, Gay' exposes how heterosexism defines gay people sexually while heterosexual men pass as normal, natural, and neutral. Yet the paper also trades in gay stereotypes and mocks the very framework—characters like Amanda Oppel ('Lesbian Identity Ends Abruptly Mid-Junior Year'), the 'Bar Skanks Announce Plans To Kiss,' and Bruce Heffernan of 'Why Do All These Homosexuals Keep Sucking My Cock?' both defy and seem to reaffirm the stability of sexual identity categories. Weighing queer theory (via Jagose) and Golden's fluid 'elective lesbians' against the parody of 'Grad Student Deconstructs Take-Out Menu,' she concludes the paper's stance is deliberately undecidable, perhaps recommending we stop over-thinking sex and treat minority sexual identities as banal, as in 'Gay Couple Has Banal Sex.'
- ch. 18 "Scientists Find Anomalies In And Then Go Back and Kill Your Grandparents" **·** David Hume, René Descartes — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; The Cogito — This chapter is a satirical fake-news 'World' section rather than an essay: 'Vigilante Group Tracks and Kills Storm-Causing Chaos Butterflies' literalizes the butterfly effect of chaos theory, 'Great Thinkers Fired From Canon' mocks citation metrics by crowning 'Ibidem' history's most-cited philosopher, 'University Restructures To Remain Financial: Becomes Bank' parodies corporatized academia as sympathetic magic, and 'ADD Sufferers Fail Cogito: Don't Exist' has distracted patients pop out of existence for failing Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am.' The title story, about physicists whose experiment lets them go back and kill their grandparents, is printed with its sentences scrambled into a reporter's phone-call fragments, enacting its own point that, as Hume noted, causal order is never perceived only imposed—and with quantum time-symmetry and the grandfather paradox, time's arrow jumps wherever it likes, even into loops.
- ch. 19 "Funny Newspaper Makes Accurate Prophecy" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Plato, Socrates — Geist (World Spirit); History Has a Direction — Auxier takes the September 28, 2001 Onion issue—'Hijackers Surprised To Find Selves In Hell,' published while late-night TV was still in mourning—to ask what makes some comedy permissible and durable, glancing back at Aristophanes' caricature of Socrates in The Clouds and the circle-men speech Plato puts in his mouth in the Symposium. Hegel supplies the machinery: comedy as a moment of Art within Absolute Spirit may only bring to naught what is already null, while irony that diminishes the noble degrades the ironist—which is why the Warren Commission is fair game for 'Smithsonian Janitor Finds Magic Bullet' but Martin Luther King, a World Historical Individual whose individuality embodies his movement, can never anchor the 'Mrs. Williams Finally Decides Dinner Guest Is Not Going to Show' story. Since 'the news' itself is the great nullity—partial time-slices pretending to explain complex events before their meanings are interpretable—The Onion's rapid 9/11 satire was legitimate and even prophetic, deflating the bullshit of those posing as arbiters of Objective Spirit.
- ch. 20 "Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy" **·** David Hume, G.W.F. Hegel, Jean-Paul Sartre, Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger — Bundle Theory of Self; Master–Slave Dialectic; The Death of God; Existentialism — Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.
- ch. 21 "Business" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 22 "World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent" **·** John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant, Aristotle, Socrates, Diogenes the Cynic — Deontology; Consequentialism; Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis) — Dan Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant, uses Onion medical stories — 'Loved Ones Recall Local Man's Cowardly Battle With Cancer,' the 'Vehicular Manslaughter Doctor,' animal hoarder Tricia McCory's 'I'm A Diseased And Deformed Animal Lover,' and the Terry Schiavo American Voices — to survey how end-of-life decisions actually get made. He runs each dilemma through Mill's consequentialism, Kant's deontology, and Aristotle's virtue ethics (with Monty Python's Philosopher's Song as running gag), then through Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics, showing that McCory's kindness to dying animals fails autonomy and nonmaleficence because kindness can be cruel. The chapter closes by restoring 'euthanasia' to its Greek meaning of 'good death,' arguing that accepting the 100 percent death rate means planning ahead with living wills and honest bad-news delivery rather than dying tube-filled in an ICU.
- ch. 23 "The Onion’s New Environmental Ethic" **·** Peter Singer, Immanuel Kant, Thomas Aquinas — Anthropocentrism; Animal Liberation; Speciesism; Ecofeminism — Matthew Altman reads Onion environmental satire as a staged escape from anthropocentrism: 'New, Delicious Species Discovered' and 'Beauty Of National Forest Enjoyed By Logger' expose that even appreciating nature is just valuing it for us, while the mascara-testing lab rabbit and 'Funny Monkey Tested On' make Singer's speciesism charge vivid against factory farming and animal experiments. He then widens the argument to a biocentric concern for species and ecosystems via 'Stuffed-Animal Biodiversity Rising' and 'Consumer-Product Diversity Now Exceeds Biodiversity,' and to ecofeminism via 'Raped Environment Led Polluters On,' where the forest as flirtatious woman links domination of nature to sexism and victim-blaming. Global stories like the Bush 'national air conditioner' piece show Western overconsumption displacing blame onto Third World overpopulation, and 'I'm Doing My Inconsequential Part' satirizes the self-satisfaction of green consumerism itself — leaving the measure of the Onion's philosophical importance as how dangerous it is.
- ch. 24 "Local" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "The Onion, Sarcasm, and the Good of Mankind" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life — Noah Levin recounts how the Onion article 'Area Man Committed To Being Spicy Food Guy' made him recognize his own obnoxious boasting about hot food and quietly change, presenting satire as continuing philosophy's self-help tradition back to Socrates' 'know thyself.' He distinguishes parody, satire, and sarcasm, then formalizes Onion jokes — the RIAA suing radio stations for giving away free music, and 'That Teen-Abstinence Rally Totally Rocked!' — as implicit reductio ad absurdum arguments whose absurd conclusions force rejection of a hidden premise. The sarcastic route beats a direct lecture, he argues, because the target must complete the three-step argument himself: identify the mocked trait, admit having it, and decide whether to change.
- ch. 26 "The Guy Is Not Alone. ." **·** Socrates, Bertrand Russell, Heraclitus — Everything Flows / Logos; The Absurd — Matt Laubenthal confesses he was the philosophy-class windbag and defends Darrin Floen of 'Guy In Philosophy Class Needs To Shut The Fuck Up' as heir to Socrates' gadfly role, noting the Athenians also wanted their relentless questioner dead. He teaches Russell's Paradox through a Burger King 's.h.i.t. load' — the set of all sets that are not members of themselves — and reconstructs Darrin's Heraclitean rejoinder that if everything flows and nothing stands still, the static either/or of set membership dissolves the contradiction. Along the way he reads the Onion's Kafka International Airport story ('Are you who you say you are?' repeated for eighty minutes) as existentialist absurdity, and the Star Trek Voyager holographic Doctor as a puzzle about whether a self could be nothing more than mathematical code.
- ch. 27 "News Archive" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Get Serious" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, David Hume, William of Ockham, Ludwig Wittgenstein, William James, René Descartes — Faith and Reason; Problem of Induction; Ockham's Razor; The Death of God — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- ch. 29 "Progress" **·** Jean-François Lyotard, Jean Baudrillard, Richard Rorty — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The End of Grand Narratives; Language Games — Gregory Gilson argues that although The Onion deliberately reports falsehoods, it embodies postmodern theories of truth better than the newspapers it parodies. Lyotard's mercantilization of knowledge and the fragmentation of dominant narratives into separate language games explain headlines like 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity' and 'Astronomer Discovers The Center Of The Universe Is His Beautiful 9-Year Old Son,' which smash incompatible discourses together, while Baudrillard's simulacrum and hyper-reality explain how The Onion — like Disneyworld — is branded fake precisely so mainstream media can seem real. Yet the chapter closes honestly: its own criticism of 'Bush Says He Still Believes Iraq War Was the Fun Thing To Do' assumed some targets were wrong, which assumes a Truth out there — the paradox of a satire whose truthfulness exceeds its own theory of truth.
- ch. 30 "Voltaire Lives" **·** Gottfried Leibniz — The Problem of Evil; The Best of All Possible Worlds — Douglas Ficek traces The Onion's God stories — 'Lord Under Investigation For Failure To Provide,' God refusing to heal paralyzed little Timmy Yu, and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways' — back through Voltaire's Candide to Leibniz's theodicy, the 'best of all possible worlds' doctrine that Dr. Pangloss keeps reciting through hanging, slavery, and syphilis until Candide concludes we must cultivate our garden. The chapter's sharpest claim is that theodicy works by victim-blaming: Jerry Falwell's 9/11 rant earned the headline-only 'Jerry Falwell: Is That Guy A Dick Or What?' because he excused God by blaming secular Americans, just as Pastor Ellsworth blames heathen tsunami victims. Following theologian Dorothee Soelle, Ficek names this 'theological sadism,' and offers the Bible-drop missionaries of 'Poverty-Stricken Africans Receive Desperately Needed Bibles' as a modern Pangloss who mistakes moral obliviousness for grace.
- ch. 31 "Entertainment" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "Point-Counterpoint Funny versus Really, Really Funny" **·** René Descartes, Bertrand Russell — Philosophical Skepticism — Andrew Terjesen starts from real cases of Onion satire taken literally — a Michigan sheriff warning about al-Qaida telemarketing, the Beijing Evening News plagiarizing 'Congress Threatens To Leave D.C.', Deborah Norville reporting that 58 percent of American exercise is televised — and explains them through the Problem of Other Minds. Descartes' hats-and-cloaks worry and Russell's analogy solution show how we infer that a straight-faced writer is 'just kidding,' but the analogy fails when cultural context, prejudice (Fred Phelps citing the gay-recruitment story, Christians forwarding the Harry Potter Satanism piece), or wishful thinking breaks the comparison with our own joking behavior. The upshot is that humor is engineered misunderstanding — the Onion works by analogy to real news, and could never warn readers off without destroying the joke.
- ch. 33 "Philosophy and Humor" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein, William James — Language Games — Thomas Brommage builds on Wittgenstein's quip that a serious and good philosophical work could consist entirely of jokes: philosophy for Wittgenstein is a therapeutic activity that dissolves pseudo-problems and lays our linguistic practices open to view, never delivering theories. Onion humor works the same way — 'Bill Gates Grants Self 18 Dexterity, 20 Charisma' needs the shared form of life of D&D-style geek culture, the 'Ask a Salmon' advice column breaks the rule that answers answer, and 'Youthful Tendency Disorder' makes the familiar (children running, jumping, and playing pretend) strange enough to skewer ADHD over-diagnosis and pharmaceutical marketing. Since Wittgenstein asks why we feel a grammatical joke to be deep, jokes that expose our conceptual confusions can themselves be serious arguments — which is exactly what a philosophy joke book, and The Onion, deliver.
- ch. 34 "Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal" **·** Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Utilitarianism — Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.

## The Philosophy of Ang Lee

- ch. 1 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Confucius, Laozi, Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche — Authenticity; Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Taoism (Daoism); Wu Wei (effortless action) — The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.
- ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Laozi, Confucius, Zhuangzi — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way); The Junzi (exemplary person); Yin and Yang — McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.
- ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Confucius, Laozi, Immanuel Kant — Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety); Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; The Tao (the Way) — Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.
- ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Xunzi, Confucius, Mencius — Li (ritual propriety); Xiao (filial piety); Human Nature Is Bad (and needs ritual) — Thompson argues that Lee's 'cowboy aesthetic' of rugged isolation in Brokeback Mountain (Ennis and Jack) and Crouching Tiger (Li Mu Bai, Shu Lien, Jen) is only apparent: the characters are always already embedded in Confucius' five cardinal relationships, read through Xunzi's darker view that selfish desire must be curbed by ritual and social hierarchy. Ennis and Jack seem lone individuals but are defined by ties to Alma, family and each other, and Jen's redemption comes when she abandons self-serving desire to re-establish her Confucian relationships. Citing Nietzsche's gloss on Aristotle that only a beast or a god lives alone, it concludes there is no truly isolated cowboy.
- ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Mencius, Confucius — Human Nature Is Good; Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Li (ritual propriety) — Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.
- ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Immanuel Kant — Yin and Yang; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime — Jameson and Brace read Sense and Sensibility and Brokeback Mountain through Burke's and Gilpin's aesthetics of the sublime, the beautiful and the picturesque, mapped onto the Chinese yin/yang and qi of landscape. In Sense and Sensibility, manicured French/Brownian gardens (beautiful, sanctioned) versus wild picturesque nature (sublime, passionate) mirror Elinor's controlled sense and Marianne's storm-caught sensibility, with Willoughby's rescue and Brandon's steadiness keyed to landscape. In Brokeback Mountain the masculine sublime wilderness (yang) versus feminine confining civilization (yin) is built through tightly framed interiors, sweeping exteriors and an 'aesthetics of isolation' that exposes American freedom as a costly illusion for Ennis and Jack.
- ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Xunzi, Mencius, Confucius, Zhuangzi, Laozi — Li (ritual propriety); Human Nature Is Bad (and needs ritual); Human Nature Is Good — Dull reads Eat Drink Man Woman through a Hall-and-Ames 'focus-field' model of personhood, analyzing harmony via metaphors of a culinary dish, music and a sports team where each element keeps its integrity within a whole. He diagnoses the Chu family by pairing Mencius (morality as expression of the four sprouts) against Xunzi (desire must be structured by ritual): Chef Chu is 'repressed as a turtle', Jia-Jen hides behind ritual, Jia-Ning acts on impulse, and Jia-Chien lacks direction. Their romantic transformations restore harmony, answering Chu's question 'is there more than food and sex?' affirmatively, as expression, desire and ritual come into balance and his sense of taste returns.
- ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Aristotle, Confucius, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — The Golden Mean; Virtue Ethics; The Categorical Imperative; The Harm Principle — Roberts argues that across Lee's 'Father Knows Best' trilogy (Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman) the clash between traditional Confucian values and Western modernity is best resolved by the virtue ethics of Confucius and Aristotle rather than by deontology or utilitarianism. Master Chu literally refusing to be pushed, the Gaos accepting Winston's homosexual relationship, and Chef Chu adapting to his daughters all require Aristotle's golden mean and habituated virtue, which accommodate special relationships and situations. Kant's categorical imperative (rejecting paternalism as treating persons as means) and Mill's harm principle are shown to be too rule-bound to reconcile tradition with modern individualism.
- ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Wu Wei (effortless action) — Kroustallis reads Lust, Caution through perception rather than hidden emotion, arguing Wong Chia Chi abandons the disengaged, sight-only aesthetic of Mrs. Mak and comes to perceive Mr. Yee's world with her whole engaged body. He uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to justify the three graphic sex scenes as bodily, essentially ambiguous cognition (the lipstick-marked cup, the flat key as motor intentionality) that links perception directly to action without unconscious representations. He frames Wong's development toward harmony via Fang Dongmei's neo-Confucian 'creative creativity' and a yin-yang polarity of meek and strong, with rain and jasmine flowers as an engaged natural environment.
- ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on the Soul; Personal Identity; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.
- ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Michel Foucault — Authenticity; Bad Faith; Discipline and Docile Bodies — Dale and Foy argue that across Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Hulk and Brokeback Mountain, Lee presents a pessimistic, Sartrean philosophy of identity in which authentic selves are irreconcilable with a hostile social world. They read Jen's caged gender rebellion and Jade Fox's rejection, Bruce's suppressed origins and rage-fueled transformation, and Ennis and Jack's concealed love as hidden identities that produce dislocation, deception and disorder. Invoking Kierkegaard and Heidegger's dasein on authenticity and Foucault's Discipline and Punish, they show society disciplining deviance so each hero is displaced or destroyed—Jack beaten to death like Matthew Shepard, the Hulk exiled to the Amazon.
- ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Jacques Lacan — Ahimsa (nonviolence); The Mirror Stage; One-Dimensional Man — Zietsma reads Hulk and Taking Woodstock as antiwar films that subvert the hegemonic culture of heroic violence, fitting Lackey's category of universal (Gandhian/early-Christian) pacifism. He argues both films disturb their genre's expected narrative and demasculinize the hero: Elliot the gay nonviolent hero and the transgender vet Vilma, and a weeping Hulk who is rescued by Betty and finally gives up his power rather than kill David Banner. He reads the bathroom-mirror 'Puny human' scene as an inverted Lacanian mirror stage unmasking America's violent militarism, framing the Vietnam War and war on terror as violence that only begets more violence.
- ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** The Buddha, Judith Butler, Michel Foucault — Heteronormativity; Compassion (karuna); Impermanence (anicca) — Kang argues Lee's Taking Woodstock desexualizes and 'recloset[s]' Elliot Tiber's gay coming-out memoir, substituting a fluid 'queer' openness for Tiber's political gay identity and framing his homosexuality as an incidental, situationally-straight product of the festival (the woman-centered threesome, the chaste kiss with Paul). Drawing on Sedgwick, Butler and Foucault's history of sexuality, she critiques how the film neutralizes homophobia and omits the gay Buddhist mentor Georgette, whose teaching on karma, samsara and dukkha grounds Tiber's self-acceptance and unconditional love—reducing a gay everyman's struggle to one 'not-normal freak' among a hundred thousand.
- ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Jean-Paul Sartre, Harry Frankfurt, Aristotle — Philosophy of Love; Struggle for Recognition; The Look (hell is other people) — Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.
- ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; The Absurd — Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.
- ch. 23 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Carl Jung, The Buddha — Being-Toward-Death; Zen Buddhism; The Tao (the Way) — Hole reads The Ice Storm's prophetic opening as a meditation on 'what is impending', weaving existentialism with Zen Buddhism and Daoism. He uses the Four Noble Truths and the Zen story of the monk 'still carrying the woman' to show the families suffer through attachment to rigid self-images, and Jung's synchronicity and the Daoist dao/wu-wei to read the ice storm's formation and Mikey's chance electrocution as an interdependent flow the characters resist. Centrally he applies Heidegger's being-toward-death—death as ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped—arguing that fleeing one's death is fleeing one's authentic being, alongside Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Nietzsche's living dangerously; he closes by applying the argument to his own mortality.
- ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" **·** Niccolò Machiavelli, Sun Tzu — The Ends Justify the Means; Virtù and Fortuna; Just War Theory — Mahon asks whether Ride with the Devil endorses the proverb that all's fair in love and war, locating the film's moral core in its outsiders—the German immigrant Jake, the freed slave Holt, and the young widow Sue Lee. Against Sunzi's undiscriminating claim that warfare is the art of deceit, he argues the film sides with Machiavelli's Discourses distinction between honorable ruses of war and dishonorable perfidy: the bushwhackers' wearing of Union blue and Jake's lies are ruses, but the Lawrence massacre and refusing to ambush women under a truce mark limits Jake will not cross. In love, Sue Lee's shift from romantic lying to 'now is the truth' shows honesty is finally required, so all is not fair.
