## The Philosophy of Film Noir

- ch. 1 "Title Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Copyright Page" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Dedication" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Contents" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Foreword" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, William James — The Death of God; Transcendentalism; Existentialism — Robert Porfirio's foreword traces film noir's dark sensibility to a native strain in American culture rather than only to imported existentialism, running from Puritan gloom through Poe, Melville, and Hawthorne to the hard-boiled pulp of Hammett, Chandler, and Woolrich. He argues that William James's pragmatism sounded the death knell of the Emersonian/Thoreauvian transcendentalist faith in self-reliance and nature, leaving the way open for Darwinism, Freudianism, and Nietzschean pessimism to reduce the individual to a 'waif amidst forces.' He connects this to the Germanic emigres who brought expressionist style, suggesting they were drawn to an American darkness already present, and closes wondering what post-9/11 neo-noir will make of the same fear and paranoia.
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Introduction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, Aristotle, Arthur Schopenhauer — Existentialism; The Death of God; The Meaning of Life; The Absurd — Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.
- ch. 8 "Part 1 The Essence and Elements of Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Nietzsche and the Meaning and Definition of Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates, Plato, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Albert Camus — The Death of God; Theory of Forms; Everything Flows / Logos; Existentialism — Mark Conard uses The Postman Always Rings Twice and Goodis's Night Squad to survey the failed attempts to define noir (genre, style, cycle, mood) and contrasts two theories of definition: Socrates/Plato's search for the essential form versus Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, in which no stable 'being' exists behind becoming and language falsifies a world in motion, making essences and definitions fictions ('I am afraid we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar'). He proposes that noir is best understood as an American artistic response to Nietzsche's death of God, the loss of transcendent meaning and value that produces noir's pessimism, alienation, and moral disorientation, citing Sam Spade shrugging off his partner's murder and Ole Andersen passively awaiting his killers. Ironically, the same flux that makes noir what it is (the death of God) is what makes noir impossible to define.
- ch. 10 "A Darker Shade Realism in Neo-Noir" **·** G.E. Moore — The Naturalistic Fallacy; Moral Relativism — Jason Holt argues that realism, especially about the role values play in people's lives, is the underappreciated essence of noir, offering a working definition of noir as 'stylized crime realism.' Surveying neo-noir detectives (Harper, Chinatown's Gittes), revamped femmes fatales who get away with it (Body Heat's Matty, The Last Seduction's Bridget), morally ambiguous protagonists (To Live and Die in L.A., Manhunter), and Lynch and Tarantino, he shows how the post-Production-Code freedom lets endings ring true to life by letting the guilty escape justice. He coins the 'normativistic fallacy' as the inverse of Moore's naturalistic fallacy: inferring what is from what ought to be, arguing that mainstream cinema's poetic justice commits it while neo-noir's downbeat endings correct it, fulfilling the realism latent in classic noir.
- ch. 11 "Moral Clarity and Practical Reason in Film Noir" **·** Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Plato — Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Virtue Ethics; The Categorical Imperative; Moral Relativism — Aeon Skoble argues against the common view that noir depicts a world without ethics, contending that noirs are actually exercises in moral clarity. He reads Frank Chambers's deliberations in Postman and Walter Neff's in Double Indemnity as Aristotelian practical reasoning gone wrong (they fail eudaimonia and are punished), while Sam Spade's decision to turn in Brigid shows objective good reasons at work. Using Touch of Evil, he shows that a corrupt cop like Quinlan being pursued affirms moral realism and refutes subjectivism, and he sides with Aristotelian virtue and Platonic objective justice over Kant's rigid categorical imperative (which would forbid the detective's useful lies or lying to Nazis). He concludes that because bad noir characters do not flourish, even films about immoral acts are morally edifying rather than corrupting role models.
- ch. 12 "Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Carl Jung — The Death of God; Existentialism; Yin and Yang; Archetypes — Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.
- ch. 13 "From Sherlock Holmes to the Hard-Boiled Detective in Film Noir" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gilles Deleuze, René Descartes — The Pragmatic Method; The Rhizome; The Death of God; Will to Power — Jerold Abrams argues that the noir detective inherits the Holmes/Dupin detective logic but inhabits a fundamentally different maze. Using Eco's three labyrinths, he maps the classical Greek maze (with faith as Ariadne's string) and the mannerist maze (with Cartesian/Kantian pure reason) onto the escapable world of classic detection, and the Deleuzian rhizomatic maze, born after Nietzsche dissolved reason into will to power, onto noir's inescapable world (The Third Man, Kiss Me Deadly, The Maltese Falcon's fake statue). He shows both detectives use Peircean abduction (the logic of guessing) rather than pure deduction, illustrating it with knife-wound examples and Calloway's trapdoor inference in The Third Man, while the noir femme fatale becomes the anti-Ariadne whose thread of clues leads only to the hangman's rope.
- ch. 14 "Part 2 Existentialism and Nihilism in Film Noir" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Film Noir and the Meaning of Life" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Albert Camus, Thomas Nagel, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Meaning of Life; The Absurd; Philosophical Pessimism; Existentialism — Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.
- ch. 16 "The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent" **·** Albert Camus, Friedrich Nietzsche, Sigmund Freud, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; The Death of God; The Unconscious; Rebellion and Revolt — Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.
- ch. 17 "Symbolism, Meaning, and Nihilism in Quentin TaranTino's Pulp Fiction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle — The Death of God; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Conard reads Pulp Fiction as a study of American nihilism in Nietzsche's 'God is dead' sense: with no transcendent framework of value, Jules and Vincent orient their lives by transient pop-culture icons (Jack Rabbit Slim's, the Fonz) and by Marsellus Wallace's arbitrary power, so the mysterious briefcase has worth only because he wills it. He contrasts this void with Aristotelian ethics, where a thing's good lies in realizing its rational essence. Jules's transformation begins when he survives the misfired shots and reinterprets his Ezekiel 25:17 recitation as a call to be 'the Shepherd,' while Butch's choice of the samurai sword over the baseball bat signals a return to an objective warrior code beyond the empty pop icons.
- ch. 18 "Part 3 Six Classic Films Noirs" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Film Noir and the Frankfurt School America as Wasteland in Edgar Ulmer's Detour" **·** Theodor Adorno, Walter Benjamin, Herbert Marcuse — The Culture Industry; The Aura of the Artwork — Cantor argues that Ulmer's Detour deconstructs the American dream in a manner that closely parallels the Frankfurt school's culture critique. Al Roberts's westward journey toward success collapses into crime and doom, dramatizing Horkheimer and Adorno's claim in 'The Culture Industry' that Hollywood sells the masses an illusory lottery of hope (Haskell's horse 'Paradisical,' Sue's failed stardom) to reconcile them to capitalism. Cantor ties Roberts's disgust at jukebox music and his 'jazzing up' of Brahms directly to Adorno's polemics against mechanical reproduction and Benjamin's loss of the artwork's aura. He finally suggests both Ulmer and the émigré Marxists project a European elitist alienation onto an America they picture as an empty wasteland.
- ch. 20 "Knowledge, Morality, And Tragedy in The Killers and Out of the Past" **·** Aristotle — The Male Gaze — Jarvie tests whether The Killers and Out of the Past rise to tragedy in Aristotle's Poetics sense and answers no. Using Aristotle's demands for noble protagonists acting on principle, a fatal error, and a catharsis of pity and terror, he shows that Swede and Jeff are self-centered moral cowers ensnared by femmes fatales (Kitty, Kathie) whose only 'error' is sexual susceptibility, which is banal rather than tragic. He argues the films' 'personal morality' is incoherent because morality is social, and that their false-appearance mystery plots plus flippant normalizing codas (Reardon's insurance office, The Kid's lie to Ann) reassure audiences and encourage the puritanical 'sexy woman as succubus' myth instead of educing genuine catharsis.
- ch. 21 "Moral Man in the Dark City Film Noir, the Postwar Religious Revival, and The Accused" **·** Sigmund Freud — The Death Drive (Thanatos); The Male Gaze — Palmer nuances the 'dark mirror' theory of noir by recovering a redemptive subgroup, reading Dieterle's The Accused through the postwar religious revival and the writings of Reinhold Niebuhr and Erich Fromm. Where Lang's The Woman in the Window only chastens its professor via a dream, The Accused stages a genuinely penitential arc: repressed psychology professor Wilma Tuttle kills the aggressive student Bill in panic, then is therapeutically forced to relive the crime (at the prizefight and in the reenactment) until love with lawyer Warren Ford delivers her from 'separateness.' Palmer argues this patriarchal, therapeutic 'conversion'—glamorizing Loretta Young out of her mannish disguise—reconfigures Niebuhr's taming of passion and Fromm's account of love as a decision, heralding a coming 'culture of narcissism.'
- ch. 22 "On Reason and Passion in The Maltese Falcon" **·** Plato — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons); The Male Gaze — Knight argues that Sam Spade is not the dispassionate reasoner philosophy since Plato has assumed the detective to be, defending instead cognitivism about the emotions (via Solomon, de Sousa, and Damasio's Phineas Gage case). Because the hard-boiled detective enters events in media res, Spade must work hermeneutically to reconstruct the real story behind Brigid O'Shaughnessy's lies, and his judgments of trust, confidence, and loyalty fuse reason with feeling. In the climax Spade sends Brigid over for murdering Miles Archer precisely because reason and emotion together tell him he cannot trust her, whereas Brigid—the film's true cold calculator—only feigned emotion to make him her sap; Knight contrasts her with the non-fatale Vivian Rutledge of The Big Sleep.
- ch. 23 "Ride the Pink Horse Money, Mischance, Murder, and the Monads of Film Noir" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Gottfried Leibniz, Plato — The World as Will; Ethics of Compassion; Monadology — Silver reads Robert Montgomery's Ride the Pink Horse as a prototypically noir embodiment of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation. The revenge-driven Gagin, like Hugo, is enslaved to money and will—'a man can do what he wants, but not want what he wants'—and takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world, blind to the monads and Platonic-cave shadows of fate around him. Against him stand Pancho's suffering kindness and the Indian girl Pila's selfless compassion, which Silver aligns with Schopenhauer's dictum that 'compassion is the basis of all morality' and his prizing of aesthetic transcendence. The carousel (tío vivo) and the burning of Zozobra, the god of bad luck, become symbols of will's pointless circular striving from which only sacrifice and art offer escape.
- ch. 24 "Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 25 "Index" *(notes)*

## The Philosophy of Horror

- ch. 1 "Half Title" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Table of Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgements" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Gynaehorror as convention and challenge" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud — The Rhizome; Woman as the Other — This introductory chapter defines 'gynaehorror' as horror rooted in women's reproductive bodies (menstruation, virginity, pregnancy, motherhood, menopause), reading films like Inside, Vigil, Teeth, Alien, The Brood and Rosemary's Baby through it. It leverages Deleuze and Guattari's rhizome/becoming to reframe the monstrous female body not as a fixed molar 'being' but as a productive, boundary-breaching 'becoming', while positioning woman as the abject Other against which the male subject defines himself. It argues horror is simultaneously conservative (punishing women) and potentially radical.
- ch. 8 "Heteronormative horrors" **·** Judith Butler, Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud, Gilles Deleuze — Heteronormativity; A Vindication of the Rights of Woman; Gender Performativity — Reading virgins and the vagina dentata as the dyad through which horror polices female sexuality, the chapter uses Irigaray's account of the virgin as prop to male subjectivity and Creed's femme castratrice to analyse Halloween's 'Final Girl', Teeth's toothed-vagina revenge on abstinence-only purity culture, Jennifer's Body and Haute Tension. It closes with Rich's 'compulsory heterosexuality' and Wittig's 'heterosexual contract' to argue horror naturalises heteronormativity by casting female sexuality as either contained (virgin) or monstrously open (vagina dentata).
- ch. 9 "‘Pro-life’ and Pro-Life" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud, Gilles Deleuze — Woman as the Other; The Problem of Evil — The chapter argues that horror films about pregnancy (Rosemary's Baby, Demon Seed, The Reaping, Prophecy, Inside) pit a foetal 'subject' against the pregnant woman, eroding her selfhood by conflating her body with an invadable house or environment. Drawing on Young's, Battersby's and Tyler's phenomenologies of pregnant embodiment and Irigaray's 'woman as place', it shows how foetal-imaging technology and abortion politics (The Life Zone versus Carpenter's Pro-Life) reduce the woman to a vessel while the foetus is granted autonomous personhood.
- ch. 10 "Brave new worlds cyborg futures and female subjectivity" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Simone de Beauvoir, Sigmund Freud — The Rhizome; Mind–Body Dualism; One Is Not Born a Woman — Examining 'reproductive technohorror' from Shelley's Frankenstein through Splice, The Unborn and The Machine, the chapter argues these films code science as masculine domination of feminised nature (via Bordo's Cartesian masculinisation and Merchant's Bacon) and eliminate the female body altogether so man can create life without woman. It contrasts this with Haraway's post-gender cyborg and Braidotti's Deleuzean metal-morphoses, using becoming-woman and the rhizome to imagine reproductive difference as productive rather than as the erasable 'female problem'.
- ch. 11 "Monstrous motherhood" **·** Michel Foucault, Jacques Lacan, Sigmund Freud — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Power/Knowledge; The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real — The chapter argues that horror films about mothers are not static representations but Foucauldian sites where 'discourses of motherhood' are produced, policed and contested; using Foucault's account of bodies disciplined through power/knowledge, it treats films as cultural artefacts that both enforce and challenge norms of 'essential' and 'ideal' motherhood. It reworks Sarah Arnold's Lacanian 'Good Mother/Bad Mother' schema (the mother who sacrifices herself so the child enters the Symbolic and submits to the Law of the Father) alongside popularised Freudian mother-blame (the 'refrigerator mother', 'tell me about your mother') to read Psycho's Norma(n), the phallic mothers of The Killing Kind and The Brood, and the doomed single mothers of The Ring, Silent Hill and Triangle. It coins the 'monstrous-maternal' to argue that motherhood is framed as always-already monstrous because no woman can meet the impossible, shifting criteria of ideal motherhood, illustrated through Grace's Vivian/Madeline generational clash and Serial Mom's Beverly Sutphin.
- ch. 12 "The ageing woman as (American) horror story" **·** Michel Foucault, Gilles Deleuze — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Power/Knowledge; The Rhizome — The chapter theorises the 'abject barren body' — the menstruating, menopausal and post-menopausal woman — connecting menarche as an upswell of feminine power (Carrie's telekinesis, Ginger Snaps, The Witch's Thomasin) to menopause's cultural construction as loss and 'living decay'. Drawing on Mary Douglas and Kristeva on pollution and abjection, and on Deleuze and Guattari's 'becoming-woman' and bodies defined by capacities rather than fixed being, it argues that the female reproductive body is more often barren than fecund and that this state is another generative modality, not an absence. It reads the Western biomedical pathologisation of menopause (Wilson's Feminine Forever, HRT) as a Foucauldian disciplinary discourse, then tracks older women through Sunset Boulevard's Norma Desmond, the hagsploitation cycle (What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?, Strait-Jacket, Hush Hush Sweet Charlotte), and The Taking of Deborah Logan, concluding that Jessica Lange's American Horror Story roles offer the fullest, sexually frank rebuttal to the abjection and invisibility of the ageing woman.
- ch. 13 "Afterword monstrous miscarriages and uncanny births" *(no index entry yet)* — The afterword uses the anthology films The ABCs of Death and its sequel to argue that 'gynaehorror' can be either reactionary or radical. Recounting a female-fan viewing of the first anthology, it catalogues its 'matrix of misogyny' — pervasive objectification, sexual assault and the reductive 'M is for Miscarriage' punchline that renders the woman's reproductive body abject and disposable. Against this it champions the sequel's 'Z is for Zygote', in which an abandoned pregnant woman keeps her thirteen-year-old unborn inside her and is finally turned inside-out and reborn as a 'mother-skin', reading the short as a provocative, generative treatment of maternity, ageing and reproduction. It closes the book's argument that gynaehorror need not belittle women's bodies but can be monstrous in the productive sense of a zygote — new life and new possibilities.
- ch. 14 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 15 "288" *(front)*

## The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "THE PHILOSOPHY OF POPULAR CULTURE" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 8 "Introduction" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Albert Camus, Martin Heidegger, Søren Kierkegaard — Existentialism; The Absurd; Authenticity — Editor Jerold Abrams argues Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent 'cinematic existentialism' in which a free subject stands against a cold, uncaring world, synthesized with strands of Stoicism and pragmatism. He surveys the volume's essays as variations on this theme: Camus' absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzschean flux in Full Metal Jacket, Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity in Paths of Glory, and Nietzsche's overman as the Star Child in 2001. The essay ties specific films (the ape's femur, HAL, Humbert, the Overlook) to the claim that each Kubrick subject must invent its own meaning in a meaningless universe.
- ch. 9 "Part One The Subject at War" *(front)*
- ch. 10 "Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre, René Descartes — The Absurd; Existentialism; Bad Faith — Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.
- ch. 11 "Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Heraclitus — Will to Power; Everything Flows / Logos; The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality — Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.
- ch. 12 "Existential Ethics Where the Paths of Glory Lead Jason Holt" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Aristotle — Authenticity; Bad Faith; Existentialism; Being-Toward-Death — Holt uses Paths of Glory to illustrate existential ethics, framing the doomed 701st Regiment as 'thrown' beings-toward-death who retain full freedom in how they meet their fate. He resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' (denying objective values while commanding authenticity) by treating authenticity as a formal, second-order virtue like integrity: Colonel Dax is sincere and consistent, General Mireau an inauthentic hypocrite acting in bad faith. Addressing weakness of will (Roget's cowardice) and the condemned Paris 'dying well' before the firing squad, Holt argues that courage—an Aristotelian character virtue—is the smuggled-in content that grounds any formalist existential ethics.
- ch. 13 "Part Two The Subject in Love" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman" **·** Immanuel Kant, Søren Kierkegaard — Philosophy of Love; Moral Luck; Existentialism; The Categorical Imperative — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.
- ch. 15 "Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Socrates, Plato, Michel Foucault — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Existentialism; Pragmatism — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (and later 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body ('I am my body'), recovering the somatic that Socrates and Plato's Phaedo denigrated. In Killer's Kiss the boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight where bodies become weapons, spatial camera work, and the theme of contingency foreground embodiment; 2001 makes viewers feel their own bodies in space, and A Clockwork Orange's Ludovico 'cure' rewires the body-mind. Drawing on pragmatists Shusterman and Sullivan and on Foucault's biopower, he argues the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut turn Merleau-Ponty's projective intentionality into domination rather than communication.
- ch. 16 "The Logic of Lolita Kubrick, Nabokov, and Poe Jerold J. Abrams" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce — The Pragmatic Method; Personal Identity — Abrams argues Kubrick's and Nabokov's Lolita is a philosophical detective story descended from Poe's Dupin tales, and that Humbert fails as a detective because he lacks the right logic. Using Peirce's abduction (and Eco's overcoded/undercoded/creative types), he shows Humbert excels at 'overcoded' guesses—spotting a nymphet at a glance—but cannot make the 'undercoded' abductions needed to see that Quilty is shadowing him, because he is all chess-like calculation and no playful 'musement' or acumen. Humbert (the resolvent) and Quilty (the creative) split Poe's 'bi-part' double-Dupin; Quilty the changeling-Minotaur controls the labyrinth and dies behind Lolita's portrait as a self without a unified identity.
- ch. 17 "Part Three The Subject and the Meaning of Life" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler" **·** David Hume, Karl Marx, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, G.W.F. Hegel, Seneca — Philosophical Skepticism; The Absurd; Existentialism; The Meaning of Life — Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).
- ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" **·** Aristotle, Seneca, John Stuart Mill — Stoicism; The Meaning of Life; Virtue Ethics; Fate and Foreknowledge — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- ch. 20 "Part Four The Subject in History" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "Spartacus and the Second Part of the Soul Gordon Braden" **·** Plato, Plutarch — Tripartite Soul; Justice in the Republic — Braden argues that Kubrick's Spartacus, despite its chaotic production, coheres around Plato's tripartite soul as mediated by Plutarch's analysis of Roman politics. He maps the film's rivalries onto to thymoeides, the soul's 'second' spirited part governed by philotimia (love of honor): Crassus's obsessive hamilla with Gracchus, and his skewed contest with Spartacus over Varinia and Antoninus. Reading Draba's trident-throw and Crassus's closing 'now I fear him' as the spirited part's competitiveness overrunning reason, Braden shows the gladiatorial paired combat mirroring republican politics on its way to the Principate.
- ch. 22 "The Shape of Man The Absurd and Barry Lyndon Chris P. Pliatska" **·** Thomas Nagel, Albert Camus — The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus; The Meaning of Life — Pliatska reads Barry Lyndon through Camus's Sisyphus and, chiefly, Nagel's distinction between conventional absurdity (a discrepancy between aspiration and reality, like the mechanical digger wasp Sphex) and philosophical absurdity (the collision of participant and external viewpoints). He argues Kubrick's painterly tableaux, slow reverse zooms, and the detached narrator force viewers from identification into an external, sub specie historiae perspective, exposing Barry's ambitions as conventionally absurd. That recognition then turns back on the audience as the inescapable philosophical absurdity of the human condition, though Pliatska finds Kubrick's tone more lamenting than Nagel's ironic equanimity.
- ch. 23 "The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer" **·** Jean Baudrillard — Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal); The End of Grand Narratives — Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.
- ch. 24 "Part Five The Subject of the Future" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — Free Will vs Determinism; Will to Power; Radical Freedom and Responsibility — Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.
- ch. 26 "“Please Make Me a Real Boy” The Prayer of the Artificially Intelligent Jason T. Eberl" **·** Alan Turing, G.W.F. Hegel, Aristotle, Boethius — The Turing Test; Master–Slave Dialectic; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Eberl argues that HAL 9000 in 2001 and David in A.I. present sufficient evidence of personhood, testing them against the Turing test, behaviorism, and Boethius's definition of a person as an individual substance of a rational nature. He uses Hegel's master-slave dialectic of recognition to explain the deadly struggle between humans and their self-conscious creations, reading Bowman's disconnection of HAL and the Flesh Fair's destruction of Mechas as humans failing to recognize persons. Invoking Aristotle's telos and virtue, he claims the Flesh Fair's real moral crime is precluding Mechas from pursuing their own flourishing, while David's Pinocchio-like leap of faith marks him as person-like.
- ch. 27 "Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato, Nick Bostrom — The Übermensch; The Death of God; The Last Man; The Noble Lie — Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.

## The Philosophy of the Beats

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "Half title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "Title" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 4 "Copyright" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 5 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — Existentialism; Cosmopolitanism — Elkholy's editorial introduction defines 'Beat' (the New York/West Coast writers) versus 'beat' (a lifestyle of weariness and disaffiliation), tracing the term through Kerouac, Ginsberg's 'Howl,' and Snyder. She frames the Beats' turning-inward and self-marginalization philosophically, noting that Brustein's charge that beats pursue aimless 'kicks' echoes Kierkegaard's critique of the Romantics as engaged in purposeless, rootless striving that evades responsibility. Against this she sets Holmes's reading of beat detachment as a search for meaning and belief, and casts the Beats' global travels as anticipating an emerging cosmopolitanism.
- ch. 7 "I. The Beats Creating a Subculture" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "The Philosophy and Non-Philosophy of Potato Salad" **·** Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, Plato — Deconstruction; Allegory of the Cave — Scribner uses Ginsberg's 'Howl for Carl Solomon'—and Solomon's throwing potato salad at a Dada lecture—to ask whether the Beats' performative acts count as philosophy at all. He argues philosophy is constituted by self-contestation, its relation to a 'non-philosophy' of madness and raw experience, reading Solomon's silence and Ginsberg's poetic mediation through Foucault's 'Madness and Civilization' and Derrida's rebuttal in 'Cogito and the History of Madness.' Ginsberg-to-Solomon is made analogous to philosophy-to-the-Beats: a betraying translator who nonetheless must give the mute event voice, grounded in Plato's failure to banish the poets from the Republic.
- ch. 9 "Laugh of the Revolutionary Diane di Prima, French Feminist Philosophy, and the Contemporary Cult of the Beat H" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Jacques Lacan, Sigmund Freud — Feminism; Objectification — Quinn reads Diane di Prima's serial poem 'Loba' and 'Memoirs of a Beatnik' through Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' and its call to 'écriture féminine'—women writing the body. She argues di Prima's she-wolf/Medusa figure, sex-positive candor, and refusal of narrative closure enact Cixous's boundless feminine writing, while Cixous's anti-Freudian, anti-Lacanian mockery of 'penis envy' and the 'big dick' illuminates di Prima's transgressive motherhood and bisexuality. Against the male Beats' dismissal of women writers (and Beauvoir's foremother status), the essay centralizes di Prima as a serious feminist philosopher-poet rather than a nostalgic icon.
- ch. 10 "Beat U-topos or Taking Utopia on the Road The Case of Jack Kerouac" **·** John Stuart Mill, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, John Locke — The Harm Principle; Utopia and Dystopia; Buddhism — Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.
- ch. 11 "Being-at-Home Gary Snyder and the Poetics of Place" **·** Martin Heidegger, Dogen, Henry David Thoreau — Deep Ecology; Zen Buddhism; Transcendentalism — Hayes reads Gary Snyder's poetry and prose on 'being-at-home' through Heidegger's claim that 'poetically man dwells' and his earth/world distinction, arguing Snyder's bioregionalism (renaming California the 'Shasta Bioregion,' America 'Turtle Island') roots identity in place while embracing Zen impermanence learned from Dōgen. Snyder's shamanic 'tawny grammar,' his pragmatic environmental program in 'Four Changes,' and his Transcendentalist lineage (Thoreau, Emerson) turn wildness into 'the state of complete awareness,' letting a place 'set free into its own presencing' and grounding a poetics of dwelling that is at once local, geological, and impermanent.
- ch. 12 "II. Beat Identities Selfhood and Experimentation" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "From Self-Alienation to Posthumanism The Transmigration of the Burroughsian Subject" **·** Jacques Derrida, Jacques Lacan, Karl Marx — Deconstruction; Alienation; The Mirror Stage — Bolton argues William S. Burroughs's fragmented subjects—split by a parasitic 'Other Half' or word virus—are not postmodernism's dissolved nonsubjects but practitioners of a productive self-alienation. He aligns Burroughs's multiply-named, body-swapping characters (Mr. Bradley Mr. Martin, Joe the Dead) with Lacan's split subject constituted in language and with Derrida's iterable 'mark' and 'third that walks beside you' as an absent-present that dissolves binaries. Through Naked Lunch, Nova Express, and The Western Lands the Burroughsian subject transmigrates from Marxian/Hegelian alienation to N. Katherine Hayles's posthuman, gaining agency by extending into its technologized environment.
- ch. 14 "“I am not an I” Performative (Self)Identity in the Poetry of Bob Kaufman" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, The Buddha — Existence Precedes Essence; Embodiment (the lived body); Ahimsa (nonviolence) — Pynn reads Bob Kaufman's poems ('Forget To Not,' 'Would You Wear My Eyes?,' 'Benediction,' 'Jail Poems') as enacting a performative, intersubjective selfhood: against Beauvoir's 'flavor of death' in American conformity and Sartre's dictum that existence precedes essence, Kaufman replaces the drive to invincibility with 'nakedness' and vulnerability. Merleau-Ponty's embodied intercorporeity and Buddhist ontology—impermanence, non-self, compassion, and ahimsa—let the poet's 'I am not an I' burn the isolated ego into a communal 'thousand me's,' with slavery's trauma inscribed on the body and Kaufman's 1963 Buddhist vow of silence as liberating practice.
- ch. 15 "Tongues Untied Beat Ethnicities, Beat Multiculture" **·** Kwame Anthony Appiah — Cosmopolitanism; Double Consciousness — Lee surveys the neglected ethnic and multicultural seams running through Beat authorship—Ginsberg's Jewish 'Howl' and 'Kaddish,' Kerouac's French-Canadian 'Ti Jean' and the cross-ethnic geography of 'On the Road,' Ferlinghetti's and di Prima's Italian America, and Chicano, Asian American, and Black Beat outriders (Acosta, Frank Chin, Baraka, Ted Joans, Kaufman). He frames these through multicultural theory—Said, Spivak, Bhabha, and especially Anthony Appiah's cosmopolitan account of ethnicity as interstitial—arguing Beat writing foreshadows the field of multicultural studies, a 'tongue untied' whose transnational, race-inflected voices reach back to 'Howl' and 'On the Road.'
- ch. 16 "Joanne Kyger “Descartes and the Splendor Of” Bridging Dualisms through Collaboration and Experimentation" **·** René Descartes, Judith Butler, Zhuangzi — Mind–Body Dualism; Gender Performativity; The Cogito — Falk analyzes Joanne Kyger's 1968 experimental video 'Descartes' and its script 'Descartes and the Splendor Of,' a condensed rewrite of the 'Discourse on Method' that subverts Descartes's mind-body dualism and privileging of reason. Kyger deflates the cogito with slang ('to doubt is a drag'), substitutes Buddhist, Taoist (Zhuangzi's butterfly dream), and Confucian terms, and—voicing and performing Descartes as a woman doing housework and as 'Mother God'—feminizes the most masculine of professions. Reading this through Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble' and gender performativity, Falk shows the parody destabilizes the mind/body, male/female hierarchy Cartesian dualism underwrites.
- ch. 17 "III. Beat Avant-Garde Spontaneity and Immediacy" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — Existentialism; The Absurd; Existence Precedes Essence — Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.
- ch. 19 "Wholly Communion Poetry, Philosophy, and Spontaneous Bop Cinema" **·** Gilles Deleuze, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Rhizome; Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate) — Sterritt reads Peter Whitehead's 1965 film 'Wholly Communion,' shot at London's International Poetry Incarnation, as 'spontaneous bop cinema' embodying Beat poetics through Bakhtin's dialogic/carnivalesque and the schizoanalysis of Deleuze and Guattari. Ginsberg's drunken recitation of 'The Change' becomes a 'body without organs' entering the 'chaosmos' on the plane of immanence; Jandl's sound poetry is pure Deleuzian sensation. Adrian Mitchell's anti-Vietnam 'To Whom It May Concern' is read through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and amor fati and Deleuze's 'difference in repetition,' its incantatory counter-words a materialist line of flight against the order-words of war.
- ch. 20 "High Off the Page Representing the Drug Experience in the Work of Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Gilles Deleuze — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Erik Mortenson argues that Kerouac's and Ginsberg's drug writing works 'through the body' to transmit the altered temporality of intoxication to the reader, using Merleau-Ponty's account of original speech and the lived body as gesture, and Deleuze and Guattari's 'Body Without Organs' and speeds. Marijuana expands the present into Kerouac's long exfoliating sentences and empathetic 'digging' (Visions of Cody, On the Road), while Benzedrine contracts it into the accelerated confessional rush of The Subterraneans; Ginsberg's LSD poems ('Lysergic Acid,' 'Wales Visitation') hit the limit of representing timelessness. The chapter concludes the writing lets the nonuser get 'high off the page' without the dependency Deleuze and Guattari warn of.
- ch. 21 "Genius All the Time The Beats, Spontaneous Presence, and Primordial Ground" **·** The Buddha, Dogen — Zen Buddhism; Non-Self (anatman); Emptiness (sunyata) — Marc Olmsted reads Beat spontaneity through Tantric (Vajrayana) Buddhism, arguing that 'first thought, best thought' and Kerouac's 'Mind is shapely, art is shapely' rest on the view that enlightenment/awareness is already present and need only be recognized. He maps Ginsberg's poetics onto the Tantric terms Ground, Path, and Fruition, tying shamatha-vipashyana practice and the doctrine of anatta (no-self) to the poet catching the first pre-conceptual thought. Ginsberg's Blake visions, his study under Trungpa and Gelek Rinpoche, and Burroughs's cut-up 'homemade yankee tantra' are offered as evidence that Beat composition enacts a Buddhist recognition of primordial, empty, self-existing awareness.
- ch. 22 "Spontaneity, Immediacy, and Difference Philosophy, Being in Time, and Creativity in the Aesthetics of Jack Ker" **·** Shankara, René Descartes — Atman and Brahman; Duration (durée) — David Need contrasts three theories of 'being in time' behind the aesthetics of spontaneity: Kerouac's debt to Spengler's organic cycles of civilization (a stereoscopic, dualist view where an arbitrary measure like a candle or page limns deep being), Olson's use of Whitehead's 'concrescence' in 'Projective Verse' (a monist, all-at-once projection of new monads), and Cage's use of Coomaraswamy's Vedanta, where silence is sabdabrahman and chance imitates Nature. He argues the real fault line is the old monist-vs-dualist divide (Advaita brahman vs. Cartesian dualism), and that each artist's notion of creative freedom follows from which metaphysical schema he borrowed, so our quarrels with the Beats reflect our own metaphysical stakes.
- ch. 23 "IV. Beat Politics Ethics and Affinities" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "Two Ways of Enduring the Flames The Existential Dialectics of Love in Kierkegaard and Bukowski" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Jacques Lacan — Philosophy of Love; The Leap of Faith; Despair (sickness unto death) — Andreas Seland argues that Kierkegaard and Bukowski offer opposed responses to a Romantic 'paradox of love': the beloved is a dialectical object, part inner imago (Shelley's veiled maid in 'Alastor,' Stendhal's crystallization, Lacan/Zizek) and part uncontrollable external person, and this gap breeds despair. Kierkegaard's Knight of Faith in Fear and Trembling resolves it by infinite resignation and the absurd leap, internalizing the gap and severing the tie to the real to love the princess only interiorly. Bukowski's Chinaski in Women does the opposite, deliberately choosing unstable 'Lydia-object' women who embody the gap, seeking the insecurity itself as a line of flight beyond bourgeois love and even beyond himself.
- ch. 25 "Anarchism and the Beats" **·** Karl Marx, Henry David Thoreau, Carl Jung — Anarchism; Civil Disobedience; Class Struggle — Ed D'Angelo argues the Beats had a philosophy after all: a romantic bohemian anarchism that made poetry a means to a religious transformation of consciousness, with political change following consciousness rather than the reverse. He shows Ginsberg inverting Plato's rationalist hierarchy (grounding reason in imagination and the body) and reads Beat 'criminality' as a shamanic journey to the unconscious underworld, distinct from Mailer's macho 'White Negro' hipster. He traces their lineage through Greenwich Village bohemia, Proudhon/Bakunin/Kropotkin anarchism, and pacifist anarchists like Rexroth and Dellinger, arguing the Beats rejected Marxist materialism and class warfare, and that the movement was 'born' out of Rexroth's anarchist poetry circle at the 1955 Six Gallery reading of 'Howl.'
- ch. 26 "Between Social Ecology and Deep Ecology Gary Snyder’s Ecological Philosophy" **·** Arne Naess, Baruch Spinoza, Dogen, Aldo Leopold — Deep Ecology; Emptiness (sunyata); Anthropocentrism — Paul Messersmith-Glavin positions Snyder as a bridge between deep ecology and social ecology. He shows how Sessions and Devall enlist Snyder's Mahayana Buddhism (emptiness/sunyata, Dogen's 'Mind means trees, fence posts, tiles, and grasses') and Spinoza's monism for a biocentric, consciousness-changing deep ecology descended from Naess and Leopold's land ethic. Against this, he sets Bookchin's social ecology, which roots the ecological crisis in human hierarchy and attacks deep ecology's ahistorical 'cosmic oneness' and misanthropic Earth First! statements. Snyder's threefold nature/wild/wilderness distinction, bioregionalism, and reading of Marx and anarchism let him hold both, insisting environmental and social justice are 'all one front.'
- ch. 27 "William Burroughs as Philosopher From Beat Morality to Third Worldism to Continental Theory" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Jacques Derrida, Herbert Marcuse, Frantz Fanon — Bad Faith; One-Dimensional Man; Deconstruction; Existence Precedes Essence — Jones Irwin makes the case for 'Burroughs as philosopher,' tracing an 'impassioned moralism' and antihumanism (human as adjective, not noun) that separates him from other Beats and postmodernists. He links Burroughs's critique of alienation to Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and to Sartrean existentialism and bad faith ('there are no victims, just accomplices'), and reads the Beats' 'third force' Third Worldism via Freire, Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, and Paz. Close readings of Naked Lunch's 'Bradley the Buyer' and the sex-and-death delirium of 'AJ's Annual Party' connect Burroughs to Artaud's body without organs, Bataille's Sadean tradition, and Derrida's deconstruction of embodiment and 'distance touching.'

## The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers

- ch. 1 "Preface" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Part - 1 The Coen Brand of Comedy and Tragedy" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Raising Arizona as an American Comedy" **·** Ralph Waldo Emerson, Plato, Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre — Self-Reliance; Allegory of the Cave; Authenticity — Gilmore reads Raising Arizona as a classical comedy (bad-beginning-to-good-ending) about the American 'optative mood' of self-creation, using Hi McDunnough's outlaw-to-family arc and his name-as-height-metaphor to figure Emerson's aspirational American self. He deploys Plato's two kinds of cave-laughter to distinguish the film's 'tender,' welcoming comedy (Hi and Ed, Gale and Evelle) from mocking ridicule, and frames Hi's need to abandon outlaw identity via Heidegger's Augenblick and Badiou's 'event' sparked in Ed's mug-shot flash. Nietzsche on dreams-as-origin-of-metaphysics grounds the film's dream/reality tension, and Hi's over-identification with the outlaw universal is glossed as Sartrean bad faith.
- ch. 9 "The Human Comedy Perpetuates Itself Nihilism and Comedy in Coen Neo-Noir" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Hannah Arendt — The Death of God; The Last Man; Will to Power — Hibbs argues that neo-noir turns classic noir's grim fatalism comic by making nihilism a working assumption, and that Nietzsche supplies the diagnosis: the 'death of God,' the passive 'last man,' and the aristocratic 'pathos of distance' of will-to-power super-antiheroes (Hannibal Lecter, the villains of Cape Fear/Basic Instinct). He reads The Big Lebowski as the Coens' comic leveling of nihilism, with Walter insisting the Germans are 'nihilists' and 'cowards' and the Dude 'abiding,' showing that full nihilism cannot be lived. In Fargo and Raising Arizona, Marge's 'banality of virtue' (a comic counterpoint to Arendt's banality of evil) and the resilience of familial/procreative instinct reassert a comic order over the noir trap.
- ch. 10 "Philosophies of Comedy in O Brother, Where Art Thou" **·** Henri Bergson, Søren Kierkegaard — Laughter (the comic as mechanical encrusted on the living); The Stages on Life's Way — McFarland explains the comedy of O Brother through Bergson's 'mechanical encrusted on the living' (the chain-gang pratfall where McGill forgets he is shackled, the toon-like plasticity of the escapees) and Kierkegaard's account of the comic as unresolved contradiction, like men bustling on a sinking ship. He argues the Klan-rally set piece refuses Jamesonian 'pastiche' by grounding its Wizard-of-Oz and Odyssey allusions in real historical guilt, forcing the postmodern aesthete-viewer, as in Kierkegaard's Either/Or, from the aesthetic to the ethical stage. The subverted ending—Penny rejecting the non-bona-fide ring—enacts Kierkegaard's view that marriage is comic because it 'binds' time and acknowledges contradiction rather than resolving it.
- ch. 11 "No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Aristotle, Heraclitus, Albert Camus, Henry David Thoreau — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Everything Flows / Logos; The Absurd; Fate and Foreknowledge — Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'
- ch. 12 "Deceit, Desire, and Dark Comedy Postmodern Dead Ends in Blood Simple" **·** Jean-François Lyotard — The End of Grand Narratives; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Woolfolk argues that Blood Simple is 'resolutely postmodern': it recycles noir motifs as Jamesonian pastiche but, unlike classic noir (Double Indemnity, Detour), offers no modernist critique of capitalist civilization and no saving metanarrative, leaving only a profane comic present. He reads the three men who go 'simple'—Ray, Marty, Visser—through Girard's triangular desire, driven by unchecked, mutually imitated passions with no external mediating authority, while Visser's sidewalk individualism supplies a minimal social philosophy. Crucially the film's world is ruled by chance, not fate (the pistol's three bullets, Abby's lucky single shot), so Abby's clueless 'health' and survival affirm postmodern contingency rather than any critique of late modernity.
- ch. 13 "Part - 2 Ethics Shame, Justice, and Virtue" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "“And It’s Such a Beautiful Day!” shame and Fargo" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Virtue Ethics — Hanrahan and Stearns read Fargo through Aristotle's theory of shame and its link to friendship, sorting the characters into his moral hierarchy: Gaear is the shameless self-indulgent man, Jerry is the morally incontinent one whose flickers of shame (before Scotty, before the swindled customer) stay inert against his greed, and Marge is the exemplar of excellence. They argue that a capacity for shame requires valuing others non-instrumentally, which the co-conspirators cannot do because they relate only through friendships of utility (Carl and the prostitute, Jerry using his son). Marge's friendship-of-the-good with Norm grounds both her decency and her ability to mediate others' shame, and her 'it's such a beautiful day' expresses the same noninstrumental valuing that makes moral concern possible.
- ch. 15 "Justice, Power, and Love The Political Philosophy of Intolerable Cruelty" **·** John Rawls, Thomas Hobbes, Plato, Niccolò Machiavelli — Justice as Fairness; The Veil of Ignorance; The Social Contract — Biderman and Devlin trace Intolerable Cruelty through three theories of justice enacted by divorce attorney Miles Massey and femme fatale Marylin. 'Justice as power' is Thrasymachus's 'advantage of the stronger' and Machiavelli's might-makes-right, seen in Miles's courtroom war-room rhetoric and teeth imagery and in Marylin's plan to 'nail his ass' via marriage. 'Justice as compromise' is Hobbes's social contract escaping the state of nature, but the film shows the Massey pre-nup's signing and tearing to be merely a mask for power. When Miles and Marylin genuinely fall in love, their indifference to each other's wealth becomes a Rawlsian veil of ignorance and difference principle—justice as fairness—though the cynical Funniest Divorce Videos ending leaves that victory unguaranteed.
- ch. 16 "Ethics, Heart, and Violence in Miller’s Crossing" **·** David Hume, Plato, Thomas Hobbes, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant — Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; The Social Contract; Justice in the Republic — Herling reads Miller's Crossing through Hume's moral psychology of passion versus reason, arguing the film's dominant 'ethics' (voiced by Johnny Caspar) is Hobbes's social contract plus Thrasymachus's advantage-of-the-stronger and Plato's 'do good to friends, harm to enemies'—a relativism of power that Tom Reagan navigates by cool calculation. 'Heart,' the capacity for sympathetic attachment Hume makes the real basis of morality, keeps breaking through: Tom spares the pleading Bernie ('Look in your heart') at Miller's Crossing, and his loyalty to Leo secretly drives his 'plays.' But Bernie's betrayal, the surreal sympathy-crushing violence (the beatings, Leo's tommy-gun ballet, Caspar shooting the faceless Dane), and Leo and Verna's reunion steel Tom into lonely noir stoicism—'What heart?'—when he finally executes Bernie without mercy.
- ch. 17 "“Takin’ ’er Easy for All Us Sinners” Laziness as a Virtue in The Big Lebowski" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant, Epicurus, John Locke, Aristotle — The Death of God; Master and Slave Morality; The Categorical Imperative; Epicurean Pleasure (ataraxia) — Douglass and Walls read the Dude's 'principled laziness' as a coherent ethos and test it against the film's rival worldviews: the villains' hollow nihilism (which they distinguish from Nietzsche's will to power and death-of-God), Bunny's Aristippan hedonism versus Epicurus, the Big Lebowski's Nietzschean master-morality egoism, and Walter Sobchak's rules-worship read through Kant's categorical imperative and Locke's social contract. They argue dude-ism works as a personal path to contentment but, lacking any objective standard, cannot condemn true evil like Bunny's threatened murder, exposing its purposeless-universe premise as its real flaw.
- ch. 18 "No Country for Old Men as Moral Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Søren Kierkegaard, Bernard Williams — The Categorical Imperative; Teleological Suspension of the Ethical — McFarland reads the film as moral philosophy: Sheriff Bell faces a post-Kantian predicament, able to reconstruct how crimes happen but unable to 'measure' why, and dooms himself by tying duty to an outcome (his promise to make Llewelyn safe) rather than to Kant's unconditional imperative, so failure yields Bernard Williams-style shame. Llewelyn is cast against Kierkegaard's Abraham/Brutus distinction as a tragic hero who cannot suspend the ethical, while Chigurh functions as an ironic anti-philosopher who alternately grounds killing in self-interest ('what good is a rule if it got you here?') and in a perverse Kantian promise-keeping, until Carla Jean restores moral responsibility by refusing his coin toss.
- ch. 19 "Part - 3 Postmodernity, Interpretation, and the Construction of History" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Heidegger and the Problem of Interpretation in Barton Fink" **·** Martin Heidegger, René Descartes, Aristotle — Dasein (being-there); Mind–Body Dualism; Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Conard uses Barton Fink as a springboard into Heidegger's theory of interpretation, contrasting it with Cartesian dualism. Barton, the 'life of the mind' artist whose skull-like hotel room symbolizes his isolation, is a Cartesian subject cut off from the practical, meaning-giving contexts (Heidegger's workshop, the ready-to-hand versus present-at-hand typewriter) in which equipment is understood and interpreted. Conard argues the film's uninterpretable elements—the box, the wall photo, the mosquitoes—resist meaning precisely because Barton is severed from the web of relations that would let anything show up as meaningful, illustrating Dasein's temporal, potentiality-driven being.
- ch. 21 "The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy" **·** Michel Foucault — The End of Grand Narratives; Power/Knowledge; Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal) — Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.
- ch. 22 "“A Homespun Murder Story” Film Noir and the Problem of Modernity in Fargo" **·** Alasdair MacIntyre, René Descartes, Jean-Paul Sartre — Virtues, Practices and Traditions; Judgment of Taste and the Sublime; Everything Flows / Logos — Abrams reads Fargo as a noir study of modernity via MacIntyre's After Virtue: humans are 'story-telling animals,' and the Enlightenment project (Descartes, Sartre) shredded the shared myth, leaving Cartesian monadic selves who float in a void as 'unscripted, anxious stutterers.' The whiteout blizzard becomes an ontological tabula rasa of Heraclitean flux where every conversation collapses (Jerry, Carl, Mike Yanagita, even Marge at the drive-thru). Abrams reads Marge as morally good but intellectually shallow—wrong to call the sublime, Kantian 'dynamically sublime' day 'beautiful'—and Grimsrud as the one who dimly 'sees' the modern abyss, so the film hands the deeper mystery of modernity's crime to the viewer.
- ch. 23 "Part - 4 Existentialism, Alienation, and Despair" *(front)*
- ch. 24 "“What Kind of Man Are You ” The Coen Brothers and Existentialist Role Playing" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus — Existence Precedes Essence; The Absurd; The Myth of Sisyphus — Gaughran argues the Coens presuppose an absurd, valueless world (announced by Blood Simple's 'you're on your own' voice-over) in which characters must, per Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' invent a self by adopting a style. He surveys the hats of Miller's Crossing, Everett's Dapper Dan dandyism in O Brother read through Camus's The Rebel, and Ed Crane of The Man Who Wasn't There as a Meursault-like figure who forges an identity through violence. Against Camus, murder and suicide are illegitimate revolts, and Sisyphus—not the nihilistic killers—stands as the true absurd hero who never resolves the tension between mind and indifferent world.
- ch. 25 "Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There" **·** Søren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus — Despair (sickness unto death); Existentialism; The Absurd — Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.
- ch. 26 "Thinking beyond the Failed Community Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn’t There" **·** Albert Camus, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Absurd; Existence Precedes Essence — Palmer reads Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn't There as a diptych re-composing James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity, whose core theme is a failed community where self-interest poisons human bonds. Blood Simple dramatizes the Cainian problem—Visser and the others destroyed by instrumentalization and fatal miscommunication—while The Man Who Wasn't There, framed by Camus's The Stranger and Sartre's Nausea, stages its utopian solution. Ed's Sartrean disgust at hair and physicality drives his dry-cleaning scheme; like Meursault he kills and is condemned for the wrong crime, but unlike Cain's solipsistic heroes he ends yearning for communion with Doris beyond the grave, imagining the restoration of the lost community.
