## The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!

- ch. 1 "Globalization and Contemporary Art" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Jacques Derrida — Philosophical Skepticism; Deconstruction — The editors' introduction argues that South Park is one of TV's most important series because it lampoons the fanatical extremists of every social, ethical, economic, and religious position, modeling the fallibilist skepticism critical thinkers need (quoting Parker's line that the people screaming on both sides are the same and it is OK to laugh from the middle). It offers Peirce's account of thinking through incomplete signs and Derrida's 'play of differences' as case studies of this healthy skepticism, defends laughing at fanatics because their reasoning withers in sunlight, and previews the volume: Murtagh's 'sledgehammer' defense of blasphemous humor, Jacoby's Clifford-style case that belief without evidence is wrong, Dueck on rationally defensible faith, Gray on the 'Douche or Turd' election, and Held on gay marriage.
- ch. 6 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Socrates, Hannah Arendt, Plato, Sigmund Freud, Aristotle — The Banality of Evil; The Unexamined Life; The Golden Mean; The Unconscious — Young argues that South Park is perceived as dangerous for exactly the reasons Socrates was tried and executed in Plato's Apology: both 'corrupt the youth' by mocking religion, questioning authority, and exposing that the supposed teachers (Mr. Garrison's flip-flopping creationism, Mrs. Broflovski's moral panics, the 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip) do not know what they think they know. He diagnoses Cartman as an Eichmann figure whose banal, thoughtless evil—feeding Scott Tenorman his parents, torturing Muslims with farts—consists in the inability to think from another's standpoint, while Kyle and Stan's friendship embodies Arendt's dialogic thinking and Aristotle's mean between ideological extremes, as when they see both the merit and the smugness of hybrid drivers in 'Smug Alert'. Freud's theory that jokes break through repression explains why the show's vulgarity is essential rather than gratuitous: it verbalizes what culture silences so that it can be thought through, making South Park a Socratic gadfly rather than a corrupter.
- ch. 8 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Blaise Pascal — Pascal's Wager; Philosophical Skepticism — Jacoby defends W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief—it is wrong to believe on insufficient evidence and the burden of proof falls on the claimant—through Stan's exposures of TV psychic John Edward ('The Biggest Douche in the Universe'), the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the faith-based story of Joseph Smith in 'All About Mormons'. The centerpiece is a South Park-illustrated demolition of Pascal's Wager: Kyle's hemorrhoid-driven despair in 'Cartmanland' shows a perfectly good God would not eternally reward evil Cartman or torture honest nonbelievers, and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' shows the wagerer cannot even know which religion pays out. Stan's closing speech to Edward's frightened audience carries the moral: comforting lies weaken the mind and slow the progress of finding the real, amazing answers.
- ch. 9 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Socrates — The Ethics of Political Violence; Socratic Ignorance (knowing that you don't know); Cosmopolitanism — Kirby reads the 'Imaginationland' trilogy as a satire of post-9/11 America interpreted through Ulrich Beck's world risk society: the Pentagon generals, still thinking in Cold War categories like 'Project X' and Chinese imagination portals, embody Beck's denial response and end up voting to nuke Imaginationland, while Cartman's Rambo-style self-interest embodies the apathetic response. Socrates' practice of demanding definitions frames the chapter's question of what terrorism actually is (via Hoffman's five criteria), and Socratic ignorance about what one does not know is contrasted with the worse condition of not being able to know what you do not know. Kyle's courtroom speech that imaginary beings like Luke Skywalker and Santa are 'realer' than most real people, and Butters' creative power to imagine Santa back to life, point to Beck's cosmopolitan 'transformation': imagination and cross-border cooperation as the way out of risk panic.
- ch. 10 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(no index entry yet)* — Arp uses the show as a logic textbook: his own prejudice against Goth kids and Officer Barbrady's post-Atlas Shrugged ban on books illustrate hasty generalization, Cartman's 'if you do drugs, then you're a hippie' chain and the Tooth Fairy syllogism illustrate deductive argument, and Towelie's appearances illustrate inductive strength. A fallacy catalog follows: Johnny Cochran's 'If Chewbacca lives on Endor, you must acquit' in 'Chef Aid' as red herring, Mrs. Broflovski's 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip as slippery slope, Mrs. Marsh's cookie outburst in 'Clubhouses' as hasty generalization plus slippery slope, Father Maxi's hell pronouncements as appeal to inappropriate authority, and cartoon Rob Reiner in 'Butt Out' as ad hominem. The chapter's claim is that Parker and Stone deliberately violate logical principles episode after episode to expose absurd beliefs, because how people reason shapes the laws they make and the beliefs they die for.
- ch. 11 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** William James, Thomas Kuhn, W.V.O. Quine — Faith and Reason; Paradigm Shifts; The Will to Believe — Johnson uses 'Go God Go's' future of 2546—where Dawkins-style atheism has become a warring religion and otter scientists intone 'Oh my Science!'—to ask whether science and religion genuinely conflict and whether New Atheism is itself a faith. Applying abduction and the four criteria of adequacy, he argues the embellished-story hypothesis beats miracle claims about Jesus (whose legend grew Gospel by Gospel), Sathya Sai Baba, Joseph Smith, and Xenu, that Mr(s). Garrison's 'you can't disprove God' and the show's sarcasm commit an appeal to ignorance, and that Stan's water-into-wine scene with Jesus shows how easily people are fooled. He allows Kuhnian theory change in science but rejects James's will-to-believe for existence claims—the moon whale Willzyx needs evidence—and concludes Parker and Stone are unfair to Dawkins: ending religion would not end violence, but it would remove the easiest justification for it, and some answers are simply true even when unknown.
- ch. 13 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** David Hume, William James, Alvin Plantinga, Karl Popper — On Miracles; The Will to Believe; Faith and Reason; Falsificationism — Dueck takes Stan's closing pluralism in 'Super Best Friends'—all religions have something valuable to teach, as the interfaith superheroes' combined powers defeat Blaine—and tests it against Hick's pluralism, exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivist 'anonymous Christians', using 'Go God Go's warring atheist factions to show exclusivity is unavoidable even without God. Hume's miracle argument explains why Jesus's look-away water-into-wine trick convinces no one in the episode: testimony can never outweigh the laws of nature, so supernatural evidence resists natural evaluation. Popper's falsificationism warns that watering doctrines down to make religions compatible (the rabbit-pope of 'Fantastic Easter Special') leaves nothing to test, while James's will to believe and Plantinga's defense of exclusivism ground the conclusion that faith can be rationally justifiable where evidence runs out—beware the Blainetologists, but do not surrender ways of life that define us.
- ch. 14 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Blaise Pascal, Alvin Plantinga — The Problem of Evil; Pascal's Wager — Johnson formalizes Kyle's crisis in 'Cartmanland'—evil Cartman inherits a million dollars and buys the amusement park while good Kyle suffers hemorrhoids and loses faith—as a valid argument from the logical problem of evil, then evaluates the town's theodicies against the philosophical ones. The Job story Kyle's parents read him fails like skeptical theism (it proves too much and ends in moral agnosticism), Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards's God-glorifying account, Stan's restored faith via Cartman's perfect misery is a greater-goods response, Augustine's free will defense purchases goodness at the price of God's control of prayers and elections and cannot explain natural evils, and Hick's soul-making theodicy founders on fawns, tsunamis, and Kenny's deaths. Pascal's Wager and Plantinga's divine sense are dismissed in turn: evil does not disprove God, but proportioning belief to evidence makes non-belief the rational stance.
- ch. 15 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** John Stuart Mill — On Liberty — Koepsell surveys sixteen years of South Park blasphemy from 'Jesus vs. Santa' through 'Red Hot Catholic Love', 'Bloody Mary', the Scientology of 'Trapped in the Closet', and the censored Muhammad episodes 'Cartoon Wars' and '200'/'201', arguing that the show's equal-opportunity mockery is legitimate cultural criticism, not a sign of civilizational decline. Tracing the legal history from nineteenth-century blasphemy prosecutions through Cantwell v. Connecticut and Chaplinsky, he adopts Mill's On Liberty case that only free and open discussion of even the most sacred beliefs can shake out truth and keep opinion from becoming dead dogma. Comedy Central's black-screening of Muhammad while airing far coarser blasphemy was incoherent capitulation: nothing on the show is sacred, tolerance requires neither silence nor immunity from ridicule, and the Mormon Gary's 'suck my balls' sums the show's loving-but-mocking attitude.
- ch. 17 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** John Stuart Mill — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle; On Liberty — Murtagh asks whether the Virgin Mary statue spraying menstrual blood on a cardinal and the pope in 'Bloody Mary' is morally wrong, and answers with a utilitarian weighing of blasphemous humor's consequences. On the negative side, offense to believers (with Cartman's sudden piety about Family Guy's Muhammad in 'Cartoon Wars Part I' articulating the utilitarian worry that millions watching intensifies the harm) and a possible desensitizing erosion of tolerance; on the positive side, pleasure and the show's power to provoke thought, as when Randy learns from Stan that his five sober days came from his own willpower, not 'divine ass blood'. Drawing on Mill's greatest happiness principle and On Liberty's defense of open discussion, he concludes blasphemous humor is morally justified when it is an important part of a presentation with significant social value, and wrong when used merely to piss people off or for profit.
- ch. 18 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Hans-Georg Gadamer, Charles Sanders Peirce, John Locke, Blaise Pascal — Philosophical Hermeneutics (fusion of horizons) — Sirvent and Baker read The Book of Mormon alongside 'Cartman Sucks' and 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe' to expose religious fundamentalism—Elder Price's 'I Believe' creed, Elder McKinley's 'turn it off' cure for gay feelings, the conversion camp that is 'fixing' Bradley—as at once naive and arrogant. Peirce's 'fixation of belief' names the dogmatist's refusal to admit a belief could be wrong; Gadamer's hermeneutics shows that Elder Cunningham's Boba Fett additions to scripture are not corruption but an honest image of how all interpretation works, against the fundamentalist's naive realism that claims one pure meaning; and Locke on religious 'enthusiasm' plus Pascal on evil done from religious conviction explain how certainty of God's will always turns out to be a self-portrait, as in Cartman's revelation that God wants everyone to give him a dollar in 'Probably'. Genuine faith, they conclude with Elder Price's final conversion, only becomes fruitful once it accepts doubt.
- ch. 19 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 20 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Karl Popper — The Open Society; Democracy — Argues that South Park performs Popper's defense of the open society by ridiculing 'enemies' on both flanks: Cartman as a Glenn Beck-style ranter in 'Dances with Smurfs' and a xenophobic border agent in 'The Last of the Meheecans', versus liberal fanatics like Rob Reiner in 'Butt Out', Rosie O'Donnell's recount antics in 'Trapper Keeper', and Tom Cruise's litigious Scientology in 'Trapped in the Closet'. The show does not silence extremists but lets them speak and then mocks them, which the authors read through Popper's paradox of tolerance: tolerance cannot be extended to those who suppress criticism, as the Church of Scientology's pressure campaigns showed. A closing section links this to Jefferson's Virginia Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom — 'truth is great and will prevail if left to herself' — making free, offensive argument and dissent the lifeblood of democracy.
- ch. 21 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Karl Marx — Class Struggle; Historical Materialism — Uses 'The Last of the Meheecans' to argue that Marx's account of labor-power needs race built into it: once Butters is mistaken for a Mexican immigrant 'Mantequilla', the couple who hit him hand him Windex and a leaf blower and he sings 'Work, Mexican, work', showing how racialization assigns his labor a demeaned value. The episode's conflicting stereotypes (lazy shiftless 'Meheecans' versus the hard-working backbone of service labor) and the mass 'Orgullo de Mantequilla' migration home reveal a super-exploited population. The author then recovers Marx's own writings on Polish and Irish liberation, American slavery, and Lincoln's reelection ('labor in the white skin cannot emancipate itself where in the black skin it is branded') to show that for Marx, racial and national domination were always obstacles to working-class freedom.
- ch. 22 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** John Stuart Mill, John Locke, Jürgen Habermas — Democracy; The Harm Principle; On Liberty; The Social Contract — Takes 'Douche and Turd' — Stan refusing to choose between Giant Douche and Turd Sandwich, Puff Daddy's gun-toting 'Vote or Die', and his banishment — plus the kindergarten tie in 'Trapper Keeper' (Flora's indecision, Rosie O'Donnell's recounts) to ask whether every vote counts in a two-party system. Through Locke, Stan's abstention becomes a withdrawal of consent to be governed by either mascot; through Mill, non-voting threatens the active participation that gives institutions legitimacy and wards off tyranny of the majority, even as the chapter catalogs real disincentives: the Electoral College's spectator states, the 2000 Florida debacle, and Commission rules excluding third parties like Nader. Habermas closes the chapter: the vote, read as positive liberty, is the paradigm of rights and inclusion in a community of equals.
- ch. 23 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Jean-Jacques Rousseau — The General Will; Social Darwinism; Class Struggle — Reads '1%' — where Cartman's failed fitness test makes him the scapegoated one percent, and the school's 99% splinter into warring 83%, 30%, and 5% factions occupying the Red Robin (and its restroom) — through Rousseau's Social Contract on freedom and equality and the dismembered social body, showing how popular solidarity shatters into meaningless percentage tribes. 'Night of the Living Homeless' (the poor as zombies who 'feed on our change', Kyle's $20 spawning the swarm, the shotgun as the only remedy) dramatizes the dehumanizing social-Darwinist picture of the economic undead, and the underpants gnomes' business plan (Phase 1: Collect Underpants, Phase 2: ?, Phase 3: Profit) mocks CEOs who cannot say why they amass wealth. The chapter's own verdict: corporations as such are good (cars, computers, canned soup), and blame falls on the greedy individuals inside them, since death — Tolstoy's two meters of burial land — levels all players.
- ch. 24 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Adam Smith, Plato — The Invisible Hand — Cantor frames South Park with Plato's Silenus image from the Symposium — Socrates' ridiculous, ass-and-cobbler talk hiding wisdom inside — to argue the show's obscenity wraps genuinely philosophical libertarianism, just as Aristophanes' Clouds gave Socrates fart jokes about thunder. Reading 'Gnomes' closely (the gnomes' Collect Underpants/?/Profit plan, Mr. Tweek's slick nostalgia advertising and sale of his son into slavery rhetoric, the boys' flip on Prop 10), the chapter applies Smith's invisible hand: business activity looks like sneaky theft to outsiders, but Harbucks wins by serving consumers, while Mr. Tweek's real sin is enlisting government power against a rival. 'Cripple Fight' (Big Gay Al defending the Boy Scouts' freedom of association) and 'Something Wall Mart This Way Comes' (the store's heart is a mirror reflecting consumer desire) extend the same lesson — freedom cuts both ways, and the market answers to shoppers, not regulators.
- ch. 26 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** John Stuart Mill — The Harm Principle; On Liberty; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Challenges the received libertarian message of 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' — Randy giving himself testicular cancer for a marijuana prescription, Cartman bootlegging KFC in a Scarface parody after Colorado bans fast food — by pressing Mill's liberty principle on what 'harm' means: Mr. Garrison's plot to murder the Queer Eye cast is immediate harm, but the S&M Mr. Slave displays to schoolchildren in 'The Death Camp of Tolerance' is only indirect, psychologically mediated harm Mill cannot clearly handle. Addiction then undermines Mill's assumption of sovereign tastes: corporations can shape desire without coercing anyone, so the libertarian 'omnicompetent individual' is a myth. Mead's intersubjectivity (Randy smoking pot before Officer Barbrady, blind to how Jimbo sees him) grounds the constructive claim that selves are socially formed, and the shark-tank defecation and Prisoner's Dilemma examples show why collective harms need rules and regulation.
- ch. 27 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** John Stuart Mill, Immanuel Kant, Robert Nozick, John Locke — The Harm Principle; Deontology; Consequentialism; Autonomy of the Will — Defends South Park's anti-paternalism on both consequentialist and deontological grounds. 'Major Boobage' shows the futility of Gerald's cat ban meant to stop kids 'cheesing' — Kenny still gets high and Gerald himself relapses — while 'Medicinal Fried Chicken' shows how the KFC prohibition births a violent black market, with Cartman's $85 snack pushing him into the Colonel's Scarface-style drug war. On the deontological side, Mill's 'over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign', Locke's self-ownership, and Kantian respect for rational agents (via Nozick's inviolability, and the authors' autarchy-versus-autonomy distinction) ground the claim that coercion is wrong even when benevolent: 'Butt Out' has Kyle and Stan tell Rob Reiner that forcing others to quit smoking is fascism, while Big Tobacco's Kevin Harris wins their approval simply by informing and letting people choose.
- ch. 28 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** John Stuart Mill — The Harm Principle; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Uses 'Follow That Egg!' — Mrs. Garrison's jealous crusade to stop Mr. Slave marrying Big Gay Al, her two-daddy egg experiment where Stan and Kyle out-parent Cartman, and the governor's 'butt buddies' separate-but-equal compromise — to demolish the standard arguments against gay marriage (scripture, dictionary definition, procreation, tradition, harm to children, the slippery slope to polygamy and incest) as post-hoc rationalizations of disgust. Mill's harm principle and negative liberty supply the positive case: unlike under-age, incestuous, or polygamous marriage, gay marriage demonstrably harms no one, so no legitimate reason remains to ban it, and rights should never be put to a referendum anyway. The 'butt buddies' label fails because separate is never equal — marriage's social recognition, not just its 1,100 benefits, is what its defenders are denied.
- ch. 30 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Peter Singer, John Stuart Mill — Speciesism; Animal Liberation; Utilitarianism; Ethical Egoism — Uses 'Fun with Veal' (the boys' bedroom standoff over baby calves, the FDA renaming veal 'tortured baby cows', Stan's meat strike punished by 'vaginitus'), 'Whale Whores' (the Japanese hating dolphins until Stan's doctored Enola Gay photo swaps in a cow and chicken), and 'Pee' (researchers peeing on rhesus monkeys) to pose the line-drawing problem: why do we protect cute animals and slaughter yummy ones? Neither intelligence (pigs versus dogs), utility, age, nor cuteness survives scrutiny as a morally relevant criterion — if it did, Nurse Gollum or Timmy would lose standing. Singer's speciesism analogy and the utilitarian inclusion of all who can suffer are then applied: Cartman, who draws his moral circle around himself, is the honest ethical egoist, while Kyle and Butters' selective vegetarianism and the adults' meat-eating inconsistency are exactly what Singer's view condemns.
- ch. 31 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" **·** Plato, Arthur Schopenhauer, Sextus Empiricus, Pythagoras — Tripartite Soul; The World as Will; Pythagorean Harmony of the Spheres; Theory of Forms — Reads South Park's music through the Greek doctrine of ethos: Sextus Empiricus' story of Pythagoras sobering drunk youths with slow aulos tunes and Plato's banishment of the soft Ionian and Lydian modes anticipate episodes where music directly changes behavior — Slayer's 'Raining Blood' scattering the hippie horde in 'Die Hippie Die', Cher blasted at the ATF standoff, and the Brown Noise in 'World Wide Recorder Concert'. Plato's tripartite soul maps how the Succubus's 'Morning After' spell enchants Chef's appetitive soul until the boys reverse the melody, while the Sirens' cosmic harmony in the Republic's Myth of Er links back to pitch-planet correspondences. Against Plato's view of music as inferior imitation, Schopenhauer's claim that music copies the Will itself explains why Grandpa's Enya torture in 'Death' communicates despair better than argument; authenticity judgments (Phil Collins appreciated only on Ritalin, Cartman's cynically reworded Faith + 1 hits) echo Plato's demand that music imitate the good.
- ch. 32 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" *(notes)*

## The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates

- ch. 1 "Series" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Titlepage" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Competing with High Quality Data" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction" *(no index entry yet)* — Editors Decker and Eberl open with William Shatner's 1986 'Get a life' Saturday Night Live skit and argue that thousands of hours spent watching Star Trek are not wasted, because the show is a treasure trove of philosophical questions. They preview the volume's ethics chapters on captains' moral psychology and the Prime Directive (asking why Kirk is so hellbent on destroying utopian civilizations), its social-political chapters on Klingons, Borg values, Federation economics versus Ferengi capitalism, and justice in the Q Continuum, and its metaphysical chapters on whether Data and Voyager's holographic Doctor are persons, Riker's duplication, and holodeck skepticism. It closes by framing Roddenberry's secular humanism against the seriously treated religious cultures of the Klingons and Bajorans.
- ch. 7 "Part I Alpha Quadrant Home Systems" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Notes" **·** Robert Nozick, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Plato, Socrates — The Experience Machine; The Unexamined Life; Eudaimonia (flourishing) — Jason Eberl uses the amusement park of 'Shore Leave', Omicron Ceti III's spore paradise in 'This Side of Paradise', Landru's hedonistic 'red hour', and the Borg's relentless efficiency to argue that edifying play and leisure are necessary for intellectual, moral, and spiritual flourishing. Following Josef Pieper's Leisure, with Nozick's experience machine (applied to 'The Thaw' and Barclay's holodiction), Aristotle's 'we work in order to be at leisure', and Aquinas on wonder, he contrasts mere utility (bonum utile) with the common good a drone-only Collective can never have. He concludes that thoughtfully watching Star Trek is itself worthwhile leisure: science-fiction thought experiments that serve Socrates's examined life.
- ch. 9 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Virtue Ethics (arete); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Jerold Abrams reads J. J. Abrams's Kirk as Aristotle's megalopsychos and 'god among men' from the Politics: too excellent to be a mere crewmember, disdainful of rank, speaking openly from love and hate, and a law unto himself. The four-on-one bar fight, reprogramming the unwinnable Kobayashi Maru, declaring 'Some should be' above the Prime Directive to Pike, and his exile to frozen Delta Vega (like the Argonauts stranding Heracles) all enact Aristotle's dilemma that a society must either exile such a man or submit to his monarchy. Spock, a great-souled man himself, becomes Kirk's 'second self' in Aristotle's truest friendship once Kirk takes the captain's chair.
- ch. 10 "Notes" **·** Plato, Aristotle, John Rawls, David Hume, Martha Nussbaum — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will); Tripartite Soul — Tim Challans treats Kirk, Picard, Archer, and Janeway as case studies in moral psychology, with the captain as Plato's charioteer balancing the horses of Spock's logic and McCoy's feeling. He reads Picard's 'there are four lights' coercion in 'Chain of Command' and his Locutus guilt in 'Family' through Rawls's shame/guilt distinction and Nancy Sherman's 'moral injury', while Kirk's 'I need my pain' refusal of Sybok and Archer's Xindi-era regrets show commanders owning guilt, regret, and remorse. Drawing on Nussbaum's 'upheavals of thought' and Hume's passions, he argues that a rare, well-integrated moral psychology—pride tempered by humility, as Q's lesson in 'Tapestry' demonstrates—is what qualifies the one-in-a-million starship captain.
- ch. 11 "Notes" **·** Immanuel Kant, Confucius, Aristotle — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; The Junzi (exemplary person); Utilitarianism — Barcenas and Bein pit Kant against Confucius on the Prime Directive, opening with Kirk's Nibiru volcano rescue of Spock in Into Darkness. Kant's categorical imperative—universalization and respect tests applied to Scotty's dilemma in 'Bread and Circuses' and Worf's 'not a matter of degree'—makes the Directive absolute, while Confucius and Aristotle ground morality in cultivated character: a junzi like Picard may bend the rule when virtue demands it, as in 'Pen Pals' and rescuing Wesley from the Edo in 'Justice'. They conclude Starfleet needs both: the Kantian rule for most officers, and exemplary persons like Picard to know when the rule fails.
- ch. 12 "Notes" **·** Aristotle, Robert Nozick, Jean-Jacques Rousseau — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Utopia and Dystopia; Moral Relativism — David Kyle Johnson argues Kirk is a jerk for dismantling utopias—the machine-god Vaal in 'The Apple' and the spore colonists of Omicron Ceti III in 'This Side of Paradise'—whose members were happy, healthy, and arguably free. Taking up objections from the Mission Log podcast, he rebuts the 'stagnation' and 'drug' charges by testing the utopias against Aristotle's eudaimonia and Maslow's self-actualization, and exposes the appeal-to-nature fallacy behind 'artificial happiness'. Using Rousseau on primitive simplicity and Nozick's libertarian minimal state, he concludes that the real threat to freedom is Kirk himself (and a Federation that, as Eddington says, assimilates without telling you), and that at minimum cultural relativism forbids wrecking harmless societies.
- ch. 13 "Notes" **·** Thomas Hobbes, Sigmund Freud — Just War Theory; The Ethics of Political Violence; The State of Nature; Utilitarianism — David Boersema reads Star Trek as a survey of peace studies, distinguishing negative peace from positive peace via 'The Cloud Minders', where Troglyte Vanna demands her people's 'right to the clouds' in Stratos. Against Anan 7's 'we're a killer species' in 'A Taste of Armageddon'—explicitly mirrored in post-9/11 drone war and 'shock and awe'—he enlists Hobbes, Freud, and McCoy's defense of the dark Kirk in 'The Enemy Within' to question whether violence is natural, and treats Kodos's 'some had to die that others might live' in 'The Conscience of the King' as the utilitarian justification for atrocity. Gem's compassion in 'The Empath', Kirk sparing the Gorn in 'Arena', and the Horta's misread attack in 'The Devil in the Dark' display nonviolence, deterrence, and corrected perception as alternatives to war.
- ch. 14 "Part II Beta Quadrant Dangerous Rivalries" *(front)*
- ch. 15 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; The Death of God; Moral Relativism — Victor Grech presents Klingons as a cultural pastiche—Mongol horde stereotypes, Japanese Bushido, Viking Valhalla, Shakespeare 'restored to the original Klingon'—whose 1500-year honor code and embrace of honorable death (Klag's dishonored father, Jadzia's rebuke of Kang) make them Nietzschean Ubermenschen who slew their own gods, echoing Nietzsche's 'God is dead'. The Kahless clone of 'Rightful Heir' ('perhaps the words are more important than the man') shows a messianism surviving deicide. He then reads Worf through Roland Barthes's 'Occidentalism' and one-way acculturation—Picard praising Worf's 'humanity' after 'Reunion'—while Azetbur's 'human rights' is racist jab in The Undiscovered Country and Trekkers' Klingon cosplay raise cultural relativism and appropriation.
- ch. 16 "Notes" **·** René Descartes — The Question Concerning Technology; Mind–Body Dualism; Utopia and Dystopia — Dan Dinello reads the Borg as the nightmare double of Data: where Data embodies Asimov's Laws of Robotics and Federation humanism, the Borg realize Jacques Ellul's and Langdon Winner's thesis that technology is an autonomous, totalitarian force assimilating its makers rather than a neutral tool. He traces the Collective's shared mind and quest for 'perfection' to transhumanism (Max More, James Hughes), whose philosophical roots lie in Descartes's mechanical body and mind-as-information—the very premise of Ira Graves's consciousness upload in 'The Schizoid Man'. Picard's tear as Locutus and Hugh's acquired individuality in 'I, Borg' show that creativity and liberal humanist values, not technology, defeat the ultimate techno-totalitarian dystopia.
- ch. 17 "Notes" **·** Immanuel Kant, Andy Clark — Autonomy of the Will; Humanity as an End in Itself; The Extended Mind — Barbara Stock uses the Borg to analyze autonomy: Picard's 'they took everything I was' names the Collective's destruction of self-governance, while Hugh's choice to return to the crash site in 'I, Borg' displays the Kantian core of autonomy—acting on universalizable principle against inclination. She defends relational autonomy through Janeway's pleading with Kes in 'The Gift' and the Ferengi woman's internalized oppression, then combines it with Clark's extended cognition to ask whether the Borg Queen's 'I am the Collective' might make the Collective itself an autonomous agent. Finally she judges Janeway's forcible de-assimilation of Seven defensible only while Seven is non-autonomous, and her promise never to let Seven return ethically suspect.
- ch. 18 "Notes" **·** Thomas Hobbes, John Locke — The State of Nature; The Social Contract; Natural Rights — Alkema and Barkman put Q himself on trial, asking what justifies his judgment of humanity in 'Encounter at Farpoint' and Trelane's of Kirk in 'The Squire of Gothos'. Hobbes's Leviathan would license Q's might-makes-right sovereignty over a savage species, but Q lacks humanity's consent and cannot show he acts for future peace; Locke's natural law instead binds even nearly omnipotent beings, as Janeway's asylum ruling for the suicidal Quinn in 'Death Wish' demonstrates. Q's repeated self-sacrifice—in 'Deja Q' and the Continuum's civil war—reveals a conscience answerable to natural law rather than raw power.
- ch. 19 "Notes" **·** Karl Marx — Alienation; Historical Materialism; Class Struggle — Jeff Ewing argues the Federation's moneyless, postscarcity economy is Marx's transitional stage on the way to classless communism: Picard's 'we've eliminated hunger, want, the need for possessions' and Troi's exchange with Samuel Clemens in 'Time's Arrow' mark Marx's shift from the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom. He reconstructs Marx and Engels on alienation, the division of labor, labor-tokens, and the withering state to dissolve the apparent anomalies—Federation credits, Quark's tab, the Chateau Picard vineyard—as survivals of transition rather than capitalism. Rom's 'workers of the world unite' in 'Bar Association' and the self-actualizing leisure of Enterprise crews complete the case.
- ch. 20 "Notes" **·** Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill, David Hume — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle; Higher and Lower Pleasures — Greg Littmann tests utilitarianism against Star Trek's heroes, reading Spock's 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few' (The Wrath of Khan, Into Darkness) as Bentham's greatest-happiness principle, with Kirk's radiation-chamber death as its mirror image. He uses Mill's higher and lower pleasures to contrast the TNG crew's improbably refined holodeck tastes with Kirk's Argelius shore leave and Quark's 'Vulcan Love Slave', and Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis to defend emotion against Vulcan suppression. Against Janeway killing Tuvix, Sisko's conspiracy in 'In the Pale Moonlight', and Kirk letting Edith Keeler die, he notes Trek never shows the many actually harmed, but sides with the utilitarians: favoring friends and the few is arbitrary discrimination.
- ch. 21 "Notes" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Courtland Lewis argues Star Trek teaches philosophy through casuistry: episodic case studies that test intuitions, moving from paradigm cases to harder ones. Its three sci-fi virtues—scientific constraint, flexible realism, and thought experimentation, shown in 'Clues' and contrasted with Doctor Who's 'Kill the Moon'—let it stage 'The Measure of a Man's hearing on Data's personhood and 'Nothing Human's dilemma over using Cardassian Mengele-style research data (analogous to Tuskegee) to save B'Elanna without the racial baggage of real-world cases. Viewers deliberate along with the crew—Janeway uses the data, then the Doctor deletes Crell Moset—which is exactly why Trek changes lives.
- ch. 22 "Part III Delta Quadrant Questing for Home" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Notes" **·** Derek Parfit, René Descartes — Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity; Mind–Body Dualism — William Jaworski argues, opening with Breaking Bad's Skinny Pete and Badger, that you should never enter a transporter: after showing the MEM converter violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, he asks whether the reassembled pattern is you or a replica. He tests three escape routes—Vulcan katra substance dualism (The Wrath of Khan, The Search for Spock) in the tradition of Plato and Descartes; constitutionalism, on which you survive total replacement by robotic parts as Picard nearly does under Borg assimilation; and Parfit's survival-without-identity answer to Riker's fission in 'Second Chances'. Each fails or costs too much: dualism wrecks moral intuitions about killing, constitutionalism faces the two-Riker indeterminacy, and mere 'survival' cannot sustain the particularity of love.
- ch. 24 "Notes" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit — Personal Identity (memory theory); Teleporter Paradox (personal fission); Personal Identity — Trip McCrossin reads 'The Enemy Within's split Kirk (with its LBJ/Vietnam subtext) and 'Second Chances's two Rikers as a crash course in Locke's consciousness theory of personal identity, from 'Turnabout Intruder's body swap and reward-and-punishment problem to the transitivity-of-identity paradox that blocks both Kirks from being the original. Parfit's degrees of psychological connectedness, he argues, explain why TNG treats the both-Rikers-survive answer as uncontroversial where TOS agonized over it. But Thomas Riker's renaming, and David Wiggins's 'only a and b' rule, reveal that identity would become an extrinsic property if branching mattered—so the survival-versus-identity debate ends 'to be continued'.
- ch. 25 "Notes" **·** Immanuel Kant, Jeremy Bentham, Protagoras — Humanity as an End in Itself; The Categorical Imperative; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism) — Nina Rosenstand reads 'The Measure of a Man' as a Kantian defense of Data's personhood: Maddox's sentience criteria concede intelligence and self-awareness, and Picard—prompted by Guinan's warning that a ruling for Maddox means an army of android slaves—shows a rational being must be treated as an end in himself, never dismantled merely for Starfleet's benefit. Bentham's utilitarianism supplies the contrast (an army of Datas would maximize happiness), while the episode's title ironizes Protagoras's 'man is the measure of all things', since the measure here is rationality rather than humanity. Louvois's open verdict becomes precedent for Lal, the exocomps, and Voyager's Doctor, and a metaphor for real struggles for recognition.
- ch. 26 "Notes" **·** Martha Nussbaum, René Descartes — Feminism; The Ethics of Care; Mind–Body Dualism; Embodiment (the lived body) — Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.
- ch. 27 "Notes" **·** Edmund Husserl — Intentionality; Phenomenology; Embodiment (the lived body) — Applies Husserl's phenomenology - noesis (the act of meaning-giving), noema (the meaning arrived at), and the life-world - to Voyager's Doctor and Seven of Nine as they build selves from conscious experience. Reads "Latent Image" (the Doctor's deleted memories of choosing Harry Kim's life over another ensign's) and "Infinite Regress" (Seven's channeling of assimilated personalities) as parallel guilt experiences whose noemata teach each that past choices remain part of identity without governing it. Their forced isolation in "One", the Doctor's unrequited love in "Someone to Watch over Me", and "Body and Soul", where the Doctor savors food and sensation through Seven's body, generate a shared noema: social interaction and embodied experience are what make a life-world, even for photons and drones.
- ch. 28 "Notes" **·** Carl Jung, Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, G.W.F. Hegel, John Locke — The State of Nature; Archetypes; Natural Goodness and Corruption by Society; The Collective Unconscious — Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.
- ch. 29 "Part IV Gamma Quadrant Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "Notes" **·** Mind–Body Dualism — Argues through Alfred North Whitehead's philosophy of organism - reality as momentary actual occasions with mental and physical poles, nested societies, and canalization - that Star Trek's advanced beings are not, and could not be, purely incorporeal. Mindless feeders like the dikironium cloud creature and the Drella show bodilessness is not sufficient for advancement, while parasitic Zetars and Ronin show it can be a liability; the Douwd, the Companion, and Amanda Rogers's Q parents voluntarily tether to bodies for love and new experience. The Q's stagnation and civil war ("Death Wish", "The Q and the Grey") illustrate Whitehead's balance of survival against creative advance: what looks like "freedom from physical form" is really "freedom of physical form", since a purely mental entity would be an unsustainable organism.
- ch. 31 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Consequentialism; Virtue Ethics (arete) — Applies Aristotle's three friendships to Trek: Ferengi Rules of Acquisition dealings and treaties as utility friendships, Bashir and O'Brien's darts and racquetball as friendship of pleasure, and virtuous friendship as requiring emotion, mutual goodwill, and irreplaceable intrinsic valuing - which emotionless Data fails at with Jenna D'Sora in "In Theory". The core argument, following Badhwar, is that consequentialism is logically and psychologically incompatible with virtuous friendship: Spock's "needs of the many" maxim and Data's "for the greater good" experimentation on Geordi in "Descent, Part II" show friends being treated as sacrificeable instruments, while the Kobayashi Maru cheat shows consequentialist reasoning blessing outcomes over means. Kirk's reversal - "the needs of the one outweigh the needs of the many" in The Search for Spock - and T'Pol's years caring for the amnesiac Archer in "Twilight" exemplify acting out of friendship rather than for any further goal.
- ch. 32 "Notes" **·** Feminism; Binary Oppositions; Authenticity — Pits Donna Haraway's Cyborg Manifesto against Star Trek's horror of the Borg, reading Locutus/Picard, Hugh, and Seven of Nine as tests of the Federation values of autonomy, individuality, and authenticity against the rival Borg values of heteronomy, collectivity, and simulation. Picard's "My culture is based on freedom and self-determination" exchange with the Borg, Hugh's discovery of his name and first-person "I", and Seven's tug-of-war with the Borg Queen in "Dark Frontier" dramatize what assimilation threatens. The chapter then defends a Haraway-inspired feminist reboot: women and minorities were long denied autonomy, individuality, and authenticity by prejudice and stereotype (Seven still must look "warp-core hot" in her catsuit), the human/machine and man/woman binaries were always false, and since we already live as cyborgs of apps, implants, and networks, resistance was negligible - the real Borg problem is their violent means, not their values.
- ch. 33 "Notes" **·** Personal Identity — Uses Odo as a case study in George Herbert Mead's theory that the self emerges only through social interaction: language begins with significant gestures (Odo's tentacle-slap at Dr. Mora, his talking to the dying baby changeling in "The Begotten"), and specific others like Mora and Kira teach the attitudes that become the generalized other. The Meadian I/me split explains Ezri Dax's nine-selves crisis and Joran's emergence in "Field of Fire", and the failed outfield calls and Sisko's ejection of Rom in "Take Me out to the Holosuite" show characters still learning to take the attitude of the team. Odo's "justice trick" is reread as instinct rather than racial memory, his confession to Kira in "Heart of Stone" shows the name odo'ital ("nothing") redeemed by internalized others, and his choice of the station crew over the Great Link marks a cosmopolitan self.
- ch. 34 "Notes" **·** David Hume, Immanuel Kant, Thomas Aquinas — Moral Relativism; Reason Is the Slave of the Passions; The Categorical Imperative; Is–Ought Problem — Tests moral relativism against absolutism through Enterprise's "Cogenitor": Trip's liberation of the Vissian third-sex being - secretly scanning its brain, naming it Charles, teaching it to read - ends in its suicide, and the chapter asks whether Trip's judgments track rational moral truth or are Humean after-the-fact rationalizations of disgust, since on Hume's view reason is the slave of the passions and is/ought are separate. Kant's categorical imperative (the cogenitor used merely as a means of reproduction) and Aquinas's natural law are offered as absolutist resources on Trip's side, while Phlox voices a Benedict-style "morally good is just habitual" relativism and Archer concludes "we didn't come out here to play God", prefiguring the Prime Directive. The chapter lands on Mary Midgley's rejection of moral isolationism via her tsujigiri example and Quark's "we're better than you" speech to Sisko: cross-cultural judgment is possible, but only after understanding, and not on the first day of first contact.
- ch. 35 "Notes" **·** Martin Heidegger, Andy Clark, David Chalmers — The Question Concerning Technology; The Extended Mind — Reads the Borg as the embodiment of Heidegger's essence of technology: assimilation as the "challenging" that sets upon nature, species and persons as standing-reserve, drones interchangeable like replaceable parts, and cube ships with no bridge because function outweighs individuality. The Enterprise cannot beat the Borg with more technology - every phaser adaptation buys only moments - because, as with Heidegger's danger, the crew tries to control technology from inside technology; rescue comes only when Guinan persuades Riker to "throw the book away" and shift how the crew relates to the Borg. The warning is extended to us through Zizek on synthetic life and a new servant class and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind: our devices already remember, plan, and identify for us, so we are being assimilated by our own creations.
- ch. 36 "Part V Beyond the Galactic Barrier The Future as the Final Frontier" *(front)*
- ch. 37 "Notes" **·** Plato, Nick Bostrom — Allegory of the Cave; The Simulation Hypothesis; Free Will vs Determinism; Philosophical Skepticism — Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.
- ch. 38 "Notes" **·** David Lewis, David Hume — Personal Identity; Possible Worlds; Ship of Theseus — Sorts out Spock-Prime, bearded Mirror-Spock, and Abrams's Spock-2 using David Lewis's modal realism, counterparts, and Humean supervenience: identity is not directly perceived but judged from adjacent similar instances, as with Hume's natural properties. The refit Enterprise versus the Enterprise-A, plus the thought experiment of downloading the old ship's computer into the new one, carry a Ship-of-Theseus-style analysis of whether swapped cells and Spock's katra-separated death and Genesis resurrection preserve identity. Mirror-Spock turns out to be a worldmate within one enlarged world (Kirk's crossover in "Mirror, Mirror" makes the universes spatiotemporally continuous), not a transworld duplicate, and Spock-Prime and Spock-2 are like two highways overlapping until Nero's arrival in 2233 makes them diverge - two similar individuals formed by different successes and failures, never identical.
- ch. 39 "Notes" **·** G.W.F. Hegel, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; History Has a Direction — Reads "The City on the Edge of Forever" through Romanticism: the Guardian of Forever strands Kirk and Spock without historical reference points - a nihilist moment of pure meaninglessness - and Kirk's Romantic response is to rebuild the narrative of the past even at the cost of letting Edith Keeler die. Hegel's philosophy of history explains the compulsion to record (Spock's anguished "I've missed taping centuries of living history"), why Edith's unwitting world-historical role is to die under a truck rather than lead a pacifist America to Nazi conquest, and Novalis's call to "make the world Romantic" frames Spock's self-rescue as young Selek in "Yesteryear". Kirk, Spock, and McCoy become Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy archetypes - Tragic Hero, Apollonian, Dionysian - converging in the street scene where McCoy lunges to save Edith, Spock waits on logic, and Kirk, seizing McCoy's arms, finds a tragic beauty in her death.
- ch. 40 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche — The Übermensch; Amor Fati (love of fate); Will to Power — Argues Q embodies Nietzsche's revaluation of values: contemptuous of herd-like safety, Q subjects Picard and the crew to trials ("Encounter at Farpoint", "Hide and Q", "All Good Things"'s "the trial never ends") meant to force growth beyond conventional morality, seek out other "supermen", and embrace risk - Q's "bloody nose" defense after eighteen crewmen die at the Borg in "Q Who?". The Borg figure as everything Nietzschean individualism despises, a mindless collectivism that robs drones of the passion the strong need to individuate, and Q's offer to join Picard as guide pictures a friendship between Nietzsche's self-mastered few. The lesson of "Tapestry" is amor fati: Picard must embrace the Nausicaan knife fight that nearly killed him, since undoing it makes a safe, unnoticed man - though the authors finally refuse Nietzsche's harsher dictum that the weak should perish, siding with healing over Q's education-by-death.
- ch. 41 "Notes" **·** The Death of God — Argues that despite Roddenberry's strident atheism, Star Trek develops a "humanist theology": godlike beings - Gary Mitchell, Charlie X, Trelane, Q, and Apollo in "Who Mourns for Adonais?" - are demoted to powerful aliens whose demand for worship disqualifies them as gods, echoing the 1960s death-of-God theology in which god-figures are consistently disappointing and the God of traditional theism is symbolically dead. Divinity is relocated into a possible human future requiring compassion above power - Kirk's charge to the dying Mitchell that "a god needs compassion", and Picard's "perhaps there's a residue of humanity in Q after all". The chapter also weighs Trek's anti-posthuman bias ("Dr. Korby was never here", the Borg) against the consensual Decker-V'Ger union in The Motion Picture, and reads Star Trek V's "What does God need with a starship?" as the uneasy remainder of Shatner's religiosity inside Roddenberry's secular vision.
- ch. 42 "Notes" **·** Plato, John Dewey — Democracy; Faith and Reason; Justice in the Republic — Charts Star Trek's handling of secularization, from the "Roddenberry attitude" of Kirk confronting fifteen would-be gods to later series' complications, using Robert Audi's nine features of religion and Benedict Anderson's "imagined community" - the Yangs' sacred flag and worship-word "freedom" in "The Omega Glory" show an incoherent civic religion Kirk can correct. "Who Watches the Watchers" inverts the dynamic by making Picard an accidental god who refuses to found a religion among the proto-Vulcan Mintakans, while real-world creationism in schools and abstinence-only sex education supply the chapter's empirical moral arguments that faith-driven public policy fails on its own terms. DS9's Bajor arc - Vedek Winn boycotting Keiko's school, Sisko's defense of the faith that sustained Bajor through occupation, and Akorem's restoration of the D'jarra castes in "Accession", likened to Plato's Republic-class soul hierarchy - grounds the claim that infallible religious authority corrodes democratic equality, with Sisko as the Emissary who synthesizes faith and secular governance.
- ch. 43 "Contributors" *(notes)*
- ch. 44 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 45 "EULA" *(front)*

## The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

- ch. 1 "Series" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Acknowledgments Legacy of the Force" *(notes)*
- ch. 6 "Introduction “The Circle Is Now Complete”" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — The editors frame the volume through fan controversies (Han or Greedo, Jar Jar, the de-canonized Expanded Universe) and the philosophical question each film raises, from whether a prophesied destiny robs Anakin of freedom to whether good and evil are mere 'points of view.' They invoke Hegel's claim that philosophy captures only its own time to concede this 'ultimate' volume predates Episode VII. The introduction connects Star Wars to philosophy by previewing the essays: Stoic Jedi, the Sith's Thrasymachus-like worldview, Boba Fett's amoralism, feminist readings of Padme and Leia, Kevin Smith's charge that the Rebels are terrorists, Joseph Campbell's monomyth, droid minds, and whether Chewie can speak.
- ch. 7 "Episode I The Philosophical Menace" *(front)*
- ch. 8 "Notes" **·** Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — Tripartite Soul; Man Is the Measure (sophistic relativism); Will to Power; The Noble Lie — MacMullan argues Darth Plagueis is a paradox for Plato: wisdom as reason ruling spirit and appetite should be impossible for a Sith who feeds on passion, yet Plagueis stays patient, restrained, and rational for over a century. He reads Sidious's 'I will make it legal' and the Sith Code as Thrasymachus's 'justice is the advantage of the stronger,' and notes Plagueis even shares Plato's noble lie and eugenic breeding programs. Finding that Plato's prediction of self-destruction fails for Plagueis, the chapter turns to Nietzsche: master morality, the will to power, and life beyond good and evil better explain a Sith who cherishes bodily life and seeks to conquer death where Yoda and Socrates calmly disdain 'crude matter.'
- ch. 9 "Notes" **·** Epictetus — The Dichotomy of Control; Preferred Indifferents; Stoicism — Hummel maps the Jedi Order onto Epictetus's Stoicism: philosophy as a way of life, virtue through wisdom, the dichotomy of control ('some things are up to us'), and treating outcomes like flying or other people's fates as preferred indifferents within the will of the Force. Anakin falls because he misconceives power as the ability to do amazing things - stopping people from dying - instead of mastery of his own judgments, and he refuses Stoic indifference toward Shmi and Padme. The chapter also indicts the Jedi's own un-Stoic lapses: mind tricks on Watto, entering the Clone Wars, and Mace Windu's attempt to execute a subdued Sidious.
- ch. 10 "Notes" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — The Leap of Faith; Teleological Suspension of the Ethical; The Stages on Life's Way; Faith and Reason — Lindenmuth reads Luke's endgame in Return of the Jedi as Kierkegaard's knight of faith, reversing Abraham's binding of Isaac: where Abraham raised the knife, Luke, pressed by Yoda and Obi-Wan to kill his father, throws his saber away. Jedi detachment ('train yourself to let go') is infinite resignation, and Han Solo's arc from self-interested smuggler to hero at Yavin traces Kierkegaard's aesthetic-to-ethical stages. Luke's double movement - resigning everything, his cause and his life, while trusting there is still good in Vader - suspends the ethical demand to kill and accomplishes what neither side thought possible: turning a Sith back to the light.
- ch. 11 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Immanuel Kant — Perspectivism; The Golden Rule; Problem of Induction — Adams pairs Anakin with Achilles to show how Palpatine's lesson that 'good is a point of view' - Nietzsche's claim that there are no moral facts, only interpretations - nearly destroys both heroes before a father's love pulls them back: Priam's tears before Achilles, Luke unmasking Vader. Against nihilism the chapter defends moral realism through Apollo's lion simile (compassion and respect are objective facts about what persons require) and Kant's self-critical inquiry, with the Jedi Council's twelve-way deliberation illustrating that some interpretations are better than others, beyond Hume's problem of induction. Both epics settle on a 'Pagan Golden Rule' - help your friends and harm your enemies, but never lose compassion for either.
- ch. 12 "Notes" **·** Confucius, Laozi — Wu Wei (effortless action); The Tao (the Way); Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Rectification of Names — Decker parallels the Republic's fall into Palpatine's Empire with the Zhou dynasty's collapse that birthed Chinese philosophy, reading three Jedi from the Dark Times comics through it. K'Kruhk, guided by the Zatoichi-like Master Zao, learns wu-wei - following the Force rather than forcing outcomes, with Laozi's Dao as the Force's Chinese analogue. Dass Jennir's struggle over what 'Jedi' means after killing a slaver becomes Confucian rectification of names and the cultivation of ren, while Kai Hudorra's loss of faith, withdrawal to a casino, and final sacrificial stand against Vader embody Mozi-style pragmatic minimalism redeemed by Jennir's virtuous example.
- ch. 13 "Episode II Attack of the Morals" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "Notes" **·** Just War Theory; The Ethics of Political Violence; Doctrine of Double Effect; Utilitarianism — Camosy takes up Randal's charge in Clerks that destroying Death Star II killed innocent independent contractors. Against utilitarian reasoning he deploys just war theory: terrorism is intentionally targeting innocents as a means, so Tarkin's destruction of Alderaan (and, he argues, Hiroshima) qualifies, while the Rebels, who would have been 'pleased' if the workers took the day off, do not. Since the crew was mostly conscripted clones and programmed droids with no moral responsibility, and destroying the station saved billions, the attack passes the proportionality test - an exercise in double-effect reasoning that asks fans to question the 'good guys lens.'
- ch. 15 "Notes" **·** Michael Walzer — Just War Theory; Ethical Egoism; Moral Relativism — LaRocca argues Boba Fett is best understood as an amoralist - neither a moral relativist nor an ethical egoist, but someone who has withdrawn from moral judgment altogether - reading his terse 'As you wish' to Vader and his insuring of Han's survival purely for payment as evidence. Through Michael Walzer's account of the soldier's constrained choice and the 'good mercenary' debate, he asks whether mercenary violence (Blackwater, private military contractors) really differs morally from a conscript's or clone's. The upshot is that Fett's grayness between Empire and Rebellion exposes amoralism as a surprisingly central part of political and military life.
- ch. 16 "Notes" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Nagel, Harry Frankfurt, Susan Wolf — Moral Luck; The Categorical Imperative; Second-Order Desires (personhood); Free Will vs Determinism — Michaud puts Jar Jar Binks on trial for proposing the emergency powers that let Palpatine become Emperor and doom the galaxy. He weighs Nagel's resultant moral luck through a two-Lukes landspeeder case, Susan Wolf's virtue-based reply that equal fault can deserve different feelings, Kant's 'ought implies can' and the categorical imperative, and a Frankfurt-style scenario in which Palpatine's hypothetical mind-trick removes Jar Jar's ability to choose otherwise. The verdict: as a deceived, politically limited character trying to do good, Jar Jar is not guilty of the Empire's crimes - only of being obnoxious.
- ch. 17 "Notes" **·** Augustine of Hippo — The Problem of Evil; The Divided Will; Fate and Foreknowledge — Eberl applies Augustine's theodicy to the Force: since evil is privation rather than a thing, the dark side is not a real half of the Force but its willful misuse by free beings, answering why a Force with a will permits Alderaan. Anakin's fall is Augustine's inordinate desire (cupiditas) for the temporal good of Padme's life against Yoda's counsel to let go, while Jacen Solo's willingness to kill for peace shows love destroyed rather than merely disordered, placing him beyond the redemption Anakin's rightly ordered love for his children still permits. Free will remains a divine gift whose misuse, not its giver, explains moral evil, and Anakin could still freely fulfill the Chosen One prophecy.
- ch. 18 "Episode III Revenge of the Alliance" *(front)*
- ch. 19 "Notes" **·** Epictetus, Zeno of Citium — Stoicism; The Dichotomy of Control; Philosophy of Love — Taliaferro and Beck trace a philosophy of love through Anakin: fatherless, he attaches compulsively to Shmi and then Padme, refusing the Stoic limits on control that Yoda and Epictetus teach, so that love curdles into the vow to 'stop people from dying.' Vader's fatherhood is the caricature of love - offering Luke power instead of care - until Luke's compassion and Vader's final self-sacrifice redeem it. The lesson: love must be tempered by humility about what Zeno and the Stoics placed outside our control, and broken family bonds can be partly repaired through costly self-sacrifice.
- ch. 20 "Notes" **·** Socrates, Plato, Aristotle — Aristotle on Friendship (philia); The Social Contract; Justice in the Republic; Man as Political Animal — Littmann shows Luke, Leia, and Han repeatedly put friends and family above the galaxy's freedom - Luke abandoning Dagobah for Bespin, the Jabba rescue, refusing to kill Vader - in the tradition of Homer's heroes, then submits them to Athenian scrutiny. Socrates's refusal to escape his Athens prison and his implicit just agreement with the city set civic duty over friendship; Plato would abolish the guardians' family and censor the Zeus-Kronos patricide myth yet approves of Luke sparing Vader; Aristotle prizes philia but holds citizens belong to the state. He concludes the philosophers mostly win: heroic loyalty is often moral failure, and good moral reasoning asks how many people an action affects, not just whom you love.
- ch. 21 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Malloy argues loyalty's moral value is exaggerated, asking what loyalty is via Royce's cause-loyalty, Fletcher's historical self, and Keller's thin motive theory, applied to Leia torn between Alderaan and the Alliance and to Luke's emotional flight from Dagobah. The Sith embody a paradox: under the Rule of Two a loyal Sith must betray, so Vader's final turn on Palpatine was loyalty to Luke and thus betrayal of the Sith itself, while stormtrooper-style loyalty shows devotion is only as good as its object. Betrayal wrongs because it irreversibly alters a relationship - which is why Lando's Bespin gamble was right - and loyalty's real value is the commitment, dedication, and selflessness behind it.
- ch. 22 "Notes" **·** Plato, Socrates — The Philosopher King; Justice in the Republic; Tripartite Soul; The Noble Lie — Barkman and Alkema map Plato's Republic onto the fall of the Old Republic: the bickering Senate and Anakin's 'someone wise' exchange with Padme enact democracy's degeneration into tyranny, with Palpatine as Plato's werewolf-like protector-tyrant and Dooku's Sith name 'Tyranus' marking Thrasymachus's justice-as-strength as Sith doctrine. The Jedi approximate Plato's philosopher-guardians - courageous, temperate, reluctant to rule, surrendering their children to the Temple much like the Republic's breeding deceptions and noble lies. Justice as each part doing its own work applies to the tripartite soul as much as the state, and the chapter closes that democracy survives Endor but only if truth stays a beacon of the light side.
- ch. 23 "Episode IV A New Hermeneutic" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 24 "Notes" **·** Simone de Beauvoir, Betty Friedan — Feminism; Objectification; Woman as the Other — Argues that Leia and Padme really are strong feminist characters, using Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to defuse the two stock objections: Padme's motherhood is 'freely chosen' rather than an oppressive role, and Leia chained in Jabba's palace keeps command of her sexuality, turning the damsel-in-distress plot around by strangling Jabba with her own chain and later rescuing Han herself. The chapter's real complaint is structural: with only six speaking women in the original trilogy, almost all of them royalty, Leia and Padme are forced to represent all women (the 'affluent few' problem), while Shmi, Aunt Beru, Mon Mothma, and the handmaidens Sabe, Corde, and Dorme never get the screen time to show their strength.
- ch. 25 "Notes" **·** Michel Foucault, Jean-Paul Sartre — Discipline and Docile Bodies; Objectification — Reads Leia's gold-bikini captivity in Jabba's palace as an image of contemporary culture's fear of fat: Jabba, the rancor, and the Sarlaac personify uncontrolled appetite and Sartre's 'slimy' being-in-itself, while Leia's thin, disciplined body epitomizes the anorexic ideal. Drawing on Susan Bordo and Foucault's docile bodies, the chapter argues the scene chains women to a tyrannical ideal of slimness so that Leia herself becomes the oppressor, and closes with Sartre's point that consciousness depends on its body, so we should suspend the fear of flesh and embrace embodied life as the Force does.
- ch. 26 "Notes" **·** Peter Singer, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill — Animal Liberation; Autonomy of the Will; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Uses the Zillo Beast arc, battle droids, mynocks, and Han shooting Greedo to test theories of moral status: Schweitzer-style reverence for life would forbid a Jedi from eating anything, genetic views breed Palpatine-style human chauvinism, Singer's sentience view makes droid suffering and Luke dropping the rancor's door morally troubling, and Kantian autonomy excludes cognitively impaired beings too harshly. The chapter weighs Palpatine as merely a 'sociopathic' goal-pursuer rather than a Kantian moral agent, and leaves the droid question open via the novel Children of the Jedi, where the droid-converted Nichos lacks even mere agency because he cannot override his programming.
- ch. 27 "Episode V Metaphysics Strikes Back" *(front)*
- ch. 28 "Notes" **·** Augustine of Hippo, Zhuangzi — The Problem of Evil; Taoism (Daoism) — Asks how an all-encompassing, good Force can have a dark side: after framing the Force as panentheistic, it tests Augustine's privation theory (Alderaan's destruction as an absence of 'measure, order, and form') and a Daoist reading of Yoda's equanimity modeled on Zhuangzi drumming and singing after his wife's death, rejecting both because Vader's evil is active, disciplined, and full of the Force rather than a lack. The answer endorsed is Schelling's: the will needs a dark 'ground' - Yoda's 'anger, fear, aggression' - which is benign when ordered by the will of love and becomes evil when it separatisitically defies it, which is what 'bringing balance to the Force' means.
- ch. 29 "Notes" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, René Descartes — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology — Reads Jedi training through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology and the enactivism of Varela, Thompson, and Rosch: Obi-Wan's blast-shield remote drill and Yoda's Dagobah obstacle course work because perception, thought, and action are one embodied flow rather than a perception-cognition-action 'sandwich.' Luke fails to lift the X-wing because his habits do not yet present the ship as liftable, while for Yoda 'size matters not'; and Jedi need no special Force-organ (so midi-chlorians are redundant) because skilled interaction, like Bach-y-Rita's tactile-vision subjects, determines what experience is like.
- ch. 30 "Notes" **·** David Hume, Charles Sanders Peirce, Socrates, Hilary Putnam — Problem of Induction; On Miracles; Philosophical Skepticism — Asks whether Han Solo's 'hokey religions' dismissal of the Force is unreasonable given his evidence, answering no: Hume's argument against miracles explains why testimony of lightsaber tricks and mind tricks should not overturn Han's experience of consistent natural law, while Hume's problem of induction and custom/habit explain why both Han's 'luck' verdict and Obi-Wan's 'no such thing as luck' are habit-based generalizations. Peirce's fallibilism (backed by Putnam's 'fallibilism does not entail skepticism') lets Han and Obi-Wan each claim knowledge without certainty, echoing Obi-Wan's line that many truths depend greatly on our own point of view.
- ch. 31 "Episode VI Return of the Non-Human" *(front)*
- ch. 32 "Notes" **·** John Searle — The Chinese Room; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Asks whether droids like C-3PO and R2-D2 can think, staging Searle's Chinese Room as a 'Bocce Room' to argue that droid anxiety, pain, and heroism might be mere input-output symbol shuffling. It then rebuts Searle with the systems reply (the room as a whole, not the person inside, might understand) and a neuron-by-neuron mechanical brain-replacement thought experiment showing the biological/mechanical divide is arbitrary, concluding that restraining bolts, memory wipes, and the Mos Eisley cantina's 'we don't serve their kind here' prejudice lose their justification if droids might genuinely suffer.
- ch. 33 "Notes" **·** Ludwig Wittgenstein — Language Games; The Private Language Argument — Pits Chomsky's structure-based verdict - Chewbacca's roars are unscripted, grammarless animal noises, hence not language - against Wittgenstein's meaning-as-use: the builder's language of 'wrench' and 'hydrospanner' shows that unstructured commands can work perfectly as a language-game. Obi-Wan's private Force-diary symbol 'S' illustrates the private language argument (no standard of correct use without a community), and viewers learn 'Sith,' 'lightsaber,' and Chewie's frustration at the medal ceremony from use alone, so Chewie genuinely communicates despite Shyriiwook having no real-world grammar.
- ch. 34 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Personal Identity — Uses Palpatine's cloning of the last Zillo Beast, Boba Fett's SCNT creation from Jango, and Thrawn's Hand of Thrawn resurrection scheme to argue de-extinction is impossible: if species are individuals (Ghiselin's species nominalism, grounded in Darwinian variation against Aristotle's species essentialism), then extinction closes the species' unique life story, so any clone is a numerically distinct new individual. The same numerical-vs-qualitative identity point shows Thrawn's clone would not be Thrawn, and only Palpatine's dark-side survival in a cloned body - not cloning itself - counts as genuine resurrection.
- ch. 35 "Episode VII The Fandom Awakens" *(front)*
- ch. 36 "Notes" **·** Carl Jung — The Collective Unconscious; Ideology and False Consciousness — Maps Campbell's Hero's Journey onto Luke's arc in A New Hope (ordinary world, meeting the mentor, crossing the threshold, atonement with the 'Dark Father' Vader), then argues both Campbell and Lucas misunderstand myth: following Malinowski, myth is a living social charter and therefore ideology, so Star Wars' cosmic dualism, male-centered monomyth, and celebration of violence conceal political and commercial power. The chapter's closing turn - 'Star Wars(TM) is the real Empire and the fans its consumer-subjects,' with Reagan's SDI and an 'insurgents vs. Empire' reading of the Rebellion as illustrations - applies ideology-critique to the franchise itself.
- ch. 37 "Notes" *(no index entry yet)* — Takes the carbon-freezing scene - Leia's 'I love you,' Han's 'I know,' Chewie's howls - to pose the paradox of fiction: we feel genuine, involuntary fear and pity for characters we know do not exist. It tests and rejects the illusion theory (we do not flee Vader's 501st Legion), the thought theory (we pity Han himself, not our mental representation of him), and Walton's pretend theory (viewers' emotions, unlike a child's Darth Maul lightsaber play, are not voluntary), landing on Radford's conclusion that our tears over the binary sunset and Obi-Wan's death are real emotions but not rational ones.
- ch. 38 "Notes" **·** Daniel Dennett, René Descartes — The Intentional Stance; Mind–Body Dualism — Uses a vintage Blue Snaggletooth action figure to illustrate Dennett's three stances - physical (AFA wear-grading of dented boots), design (why the Sears-exclusive mispack is valuable), and intentional (predicting whether Han would shoot first at a pedant correcting his parsec gaffe) - arguing that play trains a third-person science of mind that Descartes' first-person introspection and dualism could never verify. Dennett's account of religion as a misapplied intentional stance then explains begging the Falcon to 'hold together' and Zeus's lightning as projected intention, with the twist that children playing with figures know they are pretending while the superstitious mind does not.
- ch. 39 "Notes" *(no index entry yet)* — Analyzes Lucasfilm's April 2014 press release demoting the entire Expanded Universe (including Zahn's Thrawn Trilogy and the slicer Ghent) to noncanonical 'gossip,' contrasting it with the older G-T-C-S-N canon hierarchy and using Barthes' 'Death of the Author' to deny that creators can fix a fiction's meaning. Canon is shown to be dynamic, negotiable, and participatory - Aayla Secura rose from N-Canon to C-Canon after Attack of the Clones, fans picked R4-G9's color, the Holiday Special fell from Gospel - so Lucasfilm cannot unilaterally settle whether Han shot first: 'Star Wars is, after all, about rebellion.'
- ch. 40 "Contributors Troopers of the 501st Legion" *(notes)*
- ch. 41 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 42 "EULA" *(front)*
