- ch. 6 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Alan Turing — The Turing Test; Personal Identity; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.
- ch. 8 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Hall predicts what real alien Transformers would be like: any starfaring civilization is at least Kardashev Type 1 and would send nanotechnological, shape-shifting robots rather than biological explorers, since minds upload into machine bodies and colonies go all-robot. He proposes a logarithmic 'Hall scale' of ethics, arguing that interstellar cooperation requires Level 10 morality whose expanding inclusiveness would give visitors enough concern for indigenous species to leave Earth as a nature preserve, since robots need only the matter and energy of Mercury and the outer planets, not our biosphere.
- ch. 10 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Alan Turing — The Turing Test — Shook dismantles the four assumptions behind the argument that advanced aliens would already be here (that they want to find us, that travel is easy, that visits would leave traces, and that disguised visitors must be benign), showing the Transformers scenario - a warring robotic civilization that crashes into Earth unnoticed and disguises itself as Chevys and boomboxes like Bumblebee and Frenzy - is more probable than SETI's radio-based angel-alien mythology. War, not peace, drives the technology of real civilizations, as Trailbreaker's 'Simple. Disguise!' explanation of transformation shows, so First Contact will likely be with militaristic strangers absorbed in their own conflicts, not missionaries.
- ch. 11 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Maurice Merleau-Ponty, René Descartes, George Berkeley, Edmund Husserl — Embodiment (the lived body); Phenomenology; Mind–Body Dualism — Using the hidden sides of Transformers - a robot inside a Camaro, a tank inside a robot - the authors stage the philosophy of perception: Descartes's innate geometrical rules and Berkeley's bodily cross-referencing both fail to explain how Sam Witwicky can know the steelyard robot is his Camaro, while Merleau-Ponty's embodied account of focus, background, and 'indeterminate vision' explains it through the perceiver's lived body. They extend this to the 'Autobot Spike' mind-transfer episode and to CGI: virtual Transformers on screen feel hollow because light-created images have no hidden surfaces for our bodies to investigate and grasp.
- ch. 13 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, John Locke, Judith Jarvis Thomson, Thomas Aquinas — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Aristotle on the Soul; Potentiality and Actuality — Spicher argues that when Bumblebee trades his beat-up 1976 Camaro for a shiny 2007 model only his appearance changes (an accidental change), never his identity, because transforming is part of a Transformer's essence like a human wearing a mask. Locke's memory continuity and Thomson's bodily criterion each fail - the embryo, coma, and corpse problems, plus the thought experiment of Megatron's memories transplanted into another body - so he defends an Aristotelian composite of form and matter in which the Spark is the soul-like form organizing the machine body, preserving identity through transformation as form guides matter toward actuality.
- ch. 14 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Philosophical Skepticism — Steiff reads the 2007 movie as a sustained lesson in perceptual error: Sam's Porsche disappointment at the dealership, the parents' 'earthquake' misperception, and the Camaro that no one at Bobby B's lot suspects show that we see what context, expectation, and conditioning (the kitten experiments) lead us to see. She distinguishes illusion - misperceiving an object really present, as Sam misperceives Bumblebee as just a car - from hallucination, and weighs direct realism against representative realism's 'veil of perception' using film tricks from Melies's jammed camera to the Lumiere brothers' panic-inducing train, leaving Sam's knowledge resting on fallible but indispensable sense experience.
- ch. 15 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 16 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** John Searle, Alan Turing, René Descartes — The Chinese Room; The Turing Test; Mind–Body Dualism — Pike asks what the All Spark's zap would have to do to give brought-to-life vending machines and steering wheels genuine minds, testing logical behaviorism's dispositions and Turing's conversation test against Searle's Chinese Room ('syntax is insufficient for semantics'), and weighing Descartes's God-given soul against physicalist alternatives: functionalism, Searle's biological naturalism, and reductive physicalism. Since we can never access another mind from the inside, he concludes that by abductive inference to the best explanation - Optimus Prime's mourning, planning, and moral decision-making being too complex for mere programming - we have as much reason to credit a Transformer with a mind as any human around us.
- ch. 17 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle — Aristotle on the Soul; Virtue Ethics (arete); Immortality and the Soul — Eyestone argues Transformers are genuinely alive with souls by applying Aristotle's De Anima: self-motion, perception, and intellect fit Ratchet (who tells Buster 'I'm a machine, and I hear you!'), and even the troublesome nutritive faculty is secured, since Energon ingestion, agelessness, and building each other suit naturally immortal, semimortal beings whose reproduction resembles Primus's creation. He extends arete to machines - Megatron has the excellence of a military leader but not of a person, while Optimus's chosen, trained goodness (Grimlock's 'Autobot training,' the Aerialbots' decision in 'War Dawn') makes him virtuous - and answers his title question 'why not?', since Aristotle's mortal soul gives Transformers no worse a shot at heaven than we have.
- ch. 18 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — A fictional five-session counseling narrative in which a burned-out Optimus Prime - running out of gas, embarrassed by 'WASH ME' written in his own dirt - secretly sees therapist Dr. Sara Sawyer. Through the empty-chair technique he speaks to the dead Jazz, admitting the survivor guilt of a leader who was fighting Megatron when Jazz fell, and confesses the night he nearly smashed a human teenager's car mistaken for a Decepticon; the Miracle Question helps him imagine peace. The dialogue dramatizes an internal transformation: the machine learns to name grief, anger, and sadness, admit mistakes to his team, and take R and R - in the authors' phrase, becoming more human.
- ch. 19 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Arp defines personhood through five capacities (rationality, robust mental states, genuine language rather than information transmission, social relationships, and free autonomous action) and argues Transformers meet them all: Bumblebee's homing-signal syllogism, Frenzy's Air Force One hack, Megatron's curses when foiled, and Optimus's fatherly bond with Sam. A thought experiment of gradually replacing a man's brain, then body, with silicon shows that cognitive capacities, not carbon, make a person, so deceiving Decepticons are morally responsible persons who deserve blame and 'robot jail' rather than the scrapping reserved for mindless machines.
- ch. 21 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Plato, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, Zeno of Citium — Platonic Love (the ladder of love); Aristotle on Friendship (philia); Stoic Cosmopolitanism (citizens of the world); Respect for Persons — Watson and Arp ask whether Ironhide and Chromia's embrace means Autobots can love, rejecting programmed loving behavior, implanted souls, and wired-in human brains as insufficient for genuine personhood, then sort Transformer relationships into Western conceptions of love. Empedoclean cosmic Love and Strife map onto Primus versus Unicron; Platonic philia ascends to the Form of Beauty, with Transformer souls originating in and returning to the All Spark; Aristotle's three friendships separate Optimus and Sparkplug's virtue-friendship from Megatron and Starscream's mere utility; and Stoic-Kantian equal love explains Autobots saving Decepticons who immediately try to kill them, alongside Christian agape in Autobot family bonds.
- ch. 22 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Immanuel Kant, Thomas Hobbes — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Ethical Egoism — Michaud reads the Autobot-Decepticon war as a contest of ethical systems: Optimus's fair fighting, his refusal to ignore human casualties, and Bumblebee's friendship with the inferior Spike instantiate Kant's categorical imperative and the treatment of rational beings as ends in themselves. The Decepticons run through the egoist tradition - Hobbes's psychological egoism from Leviathan, Starscream's self-defeating normative egoism, and Megatron as Ayn Rand's rational egoist taunting 'You still fight for the weak; that is why you lose' - leaving the reader to choose between Kant's world of peaceful obligation and Rand's world of power where, like Starscream, you die alone.
- ch. 24 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — Master and Slave Morality; The Übermensch; Moral Relativism — Barkman takes the 1986 movie poster's 'Beyond Good. Beyond Evil.' as a Nietzsche allusion and argues the cartoon refutes it: Skyfire's 'It is wrong,' Orion Pax's repudiation of admired power in 'War Dawn,' and Optimus's humble 'Thrones are for Decepticons' make Megatron a would-be superman and villain while Optimus is a Platonic guardian of a universal moral law binding even Unicron and the Quintessons. A reductio against cultural relativism (the Decepticon invasion of Earth, First Aid's failed pacifism in 'The Ultimate Weapon') plus C.S. Lewis-style archetypes explain why Optimus - a Christ-type who died saving the world - endures while GoBots do not.
- ch. 25 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Virtue Ethics — Neil maps Optimus Prime onto Joseph Campbell's hero's journey: the naive dock worker Orion Pax is deceived and nearly killed by Megatron, rebuilt by the ancient Primus as the first Autobot, and raised to leadership through the four stages of separation, trials, supernatural aid, and return. Evolutionary 'group-fitness' psychology explains why children wept at his 1986 death, and his cooperative coaching-style leadership is cataloged episode by episode - honoring the duel he lost to Megatron's cheating in 'Heavy Metal War,' refusing to condemn Mirage without evidence, exposing the evil clone by insisting on rescuing Spike, and turning Omega Supreme from revenge to save San Francisco before his sacrificial passing of the Matrix.
- ch. 26 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** William James — Shook diagnoses Megatron through William James's expansive, possessive self turned pathological: a megalomaniac whose self encompasses everything and who must control it all ('My hunger for power!', 'Compassion is for fools!'). Reconstructing Megatron's pronouncements into a 'philosophy of Strength' - might makes right, perpetual war against the weak, 'Peace through tyranny' echoing Orwell - he identifies it as fascism on the model of Hitler and Mussolini's perpetual-war state, against which Optimus's cooperative 'till all are one' Community is not a rival regime but an ethical ideal that only we can put into practice.
- ch. 28 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** John Searle, Alan Turing, Daniel Dennett — The Chinese Room; The Turing Test; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Philosophical Zombies — Koepsell accepts that Autobots are virtuous and Decepticons vicious, then asks whether ethical war-bots are even possible, using the military's autonomous-weapons program, Asimov's Three Laws, and a kitten-sensing washing machine to argue that designed-in 'ethics' is only the designer's morality, like A Clockwork Orange's conditioned Alex, because it involves no real choice. Searle's Chinese Room and Turing's test then cast doubt on whether any mind, even our own, makes genuinely free choices, so he concludes that the appearance of virtue - behavior that reliably works - is all we ever have for humans or Autobots alike, and we should build machines as well as Optimus Prime and Bumblebee.
- ch. 29 "Transformers and Philosophy" **·** Aristotle, Philippa Foot — Eudaimonia (flourishing); Virtue Ethics (arete); Practical Wisdom (phronesis); Natural Rights — Plauche grounds Optimus Prime's line 'Freedom is the right of all sentient beings' in 'Aristotelian liberalism': since Energon, like our food, is scarce and requires labor and creativity, any volitional artificial life needs a moral code whose standard is flourishing (following Foot's natural goodness), cultivating intellectual and moral virtues from prudence, independence, and honesty to benevolence and courage. Ricardo and Mises's law of association - illustrated by Ratchet and a human mechanic both profiting from specialization despite Ratchet's absolute superiority - plus the ruinous cost of war give even superior aliens reason to respect our rights to life, liberty, and property rather than enslave or exterminate us, as Megatron would.
- ch. 30 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "Transformers and Philosophy" *(notes)*

## True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You

- ch. 1 "section-1" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "True Blood and Philosophy" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright Page" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Acknowledgments" *(notes)*
- ch. 7 "Introduction" *(no index entry yet)* — The editors frame the book with Jason Stackhouse's 'lick your mind' line and the claim that Bon Temps is a banquet of philosophical morsels: Reverend Newlin's charge that vampires are 'unnatural' opens the question of whether they are inherently evil, and vampires coming out of the coffin test whether humans and super-powered predators can share a political community as equals. It name-checks the book's guiding parallels — the gay-rights analogy of 'God hates fangs', the scapegoating around Maryann the maenad — and ends by inviting the reader across the threshold to 'think bad things', valuing the questioning itself over conclusive answers.
- ch. 8 "PART ONE - “I USED TO HATE VAMPIRES, UNTIL I GOT TO KNOW ONE” VAMPIRE-HUMAN ETHICS" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "NOTES" **·** Immanuel Kant — The Categorical Imperative; Humanity as an End in Itself; Respect for Persons — Robichaud asks whether Bill may turn Sookie into a vampire and answers with Kant's Formula of Humanity: consent matters because turning someone without letting them take up your end as their own treats them as a mere means. He argues the consent must be explicit (marriage is not tacit permission, as flirting is not consent to sex), informed (Fangtasia wannabes consent in the dark about unlife), and noncoerced (glamouring is like hypnotism, and Lafayette's begging under duress from Eric has no moral force). Even though Bill's forced turning improved Jessica's life, respecting her autonomy outweighed benefit, though Godric's turning of mortally wounded Eric may be excused by hypothetical consent.
- ch. 10 "NOTES" *(no index entry yet)* — Culver reads vampire 'mainstreaming' through play theory: using Huizinga's Homo Ludens (and Caillois), she argues Bill 'plays human' — ordering wine his first night at Merlotte's — within bounded spaces (the threshold requiring invitation), fixed rules ('she's mine', courtesy between vampires), and goals, and that play changes both species by building bonds across the boundary. Nest vampires like Malcolm and Diane who refuse to 'dress up and play human', and humans like the Fellowship of the Sun, are Huizinga's spoilsports who shatter the play-world, while Eric's incognito surveillance of Sookie in other sheriffs' territories is cheating rather than spoilsporting.
- ch. 11 "NOTES" **·** Peter Singer, Jeremy Bentham, Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, René Descartes, Thomas Aquinas — Speciesism; Animal Liberation; Anthropocentrism — Blayde and Dunn use True Blood to expose speciesism from both directions: the philosophical tradition (Aristotle's rational animals, Aquinas's divine image, Kant's dignity versus price, Descartes's denials of animal pain) justified human exploitation of nonhumans, and the show's vampires invert the ladder by treating humans as 'pets and cattle' — the magister's 'humans exist to serve us' and his verdict that Bill 'murdered a higher life form' for a pet mirror how we talk about animals. Amy's torture of Eddie Gauthier is read against factory farming, and the chapter closes with Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' and Singer's sentience criterion as Sookie's 'civic duty' grounds for extending moral consideration beyond our species.
- ch. 12 "PART TWO - “LIFE-CHALLENGED INDIVIDUALS” THE POLITICS OF BEING DEAD" *(front)*
- ch. 13 "NOTES" **·** John Rawls, John Locke — The Veil of Ignorance; The Social Contract; Natural Rights; Justice as Fairness — Foy reads the Great Revelation and the Vampire Rights Amendment as a test of social contract theory: Nan Flanagan's 'we pay taxes, we deserve civil rights' invokes the Lockean bargain of obedience for protection, but Locke's God-given natural rights falter when the Fellowship denies vampires souls, and Locke excludes atheists and never imagined vampires. The chapter's resolution is Rawls: behind a veil of ignorance where deliberators might wake up vampire or human, anti-vampire bigots like the Newlins and supremacist nests alike would choose equal basic liberties plus distributive justice — including limits on vampires' centuries of accumulated wealth — so Sookie's 'let the law do it' to Rene marks a pluralist peace no theistic contract could deliver.
- ch. 14 "NOTES" **·** John Rawls, Thomas Nagel, Aristotle — What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Curtis argues liberal society should be wary of integrating True Blood's vampires: their feudal system of kings, sheriffs, and the magister, enforced through maker bonds and punishment, violates even Kukathas's maximally tolerant liberalism because members cannot freely exit and humans are mistreated with impunity. Adapting Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' to the question 'What is it like to be a vampire?', he contends that glamouring, blood bonds, and an eroticized hunger different in kind from ours leave humans unable to verify vampire trustworthiness — echoing Aristotle's claim that one who cannot live in the polis is a beast or a god — so mainstreaming demands the AVL first expose and reform vampire institutions.
- ch. 15 "NOTES" **·** Karl Marx — Commodity Fetishism — McClelland traces the vampire's drift from demonic scapegoat — Marx's figure for capital draining the proletariat — to sympathetic protagonist, then reads TruBlood itself as a political device: the synthetic substitute is a trap that lures the ancient enemy out of opposition and into consumption-based communion, creating the 'ideal consumer' who is eternal, much as globalization absorbs adversaries into the marketplace. Godric's exhaustion with undead power struggles and the maenad Maryann's induced hedonism show, respectively, the hollowness of quasi-immortal consumer life and the human community's own susceptibility to buying bliss at the price of its principles.
- ch. 16 "PART THREE - “THEIR VERY BLOOD IS SEDUCTIVE” EROS, SEXUALITY, AND GENDER" *(front)*
- ch. 17 "NOTES" **·** Natural Law; Objectification — Brace and Arp systematically map the coffin-to-closet analogy: 'God hates fangs' echoes Fred Phelps, Eddie's leap from closeted family man to vampire lover parallels coming out, and vampire media normalization (Fang magazine, teen soaps) mirrors Ellen and Dawson's Creek. They distinguish orientation from action, rebut the natural-law argument that nonprocreative sex is unnatural (it would condemn infertile and contracepting heterosexuals too), and fix the moral line at consent — Bill asking before fang and penis penetrate is healthy, while Lorena's forced turning of Bill and the Rattrays' draining of him, 'objectified and crucified' for his blood, are violations; on that basis they argue vampires deserve equal rights under the VRA.
- ch. 18 "NOTES" **·** Feminism; Intersectionality; Dominance Approach (pornography and gender); Objectification — Craton and Jonell read Sookie as an emblem of contemporary feminist ambivalence: her 'I am woman, hear me roar' independence coexists with sexual caution, and the show stages feminism's sex wars — Lafayette's sex work and webcam pornography versus Maryann, whose 'pro-sex' liberation collapses into self-annihilating worship of Dionysus and whose death suggests unregulated sexuality is dangerous. Tara's plotline shows how race and class layer onto gender (her 'baby-daddy' scene, Maryann as failed white savior), exposing the limits of a united feminist front, while the 'kept woman' quarrel with Bill and Sookie's barmaid-versus-telepathic-detective career choice leave more questions about female empowerment than answers.
- ch. 19 "NOTES" **·** Sigmund Freud, Herbert Marcuse — The Unconscious; The Death Drive (Thanatos); Civilization and Its Discontents — Hirschbein presents True Blood as a Freudian fable: vampires live the unrepressed id's Eros and Thanatos that civilization forces the rest of us to renounce, which is why they defeat all three sources of suffering (mortal bodies, nature, hostile neighbors) and why the show's convulsive sex and violence thrill us. Glamouring reproduces the posthypnotic suggestion that proved the unconscious to Freud, Sookie's mind-reading confirms his dark discoveries about our sexualized aggression, vampire myths work as projection screens for desires we disown, and Marcuse's complaint about 'genital tyranny' and sublimation frames Sookie's love as a near-realization of Freud's St. Francis ideal.
- ch. 20 "PART FOUR - “I AM ACTUALLY OLDER THAN YOUR JESUS” NATURAL, SUPERNATURAL, AND DIVINE" *(front)*
- ch. 21 "NOTES" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Plato — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Forgiveness — Corn and Dunn read Maryann's takeover of Bon Temps through René Girard's scapegoat theory: mimetic desire breeds the resentments Sookie hears all day, the crowd's 'wild energy' dissolves the Apollonian individual into Dionysian self-forgetfulness (Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy, Plato's assembly that echoes blame until judgment drowns), and the town and the Fellowship of the Sun alike restore solidarity by uniting against vampires — or against Sam on the sacrificial oak. Godric's self-delivery to the Newlins is a failed Christlike sacrifice, so the chapter ends with Sookie's 'God doesn't punish, God forgives' as Girard's alternative to founding community on sacrificial violence.
- ch. 22 "NOTES" **·** Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, René Descartes — The Four Causes; Is–Ought Problem — The Terjesens dissect what 'unnatural' could mean for vampires: on modern evolutionary biology they are simply effective predators, so no unfairness or odd predation style (sleeping with one's food) makes them unnatural. Aristotle's four causes and Aquinas's God-ordered extrinsic finality would let 'unnatural' mean 'against the plan', but purposes cannot be observed — the source of bad medieval science — and Descartes's banishment of final causes from physics shows why; Godric's 'our existence is insanity' therefore commits the is–ought fallacy, and what remains to judge is not vampire nature but vampire choice, as Bill's mainstreaming and Godric's final 'I told a lie' about survival versus right and wrong show.
- ch. 23 "NOTES" **·** Thomas Aquinas — The Problem of Evil — Barkman answers 'God hates fangs' with Aquinas: evil is no-thing, so God creates nothing inherently evil — fangs, sex, and free will are good gifts whose misuse explains fallen angels, witches (via the Malleus Maleficarum and Allatius's demon-animated vampires), and human sinners like Rene and the Rattrays. Since True Blood's vampires stand unmoved before crosses, hold church meetings, and can choose as Bill does, they are not soulless minions of the devil but created beings who, like humans, go wrong only by misusing free will — which is why Harris's inclusive Episcopalianism lets Gran say there is a purpose for everything God makes, even a vampire.
- ch. 24 "PART FIVE - “OUR EXISTENCE IS INSANITY” THE METAPHYSICS OF SUPERNATURAL BEINGS" *(front)*
- ch. 25 "NOTES" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, John Searle, Thomas Nagel, René Descartes — Existence Precedes Essence; Bad Faith; What Is It Like to Be a Bat?; Mind–Body Dualism — Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.
- ch. 26 "NOTES" **·** Thomas Nagel, John Locke, Daniel Dennett — What Is It Like to Be a Bat? — Curry asks whether even Sookie's telepathy can breach the privacy of mind: a third-person account of shifter Sam hearing a dog-whistle leaves out the quale — the homage to Nagel's bat — and Locke's inverted spectrum (Jason and Tara both say 'green' while living different experiences) shows qualia are incommunicable. Reading the astrology-believing Maxine's mind traps Sookie in a dilemma: if she fully becomes Maxine she is no longer the Sookie who knows, and if she keeps her skeptical psychology she never experiences what it is like to believe — so, drawing on Dennett's coffee example for one's own past qualia, even the show's most powerful mind reader can never know what it is like to experience things as you.
- ch. 27 "NOTES" **·** John Locke — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — Grubb tests theories of personal identity on the supes: the bodily theory fails because Bill's and Jessica's bodies died and refunctioned at transformation, Locke's memory theory stumbles on amnesiac Eric (who stays Eric despite remembering nothing), and psychological continuity fails because vampirism inflated Bill's aggression and collie-Sam's mind when Andy draws a gun is anyone's guess. She closes with Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism — lives as long stories of temporal parts — which lets the rambunctious vampire Jessica count as the same person as the demure human girl because both are episodes in one continuing story.
- ch. 28 "PART SIX - “TALKING ABOUT YOUR FEELINGS IS A MANLY THING TO DO” SUPERNATURAL LIFE LESSONS FROM SEASON THREE" *(front)*
- ch. 29 "NOTES" **·** Philosophy of Disability; Objectification — Craton reads Sookie's arc through disability theory: her telepathy, treated by Bon Temps as a disability that barred her from college and respect, is reframed once vampires and Weres prize it — and finally her faerie 'light' — into an ability she controls for money, crime-solving, and saving a child. The chapter parallels the eugenics-era fears Sookie and Alcide share about passing on difference, and the freak-show histories of Joseph Merrick, Saartjie Baartman, and Julia Pastrana illuminate how vampires like Eric and Sophie-Anne value Sookie's blood as a possession to be consumed rather than a person to be respected, until she rescinds Bill's invitation and defends her light.
- ch. 30 "NOTES" **·** Jeremy Bentham — Utilitarianism; The Greatest Happiness Principle; Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI) — Grubb stages Arlene's decision to abort the baby fathered by serial killer Rene as a case study in Bentham's act utilitarianism: her prayer that ending the pregnancy will keep 'Rene's sickness' from Coby, Lisa, and Terry weighs pleasure and pain — the two sovereign masters — for the greatest number, from family to all of Bon Temps. The chapter shows why the calculus fails her: consequences cannot be known in advance (a crystal ball or Lafayette's visions would be needed), it is indeterminate whose happiness counts, and her premise that evil is biologically inheritable sits badly with the free-will account of sin, making the dilemma genuinely undecidable from inside the show.
- ch. 31 "NOTES" **·** Confucius, Mencius, Immanuel Kant, Plato — Xiao (filial piety); Ren (benevolence/humaneness); Human Nature Is Good; Rectification of Names — The Terjesens pit Kant's impersonal morality — Sam's contractual distance from the thieving Mickens is exactly how he would treat strangers — against Confucius and Mencius, for whom filial duties are the nursery of virtue: we learn benevolence by serving parents and revering elders, Lafayette's care for Lettie Mae and Tara shows family forming moral character, and the Upright Gong's covering for a father's sheep-stealing grounds Jason's 'sometimes the right thing to do is the wrong thing'. Mencius's King Shun, who abdicates and carries his criminal father into exile, models how Tommy and Jason should put family first while accepting the cost, while Mozi's universal love surfaces in Godric's 'forgiveness is love', and the chapter concludes that family counts only insofar as it develops our moral nature — the line between Tommy and Sam.
- ch. 32 "CONTRIBUTORS" *(notes)*
- ch. 33 "INDEX" *(notes)*

## True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness

- ch. 1 "True Detective and Philosophy A Deeper Kind of Darkness" *(front)*
- ch. 2 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 3 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "True Detective and Philosophy A Deeper Kind of Darkness" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Introduction Welcome to the Psychosphere" **·** Socrates — The Unexamined Life; The Meaning of Life — The editors' introduction asks why viewers willingly linger in True Detective's bleak Louisiana bayou and season two's Vinci, suggesting we may recognize something of ourselves in those worlds. It argues detectives and philosophers share the pursuit of truth, framing Rust Cohle and Marty Hart (and Velcoro and Bezzerides) as morally compromised lawmen who open the door to philosophy, invoking Socrates' 'unexamined life is not worth living.' It previews the book's coverage of pessimism, good and evil, tragedy, personal identity, and time via Socrates, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Lacan, and Zizek.
- ch. 6 "Part I “IT'S ALL ONE GHETTO, MAN … A GIANT GUTTER IN OUTER SPACE” Pessimism and Anti-natalism" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Notes" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer — Philosophical Pessimism; The World as Will; Ethics of Compassion — Argues Rust Cohle's stated pessimism and in-principle embrace of suicide closely track Schopenhauer's view that suffering is built into the world with no providential redemption, yet the two diverge because Schopenhauer condemned suicide as an affirmation of the will-to-live rather than its denial. The chapter traces Rust's three-stage arc — jaded wannabe-suicidal pessimist who nonetheless energetically investigates the Dora Lange case, resigned drinker, and finally cautious affirmer of life after the Yellow King confrontation — and contends his detective work is really motivated by a Schopenhauerian morality of compassion and justice, not mere 'programming.' Rust's finale conversion is read as an evidence-based judgment that thoroughgoing pessimism is intellectually dishonest, since compassion and justice do score nontrivial victories.
- ch. 8 "Notes" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Friedrich Nietzsche — Philosophical Pessimism; Eternal Recurrence; The World as Will — Reads Carcosa, the Yellow King, and Ledoux's 'time is a flat circle' as cosmic horror in the lineage of Lovecraft and Ligotti, arguing that the genre's dread — that monsters exist and the fixed laws of nature may fail — is a metaphor for realizing Schopenhauer's blind will, with Rust's car monologues in 'The Long Bright Dark' presented as a beginner's guide to Schopenhauer. It notes Rust inverts the usual Lovecraft protagonist by starting the story already horrified, and that eternal recurrence framed through Schopenhauer's sphere-of-time makes even the rescued children's torment maddeningly endless. The chapter closes by complaining that the finale 'Form and Void' betrays both genres: the occult becomes ordinary crime and Rust's 'light is winning' star-field reverses Schopenhauer's pessimistic cosmology.
- ch. 9 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer, Immanuel Kant — Philosophical Pessimism; Eternal Recurrence — Distinguishes philosophical pessimism (Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Camus, Unamuno) — the denial that the universe is an ordered place whose laws human reason can grasp — from mere gloominess, and reads Rust's 'time is a flat circle' as Nietzschean anti-metaphysics of a world going nowhere. It argues pessimism makes Rust the better detective because, expecting no rational order, he sees what is actually there, while optimist Marty's illusions about family and career multiply his losses and end with him losing both. Against conflating pessimism with despair, the chapter splits ideas (pessimism) from attitudes (hope), showing how Hart's heart and Cohle's clear sight combine into the show's ideal of hopeful pessimism.
- ch. 10 "Notes" **·** René Descartes, David Hume — Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Tests whether Rust's pessimism is a principled rationalist philosophy (Dienstag's view, versus Ligotti's temperament view) by mapping the Descartes-style rationalist and Hume-style empiricist opposition onto the partners: principled, deductive Rust versus impulse-driven Marty, including Rust's religion debate at the tent revival. It then reads the death of Sophia — Greek for wisdom, root of 'philosophy' — as symbolism suggesting Rust's pessimism stems from the death of wisdom rather than rational reflection, especially since Rust holds that the suffering of growing up is needed to become a pessimist. The finale's experience of Sophia's love is taken as a pure philosophical experience that collapses the reason/emotion distinction, so that pessimism belongs to both sides of the opposition at once.
- ch. 11 "Part II “We Get the World We Deserve” Cruelty, Violence, Evil, and Justice" *(front)*
- ch. 12 "Notes" **·** Arthur Schopenhauer, Thomas Hobbes — Philosophical Pessimism; Pendulum Between Pain and Boredom — Reconstructs Rust's scattered remarks — the world as 'one giant gutter,' procreation as the hubris of yanking a soul out of nonexistence into the thresher — into an explicit anti-natalist argument, testing each premise and conceding procreation is selfish while questioning whether every life nets more harm than good. It presents David Benatar's asymmetry between the absence of pain (always good) and the absence of pleasure (bad only for someone deprived), illustrating it with the show: contraception as procreative duty, the wrongness of conceiving in Tuttle's Louisiana, and the emptiness of Childress' temple as a good in itself. The chapter concludes that Rust's 'opt out of a raw deal' is philosophically defensible, with Schopenhauer's desire-pendulum and Hobbes' 'nasty, brutish, and short' backing the claim that most lives are bad.
- ch. 13 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, The Buddha — Eternal Recurrence; The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Master and Slave Morality — Takes Nietzsche's 'man is the cruelest animal' and argues the show's real exploration of cruelty lies not in the cult's crimes, which stay mysterious, but in the Cohle–Hart relationship, whose private cruelties are closer to the human condition. It explains human cruelty through theory of mind — knowing we make others suffer — and through the moral vocabulary of desert, karma, and Schadenfreude (Nietzsche's slave morality inventing hell) that hides our pleasure in suffering, which Nietzsche sees as the key to life-affirmation against Buddhist and Christian world-denial. The chapter maps Hart as Dionysian energy and Cohle as Apollonian form, and reads Rust's 2012 talk of eternal recurrence as a ruse concealing his search for a Nietzschean moment of ecstatic affirmation of all the cruelty he has caused and endured.
- ch. 14 "Notes" **·** Karl Marx — Ideology and False Consciousness — Applies Slavoj Zizek's distinction between subjective violence (murders, assaults, what makes the news) and objective violence — symbolic and systemic, the catastrophic consequences of the smooth functioning of capitalism — to season two's Vinci, modeled on the really corrupt city of Vernon, California. It reads Velcoro's 'we get the world we deserve' line and Frank Semyon's 'papier-mache' water-stain monologue as revelations of systemic violence, with the stain marking how the past stares back at Bezzerides, Velcoro, and Woodrugh. Through Zizek's 'cynical ideology' (a West Side Story reading) and his account of fantasy, the chapter argues the show demands we target the system producing violence rather than treat its visible symptoms.
- ch. 15 "Notes" **·** Aristotle — Moral Psychology (character, vice, weakness of will) — Confronts a puzzle in Rust's naturalism: he dismisses the occult, yet talks freely of monsters and evil, concepts often thought irredeemably supernatural. The chapter distinguishes natural from supernatural senses of 'monster' (Aristotle's explicable hybrids versus Carroll's order-violating beings) to argue Errol Childress is a monster consistent with naturalism, then defends a 'modest proposal' — the evil person just is the morally worst sort of person, whose vices are extreme in both intensity and object. Betty's line that Childress is 'worse than anybody' and his extreme cruelty and callousness fit this account, teaching that recognizing creatures like us can be evil, not positing inhuman monsters, is the first step to combating evil.
- ch. 16 "Notes" **·** G.W.F. Hegel — Punishment: Retribution vs Rehabilitation; The Dialectic — Uses Hans Kelsen's legal positivism — law as amoral coercive order sustained by sanction, validated by authority rather than morality — to interpret season two's competing normative systems, from Vinci's city hall to the cartel's execution of the informant Irina. Against this background it separates revenge from Hegelian retributivism, reading Velcoro's shift from killing his wife's rapist to persuading Lenny Osterman to seek exposure instead, and Frank's communicative, confessing execution of the traitor Blake, as conflicted exercises of justice. The finale's bloodshed is read through Hegel's theory of tragedy as a collision of spheres of justice, each justified in its own eyes, whose transgression may precipitate change in Vinci.
- ch. 17 "Part III “Everybody's Nobody” Consciousness, Existence, and Identity" *(front)*
- ch. 18 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Shankara, Zhuangzi, René Descartes — Non-Self (anatman); Atman and Brahman; Zhuangzi's Perspectivism (butterfly dream); Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Reads Rust's 'dream inside a locked room' and 'everybody is nobody' monologues through the dream-argument and illusion-of-self traditions: the Upanishads and Advaita's atman/brahman, Vasubandhu's Buddhist non-self, Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, Plato's Theaetetus, and Descartes' dream doubt, plus Metzinger's self-model neuroscience. It diagnoses Rust as a neuro-nihilist in Metzinger's sense and defines his predicament with Nietzsche's nihilist, who judges the world as it is that it ought not to be, while noting Schopenhauer misread India's religions as pessimistic. Thompson argues nihilism is a deep insight gone awry — the self is not a thing but an enacted process like dancing — and reads Rust's final near-death experience of love as proof that transcendence of the dream of being a person is possible.
- ch. 19 "Notes" **·** John Locke, Friedrich Nietzsche, Bernard Williams — Personal Identity; Personal Identity (memory theory); Eternal Recurrence — Divides Rust's season-one personae into Taxman (anti-natalist rule-follower), Belligerent (vigilante drunk paralyzed by Nietzsche's Gay Science demon of eternal recurrence), and Patient (the mystic who wakes from his coma feeling his daughter's love, compared to the Persian mystic al-Hallaj), asking what makes them one person. It tests the brute physicalist account (Williams and Ayer — the same bird-tattooed body), the Lockean psychological-continuity account, and the narrative account, arguing only the narrative theory explains how Rust changes without either ignoring change or multiplying selves in one body. The chapter ends by making Rust an exemplar for the viewer: we are narrators who choose who to become, so 'I know who I am' is a victory.
- ch. 20 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir — Bad Faith; Eternal Recurrence; Woman as the Other; Existence Precedes Essence — Reads Cohle's arc as an existentialist passage toward authenticity, using Sartre's being-for-itself to explain why Hart's 'family man' identity is bad faith — a clinging to social roles that denies the freedom of a consciousness that is an activity, not a thing. Beauvoir's analysis of women as the passive, objectified Other illuminates why Rust, despite his nihilism, persistently protects vulnerable women and children such as Sophia, Dora Lange, and Marie Fontenot: threats to others' freedom threaten our own. Nietzsche's Silenus wisdom, the spirit of gravity on the tightrope, and the shepherd who bites the head off the snake frame Ledoux's and Childress' warped eternal return as the poison Cohle must overcome before he can will life eternally and declare 'the light is winning.'
- ch. 21 "Notes" **·** Jean-Paul Sartre, Harry Frankfurt, Arthur Schopenhauer, Baruch Spinoza — Free Will vs Determinism; Second-Order Desires (personhood); Compatibilism; Philosophical Zombies — Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.
- ch. 22 "Part IV “This Is My Least Favorite Life” Noir, Tragedy, and Philosopher-Detectives" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Jacques Lacan, Plato, Immanuel Kant, Sigmund Freud — The Apollonian and the Dionysian; Ressentiment; Theory of Forms; Humanity as an End in Itself — Uses Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy and Lacan's ethics of psychoanalysis to argue season two failed as tragedy because feminist morality became the inflated 'Good' that blocks the transgression of limits through which Dionysian wisdom is won. Season one works because Rust's philosophy filters the Carcosa horrors without moralizing, whereas season two — failing Aristotle's catharsis model and repeating Euripides' mistake — represses the sexual knowledge troubling Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh, so Dionysus returns only as money and violence, as in The Bacchae. Ani's arc is read through Nietzschean ressentiment toward her father and Freud's return of the repressed, with Kantian sexual dignity ('maybe you were put on earth for more than fucking') and the male gaze as the contemporary Good the show never crosses.
- ch. 24 "Notes" **·** Plato, Gilles Deleuze — Justice in the Republic; Tripartite Soul; The Unexamined Life — Compares the noir detective's relation to Vinci with Socrates' gadfly role in Athens from the Apology, arguing both operate at the city's center and its margins as instruments of collective self-examination. Via Deleuze's 'Philosophy of Crime Novels' it contrasts the classic detective as an agent of truth (Poe, Christie) with the hard-boiled detective as an agent of action who stirs the system — Ani's undercover infiltration of the businessmen's party — forcing what Deleuze calls the 'power of falsehood' to reveal and conceal. Plato's Republic city–soul analogy then frames Velcoro, Bezzerides, and Woodrugh as disordered souls mirroring Vinci's corrupt class structure, whose cases restore equilibrium without achieving Platonic justice.
- ch. 25 "Notes" **·** Jacques Lacan, Sigmund Freud, Gilles Deleuze, G.W.F. Hegel — The Mirror Stage; The Symbolic, the Imaginary and the Real; The Unconscious — Reads the Cohle–Hart pairing through Lacan: Cohle is at peace with the constitutive lack introduced after the mirror stage, and his hysteric's fixation on the Other's desire is what makes him the superior interrogator, while Hart exhibits obsessional neurosis and 'interpassivity,' letting the preacher's congregation do his believing for him. Following Deleuze's Oedipal structure of detective fiction and Hegel's point that heroes are denied guilt, the chapter compares Rust to Oedipus — both men who, after a child's death, renounce the father function through anti-natalism — while arguing Cohle surpasses Oedipus by philosophically mastering the knowledge that Oedipus lacked. Rust's tying off of his 'circle of violence' is read as the Lacanian sinthome: putting his symptom to work in the service of the case rather than being destroyed by it.
- ch. 26 "Part V “Time Is a Flat Circle” Time in True Detective" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer — Eternal Recurrence; The World as Will; Will to Power; Philosophical Pessimism — Traces Cohle's opening monologue directly to Schopenhauer — reality as a purposeless will whose satisfied desires breed only boredom, answered by ascetic denial of the will-to-live rather than suicide. It then explains Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as the true test of life-affirmation, via the Gay Science demon and Zarathustra's ordeal with the Small Man, and interprets will to power as finding meaning in overcoming resisting conditions, so that affirmation does not mean approving everything that happens. Hatab argues the show's horrified version of the flat circle is Schopenhauerian rather than Nietzschean, and that Cohle's 'light is winning' ending is ambiguous — if it rests on a supernatural reunion with Sophia, it would betray Nietzsche's this-worldly affirmation.
- ch. 28 "Notes" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Arthur Schopenhauer, Martin Heidegger — Eternal Recurrence; Amor Fati (love of fate); The World as Will; Being-Toward-Death — Argues 'time is a flat circle' means neither a metaphysical cosmology nor M-theory physics nor reincarnation, but is Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a thought experiment about how to live. Tracing Rust's pessimism and his lack of the 'constitution for suicide' (echoing Schopenhauer's claim that suicide affirms the will-to-live, with starvation as its only true denial), it shows the flat circle operating as both trap and cure: obsessing over it keeps Rust on the Yellow King case until his near-death experience becomes the 'tremendous moment' of amor fati. Heidegger's view in Being and Time that anxiety before death can empower meaningful existence frames Rust's final affirmation — escaping the flat circle by faithfully acknowledging it, through sacrifice.
- ch. 29 "Known Associates" *(notes)*
- ch. 30 "Index" *(notes)*
- ch. 31 "EULA" *(front)*

## Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
- ch. 6 "Contents" *(front)*
- ch. 7 "Dare to Enter the Zone" **·** Friedrich Nietzsche, Socrates — The Meaning of Life — The editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone made 1950s television, dismissed as an 'idiot box' and 'vast wasteland,' into a venue for thinking: Serling, like Socrates the gadfly of Athens, built episodes as thought experiments in which experts' promises unravel. Taking Nietzsche's Twilight of the Idols epigraph ('I never found anything but the apes of their ideal'), they claim the show dramatizes the gap between our ideals (friendship, justice, truth, loyalty) and our treachery, from Henry Bemis's books to 'The Hunt,' where even the Devil cannot fool a dog. We laugh at the absurd endings because we are 'the species most deserving to be laughed at.'
- ch. 8 "First Dimension Facing the Zone" *(front)*
- ch. 9 "1. Lost in Time" **·** David Lewis — The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Rard argues that the suspended-animation heist of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' is not time travel, using David Lewis's definition (a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the time between departure and arrival). 'Last Flight' illustrates a consistent causal loop: in 1959 Terry Decker learns he saved Mackaye in 1917, which motivates him to go back and do it, with nothing changed. 'No Time Like the Past' enacts Lewis's response to the grandfather paradox: Paul Driscoll's attempts to kill Hitler and warn Hiroshima are thwarted by mundane coincidences, and at Homeville he always was the one who caused the schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent.
- ch. 10 "2. Where Is the Twilight Zone" **·** René Descartes, Sigmund Freud, Theodor Adorno — The Cogito; Mind–Body Dualism; The Unconscious — Scalambrino reads the Zone as a televised expression of surrealist philosophy: Breton's sought 'point of the mind' where life and death, real and imagined cease to be contradictions, realized in episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing) and 'The Mirror' (Dali's paranoiac-critical method). Descartes's cogito and the mind-body dualism supply the rational 'leash' that surrealism unbinds, questioned by 'Shadow Play,' where a man insists the world is his dream. Following Adorno's verdict that psychoanalytic interpretation killed official surrealism, he argues the show endures by provoking the uncanny ('The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' 'A Stop at Willoughby') without being pinned to Freudian readings.
- ch. 11 "3. The Short-Sightedness of Henry Bemis" **·** The Question Concerning Technology; The Meaning of Life — Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma about freedom and dependence: Henry Bemis's wish to escape the 'cages' of the bank, his marriage, and the clock is granted by nuclear annihilation, only for loneliness and monotony to become a worse prison. The shattered glasses are not just a cruel joke but the loss of the technology connecting him to books and other minds. The chapter argues Bemis's folly is the misanthropic fantasy of excepting himself from the technological system and from dependence on others, and that our remedy is philosophical rather than technical: glasses that reveal our limits and mutual dependence.
- ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" **·** Emmanuel Levinas, Jean-Paul Sartre — The Face of the Other; The Look (hell is other people) — Hooke uses Levinas's account of the face (and Lingis on trust) to read the Zone's faces: the bandaged woman and pig-faced surgeons of 'The Eye of the Beholder' unseat our standards of the normal, while trusted faces are weaponized by Robert Redford's Grim Reaper in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's Satan in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the gentle Kanamit of 'To Serve Man.' Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' and John and Marie Holt's wordless recognition in 'The Trade-Ins' show trust and love exceeding proof or evidence. Sartre's existential look, with Kierkegaard's Abraham and Beauvoir's second sex, frames how a face puts our freedom and trust in question.
- ch. 13 "Second Dimension Beyond the Boundaries of You and Me" *(front)*
- ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" **·** Charles Sanders Peirce, Peter Singer — The Pragmatic Method; Speciesism; Philosophy of Love — Klayman treats 'The Lonely' as a case study on whether Corry's love for the robot Alicia is true love. Using C.S. Lewis's four loves plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim (a concept's meaning is its practical effects), he argues Corry showed affection and appreciation but not Eros: he gave Alicia nothing, needed her merely against loneliness, and boarded the ship without sacrificing anything for her. Denying that a machine could be loved, he adds, would be a prejudice akin to Singer's speciesism, and Kendall Walton's 'Fearing Fictions' explains how Corry becomes fictional alongside a make-believe person.
- ch. 15 "6. In a Mirror Is Our Image" **·** John Locke, Immanuel Kant, Peter Singer, Tom Regan, Aristotle — Personal Identity (memory theory); Humanity as an End in Itself; Animal Rights (subjects-of-a-life) — Karavitis places thirteen robot and android episodes on a spectrum from the X109B14 computer of 'The Brain Center at Whipple's' to indistinguishable androids like Alicia, arguing that the moral duties we owe artificial creations depend on personhood. By Locke's memory-continuity account of identity, the mind-transferred couple of 'The Trade-Ins' remain persons, and so would androids created from scratch, which makes the routine destruction of Alicia, Grandma, and Jana murder. The animal-ethics tradition from Aristotle's property view through Kant's indirect duties to Singer and Regan's moral patients supplies the analogy, and the show's unstated definition of evil is treating persons as disposable objects.
- ch. 16 "7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me" **·** John Locke, Derek Parfit, Thomas Reid — Personal Identity (memory theory); Personal Identity — Lay applies Locke's memory theory to 'Person or Persons Unknown' and 'The After Hours': without factive memories linking David Gurney to his supposed past, and Marsha to her mannequin history, identity is lost in both directions. 'The Lateness of the Hour' strains the view, since Jana's implanted 'memory tracks' are not memories of real events yet she plainly is someone, and Reid's chain objection shows memory alone cannot span a life. Parfit's psychological continuity over the whole network of mental states resolves the cases, and 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' completes it: the post-Transformation person keeps Marilyn's memories but none of her desires or traits, so Marilyn did not survive.
- ch. 17 "8. What Are You Hearing" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Wissner shows how Twilight Zone scores mark the boundary between dream and reality: electronic instruments and reverberation in 'Perchance to Dream' (Hammond organ, Theremin-like violin), diegetic folk songs against the Willoughby theme in 'A Stop at Willoughby,' the shared recurring nightmare cue of 'Twenty-Two' and 'Shadow Play,' and the desperate piano ostinato of 'The Midnight Sun.' Framing this with Plato's view of music as unreal, image-evoking mimetic signs and Aristotle's claim that melodies carry ethos and can change minds, she argues music tells viewers what pictures cannot: whether a character is dreaming, imagining, or awake.
- ch. 18 "9. Machines Who Care" **·** Applied Ethics (bioethics, technology, AI); Objectification — Weiss reads 'The Lonely' and 'I Sing the Body Electric' as fifty-year-old anticipations of today's debate over relational artifacts: Alexa, therapeutic robot seals, and care robots for the aged (via Turkle, the Sparrows' objection, and Coeckelbergh's embrace of robots that care). Alicia's tear wins Corry's trust only to end with her shot in the face, while the electric grandma saves Anne's life, yet both are assembly-line products answering loneliness that the same consumer society produces. The chapter asks whether buying care and companionship from robotic women, designed, boxed, and disposed of by men, is fable or nightmare.
- ch. 19 "Third Dimension That Wondrous Land Called Truth" *(front)*
- ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" **·** David Hume — Bundle Theory of Self; Philosophical Skepticism — Nisley reads 'And When the Sky Was Opened' through Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence: Colonel Forbes's conviction that Harrington exists rests on memory's force and vivacity, and when testimony collapses (newspaper headlines, the bartender, his girlfriend, the general) the three spacemen are erased one by one, 'no longer part of the memory of man.' 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's belief that the woman in the speakeasy is his dead Laura is the imagination's feigned continuity, a resemblance across interrupted perceptions rather than a rational foundation. Memory alone, the chapter concludes, never grounds our beliefs that things or persons persist unperceived.
- ch. 21 "11. The Truth about Lying" **·** David Hume, Immanuel Kant, René Descartes, Blaise Pascal — On Miracles; Pascal's Wager; Methodological Doubt (evil demon) — Fallis treats the Zone as a seminar in the philosophy of testimony: truth-tellers like Bob Wilson warning of a gremlin get dismissed as insane ('The Whole Truth' forces truth-telling as a curse), while convincing liars like Arch Hammer come to bad ends, so Kant's letter recommending reticence, saying true things but not the whole truth, looks like the best policy. On the receiving end, Descartes's malicious demon returns as aliens and devils ('To Serve Man,' 'The Howling Man,' 'Printer's Devil'), and Hume's advice to reject miracle-like testimony fails because in the Zone crazy stuff is often true. The chapter ends by endorsing Pascal's wager through 'The Big Tall Wish' and Jeff Myrtlebank's threat: believe the incredible witness just in case.
- ch. 22 "Fourth Dimension As Vast as Space and Timeless as Infinity" *(front)*
- ch. 23 "12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep" **·** Bad Faith — Jones argues the Zone is not somewhere else: Serling's map-language of signposts, thresholds, and borders describes episodes that actually unfold in recognizable American places, from Nan Adams's real highway in 'The Hitch-Hiker' to an ordinary hospital in 'The Eye of the Beholder.' The show's impossible catalysts, gremlins, aliens, sentient dolls, perform a double distancing that lets viewers face mundane truths about selfishness, gullibility, and vulnerability while pretending those truths are fantastic. 'The Shelter' is the exception that breaks the shelter: with no supernatural or futuristic cause, only the very real 1961 fallout-shelter panic, it forces the audience to see that the Zone is their own living room and the monsters are us.
- ch. 24 "13. No Place like a Non-Place" **·** Alienation; Authenticity — The chapter reads the show through Marc Auge's 'non-place,' the anonymous transit space of supermodernity: the slow ocean liner of 'Passage on the Lady Anne' against accelerated modern life, Nan Adams's road in 'The Hitch-Hiker,' the Civil War road of 'The Passersby,' the diner of 'Will the Real Martian Please Stand Up?,' the airplane cabin of 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet,' and the hotel rooms and ninth-floor mall of 'The After Hours' and 'The Four of Us Are Dying.' In these spaces of interchangeable anonymity, emptied by postwar consumerism and shifting gender roles, identity crises play out, and only moments of identification, or fatally being recognized, as Archie Hammer is by Andy Marshak's father, restore or destroy a self.
- ch. 25 "14. The Science of Alternate Realities" **·** Karl Popper — The Metaphysics of Time Travel; Falsificationism; Possible Worlds — Morgan unpacks the science behind the 'fifth dimension': higher spatial dimensions as in the portal of 'Little Girl Lost,' Einstein's time as a fourth dimension with time-dilation travel ('A Kind of a Stopwatch'), and the grandfather paradox, which 'Back There' handles inconsistently (some events change, others cannot) while 'No Time Like the Past' gets right: past events are eternally true. Quantum many-worlds fits 'The Parallel,' where Major Gaines slips into a nearly identical reality, and infinite universes would make every possibility actual. But the cosmological multiverse, he argues with Popper's falsifiability criterion, is untestable and hence not science, remaining a dimension of mind and imagination.
- ch. 26 "Fifth Dimension Our Twisted Imaginings" *(front)*
- ch. 27 "15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances" **·** Søren Kierkegaard — The Stages on Life's Way; Despair (sickness unto death); The Metaphysics of Time Travel — Karavitis sorts episodes into three types to show that the past is dead and only moving forward counts: nostalgia ('The Sixteen-Millimeter Shrine,' 'A Stop at Willoughby,' 'Walking Distance'), time travel ('Back There,' 'No Time Like the Past,' where every attempt to fix history fails), and granted second chances ('A Nice Place to Visit,' 'A Game of Pool,' 'Printer's Devil'). Kierkegaard's Either/Or supplies the philosophy: Rocky Valentine's wish-factory and Jesse Cardiff's poolhall limbo depict the aesthetic stage's despair, while Douglas Winter taking responsibility for his pact shows the ethical stage. Second chances succeed only for those who, in Kierkegaard's words, live life forwards.
- ch. 28 "16. The Pleasure of the Twist" **·** Thomas Kuhn — Paradigm Shifts — Scales argues that Twilight Zone twist endings are miniature Kuhnian paradigm shifts: anomalous clues accumulate ('things are a little wrong' in 'The Hitch-Hiker,' Jana's mismatched photographs, the Kanamits' book title), then the ending forces a wholesale reinterpretation in which we 'come to live in a different world,' as when 'To Serve Man' turns benevolence into livestock. Extending Kuhn's theory-ladenness with Paul Churchland's connectionist prototypes, he explains the pleasure of the twist as the brain's reward for suddenly re-categorizing a whole story under a new prototype. The show's twist toolkit, he adds, seeded later works from Planet of the Apes to The Sixth Sense.
- ch. 29 "The Dimension that Can’t Be Named or Numbered" *(front)*
- ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" **·** Hannah Arendt — The Banality of Evil; The Problem of Evil — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited,' where SS Captain Lutze is tried by his Dachau victims and driven mad, and 'He's Alive,' where a phantom Hitler grooms the failed neo-Nazi Peter Vollmer, as Serling's two-part response to the Eichmann trial. Setting them against the film Operation Eichmann's monster-Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman, Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, and Serling's hatred of Hogan's Heroes' comic Klink, he traces a maturation: from the Nazi as heartless monster to Arendt's banality of evil, the thoughtless, frustrated everyman. Vollmer, the chapter argues, shows what Lutze's origins were, and remembering the Dachaus is the guard against becoming his like.
- ch. 31 "18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing" **·** Plato, Aristotle — Ring of Gyges (why be moral?); Aristotle on Friendship (philia) — Vuckovich reads 'Still Valley' through Glaucon's Ring of Gyges: Sgt. Paradine, handed a witchcraft handbook that freezes the Union army before Gettysburg, confronts the temptation of costless, unearned victory, and his burning of the handbook rather than renounce God preserves a principle worth more than winning. Aristotle's claim that bad men can be friends through shared wickedness explains the witchman Teague's bond with Paradine, an 'alliance' that recruits the desperate soldier to do the Devil's dirty work. The chapter ends on the shameful secret legacy: even burying the episode leaves Paradine with a private war in his conscience, a pyrrhic loss for a fighting man who almost surrendered what he holds sacred.
- ch. 32 "19. Looking Like Number 12" **·** Theodor Adorno — The Culture Industry — Busk explains why 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' is so disturbing despite having no monsters: through Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, standardized cultural products manufacture conformist subjects whose critical capacities and powers of resistance atrophy until difference itself looks pathological, as with Marilyn's doctors diagnosing her refusal. 'The After Hours' extends the diagnosis, with mannequin Marsha as the subject reduced to an industrial prop granted brief furloughs of 'free time.' Yet the very existence of Marilyn's and Marsha's doomed protests, like Adorno and Horkheimer's own theory, shows some subjectivity survives the production line.
- ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" **·** Hannah Arendt, Aristotle — Totalitarianism; The Banality of Evil — Altmann assembles a 'time capsule' of totalitarianism from Twilight Zone and Black Mirror: Vollmer's neo-Nazi rise in 'He's Alive' as Aristotle's rhetoric, persuasion by playing on an audience's anger and fear, weaponized; Marilyn's forced Transformation in 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' as Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference; and Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' at Dachau as Arendt's banality of evil, the mechanical non-thinking of the Eichmann trial. 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits' then carry the lens to Debord's society of the spectacle, where an empty cartoon bear wins crowds and even Bing's shard-wielding rebellion is instantly commodified into a product. The totalitarianism of screens, the chapter warns, needs no tanks.
- ch. 34 "21. That Unnamed Zone We Call Freedom" **·** John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Michel Foucault, Friedrich Nietzsche — The Difference Principle; The Minimal State — Hooke stages the liberalism-versus-libertarianism dispute through Serling's ambivalence about the State: Foucault's shepherd-flock model from his Security, Territory, Population lectures fails as politics, since 'The Shelter' shows the shepherd deciding who stays and who goes ends in mob violence, and in 'The Obsolete Man' librarian Romney Wordsworth reads Psalm 23 to a State that has declared God and books obsolete. The Rawls-Nozick quarrel (justice as fairness and the difference principle against Nozick's minimal state and his basketball-shooter case for keeping self-respect out of politics) frames how much State freedom requires. Wordsworth's laugh before his execution, under Nietzsche's epigraph about gods who mock, embodies the undefinable freedom no State can name.

- ch. 36 "About the Authors and Editors" *(notes)*

## Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!

- ch. 1 "Cover" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 2 "i" *(not yet read)*
- ch. 3 "ii" *(front)*
- ch. 4 "Title Page" *(front)*
- ch. 5 "Copyright" *(front)*
